Paris suburb shooting suspect targeted people of Muslim or African appearance, prosecutor says

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 19:19:23 GMT

A man suspected of a deadly shooting near Paris last week has admitted targeting people of "Muslim, African or North African" appearance, prosecutors say.

A man was killed and seven people including a child were injured last Friday when an attacker opened fire as he drove through two western suburbs.

On Thursday the suspect was charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office (PNAT) said.

President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack" and anti-racism demonstrations have been held around France.

Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was killed in the shooting.

Three of those wounded were still in hospital with one in critical condition, terrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen told reporters.

The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, chose Trappes and nearby La Verrière because he saw them as a "hotbed for Islamists", he said.

Kevin T had denied any "terrorist intent", insisted his actions were "legitimate" and said he "feels no regret", Christen said.

Police found "weapons or weapon components" in the suspect's home as well as books including a Quran, a Bible and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf and stickers celebrating the hard-right National Rally (RN) party, Christen said.

Kevin T told investigators that he had designed the stickers with slogans such as "long live France, RN, proud to be French" himself and had them printed more than a year ago, Christen said.

But the suspect also told investigators he was not a member or supporter of any political party.

On Wednesday Macron said that "certain political movements on the far right" including the RN and "those close to them" had allowed a climate of racism "to take root".

Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a prominent RN lawmaker, retorted that it was the president himself who had allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish.

France's presidential elections is six months away and RN leader Marine Le Pen is currently leading opinion polls.

Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 19:11:10 GMT

Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.

The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

"This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC.

The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).

Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case.

"We stand ready to support the workforce however we can."

The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.

The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.

It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.

Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse.

It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off.

Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.

It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.

It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.

A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allow creditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff. The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.

If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.

These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested in taking on between 200 and 250 stores.

Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.

More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.

Bally Auluk, a national officer at the Usdaw shopworkers union, said this week had been "incredibly distressing" for Poundland staff.

He claimed staff were having to "watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1".

He said Williams had "reluctantly" kicked off the administration process, to give the business time to find a rescue deal, adding that Usdaw was urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider.

The uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future has left some staff fearful about the future of their jobs.

Staff at Poundland's customer support centre in Walsall, some dressed as the Poundland "Pound Hound" mascot, held a protest on Thursday.

One employee said they were trying to "save our jobs".

There is also a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable".

"As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week.

He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds which help it run its day-to-day business.

"I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added.

In the memo, seen by the BBC, Williams said the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made".

Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.

MI5 false evidence in neo-Nazi spy case a serious failing, says intelligence watchdog

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 18:51:34 GMT

The man responsible for overseeing the conduct of the UK's intelligence services has said that MI5 lying to multiple courts while defending a violent neo-Nazi spy is as "serious as anything" he has ever dealt with.

"Oversight depends on candour," said investigatory powers commissioner Lord Leveson. "Failings of candour undermine the entire basis of oversight and accountability."

His office, the Investigatory Powers Commissioner's Office (IPCO), investigated how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts concerning the abusive informant known as agent X, as first exposed by the BBC.

IPCO's report, released earlier this year, found one senior officer lied repeatedly while another misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.

It also criticised other senior spies and found "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.

MI5 said it accepted the report's findings "without reservation" last month. The High Court is due to decide soon on what action, if any, to take against the agency or its staff.

In comments to mark the publication of his annual report on Thursday, Lord Leveson said the "case of agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as commissioner".

"False evidence was given to the High Court and the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and the prime minister directed me to find out how that happened.

"My investigation has now concluded and found that both IPCO and the courts were misled."

The IPCO investigation examined how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the violent neo-Nazi informant.

He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while he was under police investigation.

The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block our investigation into X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.

MI5 claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from Beth and everyone else, leaving her at a serious disadvantage.

But what MI5 said was untrue. It had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

A senior MI5 officer had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist. He even wanted me to meet the agent. In doing so, he repeatedly departed from the NCND policy.

That officer was found to have repeatedly lied by the IPCO investigation. He has resigned from MI5 since the BBC exposed what happened.

The IPCO also oversees and regulates MI6 and GCHQ, as well covert powers and agent-running by police forces and other agencies.

Its annual report revealed that errors by MI5 involving agents increased from four in 2017 to 21 in 2025. In the same period, errors by MI6 decreased from 10 to three.

It also criticised the National Crime Agency (NCA) for failings in how it managed a juvenile criminal informant, meaning a child under 18 who was being used by the agency.

It found that the NCA did not inform Lord Leveson of the fact it was running a child informant within the required time period, and a senior NCA officer wrongly extended the authorisation well beyond what is legal.

It also found a failure to record the circumstances which would justify the absence of an "appropriate adult", and that the child was "tasked to engage in criminal conduct" without the protection of a valid legal authorisation.

Lord Leveson said the agency's conduct fell "well short of what the law requires" and said he had written to its director general.

He also expressed concern with GCHQ, saying it "still cannot tell me what has happened to removable media that may hold sensitive data, years after I first raised it with them".

The report revealed the spy agency now estimates there are "thousands" of memory cards, hard drives and other portable media items it can neither find nor account for. The report stated that "these items are utilised extensively and are an essential component of some of GCHQ's operating processes".

"We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate", said Lord Leveson.

George Michael's Faith guitar sells for £180k after auction row

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 18:26:42 GMT

The guitar George Michael performed with in his 1987 Faith music video has sold for £180,000 at auction, after a row over the sale of memorabilia related to the singer.

The guitar was one of more than 30 items auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant. The sale fetched a total of £238,000 excluding buyers' premium.

Bailey died in 2014 and the items were sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.

Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Belcher declined to comment.

Sworders chairman Guy Schooling said Belcher had been "nothing but delightful" during their interactions over the past two-and-a-half years.

"There are two ways of looking at this - it can be cashing in, or it can be a bit of a memorial and a tribute to Siobhan, and that's the way we've looked at it," he told BBC News.

The auction house billed the 32 lots, including signed photographs, invitations to events and presentation CDs and discs, as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".

Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.

Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.

There is no suggestion that Belcher did not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.

Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.

In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considered the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name was "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".

He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" was "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".

Bailey asked that the auction should not go ahead, or be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.

Siobhan Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.

She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.

"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.

"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."

The guitar was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.

The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".

Other items on sale included a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Andrew Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.

"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.

Speaking before Thursday's auction, he said "she would never have consented" to it, adding that the sale "breaks my heart".

"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax [tour itinerary] and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.

Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".

He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".

Bailey acknowledged that Belcher had a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

George Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.

What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:59:57 GMT

Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.

Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.

Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.

The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.

The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.

However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.

Total welfare spending would also remain below the peak of around 12% of GDP in 2013 following the global financial crisis, leading some economists and researchers to question the idea that welfare spending is out of control.

But there are some welfare costs that are rising rapidly.

Spending on health and disability related benefits, in particular Personal Independence Payments (PIP), is up sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Accounting for inflation, spending on working-age disability benefits increased from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026.

Inflation-adjusted welfare spending remains lower than 2013 because several other working-age benefits, such as Universal Credit and housing benefit, were cut by Conservative-led governments as part of their austerity programme from 2010 onwards.

So spending in some parts of the system has come down while it has risen in others - and there could be a connection.

Some researchers think the post-2010 welfare cuts to benefits might have created an incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead to protect their living standards, therefore shifting costs around the system rather than generating lasting savings.

Many also see a specific problem regarding the growing number of young people in the welfare system claiming benefits, including PIP.

Official figures show the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neets) has risen by around 230,000 since 2019 to just under one million.

Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many off benefits and into work.

His interim report in May estimated that annual PIP expenditure on 16 to 24-year-olds rose from £1.3bn in 2020 to around £3.2bn in 2025. It also projected this cost would reach £6.5bn and cover 700,000 young people in five years' time.

PIP claimants can be in work, but official statistics show that only around one in five are.

Politicians are often unclear about what they mean by reducing spending on welfare.

In March 2025, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government presented a plan which it said would save £5bn a year from health-related welfare spending by 2030 by tightening PIP access and reducing the value of health-related Universal Credit payments.

But official forecasts made it clear that annual spending on health-related welfare in cash terms was still set to rise after the reform, just not as rapidly as the path it had previously been on.

However, at the time the OBR did forecast the plans would help put overall UK welfare spending on a "slightly downward trajectory" as a share of the economy over the medium term, rather than remaining flat as had been previously projected.

So this type of relative reduction in anticipated welfare spending, rather than a cut in absolute cash terms, could be what the government seeks to deliver.

The final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.

There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25, so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.

There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access, although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.

Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.

But some analysts argue that to be effective in delivering sustainable savings, such reforms are likely also to require the government to spend a lot more to enable young people in particular to get into and remain in work.

This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits, suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.

This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.

However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.

Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:58:18 GMT

The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex."

The Met added it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason for not visiting Thomas Markle and not allowing him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

Confirming that it had referred itself to the IPOC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter.

"While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said.

It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC.

The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, it contained claims of alleged offences.

There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get a copy from the Sussexes.

Meghan, in a statement last week, said she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".

But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.

There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal, and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.

Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings.

"If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble.

"I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say, 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken, why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies," she said.

"I believe those questions deserve clear, transparent answers."

Reports of the Met's handline of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims.

Philippine Police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:46:15 GMT

A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.

The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.

Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.

The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".

The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."

Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.

However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph.

The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.

Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.

In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.

"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.

"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."

Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."

Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."

The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.

In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.

"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.

A spokesperson for the House of Commons said that a prayer card for Farage - the way in which MPs reserve seats in the Commons - did not "display a valid date stamp" and therefore "was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol".

Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:13:40 GMT

Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.

Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England – just under 10% of the total.

Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.

GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.

Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.

Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.

An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.

"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."

Affected practices have been contacted by NHS England with advice on how to maintain business continuity and minimise the impact on patient care.

Silicon Practice ran the digital tool FootFall, which it advertised as reducing patient phone calls to practices by 30%, by working to "free your reception team from routine admin and manage demand more efficiently. Proven in 1,000+ GP practices across the UK".

Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: "GP practice websites are an increasingly important way for patients to access care, book appointments and find information about the services available to them.

"When websites are not working, it can be hugely disruptive for patients and place additional pressures on already stretched practice teams.

"It is vital that any disruption to practice websites is addressed promptly to ensure patients are able to access care."

She said affected practices must receive prompt, practical support from NHS England and local NHS organisations to restore their websites, minimise disruption and ensure patients know how to contact their practice and access the care they need in the meantime.

Careless dismissals give Australia route to series win

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:53:40 GMT

The winner of the third Test will finish the series top of the International Cricket Council's Test rankings

Third Test, Cape Town (day three of five)

South Africa 329 & 140-4: Ackerman 62; Starc 2-29

Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104

South Africa lead by 40 runs

Scorecard

Batters carelessly gifting wickets to Australia... we have been here before.

This time it was not England helping their opponents, although they will have taken note with a tour of South Africa to come this winter.

South Africa's attempt to fight back in the decisive third Test against Australia was hurt by two poor strokes on day three.

Having taken the last six Australian wickets for 99 runs in the morning despite Josh Inglis' second Test century, the Proteas began their second innings facing a deficit of exactly 100.

They needed runs from their experienced opener and number three. Neither Aiden Markram nor David Bedingham could deliver.

By the end, even captain Temba Bavuma had been tempted into a wild swipe to fall for 35. South Africa were 140-4, just 40 runs ahead, at the close.

Australia are closing in.

In isolation, Markram's drive off Mitchell Starc straight into the hands of mid-off for one appeared the most egregious.

The ball was the fullest of the six balls Markram faced but not there for him to play his trademark shot. Fielder Travis Head did not have to move.

Worse, though, was the dismissal of Bedingham, who showed he had not learned from the first innings.

Then, the right-hander top-edged a pull to Josh Hazlewood off the bowling of Starc. This time he repeated the shot, with Hazlewood the wicket-taking bowler.

"That is just absolutely soft from David Bedingham," said former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander.

"He knew they were going to target him in that zone. For the second time in the Test, he has fallen to the same ploy."

The delivery which dismissed Markram was the fullest he had faced but still not full enough to be a driving length

Given the prized position in South Africa's batting order on the back of strong domestic form for Durham in the County Championship and twin hundreds for Western Province in September, this score of 11 followed contributions of 49, 46 and 50 in his other four innings.

He has got in but has not made a match-winning contribution.

Batting in the key position of first drop, some would say that is more infuriating than not getting in at all.

His dismissal, again like in the first innings, came shortly after being hit by a bouncer, with Starc clattering one into his chest on this occasion.

When, after starting with two balls on a good length, Hazlewood went short again, Bedingham's eyes lit up.

Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer and co should have been taking note. It was the fifth time he has been dismissed pulling in his 18 Tests.

On average he gets out playing that shot once every 13 deliveries.

"He never looks in the right position to play the pull or hook shot," former South Africa captain Graeme Smith said. "He is always off balance. He is never in a strong position.

"You think about best pullers in the game they have a strong base. He is pirouetting on one leg.

"[South Africa great] Hashim Amla just put the pull shot away for a phase.

"That is what a player like Bedingham needs to think about."

Duckett and Dawson deliver in England's consolation win

Bavuma, in contrast, dug in for 115 balls in which he hit only one boundary.

As he had in his 179 in the second-Test win in Gqeberha which set up this grand Cape Town finale, he showed his side the way in a partnership lasting 17.3 overs with Matthew Breetzke after opener Marques Ackerman had briskly made 65 before being bounced out by Starc.

But with four minutes to go in the day, Australia captain Pat Cummins tweaked his field for spinner Nathan Lyon.

Bavuma had pushed and driven outside off stump to that point but, with a silly point now in place, he was dragged from his crease and tried to force through mid-wicket.

Australia's celebrations suggested they believe that was the crucial wicket.

The vicious turn Lyon found means any chase over 200 would not be straightforward for Australia. South Africa's spinner Simon Harmer dismissed Inglis and Alex Carey (80) earlier in the day on his way to figures of 4-104.

The Proteas have Breetzke and Ryan Rickelton at the crease - and Test triple-centurion Wiaan Mulder to come, before in-form all-rounder Marco Jansen and the tail.

This still appears a tall order, however.

As on day one and two, Australia have held firm and their opponents faltered. England know that feeling too.

Duckett and Dawson deliver in England's consolation win

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:37:15 GMT

Ben Duckett became the third England opener to pass 150 twice in ODIs

One-day international tri-series, Lahore

England 386-5 (50 overs): Duckett 167 (132); Asitha 2-63

Sri Lanka 331 (45.1 overs): Rathnayake 118 (77); Dawson 4-49

England won by 55 runs

Scorecard

Ben Duckett's sublime century and four wickets for Liam Dawson earned England a consolation win over Sri Lanka in their final match of the tri-series.

Duckett struck a majestic 167 from 132 balls as England racked up 386-5 in Lahore, which set up a tantalising chase after Sri Lanka's astonishing pursuit of 430 in their previous encounter a week ago.

In another high-scoring match with very little contest between bat and ball, the chase followed a similar trajectory, as Sri Lanka kept themselves within touching distance of the run-rate throughout and needed 87 off the final 10 overs.

But England's bowlers held their nerve on this occasion, closing out a 55-run win as the brilliant Pavan Rathnayake's 118 off just 77 balls was in vain for Sri Lanka.

Rathnayake, who made 130 in last week's carnage, set the platform alongside Kusal Mendis' 89 but Sri Lanka lost their last five wickets for just 16 runs, with Dawson claiming the key scalp of Rathnayake in the 45th over as they were all out for 331.

It meant Duckett's second consecutive century eclipsed Rathnayake's effort, as England's opener capitalised on a batting-friendly surface and a tiring Sri Lanka attack.

The opening partnership between Duckett and Tom Banton impressed again as the pair added 163 together before the latter frustratingly dragged on to his stumps for a fine 74.

Duckett kicked on to his highest ODI score and though England fell short of the 400 mark, contributions of 44 from Harry Brook, 30 from Will Jacks and a quickfire 43 off 27 from Jordan Cox ensured they still posted a commanding total.

Such is the power of England's middle order that Root was not required to bat.

It was far from ideal for Sri Lanka's bowlers to toil in the heat as they face Pakistan in the tri-series final on Sunday, while England travel to Australia for three ODIs and five T20s in November.

How good is England’s ODI side a year out from the World Cup?

While Duckett's 105 against Pakistan held a poor England innings together, here he was ruthless.

With very little swing or seam movement on offer, Duckett was able to back himself to flay anything wide of the off stump and timed the ball exquisitely off his pads when Sri Lanka were forced to bowl straighter.

They attempted to test with the short ball, too, but he was particularly prolific against it as the seamers lacked the pace to really trouble him.

It was also an impressive display of fitness from a player who has spoken about how hard he has worked at that part of his game, eventually falling in the 42nd over from a miscued ramp as the fatigue appeared to take its toll.

Duckett seems to relish opening with Banton: the pair have stands of 143, 6, 91, 74, 4 and 163 in their past six outings together. That, and Banton's form, has given England's selectors an intriguing conundrum for when Jacob Bethell returns from injury in Australia.

Bethell previously occupied the opening slot alongside Duckett but Banton, with five scores of fifty plus in his past six knocks, looks likely to have nailed down his place on this tour, despite some frustration that he could not kick on to three figures when conditions were so favourable.

"You want options, and guys to push their case when they get their opportunities," England coach Brendon McCullum told Sky Sports after the game.

"They're good problems for us to have. We will learn more about that in Australia, but we will always do what's right for the team depending on conditions and the opposition."

Bethell's versatility could potentially see him find a place in the middle order, but it is a promising indication of England's impressive white-ball depth that it is unclear who he could replace from Root, Brook and Jacks, with Jordan Cox needed as keeper in Jos Buttler's injury absence.

Careless dismissals give Australia route to series win

Dawson takes four as England complete 55-run win over Sri Lanka - as it happened

Liam Dawson has taken seven wickets in three games in the series

The tri-series has exposed some of England's inexperienced bowling, particularly in the middle overs, and with Jamie Overton missing out to Sonny Baker it looked like England were going to rue the omission of leg-spinner Adil Rashid again.

The experienced Dawson saved their blushes though, starting with the crucial wicket of opener Avishka Fernando, who picked out Jacks on the boundary to break a second-wicket stand of 82. Dawson then pinned the explosive Dasun Shanaka lbw for four after Root surprisingly had Mendis caught down the leg side.

Rathnayake raced to a 70-ball century to keep Sri Lanka in contention, and a fifth-wicket stand of 72 off just 38 balls with the explosive Janith Liyanage had England twitching before the latter fell to Baker for 27 off 17.

Dawson then added Rathnayake and Asitha Fernando to his tally when the run-rate spiralled in the closing stages, while Sam Curran and Baker also executed well at the death to recover from their expensive starts early in the innings.

The question surrounding England's second spinner remains, however, as part-timers Jacks and Root conceded 71 off seven combined overs which could have given Brook a headache had Sri Lanka's run chase progressed deeper.

"Leg-spin hasn't played too much of a role and we want to be a team who can adapt to different conditions and be quite malleable with our selections," McCullum added.

"Liam Dawson is an experienced and highly competitive player who's put his hand up here and unfortunately for Rash here, the conditions probably haven't really favoured him."

Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:48:44 GMT

It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".

Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.

A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.

It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.

It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".

This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.

The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of £65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.

The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.

If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.

It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.

The detail may come more quickly than feared. On welfare, the Milburn Review process is clearly heading for some sort of welfare-to-work scheme, even a separate system for younger workers.

It will cost money up front to subsidise work opportunities and hope to save more from welfare bills in the future. The chancellor saw at close quarters Gordon Brown do this twice two decades ago.

The Office for Budget Responsbility's (OBR) economic forecast showed the sheer rise in the welfare bill, which is set to jump to £431bn in 2031, if pensioner support is included.

There are two further areas where the chancellor laid down markers, with little fiscal cost, in terms of the long term plan.

On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power.

While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.

On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected.

There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.

How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge.

Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?

Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030.

The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.

A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.

But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.

Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:42:56 GMT

Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.

Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.

Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."

He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".

The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane said if the government could provide a plan to show "greater restraint" of the benefits bill, that would "play spectacularly well" with the financial markets.

Haldane, who has previously advised Burnham, told the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast: "If the government could get that through I think it would come with a huge bonus."

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

Reacting to government briefings and remarks on Thursday related to when a reduction in the benefits bill could take place, Badenoch said it "looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading".

She said: "Don't let anyone tell you this was a 'do no harm budget'. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they've harmed our national security."

Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.

Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.

Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.

The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030, and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.

Offshore workers turn to weight-loss jabs to meet helicopter weight rules

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:18:10 GMT

Hundreds of offshore workers have been using weight-loss jabs to help meet maximum weight rules for helicopter flights due to come into force next week.

From Sunday, anyone weighing more than 19st 7Ib (124kg) in civilian clothing and footwear will be banned from taking a flight to an offshore platform covered by UK safety regulations.

When the new rules were announced last year, about 2,200 workers were over the limit but that figure has now fallen to fewer than 250, according to Offshore Energies UK (OEUK).

The industry body told BBC Scotland News that on one platform, 60% of staff had been taking weight-loss drugs and extra fridge space had been provided to keep the medications cool.

The average weight of offshore workers has risen over recent decades, and increased by almost 1st 7Ib (10kg) since 2008.

The new weight limit policy came after the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) warned that rescue winches - which are critical during offshore emergencies - cannot safely lift heavier people.

The figure was decided upon after factoring in the weight of the rescuer, stretcher and other kit that would add to the combined total.

OEUK health and safety manager Graham Skinner said a range of measures were being used to help offshore workers manage their weight, including gym equipment and healthier food options.

Alongside those, he said many had had chosen to make use of the latest medical advances in controlling appetite and digestion.

"What we know is that offshore workers are using weight-loss jabs regardless of the policies. Last year we saw in some cases 60% of workers turning up with weight-loss jabs," he told BBC Scotland News.

"That's brought our average weight down in a very short space of time. I think that's very common in society and it can potentially be a really useful tool if somebody's got a lot of weight to lose it can get them in a good place."

He said initially staff appeared to be funding the medication themselves, although he thought it possible that some firms were now supporting them with the costs.

The weight-limit policy has been criticised by the RMT union which claimed there had been a lack of consultation, and that it could lead to experienced staff being excluded from offshore operations.

Earlier this year, BBC Scotland spoke to one occupational health expert in Aberdeen who said some clients were "really stressed" by the new rules while others had chosen to leave the industry.

Companies could offer staff alternative onshore roles but Skinner warned: "If somebody has chosen not to lose weight then there's a real possibility they could lose their job."

He said there were a number of safety reasons for having weight-limit controls such as working in confined spaces or ability to quickly exit a helicopter - but the actual numbers had been driven by the lifting capacity of the winches.

"It's the same winch on all search and rescue helicopters and if somebody needs to be rescued due to a health or safety incident the winch has limitations and we can't allow people to exceed those," he said.

Workers will be asked to declare if they are under the weight limit and this will be checked at the heliport.

He said employers in the industry had been working "really hard" to ensure as many staff as possible complied with the new rules and he hoped the number of staff over the weight limit could be reduced still further.

Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:18:04 GMT

Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.

Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.

The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

According to the latest figures up to 30 September, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.

However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.

Rob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.

After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.

However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.

If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.

Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.

While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.

Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."

Pensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule change in a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.

Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".

He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."

Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.

The change applies to payments made from 28 October.

In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.

Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner".

Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".

She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system.

"Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."

Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.

The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:11:35 GMT

Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.

The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by hundreds of pounds in January.

Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.

If you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.

It will be paid directly into your bank account.

Council tax bands are listed below - you can check which one you are in by looking at your annual bill or checking the government's website, although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.

Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.

This is designed to help with soaring energy bills, with some forecasts suggesting a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January the saving will be only a portion of that. Although it's designated for energy bills, you can spend the money on anything you wish.

The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.

The fee for connecting to your gas supply so called standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, next year "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.

These fixed daily charges will then be shifted onto the price you pay for each unit of energy.

The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will save an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most. But the saving will come after the projected big rise in bills in January.

Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.

The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.

The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.

It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52.95p per litre.

Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.

The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.

The chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).

Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.

It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.

But that plan has now been ditched.

Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.

If you have a large amount in savings, or if you fail to use the tax-free Isa allowance, then you will pay more tax from April.

You do not pay tax on all savings. There is the annual £20,000 Isa allowance, and an annual savings income allowance (in other words, the interest received on a savings pot) of £1,000 for basic rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers.

But beyond that savings tax rates will rise by four percentage points to 24% and 44% respectively from April.

Landlords could also pay more in tax. In analysis published on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said these steps along with measures over the past decade that have reduced private landlord returns "collectively risk leading to a steady rise in rents".

Minimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April. It means:

However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.

For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands, or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget.

But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.

The triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.

It means:

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.

The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.

The First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.

Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.

The penalty for withdrawing savings from a Lifetime Isa if you are buying a home above the £450,000 threshold will be scrapped.

Separately, he confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme to allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

The government has made no changes to student loan rates - saying only that it is being "kept under review".

There has been some backlash after the previous chancellor froze the repayment threshold for Plan 2 student loans, which were given out for just over a decade in England from 2012.

It means the salary at which borrowers start paying back their loans is due to stay at £29,385 in April and remain there for three years – so graduates start repaying sooner and repay more each month than they would otherwise have done.

The chancellor is tripling the allowance for extra earnings made alongside your main income.

If you sell on Vinted, offer dogwalking, earn money as an influencer, or have any other kind of small-scale side hustle, you can currently earn up to £1,000 a year before you have to report it to HMRC.

From April 2027 that allowance will rise to £3,000.

Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:08:23 GMT

The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at least 69 people dead.

But as Spain holds three days of mourning, revelations from leaked audio recordings of the apparent human error in a control room in the minutes before this disaster happened have given way to public disbelief and outrage, in a highly politicised climate, exactly a month before Spaniards go to the polls.

"You don't know what's happening, you don't know what has happened, you just know that you're being thrown around in a matter of seconds," said Iñaki García, 60.

He was on the stationary Iryo train that was rammed from behind by a Renfe train on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140km (87 miles) south of the capital.

"There were people injured, walking around, there were dead people," he said. "In the next carriage along there were a lot of dead people."

Recalling the horrific scenes around him, one young man told the BBC in a quivering voice: "I don't know if that's something I'll ever recover from."

Stories of tragedy have continued to emerge. A pharmacist from Urda was one of the first to reach the scene, bringing with him first aid supplies and medicine.

"One of [the passengers] was saying goodbye to his wife and children. His last words were 'God is good'," Antonio García told Spanish radio.

Similar scenes of grief played out only nine months ago in the southern village of Adamuz, when a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people.

Now, in the town of Urda, just like Adamuz, awful stories are combined with acts of kindness and solidarity.

Locals turned out to help the injured, bringing blankets, food and water to a nearby sports hall that was converted into a makeshift hospital for much of the day.

"We all started to turn out to help and we organised ourselves as best we could," said Rosa María Domínguez, a local woman, who described the scene as "a horror film".

However, the overriding sentiment that these two tragedies have generated is one of confusion and a failure to comprehend how this could have happened.

Not long ago, the speed, efficiency and safety of Spain's high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, was the envy of its neighbours.

The Adamuz crash triggered a nationwide debate about whether the network was fit for purpose.

This latest incident intensifies pressure on the left-wing government of Pedro Sánchez, in the middle of an election campaign where his Socialist PSOE is behind the conservatives in most opinion polls.

On Wednesday night a demonstration protesting at the government's handling of the rail network saw far-right groups turn out and clash with police.

Although the main parties, other than the far-right Vox, have suspended campaigning, Sánchez has twice visited the scene of the crash and his People's Party rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo came to Urda on Thursday.

Sánchez's transport minister, Óscar Puente, made clear from the start that a computer failure followed by human error was the likely cause of the crash. By late evening, leaked audio recordings of a control-room operator talking to train drivers appeared to back that up.

Puente has long been a hate figure for the right, and with two of the worst rail tragedies in Spanish history taking place on his watch, the criticism is only going to increase.

Spain's biggest train drivers' union Semaf condemned the leak of audio recordings as irresponsible and slanted. The union had already called a strike for Thursday in a bid to ensure that "urgency to travel is never prioritised over safety".

One train driver, Vicente Almenar, told Spanish media: "They always look for the last link in the chain, where it's weakest, but here the entire procedure failed because we don't even know what our colleague was seeing on the screen," he told Spanish media.

Sánchez had not been expecting rail safety to dominate his campaign, but that now looks increasingly likely.

After two accidents and more than 100 deaths on the same high-speed line, Feijóo told reporters in Urda on Thursday: "The Spanish people need answers. They are wondering what is happening to high-speed rail in their country."

And he emphasised that politics was not about talking - it was about acting.

'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:07:26 GMT

The world's changed a lot since Seán McLoughlin, better known to 31 million subscribers as Jacksepticeye, began making YouTube videos.

He started uploading in 2012, in what many people consider to be the platform's "golden age" when vlogging, video game playthroughs and comedy escapism were all the rage.

Like many in the content creation space, he's been branching out in recent years, taking more acting jobs and getting involved in film production.

BBC Newsbeat caught up with McLoughlin to talk about his new role, his work on bringing one of his favourite video games to the big screen and why he misses the "whimsical" days of the internet.

McLoughlin got famous playing video games, and these days there's a good chance you'll see - or hear - him in one.

After a role in the 2025 superhero adventure Dispatch, McLoughlin's got a new role in Hitman, the successful "assassination simulator" from Danish studio IO Interactive.

He plays controversial content creator Finn Colton, known as Finnvictus.

Although the fictional character shares McLoughlin's likeness and voice, he says the "manosphere-adjacent influencer" is not based on him.

As the name of the game suggests, players aren't there to collab with him.

He's one of the celebrity "elusive targets" Hitman's developers occasionally place in the game to encourage returning fans.

"If you love me it'll be funny to play and you'll get to kill me in different ways," says McLoughlin.

"If you hate me maybe that's even more fun to play."

It's not the first time McLoughlin's worked with IO - he appeared, briefly, in their James Bond game 007: First Light earlier this year.

He'd hoped to watch other streamers react to the blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo, but says many of his friends missed it.

"This time you're forced to interact with me," he says, even if that does involve thinking of imaginative ways to kill him off.

Earlier this year, McLoughlin was also unveiled as a producer on an animated movie version of Bloodborne, one of the highest-rated video games of all time.

Some parts of its passionate fan base reacted negatively to the announcement, questioning the YouTuber's credentials.

McLoughlin reassured them he's a huge fan of the games and has a tattoo of a Hunter's Mark - one of the game's key items - to prove it.

He's described himself as a "vibe-checker" and sees it as his responsibility to make sure the adaptation is done properly.

"If it feels off, especially with something like Bloodborne, people can feel it immediately, even if they don't know what they're pointing towards," he says.

"They know the game so well that if the atmosphere, or the world, or the vibe feels off, they'll pick up on it pretty fast."

McLoughlin says he's been trying to pick people for the project who have ideally played Bloodborne and "have a feeling" for what it's all about.

"I feel like I have good instincts on what works and what doesn't and what I like and what I don't like," he says.

"So the producing side of it fits a lot more naturally for me right now."

Screen adaptations are a big trend in video games at the moment, but they're not the only thing seizing the industry.

Hitman's new mission lands just weeks before the launch of the hugely-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

It won't be released on disc at launch, a move that's arguably accelerated the game industry's move towards digital-only games.

McLoughlin, who fondly remembers PlayStation cases on a bedroom shelf and getting new games for Christmas, says "it would suck to see physical games disappear completely".

"Just in terms of the humanity behind it all, I think it would be a shame to see that stuff disappear because it's a magical experience," he says.

The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in video game development is another hot topic at the moment.

Earlier this month, Epic Games, makers of Fortnite, announced a "pivot" towards using AI as a primary development tool.

Like many players, McLoughlin's opposed to its use.

So no chance of seeing a Jacksepticeye Fortnite skin any time soon?

"I think the chances of that happening were already zero before anything related to that even happened," he says.

"But now it's definitely, definitely unlikely."

Physical games, GenAI and content creators' career moves are sure to generate discourse, and conversations online are another thing McLoughlin thinks have changed since he started out.

He says there's been a "rise of anti-communities", where people will "rush to condemn a film or game before it's even been released".

"I'm just sad that the internet is such an angry place these days," he says.

"It's just zero to a thousand immediately. I think we're just not there in terms of having nuanced discussions about anything.

"But I think that's just endemic of the internet in general."

McLoughlin thinks that could be linked to people's real life worries.

"Right now, it's just people are angry in general, just at the world," he says.

"So it's harder to interact with stuff online these days.

"It's a less whimsical space. But hopefully that's something that can change."

McLoughlin's doing his bit to bring people together in December with his annual Thankmas event.

The fundraiser took a break last year but its returning to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation.

"I think it's a nice little pinprick of light in the middle of everything else going on," he says.

And while he's not afraid to speak his mind, he says he is mindful of letting others do the talking sometimes.

"I'm trying to get better about not giving an opinion about absolutely everything any more," he says.

"Because I think there's too much of that in the world."
