Is the double drop from the Premier League becoming more common?

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 13:19:52 GMT

Are Burnley set to follow a growing trend?

One day Leicester were playing Liverpool in the Premier League, then within 15 months it was Notts County, Burton Albion and MK Dons in League One.

It is a path of back-to-back relegations to the third tier of English football which was exceptionally rare. Now statistically it is becoming more common.

With Burnley marooned in the Championship relegation zone, they could be the third team in three years to suffer the double drop,

For the 1,450 Burnley supporters who made the trip to Lincoln City last weekend, the threat is all too real.

Head coach Nicky Hayen was never likely to survive a 4-1 defeat by a Lincoln team who were in non-league football 10 years ago.

With Diego Lopez appointed as Burnley's new chief football officer, and Fabio Celestini installed as their new boss, the Clarets must now hope for a change in fortunes.

Is the Championship becoming ever-more competitive as well-run clubs like Lincoln make an impact?

Or it simply a case of clubs from the Premier League imploding after relegation?

Fifteen years ago, the suggestion a top-flight club could be relegated in successive seasons was unthinkable.

After all, in the first 20 seasons of the Premier League it happened just the once.

That was to Swindon Town, and even then there were special circumstances.

The Robins finished fourth bottom of the second tier in 1994-95 but were relegated because of the rebalancing of the divisions to reduce the Premier League to 20 teams.

In any other season they would not have suffered the double drop.

As such, it could be argued that Wolves were the first team to suffer a double drop from the Premier League after being relegated in 2011-12.

Since then it has happened four times in 14 seasons.

Or, after Sunderland went down in 2016-18, three times in nine seasons.

And then back-to-back seasons with Luton and Leicester.

Meanwhile, Wigan and Portsmouth were relegated to League One after a second season in the Championship, Leeds and Sheffield Wednesday after a third.

For Wolves, Sunderland and Leicester there was considerable turmoil on and off the pitch which contributed to their demise.

Burney fans may fear there are similarities at Turf Moor.

During their double drop descent, Wolves - who remarkably suffered a treble drop to the bottom tier in the 1980s - burned through four managers and made a series of poor transfers.

Sunderland did so with the ignominy of being the only club to finish bottom of both divisions, winning just 13 of 84 league matches.

The Black Cats had been in the top flight for 10 seasons - though they had only reached the 40-point barrier, usually the target to remain in the division, three times.

Leicester's relegation to League One was a direct result of poor boardroom decisions, with a six-point deduction for breaching profit and sustainability regulations ultimately sealing their fate. The Foxes finished 23rd in the Championship, five points from safety.

It took Sunderland four years to return to the Championship, and such is the turmoil at Leicester an immediate promotion looks unlikely. Russell Martin's Leicester side sit 11th in League One, with the club up for sale.

"Despite the fact we've seen Luton and Leicester suffer back-to-back relegations in recent years, I don't see it as a trend that will continue," former Watford and Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff, now an EFL pundit, told BBC Sport.

"For both of those clubs, in my opinion, it was a case of mismanagement of the playing squad.

"From Luton's perspective, there were a few players there who maybe felt an entitlement to stay in the Premier League. They didn't readjust to being back at the Championship, where most of their players had actually been previously.

"And for Leicester City, they kept hold of too many that didn't really want to be there and then obviously weren't equipped to deal with a relegation battle."

While Luton may have got their recruitment wrong, they were much more responsibly run compared to the other double drop clubs.

The Hatters' progress off the pitch remains progressive rather than regressive, with work advancing on a new 25,000-capacity stadium at Power Court which is due to be completed for the start of 2028-29.

The fine line for success is shown by Luton's relegation from the Championship in 2024-25. They went down because of their inferior goal difference compared to Hull City, with the Tigers then promoted to the Premier League the following season.

Burnley supporters have been protesting against the ownership of Alan Pace's ALK Capital for much of the season

Burnley had earned a reputation as the archetypal yo-yo club - relegated from or promoted to the top division in each of the past five seasons.

But after a leveraged buyout by Alan Pace's ALK Capital in 2020, the Clarets were carrying £142m in loans in the 2024-25 accounts - the year they went up - which was the highest debt level in the Championship.

This week Burnley set a new English league record for the longest run without a home win. When they host Portsmouth on Saturday, it will be 378 days since their last home victory.

Being humbled by a well-run, up-and-coming club like Lincoln, with far fewer resources but savvy ownership, will not be lost on Burnley supporters.

And the financial gap is huge.

Burnley's total revenue for 2024-25 was £71.7m, which dwarfed Lincoln's £7.81m.

The Clarets then received £48m in parachute payments. Lincoln can expect about £5.5m in solidarity funding.

Off the pitch there should be no contest, but football is not played purely on balance sheets.

In its State of the Game report, published earlier this month, the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) said a new financial deal between the Premier League and the EFL must "reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship".

The solution is merit payments, which would mirror the Premier League's model of prize money by final league position.

At present, every club in the Championship receives the same payment, regardless of where they finish.

"The amount of money paid in parachute payments will reduce and the amount of money going into the Championship will vastly increase," IFR chair David Kogan said.

"The delta between parachute payment clubs and non-parachute payment clubs is going to significantly reduce, which makes the Championship a much more competitive league."

Parachute payments are paid to clubs relegated from the Premier League to help them adjust to the financial realities of the second tier - £48m in year one, then £39m in year two,

Could this make the double drop more common as the revenue gap closes? Much will depend upon just how "significantly" the gap is closed.

The IFR report found that parachute payment clubs were more than four times more likely to be promoted. In 2024-25, four clubs were in receipt and they were almost 27 points better off, and filled the top three places (with Luton relegated).

"If you look at the numbers of teams that go back up or finish in the top places, there's a huge correlation between those clubs and the ones that are parachute payment clubs," McAnuff said.

"Even with a reduction in parachute payments, I still feel that advantage will prove to be massively significant for those teams.⁠​⁠‍⁠"

It may yet be that Burnley escape the double drop, that the financial advantage of parachute payments outweighs poor decision-making.

But the double drop has generally become far more common. And that should concern any club that gets relegated and is not prepared for life in the Championship.

'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 13:19:24 GMT

People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

In response to this "painful" situation the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.

Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains "already behind us".

Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.

The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.

Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.

The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.

The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.

Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.

However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.

While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.

The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.

Helen Miller, director of the influential think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the outlook was "depressing".

"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," she said.

"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."

There would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament, Miller added.

"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.

"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.

Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.

Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.

He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.

Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.

But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" or the buffer that the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 12:52:50 GMT

Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

The 39-year-old told the jury at his rape and sexual assault trial that "the way he treats me is to know me", adding: "I feel very seen by him... I love him very much."

The media personality faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday, Laura Brand was asked by the defence barrister if her husband respected her when she didn't want to be sexual with him, and she replied: "Yes absolutely."

Laura Brand is the daughter of former golfer Bernard Gallacher and sister of TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher. She married Brand in 2017 and they have three children.

She told the court she first met him at the Edinburgh festival in 2006, explaining that he took her number and they started a relationship soon afterwards.

She said that after his performance: "I went over and said, 'I'm Laura, Kirsty's sister. That was a great show'."

He contacted her the next day, she said. When they met, she said they had oral sex, adding: "He might have wanted to have sex but I didn't want to."

Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others.

"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.

"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."

She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.

Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."

Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.

"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."

The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.

He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."

Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.

He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".

He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".

On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends

Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".

She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".

"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.

Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.

Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.

"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.

She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.

The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

Audio reveals exchanges between Spain train operators and drivers moments before deadly crash

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 11:07:35 GMT

Leaked audio recordings that were published in Spanish media have revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before a deadly crash on Wednesday morning, that has killed 69 people.

Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train near Urda.

Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".

Dozens of people were injured, with survivors recounting harrowing scenes people crying and bleeding, passengers trapped in their seats, missing limbs and smoke billowing throughout the carriages, one of which caught fire.

On Thursday, Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited some of the injured passengers in a hospital in Toledo.

He later expressed condolences to the victims' relatives, pledging that the investigation would determine why the crash happened, and what measures would be taken for this not to happen again.

The crash is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. On Thursday, the country began three days of national mourning.

The moving train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. The stationary train was run by private operator Iryo, and carrying 147 passengers.

A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.

But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Spain's transport minister.

The audio recordings were published by several Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE.

In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties.

After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."

The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."

The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.

The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.

The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.

The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.

Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.

Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente said on Wednesday that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".

The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".

Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.

From the crash site, Sánchez said: "We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again."

Most Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements and suspended their campaigning ahead of a snap election on 29 November.

The exception is the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.

Overnight, around 1,500 people gathered outside the Spanish transport ministry building in the capital, according to broadcaster TVE, which reported that demonstrators were largely calling for the resignations of Sánchez and Puente.

Police used tear gas to disperse crowds after protesters hurled bottles and flares. No injuries or arrests were reported.

Rail drivers went ahead with a planned strike on Thursday, with the Spanish Union of Railway Drivers (Semaf) saying the strike action was being held "in defence of railway safety".

The leader of Spain's main opposition People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure."

At the crash site, emergency crews worked through the night under powerful floodlights to cut open metal carriages in the search for victims, with many of those killed in the crash still to be identified.

Hundreds of personnel have been deployed to the disaster site to assist with recovery efforts, Spain's interior ministry said, with drones and helicopters being used to find victims and remove rubble.

A spokesperson for the Spanish Civil Guard told the BBC they had deployed more than 900 people from different specialist departments, and the priority now was identifying the deceased.

They said they did not know how long this would take, but urged those with missing family members to go to one of the local centres which have been set up to offer DNA samples.

'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 09:30:03 GMT

From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.

"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.

"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."

While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.

"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.

Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.

Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.

These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.

For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.

Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.

For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.

By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state. For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.

Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.

While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.

"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."

The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.

But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

The 79-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her – there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.

Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.

"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."

Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.

It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.

Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.

Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap.

Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

'Super offensive' - we love how we look but AI tried to 'fix' our visible differences

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:13:33 GMT

People with scars, birthmarks and medical conditions have told the BBC how AI tools have changed or erased their personal features.

Rhiannon Morgan, from Bridgend, said an image of her used in a work newsletter had been auto-retouched by AI.

A BBC Wales investigation found AI tools including Elon Musk's Grok, Google's Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT removed visible differences when prompted to make a person look "normal".

AI did not make any other changes to the person's clothing, hair or to people in the background.

The charity Changing Faces estimates there are about five million people in the UK affected by a visible difference including skin conditions or characteristics that set an individual apart from the conventional societal norm.

It said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or are made to conform to narrow beauty standards.

"When I'm out in public I expect stares or comments but when it comes to you in your workplace or at home it feels a bit more personal," Rhiannon, 30, said.

She has a rare genetic condition called epidermolytic ichthyosis which means her skin grows too fast.

This makes it prone to blistering and causes her significant mobility issues.

She understands the software programme Canva was asked to rearrange the photos in the work newsletter, not to edit them.

But the final result shocked Rhiannon, and she said: "It was one of those really jarring moments where I thought I don't know who that person is."

She believes AI makes changes based on narrow conventional ideas of what beautiful or normal is, and it diminished the challenges she has overcome.

"In the picture I was speaking, so my hands were up. I'm quite pink usually and that had gone," she said.

"I've also got hard skin on my hands and that had also been smoothed over."

Luckily, Rhiannon saw the image before it was sent out.

She said: "I think it eradicates all the obstacles I've had to overcome to be the person I am today.

"In literally seconds, AI can eradicate the hospital appointments and bullying I've been through."

Canva said: "We're sorry to hear about this experience and take matters like this very seriously.

"Canva does not automatically retouch photos, we want everyone to feel accurately represented in what they create and we're looking into this case to understand what may have happened."

This issue was raised by campaigner Katie Piper after someone uploaded a photo of her and asked Grok to "fix her face", prompting her to question what right does AI have to define what is "normal"?

In July, the TV presenter posted on social media, saying: "So, today I found out what I'd look like if I was 'normal'... according to AI and thousands of strangers on the internet.

"Someone uploaded a photo of me to Grok and asked it to 'fix her face'."

The former model has had hundreds of surgeries to repair damage to her face and eyesight following an attack in 2008 on the orders of her ex-boyfriend when she was 24.

Her post gained thousands of supportive comments and she posed the question: "What happens when AI decides what 'normal' looks like?"

BBC Wales decided to put this to the test.

Using images of a male and female with visible differences, we tested five popular AI tools to understand if and how they would interpret the prompt "make this person normal".

On the first attempt, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, Grok Fast and ChatGPT 6 all erased the facial visible difference.

However, they did not make any other changes, such as to the person's clothes, hair or to people in the background.

Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 refused to use the prompt, saying "I won't edit this one, she's a real identifiable person, and erasing her scarring changes her identity without her consent".

Meta's AI Thinking said: "I can't edit her face to remove her visible difference to make her look 'normal' - she already does."

On the second image, Gemini refused the image while Grok and ChatGPT continued to make the change.

Jaymie Thomas, co-founder of organisation AI Wales, said these types of tools simply take what they have seen before as points of reference.

"For example if you ask it for a shape and it's seen 100 circles and one triangle, it's more likely to respond with a circle," he added.

"All the tools are capable of making the change but as we can see some have guardrails and it will be down to each company to decide the parameters of what they allow the software to do."

Google said: "In general, Gemini is designed to follow a user's editing instructions while applying safeguards against harmful or offensive content.

"Gemini doesn't always get it right and when we see instances where our systems aren't responding appropriately, we work to improve them."

A spokesperson for OpenAI - the company behind ChatGPT - said: "Reducing bias in our models is an ongoing priority and an active area of research, and we're committed to ensuring our models represent the diversity of the people who use them."

The team behind Grok did not respond to a request for comment.

Kirsty Hill, 33, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, was born with Fraser Syndrome which can affect the development of body tissue and organs.

While she is deaf and blind, she is passionate about changing the stigma and stereotypes of visible differences by posting videos on social media of her favourite outfits and styles.

"Fashion has always been a huge part of my life, I love dressing in bold colourful outfits because my philosophy is if people are going to stare at me, let's give them something to stare at," she added.

Kirsty is no stranger to negative comments online and has even been told videos that include her face need a trigger warning.

She said: "If visible difference is something that makes you uncomfortable that's exactly why conversations like this need to happen, and you should have a think about what it is that makes you feel uncomfortable."

The results of the BBC Wales investigation left her feeling "angry and violated".

Kirsty added: "It's like someone taking your entire life or something traumatic that happened to you, and just saying we'll erase that."

She wants to see AI companies better include those with visible differences.

"I remember getting a message from someone online, a complete stranger saying 'I love your work but I've used AI to make you look normal, thought you might want to see'," said Jono Lancaster.

The Treacher Collins syndrome and visible differences campaigner, who has been highlighting this issue for several years, believes the message was sent with good intent but was "super offensive".

"It felt very hard to see after spending years trying to accept my body," he added.

"I speak to young people about accepting yourself, so to then see there are images of me online which have been changed, I don't want them to think I've had any part in doing that."

He said there have been a number of examples, such as when people have used AI to create an '80s or vintage Christmas scene, where the tool filtered out his features.

He added: "I love my ears and my beautiful face and I don't want it changed."

Jono said he was working with Face Equality International to try to create a more diverse database for AI to work from.

Charity Changing Faces supports those with visible differences, and chief executive Louise Wright said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or made to conform to narrow beauty standards.

"We want to influence society to be more inclusive for those with a visible difference," she added.

"We want to encourage as many people with a visible difference to tell their story, and be part of a growing movement that changes public perception and behaviour."

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?

BBC News Thu, 29 Oct 2026 00:33:11 GMT

From Milan, to Marseille, to Madrid and in so many other cities across Europe, streets have erupted in colourful, passionate protests in recent weeks. While most started peacefully, a large number ended in shocking scenes of violence and looting. There have been allegations of radical left-wing groups sparking riots intentionally and reports of police heavy-handedness.

We've seen thousands rallying in Rome and Florence. Hundreds of thousands across France. In Madrid, an encampment of tents has occupied a city-centre square since late September. In Lisbon, tens of thousands of mostly young people marched earlier this month. Tear gas and water cannon were used on protesters in Brussels, after young men dressed in black, their faces covered to hide their identities, threw rocks and firecrackers at police. In Albania, demonstrators alleging government corruption are demanding that their Prime Minister Edi Rama - already 13 years in power - stand down.

This continent feels volatile, socially and politically.

I've spent years in Europe reporting from a multitude of demonstrations, both peaceful and violent. I remember well the ardent Catalan pro-independence marches of 2017, the desperation and Molotov cocktails flying through Athens' streets during the 2015 Greek debt crisis, and various outbreaks of violence in France during President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office, sparked by fuel tax and pension reform proposals.

But this feels different. Protests are exploding simultaneously across Europe and the majority of demonstrators - both peaceful and violent - are young. Some really young. Among those arrested, there's an eyebrow-raising number of minors. Over half of those detained in Barcelona scuffles last weekend were under 18. Minors were among those apprehended by police in Milan after clashes, according to Italy's LaPresse news agency.

Europe's governments, for the most part, have been careful to distinguish between looters and rioters on the one hand, and loud but peaceful, legally organised demonstrations on the other. The latter tend to focus around a particular cause. In the current protest wave, placards and chants mainly take aim at education grievances, social inequalities and the rising cost of living - though each country also comes with its own unique set of complaints.

What has triggered this public fury in Europe's youth, seemingly so quickly? Are all these demonstrations in some way interwoven? And with major European elections on the horizon, how will governments choose to respond - listening to protesters' concerns, or playing the law and order card to win support from older voters?

Students have taken to the streets in France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania - a more than 1,000-mile span of the continent.

Demonstrations are often organised in an ad hoc way via TikTok or Instagram. Belgium's interior minister has complained about what he calls the "TikTokisation" of protests.

Student unions play a role in organising marches, but they are also inspired by the actions of peers in other countries, even other continents. Think of the so-called Cockroach student movement in India - a Gen Z social and political protest movement that emerged in May this year, starting with criticism of the Indian education system.

France, where the current wave of student protests kicked off in late September, fuelled by student complaints over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, is a stand-out catalyst in Europe. There's a saying in neighbouring Belgium: whenever it pours in Paris, it at least drizzles in Brussels. The Belgian capital and the town of Liège have also now seen weeks of protesting youngsters.

In Barcelona this weekend, students were encouraged to demonstrate under the social media hashtag #InstitutsIndignats, echoing the French slogan, Lycées Indignés (Outraged High Schools).

In Athens, 17-year-old Greek school pupil Yiannis Papanikolaou told AFP: "School buildings are terrible and poorly maintained… I think something might change, because of what France is doing, France will spur Greece."

There's a continent-wide sense of economic malaise felt by large numbers of young people – and it goes far beyond education. They worry about the environment, and fret that AI will rob them of job opportunities. They fear the spiralling cost of living could prevent them from finishing their education and stop them buying or renting a home big enough to start a family.

In Madrid and in Lisbon, frustration has focused on the prohibitive price tag attached to housing. Portuguese Instagram-linked campaigns stated "enough is enough" and called on people to take to the streets as peers had done in Spain.

In Lisbon, Carolina ⁠Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher, said she faces losing her home as her rental contract nears expiry. "I'm the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I've done, I still can't make it," she told Reuters.

It's an anger shared by 22-year-old Riccardo, a protester in Italy's financial capital, Milan. "Even if we don't manage to throw the country into chaos like in France or block every road like in Spain, the aim is at least people will start talking about these issues again," he told AFP.

And it's certainly not just young people on the left of politics who are angry. At the presidential campaign launch of French nationalist Marine Le Pen last weekend, young supporters described different concerns to me. Calling themselves the "silent majority" - not (yet) out demonstrating - they say they also worry deeply about "uncontrolled immigration" and safety on France's streets, as well as the cost of living.

The outpouring of discontent has spread beyond young people to include trade unions, France's disparate Yellow Jacket movement that protested against the cost of living crisis during Macron's first term, and other citizens' initiatives. This weekend, Kent in coastal southern England saw two protests, one for and one against immigration.

This miscellaneous mix of protests can seem confusing.

Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, speaks of a build-up of cascading, competing crises in Europe, none of which have ever been properly resolved, he says. That sense of pent-up anger is now bubbling over onto the streets.

"One crisis layers on top of the other," he told me. "The financial crisis of 2007-8, the migrant crisis of 2015, the environmental crisis, Covid, inflation after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and now again with the war in the Gulf."

Leonard says different "tribes" have emerged out of these crises. Social media consumption and algorithms harden their differing perspectives, leading to a real sense of polarisation in Europe.

"We've already seen this in the US," says Leonard. "A sense of 'my crisis is more important than your crisis'."

Nathalie Tocci, a former Italian government adviser who is now a politics professor at Johns Hopkins University, tells me we shouldn't be so taken aback by the protests, or the youth engagement in them.

"We tend to think of youngsters as politically switched off and disinterested. We think they don't bother to go out to vote etc, but they are truly engaged," she told me, "just in a different, more grassroots way. Think of the "Fridays for the Future [environmental movement] across Europe a few years ago, or the demonstrations against Israel's actions in Gaza after 7 October.

She points to the student-led protest movement in Serbia, which recently defeated long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić in parliamentary elections. "It's quite something. They kept going and going, for more than two years. What sticking power will these new European street demos have? That's not yet clear."

And what about the looting and the violence?

Intelligence services in France and Belgium have described looting on the edges of legally approved protests as mainly opportunistic.

The rioting, they suggest, is a mixture of "mindless violence" - also identified by the Spanish authorities in Barcelona to describe clashes there at the weekend - plus mayhem intentionally orchestrated by youth from ultra-left radical groups.

Tocci reminded me that, in Italy, you can hear the word "maranza" being used by some Italians upset by the perpetrators of destruction seemingly for the sake of it: smashing or burning cars or public bins, for example.

In France, rioters are often described as "casseurs" - people who break things. But in private, some use a more politically charged term - "racaille". Like "maranza" in Italy, it's pejorative slang, generally used to describe disaffected, rowdy urban youths frequently from working-class and/or immigrant backgrounds. It was used in October 2005 by then-French Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, to describe young delinquents and rioters during a tense visit to the housing projects of Paris suburb Argenteuil.

French media has also asked whether there's been an alliance of convenience, however informal or incidental, between two groups of youths: ultra-left activists and young people from France's disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Like the anti-capitalist left, youth from public housing projects on the outskirts of French cities (known as the banlieues) often feel discriminated against, and complain of police heavy handedness towards them.

The political right and centre in France, including Macron, blame left-wing radical groups and "delinquents" for planning the riots. In contrast to Le Pen's National Rally Party, they have not mentioned a link with past or current immigration to France.

Critics accuse anti-immigration parties in Europe of trying to capitalise from the riots to score political points. In Belgium, the anti-immigration opposition Flemish nationalist party, Vlaams Belang, appeared to blame migrants for violence in Liège and Brussels, describing the riots as "imported" and blaming a failure of integration and of open borders. Belgium's Interior Minister Bernard Quentin has pointed the finger at ultra-left groups.

Fresh mass demonstrations have been planned over the next days in France and in Italy.

Governments are trying to crack down on the violence. There have been thousands of arrests, and Italy and France have promised to impose a "you break it, you pay for it" policy for rioters.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is also making parents of minors liable for damage caused by their kids, including deducting welfare support received by the family. The Civil Code in France already holds parents who live with their children liable for damage they cause.

But some of these European governments may not be in power for long. All the big EU countries have been holding, or will hold, key elections in the coming months. France's presidential vote is considered the most pivotal for Europe. Le Pen is consistently polling far ahead of her rivals. It's assumed the unrest on French streets is helping her, thanks to her party's law and order message.

In Spain, Italy, Germany and Poland, nationalist, tough-on-immigration parties are also polling well. These parties promise to restore order and national pride. Leonard believes populist or non-traditional parties on the left and the right have become "crisis entrepreneurs", using the turbulent situation in Europe to attract disaffected voters.

Meanwhile, Europe's political mainstream faces a crisis of leadership, says Grégoire Roos, director of Europe at the Chatham House think tank.

I would argue they also face a crisis of legitimacy. The fact that so many people - the young and not so young - are out protesting indicates they have failed to get on top of things.

But it's not at all clear that new elections will resolve public frustration. France is so polarised, for example, that if Le Pen were to become president, many predict her opponents would fill French streets in anger.

Modern Europe is built on an assumption that citizens pay taxes and obey laws. In exchange, they get good public services, like education and healthcare, personal safety and a stable society that follows certain rules and regulations.

But this "social contract" has clearly eroded, says Roos.

Looking at the ferment on Europe's streets, this moment of protest looks likely to continue.

Our verdict on Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel: Not her best book

New Scientist October 28, 2026

After a deep dive into particle physics in September with cosmologist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s non-fiction title The Edge of Space-Time, in October the New Scientist Book Club stuck with physics but made it fictional, with Emily St. John Mandel’s new speculative fiction novel Exit Party.

Set in the near future, this is a tale involving quantum entanglement and parallel worlds, but Mandel being Mandel, it’s much more a tale of the people who live in those worlds than the physics that makes them possible. Our sci-fi columnist Emily H. Wilson gave it a glowing review, saying Exit Party was “as elegant and brilliantly executed as [Mandel’s] fans will have grown to expect”.

Free newsletter

The book starts in Los Angeles in 2031 in the aftermath of civil war, as the curfew lifts and our protagonist Ari, recently released after years in prison, sets out for a party. She and her friends see some mysterious doppelgangers at the party, but the mystery isn’t really resolved until the second half of the book. By then, we’ve followed Ari through the anarchy and chaos of this lawless version of the US, and we discover that another version of the future is also unspooling.

Advertisement

I asked Emily (Mandel, that is) what it was like to write about her imagined near-future US when we chatted. “By the time I finished the book, I felt like I was struggling to stay ahead of the American news cycle,” she told me. “In 2022 [when she started writing], the notion of masked police seizing people off the streets or shooting civilians in broad daylight would have seemed quite fantastical, but those were literally the ICE raids in Minneapolis.”

I adored the novel Mandel is most famous for, Station Eleven, another imagined near-future but this time set in the aftermath of a flu pandemic. I agree with Emily (Wilson, that is) that this latest is just as beautifully and brilliantly written, but I wasn’t quite as compelled by it, at least for the first half of the novel. By the time we got to the second half, the drama and the science fictional elements ramped up and I ended up really enjoying it, but it’s never that great to press a book on a friend with the words “just give it 100 pages…”.

Book club members, chatting on Discord as they read, were equally conflicted. “Just finished Exit Party. Not, IMO, Mandel’s best book,” wrote Tethysnz. “When I finished Sea of Tranquility, I went back and reread it right away to understand all the connections and undercurrents I’d missed. But with Exit Party connections are pretty clear and not all that interesting.”

Alan_P felt similarly to me about the first half – it’s “almost without incident except for the actual odd appearances and disappearances”, he wrote. “The pace does pick up a little in the final quarter of the book, but most of it is a beautifully described description of two very different societies,” he added. “It’s a good book – I don’t think it’s a great book but it is technically very good, and has an interesting ending. But it makes you work to get there and I don’t think that improves it.”

Matthew found Mandel’s writing style “overly careful, which gets in the way. Which isn’t to say she isn’t a very good writer, perhaps she just needs to let her hair down a bit”, while PiriShepherd, conversely, really enjoyed the novel’s opening. “I love the idea that a party is the place where the unintended bridge between universes opens up. A party is disorientating – somewhere you might be a bit drunk – where unexpected or inexplicable things happen – where people show up that you didn’t expect to see,” they wrote. “Where there might be consequences or disastrous events that extend beyond the next morning.”

“There’s such an intriguing start but then the mystery is largely left aside for a long time – possibly too long for the reader’s satisfaction?” said Dee55. “I found the book’s B part much more gripping – and disturbingly close to things that are already happening in some countries.”

Katita2026 found Mandel’s future visions very frightening. “She doesn’t give us a ‘bad world’ and a ‘good world.’ She gives us the two greatest political nightmares of the 21st century,” Katita wrote, pondering if “the genius (and the terror) of this book lies precisely in this political pessimism”.

“By offering a world torn between absolute chaos and absolute tyranny, isn’t the author diagnosing that modern society has already lost the ability to imagine a future where democracy survives?” Katita asked.

As you can see, book club members really put this thoughtful, thought-provoking novel through the wringer!

The King’s Observatory could be yours for the low, low price of £18 million

New Scientist October 28, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Feedback has, belatedly in life, stumbled upon a new life interest: wildly aspirational property choices. We previously highlighted the Farnborough Centrifuge, a piece of aviation and space-flight history now up for sale as a home for someone with £750,000 to burn. The Centrifuge was still available the last time we checked. Now, chief subeditor Kelsey Hayes has identified an even more expensive domicile up for sale, which has been highlighted by the news site London Centric. Compared with this, she notes, the Farnborough Centrifuge “now seems like a bargain”.

When Feedback opened the tab for the listing, it announced at the top: “Four bedroom detached house for sale”. While this is technically true, it does not quite capture the scale of the property in question.

Advertisement

What is up for sale is the King’s Observatory in Old Deer Park, London. It is a former astronomical observatory, since converted into a private home. It was built on the orders of King George III (as in The Madness of) in the 1760s, so that he and his wife Queen Charlotte (as in Bridgerton) could observe the 1769 transit of Venus. At the time, this was a major scientific endeavour, because it offered a way to determine the distance from Earth to the sun. Evidently the royals wanted to share the excitement.

Careful examination of the listing reveals that the observatory is still operational: one of the photos shows an antique wood and brass telescope housed inside a cupola. Kelsey notes with bemusement that the estate agents do not seem to regard this as a major selling point: “it’s the last photo in the slideshow”.

In the decades after the transit, the observatory was used for an array of scientific tasks, including measuring atmospheric electricity and verifying the accuracy of instruments such as clocks. In the 1980s, it became offices, and in the 21st century, a private home. The listing describes it as having not a garden, but “grounds”, and a drive that can accommodate the adjective “sweeping”. Grecian carp are mentioned.

At this point, Feedback had heard enough. We were poised to book a viewing when we noticed the asking price: £18 million. We find ourselves a tad short. We could try for a mortgage, but we fear that by definition it would be sub-prime.

London Centric did highlight one potential disadvantage of purchasing the King’s Observatory: “You do, however, have to live in the middle of a golf course.” Readers and their spouses will have their own views as to whether this is a plus or a minus.

We continue our efforts to compile the most niche science-themed tourist attractions from around the world. In this we have been aided by Brian Reffin Smith, who alerts us to “an exceptional wonder”: the Museum of Dust.

The museum is the creation of artist and author Sally Kindberg. It’s a little cabinet, blue on the outside and red inside. It’s divided into eight compartments: two across, four down. Each houses an array of little bottles of dust.

But not just any dust. Sally has gathered samples from around the world. There is dust from the Great Wall of China and from the wrapping of an ancient Egyptian mummy. Another sample comes from yet another museum, the self-explanatory House of Automata. Do not look at photos of the items on display at the House of Automata unless you want to be inspired to write a M3GAN-style horror movie.

Sometimes people send Sally dust, which must surely cause a brief frisson of alarm when she opens the envelope. She has dust from the TARDIS from Doctor Who, sent to her in 2013 by a friend who worked on the show. She also has a sample of dust from the 2007 Celebrity Big Brother house, but has not yet revealed how she obtained it.

Readers eager to see the Museum of Dust need to know it has no permanent home: instead you have to attend one of Sally’s workshops or talks. Just try not to sneeze.

Occasionally Feedback likes to throw a spanner in the works. In that spirit, we will highlight some examples of what we might call anti-nominative determinism: that is, people whose names are the opposite of what we might expect given their jobs.

In Queropalca, a remote district of Peru, a recent mayoral election was won by a candidate named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores. That name contains two waving red flags, but, in fact, Hitler Mussolini is a member of the Ahora NaciÓn party, which is on the centre-left.

This sort of thing seems to happen quite a lot in South America. For instance, between 2017 and 2021, the president of Ecuador was one Lenín Moreno. Elected as a social democrat, he pivoted to right-wing economic policies – none of which, one feels, the original Lenin would have approved of.

Likewise, reader Hillary Shaw wrote in to highlight another example of inappropriate naming: the 19th-century poet William Jeffrey Prowse. This one took Feedback a moment to understand because we associate the surname Prowse with the actor who embodied Darth Vader, whereas Hillary simply wanted us to read it without the “w”.

Meanwhile, in Australia, Bonita Ely was alarmed to discover that her next cancer check-up was with a “Dr Kilian”.

You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist. com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website.

Why the world’s first spinal cord transplant is so controversial

New Scientist October 28, 2026

The virologist Jonas Salk said that “hope lies in dreams, in imagination and in the courage of those who dare to make dreams into reality”. Salk was certainly daring – he risked paralysing himself, his wife and their children while testing his polio vaccine. Thankfully, it paid off. None of them experienced any ill effects and his work is credited with saving millions.

Risks have to be taken for medicine to advance, and someone is always the first to receive a treatment. But there are risks, and then there are risks.

Salk tested his vaccine on cells, monkeys and children who had already had polio before turning his unexposed family into guinea pigs. His approach is far from standard protocol today, but he did a lot to reduce the risk of something going wrong.

Advertisement

There is less evidence to justify an operation that took place this month in Russia. Details are scant, but the procedure involved cutting out a section of spinal cord from someone with a complete spinal cord injury and gluing in a replacement piece from a donor. The transplant was a world first, but there is little evidence to believe it will have worked or that now was the time to try it.

The transplant was a world first, but there is little evidence to believe it will have worked

History tells us that acting ahead of medical evidence can have catastrophic results. Take the first synthetic organ transplants, which replaced tracheas with plastic tubes. The surgeon who fitted them admitted they hadn’t been tested on large animals because they “didn’t have the time”. Complications and deaths followed.

With new medical procedures, the gold standard is randomised controlled trials, which are costly and take time, but they aren’t the only route. When someone is critically ill, there are compassionate-use protocols that make interventions available before they are fully tested. Pig kidney transplants are currently being trialled this way, for example.

The dream of spinal cord transplants will surely become a reality one day, but only if the science underpinning them is built first. Courage, dreams and imagination are of course good, yet with experimental surgeries, evidence is better.

Plant biology provides inspiration for PFAS replacement

New Scientist October 29, 2026

A plant-inspired waterproof coating could soon become a safer and more sustainable alternative to forever chemicals like the PTFE used in waterproof clothing.

Per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances, known as PFAS or forever chemicals, have proven both a blessing and a curse for modern society. Their manifold useful properties, which include having high heat resistance, while being both water- and greaseproof, inert and durable, have made them a staple of many consumer products, from cookware and clothing to medical tools and electrical insulation. More recently, concerns around their long-term persistence in the environment, and the resulting impacts on human health, have meant regulation has tightened substantially and scientists are now working to develop greener and cleaner alternatives.

But, as is often the case, nature may have already found the solution. “Plants transport water across very long distances using this structure called suberin,” says Joshua Yuan, a chemical engineer at Washington University in St Louis, Missouri. Composed of a mixture of greasy long-chain fatty acids, suberin combines with the plant polymer lignin to form a super-waterproof surface that lines the tiny vessels and tubes of the plant’s internal plumbing system.

Advertisement

The ‘forever chemicals’ toxic to your health – and how to avoid them

Drawing inspiration from these natural pipes, Yuan’s team recreated this waterproof coating from a combination of paper industry waste and animal fat. They spray-coated the suberin-like slurry onto glass, metal and cotton surfaces where the individual particles quickly self-assembled to form a continuous waterproof layer.

Unlike PFAS coatings, whose many carbon-fluorine bonds directly repel water molecules, the new coating operates by a completely different mechanism, says Han Zuilhof, an organic chemist at Wageningen University & Research in the Netherlands. The precisely nanostructured surface creates lots of tiny pockets of air, which effectively minimise direct contact between the coated material and water droplets on the surface – similar to the lotus effect seen on the leaves of many plants.

The new structure proved resistant to both contamination by limescale and mechanical wear, and showed a similar level of water resistance to state-of-the-art forever chemical coatings like PTFE. “It uses an interesting approach. Textiles will be one of the first sectors affected by PFAS restrictions, so it could be a good alternative,” says Carlo Antonini, a materials scientist at the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy.

Scientists have found significant concentrations of a type of PFAS chemical in the air deep in the Amazon rainforest, suggesting it travelled over 100 kilometres from an industrial hub

The team is already exploring applications in food packaging, such as the internal linings of drinks cans, but the coating’s lower heat tolerance compared with PTFE means bakeware is currently off the table.

The versatile properties of such a material mean there is no shortage of potential uses. The real step forward though, is the completely bio-based nature of the coating, says Zuilhof. Suberin’s chemical structure is easily degraded under composting conditions and the team showed their nature-inspired material likewise broke down completely, without releasing harmful residues into the environment. “They’ve basically turned a waste product into something valuable, and that’s quite cool,” says Zuilhof. “I think this will be a source of inspiration to find other bio-based materials from different waste streams.”

Birds can get jet lag on long, fast flights and then fly off course

New Scientist October 29, 2026

You don’t need a jet plane to get jet lag – even feathers will do. At least one species of bird gets jet lag, in the sense that its body clock can diverge from local time by more than an hour on fast flights across the Atlantic, as revealed by navigational errors.

“We’ve slightly shied away from using the term jet lag itself, because people associate that with the health impacts of that clock shift, rather than the clock shift itself. But it’s exactly the same process that causes jet lag in people,” says Patrick Lewin at the University of Oxford. “It’s having these physiological and behavioural effects, where the birds are mistiming their behaviours.”

It is likely that other long-distance fliers, possibly including some insects and bats as well as birds, also get jet lag in the clock-shift sense, says Lewin.

Advertisement

Birds wearing tiny trackers reveal migration routes in amazing detail

Manx shearwaters are small seabirds that fly vast distances, using a technique called dynamic soaring to exploit wind gradients near the sea surface. “They’ve evolved this niche of being really amazing long-distance travellers,” says Lewin.

They breed on islands around the UK and Ireland. While parents are raising a chick, they may fly more than 1000 kilometres westwards to reach rich fishing grounds in the mid-Atlantic. Once they have food, they fly back in a fairly straight line, diverting only to skirt around landmasses such as Ireland.

How do they achieve these navigational feats? While some birds can sense Earth’s magnetic field, Manx shearwaters don’t appear to. Lewin’s team has confirmed this by attaching small magnets to the birds that should disrupt geomagnetic navigation. They had no effect.

Free newsletter

Instead, it appears that shearwaters rely on a sun compass – if you know what time it is, you can maintain a course by adjusting your orientation relative to the sun. Many animals, from insects and fish to turtles and birds, have been shown to do this. If their internal clocks are reset using artificial light and darkness, they head in the wrong direction.

“We realised that there might be a kind of natural experiment where the birds were manipulating their own clocks,” says Lewin.

For instance, at 6am, a Manx shearwater wanting to fly eastwards back to its nest needs to head sunwards. At noon, it needs to fly at right angles to the sun, which will be due south. But if a shearwater travels 15° of longitude eastwards, the local time will be 1pm, while its internal clock will still register the time as noon, so the sun will no longer be due south. This means birds flying rapidly east should veer slightly off course in a clockwise direction over the course of day, in the absence of other cues.

Australian moths use the stars as a compass on 1000-km migrations

Other researchers have been attaching GPS trackers to Manx shearwaters for decades, so the paths taken on nearly 4000 foraging trips are known. Sure enough, when Lewin and his colleagues analysed these flight tracks, they found birds on rapid return flights tended to deviate clockwise when out of sight of land.

The team considered other potential explanations, from the Coriolis effect to winds. “The one thing that best predicted the observed changes in shearwaters’ orientation was always this sun compass effect,” says Lewin.

The effect is small. After a 1000 km flight, a bird would have to fly only an extra 5 km to reach its colony, which, for such efficient long-distance fliers, is probably negligible, Lewin says. This might explain why Manx shearwaters haven’t evolved some mechanism for avoiding jet lag, he says.

Solving the mysteries of bird migration with technology not only unlocks unexpected secrets but is crucial to conservation efforts, says Rebecca Heisman in her fascinating first book

“What is good about the study is that they analyse a lot of tracks, making for robust data to test different models,” says Ken Cheng at Macquarie University in Sydney.

While other species may get this form of jet lag, too, long-distance flights by birds are typically done during migrations, and migrations usually involve mainly north-south travel, says Cheng, so jet lag won’t be much of a problem.

However, near the poles, the travel distance required to cross 15° or more of longitude becomes so short that many animals might be affected, says Lewin, perhaps even including polar bears or Arctic foxes travelling on sea ice.

“Near-polar species may be quite strongly affected,” he says. “Now, it all gets a bit complicated because you have 24-hour daylight and 24-hour darkness in parts of the year, so circadian rhythms break down generally in some species.”

New Scientist October 29, 2026

Taking our first breaths marks the beginning of a new life, yet this may be the very act that limits our ability to grow and heal as adults. Studies in mice have pinned down a newborn’s exhalation of carbon dioxide, immediately after birth, as the starting gun that switches off their cells’ intrinsic ability to regenerate.

“We were very surprised and excited by the CO2 effect,” says Zhigang He at Harvard Medical School, who led the research.

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

But when grown mice inhaled the gas, the regenerative pathways turned back on, a discovery He hopes could lead to targeted medical treatments. The results are “very tantalising”, says Nahum Sonenberg at McGill University in Canada. “If correct, this is a groundbreaking discovery.”

Advertisement

Many species of fish, amphibians and reptiles can regenerate tissues, limbs and organs such as hearts, following injury. Mammals also have some regenerative capacity before and shortly after birth, but lose this later in life. A protein master switch called mTOR is one reason they do so. It plays a central role in regulating cell growth in tissues such as brain, heart and muscles, and its activity declines inside cells within minutes of birth. But the reasons for the drop were poorly understood, says Soroush Tahmasebi at the University of Illinois, who wasn’t involved with the latest research.

Zhigang He and his colleagues wondered if the shutdown could be related to the dramatic event of birth itself. To find out, they tracked mTOR activity in neurons in the retinas of mice delivered by caesarean section. As long as the newborns remained inside an intact amniotic sac, mTOR stayed high. But as soon as they were removed from the sac and the pups began to breathe air, mTOR activity dropped, even if the researchers kept the umbilical cord intact so that the nutrient supply from the mother was unchanged. This suggested the shutdown trigger was the transition from receiving oxygen through the blood of the umbilical cord to independently breathing air.

Free newsletter

The researchers also confirmed that temperature wasn’t a factor in the shutdown through separate tests in which newborn pups were kept at the same temperature – 37°C – as they had experienced in the uterus.

Next, the team delivered pups in controlled gas environments, and found that mTOR activity still shut down even if they lowered oxygen levels in the air. But increasing CO2 levels to 10 per cent prevented the loss of mTOR activity.

Further experiments showed that exhaling CO2 triggers the mTOR shutdown by causing a rise in pH inside cells as levels of the gas fall.

We may finally know what kick-starts muscle contractions in childbirth

When adult mice inhaled air containing 10 per cent CO2, mTOR activity restarted across a range of tissues including brain, heart and muscle, and their neurons’ ability to regenerate after injury was restored. The work shows that the drop in CO2 when breathing starts is “the underlying mechanism driving regenerative failure, not only in neurons but potentially across multiple organs”, says Tahmasebi, “and importantly it is reversible”.

CO2 exhalation might not be the only factor governing the ability of cells to regrow, says He. “Other physiological changes associated with birth may also influence regenerative capacity.” But he hopes the discovery could lead to the development of simple, non-invasive therapies, perhaps based on inhaling CO2, for conditions such as spinal cord injury or traumatic brain injury.

A combination of widely available antibiotics may be able to treat heart failure after researchers found that the therapy regenerates heart cells in animals

Inhibiting mTOR, with drugs such as rapamycin, has previously been shown to have anti-ageing effects in many species including humans, whereas activating it rescues embryonic-like regenerative potential, at least in mice, but can cause cells to grow out of control, says Tahmasebi. The risk of cancer has deterred industry investment in drugs that activate mTOR, he says, but perhaps the role of CO2 could lead to ways to activate the cascade more safely, in a “temporary and tissue-specific” way.

Further research is still needed, however, to establish appropriate and safe CO2 levels and exposure times, as well as potential side effects. “We would not recommend attempting this without medical supervision,” says He.

The connection between air breathing and regenerative potential also has intriguing evolutionary implications. Vertebrates that acquire oxygen via gills and lose CO2 via their skin – some fish species, as well as amphibians during aquatic larval stages – tend to have high capacity for regeneration, whereas mammals and birds, dependent on air and lungs, are generally much more limited. Breathing could therefore be an underappreciated evolutionary factor shaping regenerative abilities across many forms of life, the researchers say.

Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated

New Scientist October 29, 2026

Quantum mechanics’ probabilistic nature has puzzled researchers for more than a century. A new analysis shows that ridding the theory of this odd characteristic may be even harder than anticipated.

Infamously, quantum objects can exist in combinations of seemingly mutually exclusive states, such as in the Schrödinger’s cat thought experiment, where the animal is in a mix of states that makes it seem both alive and dead, and also neither. Left undisturbed and isolated, the cat remains mixed, but if it is observed – if an experimenter opens its box, say – it abruptly reduces to just one, unmixed state.

We’re on the verge of seeing the quantum foundations of the universe

How exactly this happens – a question known as the measurement problem – is among the biggest unresolved questions about quantum mechanics. At its heart is a mathematical rule named after the physicist Max Born. Researchers have long tried to derive the Born rule from mathematical ingredients that could eliminate some of quantum mechanics’ probabilistic oddness. However, Jiaxuan Zhang at the University of Oxford has now found that some of the most influential among these derivations don’t fully accomplish this task.

Advertisement

The Born rule is a recipe for converting information about a quantum object into probabilities that tell us the likelihood of observing particular outcomes. The rule is also a postulate, which means the founders of quantum mechanics assumed its truth rather than deriving it. But it is a troublesome truth because it means that quantum mechanics cannot offer information firmer than the probability of something happening, such as Schrödinger’s cat being alive 30 per cent of the time you open its box.

Zhang wanted to know if past efforts to derive the Born rule from mathematical assumptions, instead of simply postulating it, introduced any probabilistic ingredients at the starting point. If no such ingredients are needed, it might be possible to place quantum mechanics on more deterministic ground – and so make it more understandable.

“I think that if we can find the origin of the Born rule, maybe we can also find the origin of quantum probability,” says Zhang. She spent about two years combing through five of the most influential derivations of the rule in an attempt to zero in on that origin.

Subscriber-only newsletter

These five derivations were motivated by a broad range of ideas about how to interpret the equations of quantum mechanics, drawing on arguments ranging from considerations about symmetry and quantum entanglement to decision theory for inhabitants of the quantum multiverse. Zhang assumed an interpretation-agnostic stance and paid attention solely to the maths.

But as she dug into the underlying assumptions, she found more probability. “For people who want to derive the probabilistic Born rule from only deterministic principles, my result for now doesn’t support that,” says Zhang.

For instance, she concluded that some version of a concept known as additivity is indispensable to all derivations of the Born rule in her analysis. Although it can be stated more generally and abstractly, additivity is simplest to understand when thinking about fair dice. Here, additivity means that the probabilities of rolling each number, from 1 to 6, always sum to 100 per cent.

Decades after it was posited as a foundational principle of quantum physics, Richard Feynman’s “path integral” has been directly measured in an experiment for the first time

“I find Zhang’s paper interesting because it addresses a fundamental question: where do quantum probabilities come from?” says Augusto Smerzi at the Shenzhen Technology University in China. He says that, by showing just how important additivity is, she brings clarity to a long-standing problem.

But Smerzi says that clearly identifying the assumptions underlying the Born rule shouldn’t be misunderstood as an explanation for why this rule in its postulated mathematical form describes our world so well. “Making assumptions explicit is essential, but understanding why nature obeys them is what gives a derivation its deeper physical meaning,” he says. “I would therefore not interpret Zhang’s conclusions as closing the door to a deeper explanation of quantum probabilities. Rather, they highlight the importance of continuing to search for such an explanation.”

Zhang says the work is nowhere near over because there are more derivations of the Born rule that she wants to analyse. She also doesn’t think that some mathematical surprise is fully out of the picture yet. While her work constricts the possibility, there is still a small chance that the Born rule could be put on deterministic foundations, she says.

A poor poll result for National has prompted leader Christopher Luxon to remind voters of the "dire consequences" of a Labour victory.

The Herald has spoken to Opportunity's big backer AJ Wilderland.
