The provisional enrolment rate for the 2026 General Election is 93.6% with 3,790,946 people enrolled to vote.

This covers everyone enrolled by the 25 October deadline - the final rate won't be confirmed until after the election.

The final enrolment rate at the 2023 General Election was 94.7%. It was 94.1% in 2020, 92.4% in 2017, and 92.6% in 2014.

Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said this year's provisional rate shows "a good level of awareness of the change in the rules and the new deadline to enrol before voting started this year".

The provisional enrolment rate for 18- to 24-year-olds is 74.2%, up significantly from 53.9% on 31 July this year, and close to the 76.7% enrolled in 2023.

The provisional enrolment rate for voters of Māori descent is 85.9%.

There are 603,968 Māori voters enrolled, 272,513 (45.1%) on the general roll and 331,455 (54.9%) on the Māori roll. The total number of Māori enrolled in 2023 was 567,012.

The last day to vote is election day Saturday 7 November when more than 2300 voting places will be open from 9am.

Act leader David Seymour is floating a potential bid for the finance portfolio if the coalition Government is re-elected.

Current Finance Minister Nicola Willis is facing losing her place in Parliament, with National's low polling meaning it may not elect any MPs off the party's list.

Speaking to Newstalk ZB Canterbury Mornings host John MacDonald, Seymour was asked whether he would be seeking the finance role in coalition negotiations.

"Look it's very possible, let's see first of all if the coalition's re-elected, that's not guaranteed, this election is going to be absolutely razor tight, razor thin," Seymour told MacDonald.

"I'm running for office, I'm prepared to serve, I'll serve in whatever I think is the best capacity if the coalition is able to form a new government but far before we get to that, rather than measuring up the curtains politicians should be looking out the window to see that we're actually having an election out here and what's critical is that we win enough party votes for Act to first of all re-elect the coalition, second of all have more Act in it and then let's see how it forms up."

National Party leader Christopher Luxon is confident Willis will return to Parliament, saying she is the best finance minister New Zealand has ever had.

Asked if he agrees with Luxon's assessment of Willis' performance, Seymour said "well, let's see".

"First of all will she get another term? That's why we've actually got to win the election first," Seymour said.

"I think Nicola Willis is a very capable person but of course he's the leader of the National Party, she's a National MP, you'd expect him to say that wouldn't you?"

"Our hope, David, is that you'll be like Winston," says a resident speaking to Act leader David Seymour as he door-knocks his way through Kohimarama, an affluent beachfront suburb in Auckland's Tāmaki electorate.

Seymour is with James Christmas, a veteran of the Sir John Key Government, a former staffer to Attorney-General and Treaty Negotiations Minister Chris Finlayson (and co-author with Finlayson of a book on Treaty settlements), an unlucky National Party list candidate from 2023, and Act's candidate for Tāmaki this year.

Act's then-deputy leader Brooke van Velden convincingly won the seat in 2023, but after announcing she would retire from politics at the end of the parliamentary term, the party had to find someone else to run in the seat, eventually alighting on Christmas.

The Herald accompanied Seymour and Christmas for an afternoon of door-knocking as part of a series looking at how issues play out on the doorstep.

Recently, we spent time with Labour's Arena Williams in Manurewa, where Labour volunteers were often more concerned with making sure people were enrolled to vote than who they voted for.

The conversation is different in Tāmaki, with Act keen to ensure it holds the seat it fought so hard to win off National in 2023.

Read more of Political Editor Thomas Coughlan's Premium piece below.

Labour is not prioritising law and order this election and that comes through loud and clear in its just-released manifesto.

There is barely anything substantial in it.

Nor is there any pledge to reverse what the coalition Government has done: the gang patch ban, the longer sentences, Three Strikes 2.0 or the public funding of cultural reports.

Labour highlights the need to tackle methamphetamine and strengthen support for crime victims, both of which the coalition has prioritised.

The policy platform essentially means Labour has raised the white flag on law and order and broadly accepts the current direction of travel; whether a Labour-led left governing bloc would also do so is another matter.

Read more of Derek Cheng's Premium analysis below.

Labour's Willie Jackson has shot back at National's plan to cut public service jobs by 15%.

"We've got record unemployment, inflation is going up… People leaving for Australia, 2-300 a day are leaving.

"Wellington is struggling and these guys want to gut Wellington," he told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

"I think it's shocking… They don't care. They just see numbers and they don't see people."

National's Paul Goldsmith was adamant the party was working to bring the public service sector down to a "reasonable" size again after it shot from 47,000 to 65,000 employees under the former Labour government.

"There's not a perfect relationship between the number of people working in a department and the outcomes.

"It's about the clarity of purpose and the quality of management, all those sorts of things… "

Goldsmith said the goal was to have 55,000 public service workers in the next three to four years.

National's Paul Goldsmith is maintaining optimism for his party whose numbers took a dive in the latest poll.

The RNZ-Reid Research poll yesterday put the party on 24.8% and Labour on 30.6%.

"The election is tight, there's no doubt about it," said Goldsmith.

"We're on the cusp of three great years, this country is up off the floor, we don't want to put it at risk going the other way."

When asked on Ryan Bridge TODAY if he was worried his job was at stake, he said politics was a "hazardous business".

Labour's Willie Jackson said it was a "flip a coin" situation.

"[I] think we both probably agree this could go either way, but we are stronger going into the last week."

Meanwhile, former National and Act party leader Don Brash, who recently supported the idea to vote-split, yesterday put a personal ad in the Herald newspaper encouraging people to vote for Act in both Epsom and Tāmaki electorates.

Goldsmith, National's candidate for Epsom, said Brash had "gone off the rails".

"It's very simple. If you want a strong, stable government, party vote National."

Former Prime Minister Sir John Key is repeating a call not to engage in strategic voting, telling Newstalk ZB's Mike Hosking Breakfast it was "not a smart idea" to split the vote.

"The centre-right political party, the biggest party in the parliament, needs to have a strong core," the former National leader told Hosking.

"If you eat away at that and you say, 'okay, well, I'll give my party vote somewhere else', then then you put Labour right in the box seat to be the first party that can form a government."

Sir John released a video earlier this morning urging people to vote - telling Hosking he wasn't worried, but it was a very tight race.

"If people don't vote, you know, I would worry that they would wake up on November 8 and have buyer's remorse," he said.

Sir John suggested voters were lethargic as the campaign had lacked "drama" compared to some elections he had been involved in.

"People just go, 'oh, I'm bored with all this, I just won't vote'. But the consequences of a change of government are very, very significant."

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little says he is beginning to change the culture of a council long plagued by infighting and value for money concerns, but a year into the city’s top job, some of his key promises remain unfulfilled.

Speaking to the Herald in his office 12 months on from his historic landslide win, Little has shared his best and worst moments on the job, and revealed progress has paused on the policy that motivated him to run for the mayoralty in the first place.

Little was sworn in on October 30, 2025, after campaigning on a platform of bringing “serious leadership and real change” to council.

According to many of his council colleagues, Little appears to have largely succeeded on the former; councillors from across the political divide say the culture is more unified than in previous years, and the threat of further intervention from the Government has remained at bay.

Little said that while he didn’t make councillors join in team-building exercises or “compulsory fun” (like he said he experienced in the Labour Party), the culture across the table now is “constructive”, after years of infighting.

Hamilton and Auckland Pak’nSave stores fined $580,500 for fair trading breaches

New Zealand Herald October 29, 2026

Pak'nSave on Mill St in Hamilton. Photo / Dean Taylor

Two Pak’nSave supermarkets have been fined a total of $580,500 for repeatedly breaching fair trading rules and misleading customers.

But the consumer watchdog says the penalties are a “drop in the bucket” and will do little to deter future behaviour.

“New Zealand consumers deserve better than this given what they are paying for groceries,” Consumer NZ chief executive Jon Duffy said.

In March last year, the Commerce Commission filed criminal charges against Pak’nSave Silverdale in Auckland and Pak’nSave Mill St in Hamilton.

Both supermarkets advertised prices that did not match charges at the point of sale, and promoted specials or discounts where no special price existed.

The Mill St store pleaded guilty to eight charges and the Silverdale one admitted 10 charges.

Each charge carries a maximum penalty of $600,000.

The sentencing was heard in Auckland District Court in May before Judge June Jelas, who reserved her decision.

The judge’s written findings are still pending, but a decision on the financial penalties was released this morning.

Pak’nSave Silverdale was fined $234,000, and Pak’nSave Mill Street $346,500.

Commerce Commission deputy chair Anne Callinan said the watchdog had long put big supermarkets on notice about meeting their fundamental responsibility to ensure the ticket price on the shelf matched the price at the till.

“Despite this, Auckland’s Pak’nSave Silverdale and Pak’nSave Mill St, in Hamilton, have now been criminally convicted for repeated pricing errors that misled their customers.

“The commission will not hesitate to prosecute other supermarkets if we believe there is wrongdoing. Consumers are entitled to rely on accurate pricing; that is the bottom line.

“These are highly profitable stores who should be investing in pricing systems that ensure these errors that mislead consumers do not happen.”

Callinan said the commission was satisfied with the penalties, but the case showed the need for the Government’s current review of the Fair Trading Act.

“Increasing the penalties and changing to a civil regime as proposed will give us the option to push for fines of up to $5 million for each breach, compared to our current maximum of $600,000.

“Fines in this range would have a much stronger deterrent effect and encourage genuine behaviour change.”

Proposed changes to the act would support fairer outcomes for consumers and level the playing field for businesses that followed the rules, she said.

The commission’s case against Woolworths NZ for similar conduct was ongoing, Callinan added. Woolworths has pleaded not guilty.

Breaches in the grocery sector remain an area of focus for the commission, with several ongoing matters involving the major supermarkets.

The commission also has current proceedings against Foodstuffs North Island and Gilmours alleging cartel conduct.

Separately, in August, it announced civil proceedings against Foodstuffs South Island for allegedly implementing and enforcing a restriction on independently owned Pak’nSave stores discounting selected products.

“We will continue to act within our current remit to hold the major supermarkets to account on behalf of Kiwis,” the commission said.

Duffy said the prosecution originated from a Consumer NZ complaint about inaccurate pricing.

Consumer NZ agreed the level of the fines imposed, while substantial under the current available penalties, “are a drop in the bucket for a major supermarket and will not do much to deter future conduct of this nature”.

Duffy it was important that proposed increases to penalties under the Fair Trading Act proceeded in the next term of Government.

“Pricing errors and misleading discounting practices are widespread in the sector. The conduct demonstrates how a lack of meaningful competition is not only producing excessive profits, but also allows supermarkets to get away with declining customer service and low levels of investment in innovation.”

Earlier, Commerce Commission prosecutor Nick Flanagan called for “significant” penalties for the two supermarkets, “substantially” higher than in a previous case.

He argued that supermarkets could be incentivised to take risks if the penalties imposed were not significant.

Being a high-volume business that made frequent price changes was not an excuse for the breaches, he said.

Flanagan pointed out that another Pak’nSave had earlier been before the courts for similar breaches.

This indicated that the level of penalty in the previous case, against Pak’nSave Māngere, was not enough to prompt the supermarkets to ensure prices were accurate.

In the 2020 Māngere case, the supermarket was fined $78,000 for discrepancies between the promotional price displayed or advertised and the price charged at the till.

Flanagan argued that the fine imposed on the two latest stores needed to “substantially increase” from that figure.

In the latest cases, he told the court that prices had been advertised as specials when they were “nothing of the kind”.

For instance, one product was advertised as “extra low”, when it was actually priced at that level for 90.7% of the year.

Staff were manually updating prices at Silverdale, he said, without a systematic approach. An electronic system came into effect at the store in October 2024.

However, Flanagan said errors continued because there was so much confidence in the new system that prices were not being checked as often.

At Mill St, which had an electronic system, the store did not have processes to properly record price complaints before June 2024.

This failure would have led to more breaches, he submitted.

He argued that the excess revenue from breaches recorded at Mill St “materially understates” the true gain the store would have received from its misleading prices.

He sought a penalty starting point of $550,000 and, in the Silverdale case, $400,000, but accepted that the operators should get a 25% discount for pleading guilty at the earliest opportunity.

Defence lawyer Iain Thain argued that both stores should get a further 10% discount for co-operation.

It was “not right” to say the two stores had learned nothing from the Māngere case, he said.

The Māngere store used paper labels in its product pricing, while Mill St used electronic shelf labels, in part due to increased errors associated with paper pricing.

Pak’nSave Silverdale had also moved to digital labels before the prosecution commenced, towards the end of the offending period.

Thain said that, on some occasions, consumers had benefited from breaches.

For example, a wooden display board had advertised a Vogel’s product for $5, but customers were charged less at the checkout, in most cases $4.

At Mill St, a staff member with a scanning gun would check prices every morning in the fresh food section to ensure they were correct, Thain said.

As a result, only two of the 18 breaches were related to the fresh food department.

Unless staff were “constantly” scanning, errors could still occur with electronic prices if, for example, someone bumped an electronic label or the scanner ran out of battery.

Thain said each store had made further improvements to their systems once the proceedings began, which he argued showed remorse.

After media applications, the supermarkets asked the judge to suppress some aspects of the summary of facts, citing commercial sensitivities and disputed facts relating to Mill St.

Animal control worker’s fingertip bitten off as staff face more threats

New Zealand Herald October 29, 2026

Auckland’s shelters are facing challenges in holding dangerous and aggressive dogs Photo / RNZ, Felix Walton

A dog in an Auckland Council animal shelter is so aggressive it has bitten off the tip of a staff member’s finger – and has to be sedated with a blow dart so it can be moved between kennels.

Animal management staff are facing increasing threats from aggressive dogs and their owners in Auckland, with the latest figures revealing that abuse has more than doubled from the previous year.

Auckland Council head of animal management Ellie Waitoa said having to deal with a dog by sedating it should give people a fair idea of how aggressive some dogs could be.

“We’re dealing with some pretty gnarly behaviours, unfortunately.”

The dog seriously attacked one of its owners, but they still want it back.

Thirty-three new kennels were being built at the Manukau Animal Shelter, and an extra 14 kennels were being built at the same shelter to hold dangerous and high-risk dogs.

“Some of these dogs are so aggressive ... we can’t risk handling them.”

The report also highlighted an increase in staff exposure to high levels of violence and aggression while carrying out their duties in the community.

In the past year, 759 incidents were recorded in the council’s health and safety management system, up by two-thirds from the previous year.

Of these, eight cases were classified as high-risk.

A total of 291 incidents involved violent or aggressive behaviour from members of the public towards staff, representing a 112% increase from the previous year.

The three most commonly reported risk categories were violent and aggressive behaviour from people, animal aggression and movement, and psychosocial risk.

“People are very, and understandably so, attached to their dogs and it’s not a nice situation to be [in] when council have to impound your dog and hold it potentially.

“But it does not excuse the behaviours that stem from that. We’ve had staff that have been assaulted, physically threatened, [there’s been] threats against the shelter.

“We have security at the shelters because we’ve had people try to break in, it’s typically just really appalling behaviour.”

Waitoa said desexing the animals would help minimise a lot of the issues, including the uncontrolled dog population.

“The officers are all animal lovers, despite what may be posted on social media. You look at those shelter staff: they’re cleaning, picking up poo, feeding, providing medical attention, exercising, providing enrichment for the dogs and their care each year.

“You wouldn’t do that if you didn’t love dogs. So it’s kind of a misdirected anger, whereas owners should be really focused on the people who’ve let these dogs down in the first place and let the public down.”

Firefighter training deficiencies report includes disputed claim of ‘beasting’ recruits

New Zealand Herald October 29, 2026

Fire and Emergency NZ's reset covers recruits and volunteers, not 1000-plus career firefighters.

By Phil Pennington of RNZ

A Fire and Emergency report has revealed major flaws in the way firefighters are trained – including a claim that an old-school military style approach called “beasting” is used to belittle trainees.

In response, Fire and Emergency NZ has launched a training reset but didn’t share the report with firefighters or the Minister of Internal Affairs.

The report found training was often outdated, disjointed, or did not teach new recruits or firefighters getting a refresh what they needed for the job, and was unsafe for learners.

“Trainers use old military-style approaches [beasting] to belittle learners if they fail to meet the required standard,” it said.

“These mindsets and behaviours do not promote our courses as safe learning environments.”

Fire and Emergency said the reset would be “short” and aim to improve safety.

However, it was confined to new recruits and volunteers, and not extend to the 1000-plus professional firefighters.

National training leader Joe Stanley said he blocked the extension, saying: “We’re going down the wrong path.”

He faulted the training report for taking aim at individual instructors when they were doing their best in an underfunded system that needed to change.

Fire and Emergency NZ is under intense pressure.

Its chief executive quit last week over a month after Minister Brooke van Velden said she did not have confidence in him.

She told RNZ on Tuesday: “I was not made aware of the 2025 report you refer to, which I understand was an internal Fire and Emergency working document.

“I am advised the report helped shape this year’s redesign of recruit and volunteer training. I expect the board to ensure Fire and Emergency provides recruits and volunteers with safe, effective training that meets operational requirements and prioritises firefighter safety.”

Bill Butzbach, head of the United Fire Brigades’ Association that represents 12,000 volunteers, said he would be asking to see a copy.

“We’re quite disappointed that we didn’t see it.”

He put that down to an oversight.

The training deficiencies are long-running and systemic, according to the report.

Butzbach said this came as no surprise.

“It’s been on our radar.”

Firefighters RNZ has spoken with have for several years said training did not get high enough priority.

The problems with it come on top of the fire truck fleet management woes investigated by MPs.

A few lines in the report refer to “beasting”, and the extent or nature of it is not detailed.

Historically, it is a military practice of verbally dressing down or ordering a trainee to do arduous physical exercise – 100 push-ups – as a reprimand.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand told RNZ it “does not condone or tolerate the behaviour described, and it is not part of our training”.

The United Fire Brigades’ Association said it knew of one case in the past two years, of a volunteer recruit. The details were confidential but verbal rather than physical belittling was the issue.

They worked on it with Fire and Emergency, and Butzbach recalled one instructor was censured.

“We were satisfied with the outcome.”

He would tell recruits and their families that there were sufficient safeguards in place and Fire and Emergency NZ had changed that culture.

But Stanley rejected the “beasting” assertion entirely.

“That’s wrong. I’ve never seen any beasting,” he said.

He works at the Rotorua national training centre, running officer development, and is also national president of the Professional Firefighters’ Union (NZPFU).

They ran fitness “boot camps” but these were voluntary, he said.

Other sources said non-uniformed staff may have got the wrong idea. The training report was authored by an educationist rather than a firefighter, though it drew on some firefighter input.

The report goes into much more detail about other training shortcomings.

It cast deep doubts on whether “we do enough to embed safety in the training we provide”.

Citing the deaths of two volunteer firefighters in a landslide in Muriwai in Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023 and a volunteer firefighter injured by a car last year, it said: “While these examples relate to volunteers, feedback from interviewees suggests there is not a strong safety culture in career firefighting either.”

“Personal and crew safety training is not woven through all training activities.”

Stanley once again said that was wrong.

“That’s a backhanded insult against the programmes that I run.

“I wear the deaths of those two firefighters in Muriwai as a motivation to ensure that everyone that comes through the national training officer development function knows how to make good decisions.”

Butzbach said Fire and Emergency NZ and his association had the safety of personnel as a top priority.

Recruits do a 12-week course at the Rotorua centre. Firefighters undergo refreshers and specialised training there, as well as at fire stations.

The report featured a long list of deficiencies in training generally:

Overall, “there is no clear and documented alignment of course content to an overarching purpose”.

“This exposes the organisation to operational and reputational risk,” the report said.

Fire and Emergency New Zealand’s board got the training report in February. A team was set up to improve training but it has recently been shedding staff and a request for more funding was turned down, RNZ understands.

The report was used to begin redeveloping recruit and volunteer training.

Stanley said he blocked that being extended to career officers.

Fire and Emergency said it recently reviewed its improvement programme to “further improve delivery, effectiveness, and value for money”.

Changes would be put in place during a short reset period.

A key initiative would be improving the main safety concepts, it added.

RNZ understands managers have talked about slowing the pace of the reset to find a more sustainable model.

Stanley said Fire and Emergency NZ was wasting resources on a training reset that had far too little frontline input.

“Perversely, it’s become an opportunity to save money rather than reinvest the organisation’s resources into better training outcomes,” he said.

“I’m very, very protective over the programmes that I’m running. There is constant pressure on reducing the cost of those programmes and I push against that.”

Butzbach said the reset was at a very early stage with his association in talks with Fire and Emergency NZ about it.

“It’s just started. It’s miles away from being completed and it will require significant investment.”

Cost cutting on training had not come up with Fire and Emergency, and any move towards that would be counterproductive, he added.

One problem was what training should cover, Butzbach said: it had to match firefighters’ core jobs but these were still being debated in the face of a greater range of emergency demands.

Fire and Emergency said late on Thursday that there had been isolated instances of poor behaviour by its instructors but called them “issues of the past”.

“Like any large organisation, we are not immune to pockets of poor behaviour and are aware that in the past there have been isolated instances of poor behaviour by some of our people. Where known, these instances were addressed,” said deputy chief executive of prevention Stephen Hunt in a statement.

Instructors had a critical role and influence, so Fire and Emergency had strengthened the standards they were held to, including how they were selected and supported.

“We have revised guidelines that set clear expectations of professional conduct in the training environment.”

Behaviour on courses was monitored.

“We are confident these changes have addressed the issues of the past,” Hunt said.

He added Fire and Emergency NZ had put a lot of work into training in general to embed safety concepts in the past two years, with help from operational personnel to close any gap in knowledge that existed.

Revised safe-person and risk assessment were “now built into every practical lesson”.

The career recruit course had clear outcomes and assessment to ensure people got the skills they needed, and similar for volunteer recruits.

“We have not yet completed the reviews in full. We deliberately prioritised the recruit courses because they set the foundation for every firefighter. We will advance to the officer programmes through the review cycles.”

Fire and Emergency would keep making incremental changes and routinely examine and continuously improve training, Hunt said.

Townline Cabs under investigation by NZTA over alleged passenger overcharging

New Zealand Herald October 29, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

NZTA has launched an investigation into a taxi company accused of charging customers hundreds of dollars for short journeys from Auckland’s waterfront.

Two customers who recently used Townline Cabs told the Herald they felt “stupid” and had been unable to recover their money. One paid $187 for a journey of less than 2km.

An NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA) spokesperson told the Herald the matter was under investigation following three complaints about alleged overcharging by Townline Cabs.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

Earlier this month, a customer who did not want to be identified was charged more than $380 for a 16km trip home from Auckland’s Viaduct Harbour.

The Beach Haven resident had been celebrating a 50th birthday when he decided to go to the Viaduct taxi stand about midnight to get a ride home after a few drinks.

His wife said he saw a white taxi with a blue light on top and “assumed it was legit”.

“I know there’s scams and stuff. We’re really aware of online stuff, but we’ve always kind of trusted taxi drivers,” she said.

His wife said he had agreed on a $60 fare with the driver.

She said the driver held out an Eftpos machine and her husband paid via PayWave.

At the time, he did not realise he had paid $196.90.

“My husband didn’t even think to look at the screen.”

She said her husband described the driver as “friendly” throughout the 16km journey across the Auckland Harbour Bridge.

“He went to get out, and he [the driver] said, ‘Oh, your payment declined. Can you try again?’”

She said her husband was confused because he knew there was money in his account.

He tapped his card again, and $184.58 was taken by a different business than the first transaction.

The next morning, the man’s wife was checking whether a payment for something else had gone through when she made the startling discovery.

She asked her husband why more than $300 had been spent on taxis and where he had gone.

Her confused husband said: “I just came home.”

“At first we were like, ‘Oh, is this a mistake?’ And it’s like, ‘Oh, no. This is a full-on scam.’”

She said that, in an attempt to stop the payments, they contacted the bank.

The couple were told to check that the double payments were not a mistake made by the company, and they were also advised to cancel the card.

“It’s kind of a horrible feeling when you’ve been scammed by someone. You sort of think, ‘I should have been more on to it’.”

After they Googled the company, they found a social media thread in which multiple people claimed to have had similar experiences.

The couple said they could not find contact details for the company online.

“I would never get a taxi again. I probably would always do Uber,” she said.

The couple reported the incident to police and NZTA.

In a second incident, a Hamilton man visiting Auckland for an event said he initially wondered whether the driver had accidentally added an extra zero to his fare.

He said nothing appeared untoward when he caught a taxi near Danny Doolan’s on Auckland’s Viaduct on September 25.

He was charged $187 for a 1.8km drive.

“I thought $18.70 would be a fair kind of charge from there,” he said, initially dismissing the fee as a mistake.

“Surely they’ve just added an extra zero by error.”

His bank advised him to contact the company, but he said he could not find its contact details online.

Seven other people have contacted him and said they had a similar experience.

Auckland rideshare driver Paul Strand said situations like these were giving the industry a bad name.

“It’s doing a lot of damage to the industry.

“From a ride-share perspective, you see these taxi companies or other drivers independently who are making it unsafe.”

Strand said he understood other small groups were doing similar things, such as “consistently ripping people off” and not agreeing to a fee upfront.

NZTA said Townline Cabs did not hold a Transport Service Licence (TSL).

A TSL is an official authorisation issued by NZTA allowing individuals or businesses to operate commercial transport services.

However, the spokesperson said there was a Small Passenger Service (SPS) TSL holder associated with Townline Cabs.

“Further checks are underway.”

Detective Senior Sergeant Craig Bolton from the Auckland City Financial Crime Unit said they have received two recent reports from people being overcharged for taxi rides.

“Both reports concern the same Toyota Prius, with complainants being picked up at central Auckland locations,” Bolton said.

He said police have made initial attempts to contact the vehicle’s registered owner to discuss the reports.

“For police, these types of complaints are difficult to investigate. It is difficult to prove who was driving at the time, as it is not necessarily the registered owner.”

He said any criminal complaint requires police to consider the Solicitor-General’s Guidelines.

“These guidelines include an evidential sufficiency test. Based on information that we have available at this stage, we have assessed that threshold is not met to prove a charge beyond any reasonable doubt,” Bolton said.

He said being overcharged is the last thing anyone wants after a night out, and acknowledged the customers’ frustrations.

“It’s timely to warn the public about this fraudulent behaviour.

“While you can agree a fare with a taxi driver beforehand, you should never swipe or tap your card before the journey begins,” Bolton said.

He said swiping your card before a journey with no agreed price can also mean the matter becomes civil with any disputes.

“If a driver insists on you doing this prior to the journey beginning, we strongly advise that you walk away.”

Townline Cabs could not be reached for comment.

Pace of government digitisation a ‘real cause for concern’, says Manage My Health inquiry

New Zealand Herald October 29, 2026

The breach compromised over 400,000 HNZ documents and over 22,000 uploads. Photo / RNZ, Finn Blackwell

By RNZ

A report into a big health cyber breach says AI is being flagged as an emerging risk that could amplify existing vulnerabilities if governance frameworks are not strengthened now.

Privacy Commissioner Michael Webster’s second and final report into the Manage My Health breach in December 2025 is out today.

It found strong agreement that the spadework had not been done.

“There was strong consensus that foundational issues, forms, consent processes, and privacy arrangements must be resolved before expanding digital health infrastructure at pace.

“The pace of government digitisation was a real cause for concern; the health sector was not seen as ready for a ‘big digital one-stop shop’.”

AI’s growth made that worse.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC) had warned Health New Zealand about a digital rollout of health portals in Northland.

“It needs to engage directly with the community and ensure that the proper foundations are in place ... co-design with Māori would be particularly beneficial”.

The hackers compromised over 400,000 HNZ documents and over 22,000 uploaded by patients. About 90% of patients were from Northland.

Webster already found Health NZ and Manage My Health had failed to have enough security controls and ordered compliance by next year with privacy rules.

He said on Friday that the breach had significantly damaged trust in health portals, which were a small but vital part of the modern health information environment.

Health NZ responded that: “The Phase Two report does not identify any new privacy breaches by Health NZ and confirms we have met our legal obligations following the incident, including notifying the Privacy Commissioner and affected people.

“We are working with the Ministry of Health, primary care and wider sector partners to strengthen privacy and security settings across the health system.”

Friday’s report makes 10 recommendations with a stress on the two entities engaging “face-to-face” with Northland communities.

In July, HNZ said in an action plan in response to the OPC that it would roll out a digital solution for Northland next year and might extend that nationwide.

It was told in today’s report to get the 2027 rollout right – such as by ensuring accounts are created and activated securely, and expressly include Māori data governance considerations.

A flaw allowed some Northland hospital information to be saved into accounts patients never activated. The flaw was corrected in January 2026.

Health NZ said in a statement it would strengthen protections to ensure security of patient information in Northland and elsewhere.

“People can be confident they will receive care in our hospitals and clinics across Northland.”

The hospital flaw was not the only gap.

The report said: “It has been apparent from the start of this inquiry that large numbers of patients were unaware that they had an MMH account at all, or that MMH still maintained an account for them despite the fact the patient had moved practices or their practice had ceased to use MMH.

“They were therefore taken entirely by surprise to find that they were affected by the breach.”

A privately owned patient portal, Manage My Health still had a 24-month dormant account process for patients who were registered with active practices, which was too long.

“We consider that MMH retains contact and other details in non-activated accounts for too long.”

After three months, it should be deleted, the report recommended.

It noted there had been no readily accessible information for representatives of people who have died about how to find out about and manage their accounts. There was more information now but Webster told the company to do full user testing with patients and doctors.

Webster said other organisations must learn from the crisis to have a plan ready to go in a cyber attack.

“It’s going to be a lot more stressful for your customers and your staff if you have to create your crisis management playbook as you respond.”

Otara street fight killer Tailasa Pongia bailed after home invasion hours before fatal stabbing

New Zealand Herald October 29, 2026

Just hours before teenager Tailasa Pongia stabbed a man to death during a fight in South Auckland, he was involved in a terrifying “home invasion” in Palmerston North.

Yesterday Pongia was jailed for 18 years after he admitted murdering 19-year-old Greig Temarama-Abela on August 1 last year.

He avoided a life sentence due, in part, to his age, “impulsivity” and prospect of rehabilitation.

READ MORE: Street fight killer escapes life sentence

And the court heard that at the time of the murder, while Pongia had “helped another or others commit a burglary” the day before - he had “no other criminal record”.

The Herald can now reveal that on July 31, Pongia, then 19, and others stormed onto a property where a man was spending the evening with his wife, daughter and baby granddaughter.

Pongia was arrested and released on bail early on August 1.

He travelled back to Auckland and shortly before midnight on the same day, murdered 19-year-old Greig Kelvin Temarama-Abela.

Police are satisfied they handled Pongia’s earlier arrest properly.

The victim of the home invasion disagrees.

He cannot understand why Pongia was released so quickly and believes the fatal offending that followed could have been prevented.

He spoke to the Herald about his ordeal, and shared the footage of the offenders converging on his family home, captured on security cameras.

The footage clearly shows the offenders passing a weapon to each other - which looks to be a bat.

However police confirmed Pongia was charged with wielding a knife.

In August Pongia, now 20, pleaded guilty to murdering Temarama-Abela.

He also admitted a charge of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm in relation to another man he stabbed during the same fight.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Court documents released to the Herald this year outline how Pongia had been drinking with four friends at a Bairds Rd home in Ōtara just before midnight on August 1 last year when three young men - including Temarama-Abela and the other victim - showed up on foot at the front fence.

The visitors, who had also been drinking in a home about a kilometre away, had an “unresolved dispute” with one of Pongia’s friends.

“A verbal exchange ensued, which escalated into shouting profanities and physical challenges,” the police summary of facts said.

“The confrontation spilled outwards onto Bairds Road, where more members of the defendant’s group joined in. A widespread physical altercation broke out, with members of both groups throwing punches and fighting.

“At an unknown point, Mr Pongia armed himself with a knife.”

Temarama-Abela turned away from Pongia, who stabbed him in the upper back.

The 8.5cm deep wound entered through Temarama-Abela’s ribs and cut a small internal artery, resulting in a fatal haemorrhage, a pathologist would later determine.

A half-centimetre incision was also found on his upper arm.

The other victim witnessed the stabbing and punched Pongia, causing him to drop to his knees.

He managed to stand up and adopted a boxing stance, then lunged forwards and stabbed the man in the abdomen.

“The fighting continued intermittently, and both groups moved towards the intersection of Bairds Road and Wymondley Road,” court documents state.

“However, the fighting eventually petered off, and the groups began to disperse.

“By this point, Mr Temarama-Abela sat down at the intersection of Wymondley Road and Laxon Avenue. He quickly lost consciousness.”

He was pronounced dead a short time later at Middlemore Hospital.

Pongia initially told police he had been asleep and knew nothing of the confrontation.

Soon after Pongia was arrested for murder, the victim in Palmerston North contacted the Herald to share his story.

The victim, who did not want his name published to protect his family, was at home with his wife, daughter and 7-month-old granddaughter when the terrifying ordeal happened.

The man has a criminal history but has not had any convictions since 2013.

He said all hell broke loose just after an old friend came to visit.

The victim suspects that friend may have some kind of connection to Pongia and or his co-offenders.

However the victim said he did not know, or have any connection to any of the men who converged on his family home that night.

“They came straight in, they tried to get through my gate and I closed it thinking ‘what the f***’s going on here?’ One of them had a weapon in his hand, like a baseball bat and he jumped straight over the fence and I gapped it,” he said.

“I made it inside and my wife was standing there holding the baby … I grabbed the door handle, and they were trying to rip the door handle open.

“It all happened so fast … They ran off because my dog started barking - one of them started shouting ‘pitbull, pitbull’ and they took off.”

The victim said the men also attacked his mate on the street.

The assault was also caught on camera but no one was charged with anything related to the assault.

The victim’s wife called 111 and set off the panic alarm in the house.

He said while she was on the phone several of the group came back “for a second run” at his home.

They managed to get the gate open … they came to the house and started smashing windows.”

The victim gave a full statement to police and sent CCTV footage to assist the investigation.

He later found out that just two of the group were arrested.

Soon after, they were released and “told to go back to Auckland”.

“They f***ing jumped my fence, and they tried to kick their way in my house and threaten not only me but my partner and my daughter and my granddaughter… and they got bailed?” the victim said, shocked.

“The police f***ing let them go and he committed a more serious crime hours later. Can you just imagine the family of that young man who was stabbed? They’ve lost their son, they’re going to read this and they’re gonna go ’what the f**k?’”

“Their boy could be with them today … the only reason why I’m pushing this story is because I feel for that family … it’s f***ed up, it’s not good.”

Police stood by their decision to release Pongia on bail.

Central District crime manager Detective Inspector Craig Sheridan confirmed Pongia was later convicted of “burglary and unlawful possession of a knife and sentenced”.

The other offender admitted charges of “unlawfully entering an enclosed yard” and was discharged without conviction.

Sheridan said at the time of the arrest, the offenders “did not meet the threshold to be remanded in custody” and were released.

“He had appropriate and enforceable bail conditions, which included being forbidden from entering Palmerston North, and to reside at an Auckland address.

“Police conduct rigorous risk assessments at the time of any arrest, and this individual’s initial offence did not meet the strict legal threshold under the Bail Act 2000 to hold him in custody.

“Police understand that the outcome of the Palmerston North investigation was not what the victim of that incident and their family were hoping for; however, the file was reviewed at the time, and I am satisfied that police exhausted all possible lines of inquiry.”

The victim is considering a complaint to the Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA).

“It’s just the slackness … it’s f***ed up, it’s not good,” he said.

“I mean, if I jump a fence and I go into a property and I start lurking around with a bat and a black hood on … smashing windows, I’m going to jail …”

Opportunity’s big backer, AJ Wilderland, on the party’s coalition negotiation strategy and why working with the left could be easier

New Zealand Herald October 29, 2026

Opportunity donor AJ Wilderland (left) with fellow Serato co-founder Steve West.

AJ Wilderland says he isn’t interested in politics. Yet the co-founder of Serato, a $175 million DJ software company, has bankrolled Opportunity and helped shape its strategy, as the party hopes to become kingmaker after the election.

The Herald spoke to Wilderland about how Opportunity could negotiate with multiple parties at once, why he believes the left might be easier to work with than the right and what Opportunity would do without a big donor.

“I’m not interested in politics.”

Wilderland’s introductory comment echoed that of Opportunity founder Gareth Morgan, who nearly a decade ago unsuccessfully ran for Parliament in a bid to reform the tax system.

Wilderland, who owns about a quarter of Serato’s shares and sits on its board, has no appetite for becoming a politician. But he feels “morally obligated” to contribute to Opportunity.

He believes it hits the “sweet spot” in terms of being socially and environmentally responsible, business-focused and set on using simple rules and markets to achieve its goals.

Wilderland started volunteering for Opportunity shortly before joining its board in 2025 and ramping up his donations in 2026.

Since 2024, he has donated more than $280,000, either personally or via one of his companies.

His support accounted for 28% of the donations Opportunity received last year and half of the $20,000-plus donations it has received so far this year (the value of all its 2026 donations will only be reported next year).

Wilderland has also helped the party with governance, strategy and marketing. Policymaking is left to a team with a “high level of autonomy” and “domain expertise”.

“I have always been really interested in how you get better results when you set the right incentives, create the right systems, and you make the right thing to do, the easy thing to do,” Wilderland said.

He explained his involvement in policymaking was limited to marketing.

“One of the problems that Opportunity had in the past is feeling a little bit inaccessible, more like a bunch of policy wonks who know better than everybody else. We really wanted to change that perception.”

MORE: Serato sale gets Canadian remix as Tiny takes majority control in $175m deal

He conceded that before backing Opportunity, he voted for the Greens – a party he believed appealed to a relatively small activist constituency. When Wilderland was younger, he was an Act supporter.

Asked whether he preferred Opportunity forming a Government with Labour or National, he questioned why it mattered what he thought.

However, Wilderland said working with the left might be easier, as the likes of Labour and the Greens want many of the same outcomes as Opportunity.

The parties differ when it comes to the best way to get there.

For example, they all want to broaden the tax base. But in Wilderland’s view, implementing a land tax is administratively easier than applying a capital gains or wealth tax.

While he believes Opportunity and Act see eye-to-eye in terms of valuing markets and pragmatism, he disagrees with who benefits most from Act’s policies.

As for New Zealand First, Wilderland reckons its rhetoric about race and its approach to good faith negotiations would make it the hardest party to work with.

Wilderland said Opportunity’s approach to working with the right would be to push the other parties to be more socially and environmentally responsible.

While he sees the left being more like-minded, he conceded, “I have never spent any time in politics, inside of a party, and I don’t know how complicated it is to get the left to agree to do things differently. So I could be completely wrong”.

Wilderland is unsure whether he would be involved in negotiations if Opportunity reaches the 5% threshold required to get into Parliament.

While leader Qiulae Wong has said Opportunity would talk to the party with the most support first, he cautioned that didn’t mean Opportunity would be “forced to do anything with that party”.

“It just means that as a courtesy we would talk to them first, and there are other options.”

Wilderland said Opportunity could also talk to different parties at once.

“I don’t want to come across as an authority on what’s going to happen in a negotiation, but my understanding is that there are no rules.”

Wilderland sees Opportunity negotiating from a strong starting point because it isn’t set on being in government.

“We’re not so desperate to be in government that we would accept things that were against our values … That’s why I am happy to put such a healthy chunk of money into promoting this party,” Wilderland said, talking up his confidence in the integrity of the party’s leadership.

He assured Opportunity’s pitch to couple a land tax with a universal basic income remains in its DNA, even though it isn’t one of its bottom lines.

He said the party was realistic about what it could get across the line, recognising it was perhaps being “too honest” about what it could achieve with the support it was getting.

“If we got 15% of the vote on polling day, well, that’s a whole different story, isn’t it?”

Asked about the risk of him pulling the pin on Opportunity, Wilderland said he would only walk if the party strayed from its “stated values and goals”.

Ironically, one of Opportunity’s bottom lines is to introduce a “cap on donations per donor”.

While Opportunity has kept the wording of its bottom lines broad, its policy is to cap donations at $30,000 per party, per donor, per election and ban donations from companies and trusts.

“I feel like what I’ve done this campaign is kind of a one-off injection that helps get Opportunity a seat at the table,” Wilderland said.

“And then our track record that we start to produce, and our reliability and what we actually bring to the table, will be what gets us the votes in the future.”

Jenée Tibshraeny is the Herald’s Wellington business editor, based in the Parliamentary Press Gallery. She specialises in government and Reserve Bank policymaking, economics and banking.

The suspected Chinese spy who sparked panic at the White House

Sydney Morning Herald October 30, 2026

American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence.

A top executive at a Singapore-based data centre company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China. And now US officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funnelling information to Beijing.

But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO.

For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in AI. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Jensen Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution as well as an influential ally of President Donald Trump, set off alarms at the White House.

Roughly a year ago, Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.

This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts.

US officials already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced AI chips.

But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Jensen Huang had insights into Trump’s thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge AI models.

Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services, people briefed on the surveillance said.

The surveillance of Alice Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia said the company that employed her, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Nvidia is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” Rizzo said. Customers like Megaspeed, he added, “receive ordinary business information — not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”

The White House, the CIA and the National Security Agency all declined to comment. In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said its “current leadership” takes the matter “extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations.” It added that “outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the US government that we are fully committed to cooperating.”

Alice Huang did not respond to requests for comment. It is not clear how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed. A person familiar with Megaspeed’s operations said she had become less active in the company in the wake of the US investigations.

Asked about the American conclusion that Alice Huang has been collecting intelligence on behalf of Beijing, Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said the United States was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China.

When Trump was initially briefed on the intelligence last year, US officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Alice Huang was gathering information for the Chinese. It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment, but some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Jensen Huang could have remained unaware of what they had concluded was her intelligence-gathering role for China.

Questions about whether Megaspeed was providing AI chips to China became public through articles published last year by the Times and Bloomberg News.

Senior business columnist

Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the administration during Trump’s second term to loosen regulations on AI companies and roll back tighter restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China. He also negotiated a deal with Trump that allowed the US government to take a 25 per cent stake of certain Nvidia chips that the government allows to be sold to China.

The close relationship between the president and Jensen Huang has impeded efforts to clamp down on Nvidia’s chip sales abroad, current and former US officials said. They described some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia as having ground to a halt within the Commerce Department, the agency in charge of regulating chip exports.

Nvidia has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China. Rizzo said China’s government has “blocked US AI chips, protecting its own industry.”

Many questions about the situation remain unanswered, at least publicly.

It is unclear whether concerns about protecting the surveillance played a role in the decision not to inform Jensen Huang. Telling him could have alerted Alice Huang that she was being watched, which is a common reason intelligence officials hesitate to give defensive briefings.

It could not be determined which intelligence agency or agencies have been involved in monitoring Alice Huang, or what prompted them to start. It is also not clear under what circumstances she began gathering information for Beijing, what information she passed along or its value to China.

The previous reporting about Alice Huang by the Times described her meteoric and somewhat mysterious rise. A Chinese businessperson and investor, she eventually became a top official with Megaspeed, which the Commerce Department, toward the end of the Biden administration, began to suspect was helping China evade US prohibitions and gain access to the computing power of Nvidia chips.

The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there.

Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Alice Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her.

The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed over this year to the Justice Department, administration officials said.

Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centres and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. It has bought Nvidia chips from the American arm of Inspur, a Chinese server maker. The US has blacklisted Inspur’s parent company for funnelling technology to the Chinese military, though the US firm remains free of sanctions.

Megaspeed has then provided that computing power to Alibaba and other Chinese companies. US officials believe the firm is one piece of a sprawling international effort by Chinese companies to access the chips needed to build and run AI. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China.

Megaspeed’s sister company in Malaysia bought at least $US4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records obtained from ImportGenius, a trade platform. It was an exceptional amount of money for a small, obscure company.

Nvidia and Megaspeed have continued to do business this year. The limited data available for most of this year shows that Megaspeed and its affiliates kept buying Nvidia products, often through intermediaries.

To prevent chips from being smuggled to China, Nvidia evaluates buyers before approving a chip purchase and sometimes checks later whether the buyer still has the chips. The company continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. Megaspeed advertised the relationship as recently as this month. In a job ad, Megaspeed’s Indonesian branch called itself “a premier business partner of Nvidia.”

Megaspeed has continued serving its primary client, Alibaba, according to that person and other tech industry analysts.

In June 2024, just weeks before Megaspeed began its purchases, photos posted to LinkedIn showed Jensen Huang alongside Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan, following a local technology trade show. They drank whiskey with other AI executives.

One year later, in May 2025, they were seen together again, leaving a restaurant in Taipei after a business dinner with other AI suppliers. She waited behind Jensen Huang as he spoke to Taiwanese journalists outside the restaurant.

Those details were described in a Times article last October. But the deeper intelligence involving Alice Huang remained closely held inside the administration.

People with knowledge of the matter said US agencies had been conducting electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. That surveillance showed that she was in contact with an American citizen.

US intelligence agencies generally cannot legally surveil American citizens without a court order. But when communications involving Americans turn up in surveillance, citizens can be identified to government agencies who can show a need for the information through a process known as unmasking. In this case, the unmasking process identified Jensen Huang as the US citizen.

Before 2025, Huang seldom visited Washington and stayed out of politics.

But as the Trump administration was considering a ban on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Huang and his wife travelled to Mar-a-Lago, the president’s private club and residence in Florida, to meet with Trump at a high-end donors’ dinner and sell him on the idea of allowing chip companies to do business with Beijing.

At the event, according to people briefed on the discussion there, the Nvidia executive appeared to wow the president with his descriptions of his own rise.

Nvidia later donated at least $US20 million to Trump’s ballroom fund, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The company also pledged to invest $US500 billion on manufacturing in the United States.

And when Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited the White House for a state dinner last month, Huang was at the head table.

Last year, Trump approved the sale of an older generation of Nvidia chips to China in return for a cut of the revenue. As the president sought warmer ties with China before his meeting with Xi, he entertained a push by Huang to sell the Chinese even more powerful technology, rankling some administration officials and Republicans in Congress, before ultimately deciding against it.

People who have watched the two men interact say Trump has been won over by the lavish praise Huang has given the president in public, and his immense wealth and success.

It is not clear when Jensen Huang and Alice Huang of Megaspeed first met. Before the Times reported last year on her role in purchasing Nvidia chips, she posted photos of herself with Jensen Huang on her social media feed, according to a person who viewed it.

Alice Huang has a slim profile on the Chinese internet. She has described herself as Megaspeed’s CEO, and the company listed her as its managing director for its first eight months before removing her from that role in its corporate paperwork. Megaspeed’s current director is from Singapore but has recently lived in Shanghai, according to business records and his social media accounts.

According to information posted online by a Chinese investment fund where Alice Huang worked, she was formerly employed in China as a TV reporter, but the Times could not find any information to verify that. She later worked at several major Chinese banks, then joined a Shanghai-based fund, Hexi Capital, which has invested in a variety of semiconductor- and AI-related firms, according to WireScreen, a data platform.

According to tech investors familiar with the company, Huang and her associates bragged about her connections to Jensen Huang and used it to raise funds and promote their fast-expanding network of businesses, which has invested alongside the Chinese government in data centres around China. In Southeast Asia, Megaspeed has continued to pitch new data centres, hire employees and trumpet its close connections to Nvidia, according to industry analysts, online job posts and other records.

Megaspeed is pushing ahead with construction of a large data centre in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new AI facilities have risen between palm oil plantations. In a stock filing last month, a Malaysian property developer said it had received the final payment for the 53-acre plot where a Megaspeed subsidiary has promised to build the data centre.

When a Times journalist visited recently, rows of construction materials sat between the skeletal frames of partially built data centres. Outside the park, backhoe loaders dug into the reddish brown earth as workers installed concrete pipes.

The company had already secured the chips necessary for the build out, according to a person with knowledge of the plans.

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Patrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 20:54:36 GMT

Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’

Patrick Stewart dies aged 86 – latest updates

Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, has died. He was 86.

The Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men star died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, said Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, to the Hollywood Reporter.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” she wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

With his authoritative baritone voice and commanding visage, Stewart was already a staple of the British stage by the late 1980s when, at 47, he was cast as a graying Capt Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: the Next Generation, the first live-action spin-off of the groundbreaking 1960s TV series. Over seven seasons aboard the Starship Enterprise, Stewart’s even-keeled performance and steely directives – “engage!” and “make it so” – turned him into a global star.

Stewart reprised his role in four feature film spin-offs – Star Trek Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002) – as well as the TV series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 until 2023.

Fellow Star Trek actor William Shatner paid tribute on social media today. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did,” he wrote. “Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original series, also wrote about Stewart on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity,” he posted. “Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”

His other most well-known role was playing Prof Charles Xavier in the X-Men series. The actor had found work hard to obtain after feeling typecast as a result of his Star Trek role but had been intrigued by working with director Bryan Singer for 2000’s X-Men.

He went on to play the role in seven films and will be seen reprising the role in this December’s Avengers: Doomsday.

Marvel chief Kevin Feige has paid tribute in a statement calling him “brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas”. He added: “Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”

His other film roles included gay comedy Jeffrey, romantic thriller Conspiracy Theory, violent horror Green Room and voice roles in Ted, Gnomeo & Juliet and, most recently, The Sheep Detectives.

Born on 13 July 1940 in the small industrial village of Mirfield, England, Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to Alfred Stewart, a British military veteran turned semiskilled laborer, and Gladys Stewart, a weaver at a textile factory. His childhood, in a small house with no running hot water, was marred by alcoholism and domestic violence, a situation he later described, in an article for the Guardian from 2009, as “barely tolerable”.

He found respite in acting, first in school – he was 12 when an English teacher assigned him the part of Shylock in Shakespeare’s the Merchant of Venice – and then local drama groups. “I managed to find my own refuge in acting,” he wrote. “The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home – it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time.”

After graduating from secondary school at 15, he worked as a local reporter and furniture salesman before a local arts council provided the funding to attend the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theater School, where he enrolled in 1957, at 17. Having shed his Yorkshire accent, he took his first professional theater role two years later, and in 1966 joined the Royal Shakespeare Company. During his 16 years with the company, Stewart developed a reputation as one of the finest thespians of his era and a representative of Shakespeare to new audiences; it was while conducting master classes on Shakespeare in LA, at the invitation of a friend, that he first caught the eye of a TV casting director for Star Trek.

Stewart made his Broadway debut in 1971 in Peter Brook’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and appeared again 20 years later in a solo production of A Christmas Carol. The holiday season show, which he revived in 1992, 1994 and 2001, received a Drama Desk award.

Over the course of his career, Stewart embodied many of Shakespeare’s signature roles, including Macbeth, Othello, Prospero, Shylock and Mark Antony. He was the recipient of two Laurence Olivier awards – in 1979, for Antony and Cleopatra, and in 2009 for Hamlet – as well as a Grammy in 1996 for a spoken word children’s album Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf. He was also nominated for a Tony and four Emmys.

His final major stage role was in 2016, when he appeared as Hirst in Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land at London’s Wyndham Theatre. In 2023, he released his memoir called Making It So.

Stewart was a vocal fan of Huddersfield Town FC since he was a child and was seen cheering them on most recently in 2024. In a Facebook post from the official team, he was called “a titan of his craft and a legend and hero to millions worldwide”.

Stewart was married three times: to theater choreographer Sheila Falconer, from 1966 until 1990 and with whom he had two children, fellow actors Daniel and Sophie; to Star Trek producer Wendy Neuss from 2000 until 2003; and to jazz musician Sunny Ozell from 2013 until his death. His friend and occasional collaborator Ian McKellan, with whom Stewart starred in two Broadway productions with in 2013, officiated his final wedding after a rehearsal.

“I think I’ve been in denial about my life for a very long time,” he said to the Guardian in a 2023 interview. “I never really took on board how successful I had become. Even today I sometimes think, ‘You’re a lucky son of a bitch, Patrick,’ when something unexpected or good happens to me.”

Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost despite warnings of public finance shortfall

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 20:02:16 GMT

Experts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisions

John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.

Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking big tax and spending decisions.

In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.

Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts.

“Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face, “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”.

The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”

He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”

However, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”

Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms, on disability benefits.

Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.

The Office for Budget Responsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.

With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be for an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.

But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market than the prime minister. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.”

Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to reenter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”

The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.

The Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.

Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.

“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”

Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.

The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.”

As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.

The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.

Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.
