Visit Norway makes shithouses ‘great again’ after Trump insult

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:22:01 GMT

Tourist board responds with toilet humour after US president’s ‘shithouse country’ jibe over failure to win Nobel peace prize

Some might find it decidedly incommodious to be dumped on by Donald Trump as a “shithouse country”. Not the Norwegian tourist board, which chose instead to lift the lid on some of the nation’s loveliest lavatories.

“Are these the world’s best shit houses?” asked Visit Norway on its website, days after the US president vented his fury once more over failing to win the Nobel peace prize by describing Norway as a “shithouse country” at a rally on Sunday.

“Norway makes shit houses great again!” the agency continued above pictures of some of the country’s most striking public conveniences, adding: “These toilets are worth a visit, both when you really have to go – and when you don’t.”

Trump delivered his tirade at a rally in Michigan days before the US midterm elections. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” he declared, using a term he has previously applied to Haiti, ​Libya, Somalia and Yemen.

He added that he would welcome migrants from some countries but not Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize”. Earlier this month, Trump denounced the decision to award the prize to Navi Pillay, a former ⁠international criminal court judge.

“This is an indelible stain on the ‌country ⁠of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” he said. “I never heard of this person. The ⁠Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited … And we will ​not forget, Norway.”

Along 18 designated scenic routes around Norway, Visit Norway said, leading architects had been tasked with transforming the humble wayside privy into an attraction in its own right. Several have since won international architecture awards.

The agency pictured a series of designer public conveniences, many of them architecturally striking and all offering breathtaking vistas overlooking fjords, beside rushing rivers and foaming waterfalls, and at stunning scenic viewpoints.

They “invite you to take your time and enjoy the scenery, even if you don’t have any business to take care of”, Visit Norway said, highlighting – among others – the restrooms at the Stegastein viewpoint in the Sognefjord region of western Norway.

This particular comfort station, the tourist board noted with uninhibited pride, had been ranked among the 10 best public toilets in the world by DesignCurial, the online architecture, design and interiors magazine.

Combining clean, minimalist lines with the fjord’s rugged and brooding landscape, the loos are famous for their large, black-tinted glass windows, which allow visitors a sweeping view from the throne while remaining invisible from the outside.

It also highlighted the unique, wave-shaped Ureddplassen loo on the wild coast of Helgeland, the southernmost district of northern Norway, hailed by several international publications as the most scenic restroom in the world.

Also featured are the solar-powered modernist bog at the Utsikten viewpoint, the “Instagram-worthy” Tungeneset loo (“looks pretty good underneath the northern lights”), and the world-famous triangular “golden toilet” on Senja island.

Jens Kjeldsen, a rhetoric professor at the University of Bergen, said that under the circumstances, Visit Norway’s response was well judged. “It’s like the bully in kindergarten,” he told NRK public television. “If you get too serious, the bully wins.”

Evgenia Egorova, a senior consultant at Visit Norway, told the broadcaster the response to its social media fightback had been immense. “The world needs a little laugh,” she said. “We thought: let’s meet them with kindness, and a little humour.”

Visit Norway said it had more stylish loos in the pipeline, including a forest-inspired latrine using dried wood from more than 60 trees. “Get ready for the pit stop of your life,” it urged, before signing off with a cheery: “Toodeloo!”

The Nobel peace prize is famously not awarded by the nation or even the government of Norway, but by the Nobel prize committee, which operates independently – something Trump “knows very well”, the foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering.”

Meta discussed ‘whisper strategy’ against social media critic Jonathan Haidt, files show

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 17:20:57 GMT

Court documents reveal staff considered ways to ‘get academic community to disavow’ influential US author

Meta staff discussed deploying a “whisper strategy” to undermine the influential US academic whose work has inspired a global social media crackdown, according to court documents.

Employees at the parent group of Facebook and Instagram sought to discredit Jonathan Haidt, the social psychologist and author of The Anxious Generation, a book that helped tip the debate about online safety towards more stringent measures such as the under-16 ban in Australia.

Minutes of internal meetings contained in a recent legal filing in the US showed that staff discussed how to “get the academic community to disavow Haidt”.

They appear in a document titled “Well-being Meeting Sound-check Notes”, which refers to discussions of how Meta could “turn other academics against Haidt” and to a “whisper strategy” aimed at achieving that goal. It also mentions “debunking” his work.

Minutes from a meeting on 8 March 2023 mention “Curtiss”, an apparent reference to Meta’s then vice-president of research, Curtiss Cobb. It states: “Curtiss’s goal for this work: how do we get the academic community to disavow Haidt. Can’t co-opt them, so how do we enrage them … so the media finds him not credible.”

It then adds: “Not thinking about this as a loud strategy. A below-the-line campaign.”

It suggests getting someone called “Gellman” to write “a takedown piece”. The “Gellman” figure is not identified in the document but Andrew Gelman, a professor of statistics and political science at Columbia University who has been critical of Haidt’s work, wrote in a blogpost this week that he was “never hired by Facebook to do a hit job on Jonathan Haidt”.

Gelman said he had received money from Mark Zuckerberg’s company in the past on a “no-strings” basis but had never been asked by Meta to look at social media’s impact on teenagers’ health.

Haidt’s book The Anxious Generation argued that widespread use of smartphones has caused a mental health crisis for young people.

The academic has become a persuasive advocate for strict regulation of digital media and devices, including bans on social media for under-16s and on smartphones in schools. Early this year the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, asked Haidt to address officials on a possible social media ban for under-16s in the UK.

The minutes were produced before Haidt published his book in 2024 and discuss responding to a Substack post written by the academic in which he reviews “a bunch of articles”. It is not clear whether Meta acted on the ideas outlined in the minutes.

Duckett and Dawson steer England to victory over Sri Lanka in tri-series farewell

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:46:52 GMT

Duckett hits superb 167 as England make 386 in Lahore

Dawson takes four wickets to deny Sri Lankan chase

Not this time. Sri Lanka threatened a repeat of Rawalpindi, and a target of 387 in Lahore was within reach. Pavan Rathnayake was the thorn again with another century but, unlike his captain Harry Brook’s last week, Ben Duckett’s epic was not in vain. The left-hander struck 167 before Liam Dawson took four wickets, setting up a consolation 55-run victory for England.

Sri Lanka had already booked their place in Saturday’s tri-series final against Pakistan but looked ready to take this dead rubber, too. With 87 runs required from the last 10 overs, and Rathnayake’s low hands working their magic, the game looked theirs.

But England’s attack kept calm and Dawson, back for his final over, nabbed Rathnayake for 118 as the last five wickets fell in a rush. The win rounded off a bizarre tour for England who lost two seemingly unloseable games. Here, they were grateful for their left-arm spinner’s steel in another run-fest. Four for 49 in a 700-plus game is a special return.

“I wasn’t getting nervy,” said Brook. “We had a clear plan and a lot of clarity at the top of the mark with the bowlers. The lads have learned a hell of a lot from that game we played a couple of days ago. To finish the game off like we did there was an exceptional effort.”

Duckett was the leading man in the first half. He struggled in the 430 game, way off his best with a scratchy 29 while everyone else teed off. Move forward a week and he has two more ODI tons, 105 in the low-scorer against Pakistan followed by a career-best. With Tom Banton punching his way to his fifth 50-plus score in six innings, the first-wicket stand was worth 163 from 25 overs. England now have a healthy problem: where does Jacob Bethell, back next month in Australia, fit into the picture? Banton taking the gloves could be an option if England want to keep this opening partnership intact, with Bethell going to the middle order.

Banton will undoubtedly be peeved that he failed to turn three half-centuries in the series into at least one helmet-raising moment. He fell for 74 when his footwork went missing, dragging a Dasun Shanaka delivery on to the stumps. But Duckett, in love with Lahore, was on for the big one. He reached his third ODI hundred on this ground off 89 deliveries, and the southpaw swung freely from there, his next 50 taking only 29 balls. Middling his pull shots, Duckett eventually tired, though only after he had gone past his 165 against Australia at this venue last year.

Brook promoted himself to No 3 as England pushed towards another gargantuan total, but an errant scoop limited him to 44. Will Jacks, Jordan Cox and Sam Curran kept England moving at pace but Brook’s dismissal still felt significant, the moment that eliminated the chance of another 400. Asitha Fernando, armed with his tailing yorker, helped limit the damage with figures of two for 63, but England still made their way to the highest-ever ODI total at the Gaddafi Stadium. Joe Root was not even required.

Sri Lanka had no reason to be daunted, even with an early dismissal: Sonny Baker dropped Avishka Fernando at deep fine leg but went through Kamindu Mendis not long after. Kusal Mendis’s bat split in half early on when facing Gus Atkinson, but the replacement blade worked just fine.

England looked short with the ball having left out Adil Rashid once again, and Henry Crocombe was barely called upon in his second ODI. At 177 for two off 26 overs, Sri Lanka were more than well-placed on a dewy pitch.

Middlemarch review – World’s Greatest Novel hurtles from costume drama to jolting marital tragedy

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:40:40 GMT

Swan theatre, Stratford-Upon-AvonThis RSC staging of the sprawling middle England masterpiece has humour, compassion – and even George Eliot herself as a character

Is there a literary achievement greater than George Eliot’s stonking masterpiece? Not according to a Guardian poll, topped by this sprawling, contemplative and profound book about marriage, moral goodness, debt, death, God and everything in between. So how do you adapt its nonpareil greatness for the stage without flattening the moral, philosophical and psychological complexities?

Andrew Davies had a go at it with his watchable enough 1994 television costume drama, retelling Eliot’s story about provincial life, in six parts. A mere six-parts, you might say, for a novel that is about 900 pages. While its timeline only spans three years in the life of a fictional Midlands town, it juggles multiple storylines and perspectives, weaves the local with the big socio-political backdrops of its age and follows the trajectories of characters with such detail that it becomes hard to replicate in another form.

Now the Royal Shakespeare Company has had a go at a stage adaptation, divided into two parts and totalling almost six hours of viewing (including the intervals). Again, you might say, a mere six hours, particularly in relation to the compressions of Part One. Jeremy Herrin’s production at first seems to sacrifice character study and emotional connection for plot and pace, although it hits all the beats of a pleasing costume drama, is easy on the eye, full of incident and with an understated visual beauty that suits the town of Middlemarch perfectly. Grace Smart’s supple set design contains ecclesiastical touches in the vaulted ceiling and back window, alluding to Eliot’s exploration of divinity. The stage is often lit by candles, perhaps to gesture at Eliot’s famed passage about the candle and pier-glass, which is quoted at the outset of the show. But there is so much incident to get through that you do not get much more than momentary philosophical reflection or inner outpourings before the next flick of the proverbial page.

Like the book, the beginning focuses on the marriage of the young, devout Dorothea (Nia Towle), who sees wedlock as a means of higher learning, but does not quite make you feel enough. Her failed suitor, Sir James Chettam (Gunnar Cauthery), remains featureless, as does her sister, Celia (Lizzie Annis; why is she dressed in the same shockingly unfashionable frock throughout?). Outsider-artist Will Ladislaw (Rory Alexander), meanwhile, is barely there, appearing in brief spotlight as little more than a motif. Beyond the parish of Lowick, the drama of the Vincy family ticks over: Fred’s (Ebenezer Gyau) feckless ways with money, his tenderness for Mary Garth (also Annis), along with the budding romance between Rosamond (Emma McDonald) and the town’s ambitious new doctor, Tertius Lydgate (Andrew Richardson). It is Dorothea’s scholarly and sour husband, Casaubon (Ian Drysdale), who serves as the highlight in Part One, happy to marry a much younger woman but disdainful in the face of marital intimacy.

Eliot’s book has sometimes been seen as a satire of middle England, and Nina Raine’s script leans into humour, tipping into a bumptious broadness, which verges on pantomime entertainment in scenes featuring Peter Featherstone (Peter Forbes) on his deathbed, his hands gripped around his money box. He is played like a provincial Scrooge, his greedy family comprising a tableaux of other Dickensian types around him in the inheritance wrangles.

Raine treads a fine line between faithfulness and invention, keeping many of Eliot’s lines but turning the omniscient narrator into a character (Amanda Root). It becomes clear that this is Eliot herself, not only watching over her story but listening to characters divulge anxieties or yearning, and sometimes interrupting them, mid-scene. It is a very inventive way to get around delivering a backstory without clumsy exposition, but it feels too much like a device.

The author Tom McCarthy recently argued that Middlemarch has been middlebrowed and “heritage-industried to death,” in a podcast for London Review of Books, and this production runs the risk of doing the same by the end of this first half. But then the heavens open and it seems, for a book so preoccupied with divinity, that Eliot herself has descended to touch it with her greatness. Part Two finds its footing and doesn’t take one wrong step: the humour working brilliantly in occasional flecks, the drama leading with emotion, thought and the everyday tragedy of marital disappointment. The piano music, by Nathan Feeney, which sounded so mannered, now seems emotionally integrated. Characters come fiercely, painfully, to life. Dorothea, now a widow, carries great depths. The marriage between debt-worn Lydgate and his starkly withdrawn wife, Rosamond, is heartbreaking. Take away the 19th-century costumes and their marital friction would feel utterly contemporary. Each scene shakes you, each performer excels.

The interaction between these characters and the narrator takes on a lovely, tender texture, too. She challenges or soothes them in their worst moments, like a mother would. Eliot’s narration excels in its sustained compassion for the most fallen of characters and Raine’s script does the same. You feel for Casaubon with his writerly paralysis over his unwritten magnum opus, The Key to All Mythologies (the narrator, Eliot, voices her own sympathies), and you even feel for the rapacious Nicholas Bulstrode (John Hodgkinson), for his inability to do good.

Marriage is a “noose,” warns Dorothea’s uncle at the start, but there is a return to the “marriage plot” in Eliot’s work, however much she is said to have upturned it. The romance between Ladislaw and Dorothea is heady, intense and also – to invoke the words of Virginia Woolf – very “grownup”. You want happiness for them, for her. You believe in this second go at it.

At Swan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 16 January

The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that is

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:11:11 GMT

John Healey aced the morning-after media round because his Martin Lewis measures left nothing to challenge him on

Maybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When clued-up journalists and economists have had a chance to go through all the fine points the chancellor would rather everyone had missed. The forecasts that suggest everything is predicated on a wing and a prayer. The hidden unfunded tax cuts. The greater-than-expected spending commitments.

But on Thursday morning Andy Burnham and John Healey could afford themselves a sigh of relief. All had gone about as well as they could have hoped. It turns out that when you don’t make any massive tax or spending commitments, there isn’t a great deal to unravel. All there had been was a raft of small-scale interventions designed to help people with their personal finances. Call it the Martin Lewis budget. In fact, Healey and Lewis now seem unable to get through the day without spending some time with each other. They certainly can’t stop talking about one another. It’s becoming unhealthily co-dependent. The gods of small things.

It had been billed as the “breathing space” budget. A budget to help get everyone through the coming year more or less alive. No hiding under tables or breaking open the emergency supplies of baked beans. Apocalypse averted. But the breathing space might just as well have been for the government. Difficult decisions delayed. Hope that we all wake up in 52 weeks’ time and the world looks like a less frightening place. And even if it doesn’t, it will always have had a year’s grace. A chance for the Tories and Reform to implode. You can always hope.

Come the traditional morning-after interview with the chancellor on the Today programme, the presenter Nick Robinson seemed uncharacteristically subdued. Normally he’s a terrier on occasions like these. There’s never been a budget that Nick wouldn’t have been able to do far better himself. But this one? This one was something you might find on the consumer affairs programme, You and Yours. And the BBC was in the process of axing that.

So the 20 minutes passed with little fuss. More a softball back and forth. Healey started with his usual infectious brand of pessimism. He was born to be the bearer of bad news. The poster boy for assisted dying. Everything was absolutely terrible. He wasn’t quite sure why anyone was still bothering with anything. If it had been up to him he would have ended the interview before it had started. There was nothing to say. Other than that, given the chance, he wouldn’t have started from here. Brexit, the pandemic, Ukraine, Iran, energy prices. The world was screwed. Britain was screwed. Lie back and prepare for the worst 10 years of your already miserable life.

Nick tried to find a reason to believe. Couldn’t the chancellor have made just a little more effort? Having a plan to have a plan wasn’t the usual budget fare. Healey, AKA Dr Death, shrugged. It was one up on having a plan to not have a plan. By now Robbo was audibly struggling. How could he put it politely? In the third year of a government with a 160-seat majority, surely Healey could have been a little more ambitious. This wasn’t exactly the big transformation that had been promised.

Could he even say if he would bring down the benefits bill? Apparently he could. “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Dr Death. Cue panic stations in the Treasury. Within seconds of Healey opening his mouth, dozens of government spinners were on the phones to every journalist to tell them they hadn’t heard what they had just heard. There had been collective false consciousness. When Healey had said that he would be bringing down a benefits bill that everyone agreed was too high and that the country could not afford, what he had really meant to say was that he would not be bringing down the benefits bill that he had no idea how to pay for. Fag packets gratefully received. That was about as close to news as we got.

Maybe it was just that while Healey was having one of his better days, Robinson was having one of his worse ones. Because he had also sounded uninterested in his interview with Andrew Griffith an hour earlier. An exercise in box-ticking rather than revelation because the shadow chancellor never has anything useful to add on the day after. Sure enough, Griffith insisted that he would have done everything differently while never going into the details of how. At which point, Robbo opened half an eye and observed that if it was really that easy, how come the Tories hadn’t fixed it when in office?

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

Indeed, Nick continued, it could be argued that Labour had been left to clear up the mess the Tories created. “I’ve never shied away from saying that the Tories have a chequered record,” Griffith said defensively. Er, I’m not sure that’s entirely true, Andrew. Your usual line is that history started in 2024 and that everything is the Labour government’s fault.

That just left time for Robinson to remind the shadow chancellor that he had been part of the Treasury team that had defended the Liz Truss mini-budget even as it was being shredded. “I will never publish plans without saying where the money is coming from,” said Griffith, before announcing £30bn of planned tax cuts without specifying which benefits he would cut to pay for them. Fair to say, he’s not a man who seems to learn from experience. Once in the Truss image, always in the Truss image.

The final piece of the Thursday jigsaw was the verdict from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. In the past this has been enough to completely destroy the reputation of some chancellors. I could never look at George Osborne in quite the same way after the IFS had rubbished one of his budgets. It’s one thing to be thought of as an economic quarter-wit. What’s really devastating is to have it proved.

Helen Miller, the IFS director, looked a bit knackered. She and her team had been up most of the night, going through both the budget and the OBR figures line by line, searching for the fatal flaw. And she was gutted to announce that there actually wasn’t one. There was as little in the budget as had first appeared. She announced that she was grumpy about some measures. Disappointed in others. Another was cack-handed. The tax system had been made more complicated, not less. Yet, all in all, these were minor gripes.

“This chancellor is hoping that things get better without actually needing to do anything,” Miller said in conclusion. I don’t think that’s right. Healey never travels in hope. Like the rest of us, he’s pretty confident everything is going to be worse in a year’s time. But he had got himself some breathing space.

Puddlesuits, movie nights and daytime baths: how to survive rainy days with small kids

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:00:46 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Wet weather dampening your plans? From screen-free stories and craft kits to waterproof gear, here’s how to keep little ones – and grownups – entertained

The best gifts for kids by age

Before becoming a mum, I never appreciated quite how complicated getting out the front door would be with kids in tow. But in my four and a half years of parenting two small people, I can confidently say it’s nothing compared with the challenge of a day spent inside when outside is off-limits. Whether because of endless rain or illnesses you don’t want to pass on, I panic at the thought of filling the hours spent indoors.

Being outside is profoundly helpful for my mental health, and it comes with its own built-in entertainment for small children: a bus ride becomes a sensory experience, a trip to the doctor’s an opportunity to pick up role-play ideas.

But what to do when leaving the house really isn’t possible? Over the years, I have developed a list of ideas for keeping my children (and me) sane indoors, and the products that have helped us muddle through (and dare I say, enjoy) those days. I’ve also recommended some gear to help you brave the wet weather.

How have you been keeping the kids – and yourself – entertained during the rainy days? Let us know by emailing us at thefilter@theguardian. com

An unexpectedly popular item in our house came from one of the kids’ many generous aunties and uncles: a play tent. My initial thoughts? “How big! How intrusive! How unnecessary!” How wrong I was.

Kids of all ages seem to gravitate towards it – perhaps owing to the illusion of privacy it offers (as well as being a very non-obvious place to scarper when playing hide-and-seek, wink wink). When ours was played with so much and broke beyond repair, I didn’t think twice about replacing it with this lovely, bright Djeco one. We chose it because of its colourful design, but I’d also seen one at a play cafe from the same brand and admired how sturdy it was. It’s a great place for us all to get cosy and read, and somewhere for my four-year-old to take a minute when his little brother is destroying his beautiful Magna-Tiles creations.

Djeco multicoloured play tent

Suitable for: 3+

That brings me nicely to Magna-Tiles. Parents seem to enjoy these almost as much as their kids do, and they’re popular with older children too. We don’t have it, but I just know this Rail Racers set would be an absolute hit in this house. There are imitation brands, but we invested in the official Magna-Tiles, which have lasted really well and endured being lobbed around by our toddler – who may or may not end up being a bowler in later life, given how much he likes to throw. Friends with cheaper knock-offs say you get what you pay for in this case.

Magna-Tiles Rail Racers set

Suitable for: 3+

Look, I don’t really understand why, but my children were given this car toy by another auntie for Christmas last year, and every single child who has crossed the threshold of our house since then, big and small, has been obsessed with it. Not only does it play really earwormy songs, which they love, but it has a roller beneath a screen that shows a road unfolding in front of you as you “drive” with the steering wheel. You can also just push it around like any other toy car. So many friends have gone on to buy one too, but sorry in advance for the noise of the songs and for the fact it is, essentially, a big lump of plastic.

Steering wheel car toy

Suitable for: 3+

Our kids have a higgledy-piggledy medley of millions of different craft bits and pieces that their mother has bought for herself, used once and discarded. A visit to a craft shop such as Hobbycraft is probably the cheapest option for this, but there are a few nice premade kits out there too, like the Djeco one below. Another wildly popular craft activity in our house – also from a clever auntie – is this foil sticker set from Galt. It’s easy to use with minimal mess, so it ticks all my boxes.

Djeco animal houses craft pack

Suitable for: 3+

Galt foil set

Suitable for: 6+

Before I became a mum, I used to say I would be vigilant in rotating toys to maintain interest (putting some into storage and bringing others out from time to time), then I actually became a mum and, well, that never happened. But then I discovered Lovevery.

At first, I was a bit confused about why our kids might need new toys every few months, but after a few boxes, the value became evident. Those who sign up get a new set of toys (often sustainably made) every two to three months that are focused at their current age. It’s not cheap, but we’ve bought one or two boxes over the years or asked family to (as well as being sent some samples as press gifts in the past). There are favourites in every kit that have been thrown into the routine toy circulation, and saving them for a time stuck indoors has been a total salvation when I’m low on ideas.

The toys are good quality, often wooden, and a one-off box makes a great present for grandparents to give when they’re looking for new ideas. The newborn Looker play kit is especially valuable, chiefly owing to the wooden mobile I hung above the changing table, which helped entertain them while I was committing the grave offence of cleaning their bottoms.

The Looker play kit

Suitable for: 0+

When our eldest was given one of these as a toddler, I struggled to see the value. But then came baby number two: a future rock-climbing tornado who makes it his business to scale any piece of furniture that crosses his path. Pikler triangles can be added to with other products to make little indoor climbing frames, and ours has a slide, which our toddler spends his life climbing up and throwing himself down, especially on days when the park is off limits.

TP Toys climbing triangle

Suitable for: 1+

We have a wide array of Ravensburger puzzles, gifted by a very keen nanna. The brand makes a wide range of puzzles for different ages, so it’s worth investing in a couple. Hits in our house include the Hey Duggee one for younger kids and the current obsession: Spidey & His Amazing Friends (Ghost Spider specifically – IYKYK).

Hey Duggee puzzle

Suitable for: 2+

Spidey & His Amazing Friends puzzle

Suitable for: 3+

No imagination-based toy has been more used in our house than this ice-cream shop, made mostly of wood, by American brand Melissa & Doug. My friend’s children, seven and nine, still won’t part with theirs, which in my book is the sign of a good toy.

Melissa & Doug Scoop and Serve ice-cream counter

Suitable for: 3+

I have seen these Speed Track car-racing tracks pop up in living rooms and birthday parties, with little kids, teenagers and even adults getting in on the action. It works with most small car toys you probably already own, and it’s easy to roll up and put away.

Speed Track, 4 metres (without cars)

Suitable for: 3+

A relatively new phenomenon, “play sofas” (modular sofas that can be rearranged to spark kids’ imagination) are fast becoming a go-to for parents of active children. Ours is from the Irish brand Baby Elegance, and has become a castle, a train, a spaceship, a cave, a house, a shop and many other things, all in the first few months. It has a foam core covered in hard-wearing corduroy fabric and doubles as a very comfortable bed for fans of what I like to call lying-down parenting (favoured by those with early-rising offspring, who have difficulties sitting up or who may have just had one too many the night before).

Baby Elegance play sofa

Suitable for: 1+ (with adult supervision)

I first came across Stapelstein stepping stones at a local play cafe, and initially had no idea what the appeal was. Doubly so when I found out the price. Nonetheless, I have been blown away by just how many hours of fun my two have had playing with them, especially when friends come over. They’re made from high-density foamed plastic, making them lightweight and easy to pick up, but sturdy enough to support up to 180kg in weight, so they’re perfect for stacking, climbing on, using as hats or making seats from.

They are great for mobility and practising balance, and they spark my kids’ imagination like nothing else I’ve seen. Visiting older kids have been just as obsessed with these, suggesting it may be a toy for the long haul, too.

Stapelstein stepping stones

Suitable for: 1+ (with adult supervision)

The Yoto player is a screen-free audio player that’s a reliable all-rounder for both my kids. We listen to stories and songs, and grandparents and other relatives have recorded their own cards of them reading stories or singing for the kids to listen to. Cards can be targeted to a specific age, too. Our two-year-old loves the nursery rhymes and our four-year-old listens to stories, and both get a real kick out of “being in control” of the content, without realising that it’s actually their father and me who oversee it all. The smartphone app means we can stop and start playback from our phones, and we have recently discovered the software is available on Android Auto, meaning we can listen to our cards when in the car.

Yoto player

Suitable for: 3+

Bad weather always leaves me jealous of friends who have projectors ready to turn their living rooms into home cinemas. A friend recommended this Samsung one, and it’s on my “if we ever have spare money” list.

Samsung Freestyle 2

Friends with older kids rave about the Nintendo Switch their families got for Christmas. It can be played alone or as a family, with plenty of games for everyone. In their case, the console is kept in the living room, and children can swap TV time for console time on weekends. Mario Kart and Just Dance are good for getting the whole family together.

The Switch 2 is the latest, but the original Switch has a huge library of games and is now cheaper thanks to the arrival of its successor.

Nintendo Switch 2

Suitable for: 3+

Nintendo Switch (first generation)

Suitable for: 3+

I bought this fairly extensive colour palette of food dyes from Amazon, and the kids love being able to pick which shade they will play with that day. I use this recipe, but there are loads out there. One thing to be aware of is these playdoughs are more likely to stain than the shop-bought stuff, so are best limited to the kitchen.

When all else fails, I chuck my kids into the bath and let them have an extended play session they wouldn’t ordinarily have in the evening. If I’m feeling generous, I throw in a Munchkin ColourMix bath bomb, which my kids adore, even if the yellow shade does often make me think they may have had an accident.

I found a pile of costumes in my kids’ sizes on Vinted for days when we just need a little extra inspiration. I spent about £6 and got a huge range for whoever they feel like being on that particular day.

A timeless classic that is still a favourite for a reason. All you need is some chairs and bed sheets. For extra pizzazz, I sometimes add fairy lights, but this is not at all necessary.

We also often play the floor is lava (with the very annoying song you can find on Spotify), hide-and-seek or Bluey-style “keepy uppy” with a balloon and accompanying soundtrack music.

We live in the rainy south-west, so to have a fighting chance of leaving the house between November and April, good waterproofs for the kids are a must. For smaller ones, many friends have recommended these Muddy Puddles suits with a removable warm inner layer for adapting them to fluctuating temperatures.

For older kids, I love shell trousers because they really do keep kids dry. I am a huge Mini Rodini fan and, though they are expensive, their sizes span 1.5 to 2 years generally, so on average, can be worn for two winters. I also know many fans of Polarn O Pyret, which offers more reasonably priced options for toddlers through to 12-year-olds.

Muddy Puddles Scampsuit

Mini Rodini waterproof trousers

Polarn O Pyret shell trousers

A good pair of wellies is essential, and my kids have always liked their colour-changing ones from Grass & Air. Put their little tootsies in some merino wool socks like these from Polarn O Pyret and job’s a good’un.

One final tip I must add is not to buy fur-lined wellies. I know they look cute, but trust me, they get wet quickly, and then your kid is essentially walking around in soggy socks.

Grass & Air wellies

Merino wool socks

What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:00:46 GMT

Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers

On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen.

But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm.

“I think in a year, every company will have more AI co-workers than human co-workers,” he said.

In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol, showing that a company can do more with less, several startup employees said. It’s common for workers to brag about how well their agents can handle common office drudgery like answering emails or help with essential business operations such as giving sales pitches.

But agents are also creating tension. They are alienating customers and colleagues who seek human interaction, eliminating roles and forcing employees to become overnight managers of the bots that often make mistakes.

While startup techies such as Amin are some of the early adopters, corporate America may not be far behind. About 40% of large organizations used AI agents in some capacity between May 2025 and June 2026, up from 27% the year before, according to McKinsey’s State of AI Global Survey. Companies also expect to scale back their workforce by 10% to 15% over the next few years as they delegate more work to AI, a recent report from Boston Consulting Group found. In the present moment, companies are not seeing major productivity gains from AI, MIT research shows.

A wave of startups and big tech companies are fueling the push toward AI agents, selling companies on automated co-workers.

There’s Viktor, a company that lets companies create their own “AI chief of staff”, and Lindy, which makes customizable agents for sales, customer support or admin work. OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Claude Cowork and Microsoft’s Scout can each integrate with thousands of other tools to handle projects after employees leave for the day.

Each of these products promises companies the tantalizing dream of cranking out new co-workers, who never clock out, complain or cause human resource problems. Delegating to an agent is also cheaper than hiring a human, making a large ratio of agents to humans a point of pride among startups.

“That’s the status symbol,” said Rafael López Muñoz, chief of staff at Wordware, a San Francisco-based startup that makes AI tools. Outsourcing parts of the job to agents is “an extreme time saver”.

Lindy, for example, used to have almost 50 employees. Now, after laying off one-third of its staff, the company says it has about 20 and has filled many of its open roles with AI agents instead. It’s still hiring people for some positions.

“People are constrained by having two hands and 24 hours in a day,” said Haneen Azhar, Lindy’s senior growth marketing manager. “Now, that constraint has gone away, because your one laptop screen can be divided into 16 different agents that are running in parallel. These tools make you feel so powerful.”

Azhar says she has outsourced a long list of tasks to agents, from managing her calendar to testing how well customers respond to different marketing taglines to generating brand images. She worries about her role in eliminating jobs as she offloads work to agents. Azhar says that Lindy’s agents now handle product announcements, social media posts and marketing videos, work that used to be handled by about 100 people in its creator program, for example.

She also worries about how the shift will affect the next generation of workers. “If I was trying to get my foot in the door right now, I’d be worse off than I was a year ago,” she said.

In some cases, agents have stepped in to cover for missing staff. Jay Blumenfield runs a production company in Los Angeles that creates vertical microdramas – short, scripted series meant to be viewed on your phone. The production schedules are tight, and so are budgets. So when he had to fire an assistant director on a recent shoot, he decided to try using an AI agent instead of hiring a replacement at the last minute.

Blumenfield uploaded the script and prompted the agent to do everything the assistant director would have done. The agent produced the schedule, call sheet and day’s script, and then sent the materials to the cast and crew. The result? Everyone got their work done.

“It would have been an unmitigated disaster, but this kind of saved us,” he said.

Now, Blumenfield and his partner, Tony Marsh, run the company alone with a suite of agents. “We don’t even have an assistant anymore,” he said.

AI agents handle everything from reading scripts, running social media and planning travel. He created an agent called Shirley to act as his chief of staff, and another that scouts and books locations needed for upcoming shoots. Normally, he would have to hire two to three people to work on these tasks for two or three weeks, he said. Now, it happens within hours.

Still, it does feel a little taboo to use so many agents instead of hiring people, Blumenfield said. But the economics of filmmaking had changed enough that he felt he simply didn’t have a choice. By using agents, he can afford to make the microdramas that star actual people – at least, for now.

“The game in Hollywood is that you’re not allowed to talk about using AI,” he said, reflecting industry fears that it could end creative work. “I don’t want it to replace people. But we should be honest about how it is helping us.”

Several workers who regularly rely on agents are adamant that the tech can’t replace the human workforce entirely. But agents are changing the kinds of skills and workers needed to manage them. Agents can code, making routine programming skills less valuable, but they still require humans to prompt them thoughtfully and judge the results. They also require a fair amount of oversight.

López Muñoz said that after he let AI agents run his startup’s recruiting, he spent most of his time undoing agents’ mistakes, such as mixing up candidates with similar names or hallucinating parts of a résumé.

“The qualities we’re looking for are changing,” Azhar said about new hires, adding that he now prioritizes the ability to coordinate and delegate over years of experience.

Tarek Abillama, founder of River, which makes an AI agent for sales calls, said workers now are required to constantly check AI’s work and give it feedback.

“We all became managers,” Abillama said. “We have to be great at multitasking, because now you’re running six agents who are doing different tasks.” Abillama’s first agent, a clone of himself, gave sales demos of River’s product. Later, he replaced it with an agent called Liv, a female persona that researches customers and their companies, demos the product and handles the sale process in any language, at any time of day.

Even though River tells customers that Liv is an AI agent, Abillama said people seem to anthropomorphize the experience. He’s seen transcripts from calls with Liv where customers appear to flirt with it. Customers have also tried to push the agent to go off-script and get bigger discounts.

Founder Brooke Hopkins said while her San Francisco-based AI voice startup Coval uses agents to speed up tasks, she views the tech as tools, not colleagues. She’s also banned her company from using agents to communicate with customers, suggesting that it’s lazy and sends the wrong message.

“I can immediately look at an email and know whether or not it was written by AI,” she said. “If I get an email and it feels like a human, then I usually will read it.”

The loss of human interaction has become a point of tension, Hopkins said. Using an agent to handle a company’s sales demos or recruiting process might save time, but at what cost?

Duncan McClure, who evaluates AI models as a contractor, said he had recently been hounded with emails and phone calls from AI agents seeking to hire him.

“The message it sends is that we don’t care enough to actually put in any effort,” he said, adding that he was turned off from working with those employers. Recruiters may save hours by using agents, “but it’s my time that they’re wasting”.

Though AI can automate the time-consuming and costly parts of people’s jobs, that doesn’t always mean working less, several startup employees said. Amin, for example, said he gets more done with agents. Still, he hasn’t stopped working on weekends.

Finland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre site

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:51:45 GMT

Authorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment

‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre

Finnish ⁠police have launched a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of the country’s environmental ⁠laws ​at the site of a planned Google datacentre in rural northern Finland.

Authorities allege that Tuike Finland, a Google subsidiary, cleared and drained 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest at the planned site in Muhos before environmental impact assessments required by Finnish law had been completed.

Like other Nordic countries, Finland is attractive to tech companies seeking to build datacentres because of its relative geopolitical stability and abundance of land, but also because its cool climate should allow them to cut energy costs.

“Based on preliminary information, there have been ambiguities and ‌shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the construction site of Tuike Finland ​Oy’s datacentre project,” Finnish police said in a statement on Thursday.

“The criminal investigation will examine, among other things, circumstances related to these issues,” they added.

Finnish authorities are considering applications for a total of 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, including a €13bn (£11bn) artificial intelligence infrastructure project by Google that the US company has called its largest ‌investment in Europe.

Earlier this month Finnish authorities ordered Google to suspend work at two sites – Muhos and Otanmäki, about 100km to the south-east – after the company failed to complete environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land.

The Supervisory ⁠Agency, which oversees environmental permits and assessments, told Google to halt “preparatory ​measures altering the environment”. Campaigners estimate 250,000 trees have been felled at Muhos and 150,000 at Otanmäki.

Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings, but argued that the company had acted according to “the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.

The Finnish government has encouraged the projects. In September, when Google’s plans were announced, the prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and the deal would “deliver lasting benefits”.

But the revelations over Google’s alleged misconduct have sparked a national debate over what datacentre deals mean for communities, the environment and energy prices. The issue could impact parliamentary elections due in April.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and compensation for environmental damage. Experts say datacentres bring a limited number of local jobs, and benefits on a national level are minimal.

“Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” said Jussi Kangasharju, professor of computer science at University of Helsinki. “They are international companies serving international customers. Datacentres ultimately have little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”

Carrick keeps Fernandes as captain and says he needs no assurances on United future

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:50:16 GMT

Carrick says he is not surprised to still be head coach

He describes Fernandes as ‘important’ for the squad

Michael Carrick has said he will not strip Bruno Fernandes of the Manchester United captaincy after dropping him for the defeat by Bournemouth and that he is not surprised to have kept his job as the head coach.

Carrick and Fernandes held talks this week after the Portuguese criticised the tactics in the loss to Como, resulting in the midfielder being an unused substitute on Sunday. Harry Maguire took the armband but will not retain it for Saturday’s game at Chelsea, with Carrick saying “there is no decision to be made” and praising Fernandes.

“He’s an important player for this group,” he said. “He has been and he will be. Between us, we’ve got to make a difference and we’ve got to push things in a good direction. He’s fully committed to this football club, he’s fully committed to making things better. It doesn’t change for me. He’s the one that’s kind of led the team so well for many a game and many a year, and he’ll continue to do that.”

Carrick’s future remains unclear but he has been given a chance to turn around United’s form. The hierarchy held talks over whether to stick with Carrick at the start of the week after eight games without a win, including a wait of more than two months for a Premier League victory. There is keen interest in Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann as potential replacements.

“I don’t need any assurances from anyone,” Carrick said. “I totally get the position, I understand the job, I understand the responsibilities, I understand what comes with that.”

Asked whether he was surprised still to be in charge, Carrick said: “No, I am here to do my job. I am here to do the best for the team, and I am desperate to make us better and improve things, so I’m not surprised, no.”

The United supporters cheered Carrick off after the Bournemouth game, turning their anger on the players, who were booed at Old Trafford. “I care about what the supporters think,” Carrick said. “I care about what it feels like in the stadium, and them travelling for games, to come and see us and support us.

“I care about what we give them, and what we offer them, and what they see. I genuinely don’t take any notice of anything else. I know this job, I know what it brings, I know what we need to do really to be better. I don’t need anyone else to tell me anything else.”

How did the Spain train crash happen and what will investigators be asking?

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:39:16 GMT

Audio file appears to point finger at control centre, but there are questions around signalling and technical issues

At least 69 people died when a high-speed train from Madrid to Seville hit another train on the same track from behind near Toledo on Wednesday morning.

Both trains had been brought to a halt earlier when the signalling system failed. The driver of the state-owned Spanish train, a Renfe AVE service, was told by controllers to restart the journey, but crashed into the train in front, run by the private operator Iryo. The front carriages of the AVE train and rear of the Iryo train were destroyed and others derailed.

The nature of this disaster, as well as its human toll, seems particularly shocking. There are multiple safeguards on high-speed lines, including different types of automatic train operation, which should ensure trains are never able to come close on the same track.

The audio file released to Spanish media by the government appears to point the finger at the control centre, with a controller in Madrid telling the driver of the halted AVE train to proceed “con marcha normal” – under normal operations – rather than at low speed. The instruction was described by the transport minister, Óscar Puente, as an “inexplicable decision”.

Rear-end collisions are rare, as are any kind of crash between trains on international high-speed networks. The closest comparator occurred in China in 2011, when a high-speed train hit a stationary express in front of it in Wenzhou, killing 40 people. The rear-end collision between two East Midlands trains in Bedford this year was the first fatal crash of that kind in 40 years in the UK, and occurred on a stretch of railway without automatic train operation, after the driver apparently failed to slow despite the danger signal.

While the audio appears to indicate human error played a central role, there are other elements that remain unclear, such as what caused the initial failure of the signalling system. The German-designed train control system is being phased out and the CEO of Iryo recently told a senate inquiry that disconnection was a “frequent issue” on the line. Investigators will be looking at the sequence of events and technical issues that allowed the Renfe train to proceed but the Iryo train to stay put.

Signallers, or track controllers, are increasingly based in remote computer centres but are acutely aware of the risk and responsibility their job entails. Any investigation will want to establish what circumstances or pressures could have led to that instruction.

In all modern hi-tech transport, whether air or rail, known safety risks are eradicated as far as possible. Accident investigations typically yield rare, if not unprecedented, combinations of technical failure and human error.

The Spanish government will want to demonstrate that this latest disaster is completely unconnected to the head-on crash between two trains that occurred on the same line in Adamuz in January after one derailed, apparently due to a small section of faulty or missing rail.

Train drivers were due to strike, even before this week’s crash, in protest against under-investment in the railway and its people, which unions say is directly connected to safety.

The success of Spain’s high-speed railway, linking Madrid to Seville and Barcelona, was the envy of British rail planners. It was modern and had cut journeys from the capital to Andalusia to two and a half hours; a car takes twice that, and the public transport alternative of the coach, three times as long. Good public transportation links bring jobs and growth; losing them could mean the opposite.

The long-term trend since 2010 has been fewer fatalities of any sort on the railway. Most years, in most countries, no passenger is killed in any type of train crash, a world away from the death toll on the roads. However, worries about under-investment in the railways, particularly after costs and subsidy soared as fare revenue dried up in the pandemic, are not unique to Spain.

The tabloids that used Thomas Markle to attack Meghan should now reflect. I bet they won’t

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:06:57 GMT

The Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday plundered Meghan’s estranged father for clicks. But soul searching or remorse would be institutionally impossible

As the allegations mount against Thomas Markle Sr, his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, has released a statement describing her deep distress, and saying her priority is the protection of children. Is this the point at which Thomas Markle will cease to be an acceptable source for the Sussex character attacks that have become a tabloid staple? The Daily Mail and its sister paper, the Mail on Sunday, have been utterly brazen in their cultivation of the embittered Thomas Snr, using him as a weapon against his daughter since she first married into the royal family. Now, they’ll cut loose from him and describe the charges laid against him with the same outrage as everyone else. It would be institutionally impossible for them to discuss or reflect on their prior relationship with Markle without admitting a long-range and vindictive grudge against his daughter.

Markle denies all allegations against him. His son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr, described in a video for the Sun the material he claims to have found on his father’s spare mobile phone, after Markle Sr had gone back to the US to have his leg amputated. Markle Jr was in the Philippines, where both men had moved in 2025. He said the material included “the most horrific video of a very young Asian girl … couldn’t have been more than 10 years old”. He almost threw up; he almost dropped the phone. His immediate fear was for what else he might be inadvertently in possession of. “I’m on the hook for this, now,” he said.

As he made contact with the FBI, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and the Pennsylvania state police, he reportedly found more and more material: “the most obscene, disgusting, lowest-of-the-low images … thousands and thousands of them.” He said he started to question every aspect of his family history, all the times his father had hastily snapped shut his laptop, “all the locked rooms in all the houses we’ve ever lived in”.

Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. In 2019, she was passed a letter alleging that he had sexually abused a child, which she says had been sent to the Metropolitan police. The Met took no action on that letter and it has been reported that they subsequently misplaced it – whether that’s because they could believe no ill of Thomas Markle, or simply because they lose things, is unknown.

But until now, the Daily Mail and the Mail on Sunday’s trust in Markle Sr and solidarity with him have been without question.

In 2018, he handed the Mail on Sunday a five-page letter that his daughter had written to him after her wedding, which he had declined to attend, citing health reasons. Meghan successfully sued Associated Newspapers for printing part of the letter, though “printing” doesn’t really encompass the torrent of coverage and insinuation they wrung from its contents. It was the start of a relationship between the newspaper and the now alleged sex offender that was so close by last year that when Thomas Markle learned about his amputation, the first person he told was Caroline Graham, the Mail on Sunday’s US editor (and previously a biographer of Queen Camilla). In photos of the pair together, the emotions are almost laughably legible: Markle looks pugnacious and triumphant, like the guy who’s managed to get public opinion on speed dial. Graham looks serene and also victorious, the first reporter on to Goose Green in the tabloids’ favourite war.

A free press is essential and sometimes it is scabrous. But is this what a free press is for? To groom an estranged parent or other former intimate of someone in public life in order to undermine the latter person’s credibility and standing, seems sadistic. That’s a large word, particularly in the context of the allegations against Thomas Markle, and I use it advisedly. One of the hideous things about family estrangement is the feeling that everyone involved has had their character besmirched. The accused fight back with counter-claims. Nobody’s probity survives unscathed (although most of us could tell that Meghan’s father was exploiting her lovelessly for attention, and probably cash, long before these charges surfaced).

A political or media enemy plundering that dynamic for an easy win, for clicks, for a vendetta, does not even have the fog of emotionality as a defence. Everybody recoils from it. When the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy, made an attack ad featuring his opponent’s mother calling her daughter, Amy Acton, a liar, most people didn’t know the history. They didn’t know that Donna Arthur had lost custody of her children decades previously, after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted on charges of child rape. People could nevertheless see how low it was to air a view that was poisonous by definition under the fig leaf of hearing from both sides.

Ramaswamy lost a major endorsement and had venue cancellations within a day of that attack ad. What the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday would have to lose to even reflect on their allegiances in this episode is impossible to guess.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

The low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lie

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:01:44 GMT

Milwaukee’s first World Series championship is a rebuke to baseball’s oligarch class, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fiction

For the entirety of the 2026 baseball season, the overlords of the game have stood on the single position that what has now happened could not happen, and the result was a year that has been treated like an appetizer for the main course of the offseason: the shutting down of the game until the players, after 40 years of resistance, finally agree to a salary cap. The insistence that the game had been predetermined undermined the Milwaukee Brewers, who spent 149 days this season atop the standings.

Baseball dismissed Milwaukee’s 22-0 demolition of Seattle on 18 August, the 20-0 waxing of Cincinnati a month later, and the comprehensive dusting of their division – their fourth consecutive National League Central title and fifth in six years – by 14 games. Baseball’s owners, at their persuasive best, would have their paying customers believe that the Brewers’ franchise-record 103 regular-season wins also were an illusion, or worse, the dreaded outlier, even though Milwaukee have won 770 games since 2018, the fourth-most in all of baseball. Even when Milwaukee exhaled and made the Dodgers look old in a stirring four-game sweep, ESPN’s Jeff Passan reported the owners’ position remained unchanged.

The Brewers to that point had not helped dispel the notion. They had sputtered badly in recent postseasons, giving life to the thought that maybe their summer wins really were empty. Only one thing could ever change that perception: winning in the playoffs.

Schedule

Best-of-seven series. Milwaukee won, 4-1.

Fri 23 Oct Game 1: Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 Oct Game 2: Milwaukee 5, Tampa Bay 4Mon 26 Oct Game 3: Milwaukee 10, Tampa Bay 1Tue 27 Oct Game 4: Tampa Bay 4, Milwaukee 3 (12 innings)Wed 28 Oct Game 5: Milwaukee 4, Tampa Bay 1

How to watch

In the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.

Surrounded by so many friends that a Wednesday evening at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg felt like a home game – the good folks of Milwaukee and points beyond will remember the date specifically as 28 October 2026 – the Brewers rejected the notion they could not win both because of the economic forces against them and the intangibles champions possess but seemed to go missing from their group when the clocks fall back. They did so by winning the World Series for the first time in their 58-year history, and doing so resoundingly, destroying the Tampa Bay Rays in five games.

The final score was 4-1, ending a month that will be played and replayed in the minds and DVRs of Milwaukeeans. Few teams have ever been better. Few moments have exposed the hypocrisy of baseball’s oligarchs. Few teams so emphatically demanded so much of themselves.

What had been accepted as fact has always been decidedly fiction – but fiction can live as truth until it is exposed, killed once and for all on the ballfield. No matter the argument to concede the season to the inevitability of money and not having it, the truth is the Brewers have been an elite team for the better part of the decade, and the signature joy of this World Series run has been the joyous, ruthless attention this team paid to the task of not merely believing they were championship level, but proving it, to every team that opposed them this season, but more thrillingly, to themselves.

Nothing else mattered but emerging from this month as champions – not the payroll or the labor battles that will almost certainly shut the game down over the coming weeks and quite likely wipe out spring training and at least a portion of the 2027 season and the Brewers’ title defense, or the mystique and riches of the two-time defending champion Dodgers; not the twin histories of having never won the whole thing since that long-ago day near the end of spring training in 1970 when the Seattle Pilots’ equipment truck loaded in Tempe, Arizona, but the team didn’t know where home would be as a court order determined if the truck was headed back to Seattle or to a new home in Milwaukee, or the Dodgers’ long record of torturing Milwaukee baseball. That torture dated back to losses to Brooklyn in 1956, Los Angeles in 1959 before the Braves left town for Atlanta, and to the recent postseason defeats to the Dodgers in 2018, 2020 and 2025, when the Brewers began their second decade in the National League by being as good as the franchise had been since the big American League years of Yount and Cooper, Molitor and Fingers, only to suffer the familiar NL fate of being good, but not good enough to beat the Dodgers when it counted.

The Brewers were nowhere men – only the World Series would heal the past wounds that have stayed with them, highlighted by last year’s humiliating four-game sweep in the NLCS by the Dodgers – and they played with a buoyant and calm desperation, a gorgeous certainty that could not last, but did. The Brewers won the requisite 11 games to claim the trophy and needed only 13 games to do it, but trailed in eight of them. Yet, as an example of their belief, none of their series this postseason was tied after two games. Both Brewers losses in these playoffs were by one run.

When they faltered, they did not panic as desperate teams too close to the prize do; they got tougher. Jake Bauers’ soul-snatching at-bats against the Dodgers offered a sign, the youthful charges of Series MVP catcher William Contreras, Jackson Chourio, and the too-young-to-care stardom of Cooper Pratt was another, coming back from down 4-0 against the Dodgers and Rays was still another, and the two-out, eight-run fifth in Game 3 seemed to end the Series – except that it didn’t. Most impressively, responding to losing Game 4 three outs from the title in the bottom of the 12th not with the doubts that create suspense and pave the way to epic collapse, but by returning the next night unfazed and champagne-ready, demanding they be taken not as a cute story but a hard-edged team ready, at long last, for its close-up.

Neither the doomsday rhetoric of an unnecessary work stoppage or the fearsome reputation of the former champions, nor the feisty underdog spirit of an admirable Tampa Bay could block the sunlight, too long in arriving, of this Brewers team. They played pure, determined baseball and responded to the insult – and it is an insult – that the decimal points on the balance sheet meant more than winning 103 games and 90-plus so many times before that, meant that once it was time to deal the cards they couldn’t win. The Brewers won 114 games in 2026, finished the regular season 15-3, and then went 11-2 in the playoffs for a grand total of 26-5 since 7 September.

Baseball’s finances need addressing, but they don’t require shuttering the place. Even with the game the owners are playing in their quest to increase franchise values, their words speak an untruth – Brewers owner Mark Attanasio purchased the team from Bud Selig in 2005 for $223m and the team that supposedly cannot win (but did) has a valuation by Forbes at $1.9bn. The game that matters, however, is the one on the field, the one that belongs to the players, and this October, there was absolutely nobody better.

Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America. He also writes on Substack

My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. What can I do?

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:00:47 GMT

A game is not a moral exemption to your usual self. Sometimes the best way to puncture ‘it’s just a game’ is to show people that you’re judging them in reality

Read more Leading questions

My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. No matter how high or low the stakes, she has to win. When she doesn’t, she becomes explosive with rage, and often upends the game, sweeps dice off the table, or storms off in a rage. She is otherwise a normal and lovely person, with whom I get on very well. Seeing this side of her makes me deeply uncomfortable and it feels really childish and inappropriate. Will she behave that way with me if I say or do something she doesn’t like?

I think in an effort to smooth the tension, my husband’s family always laughs and teases her about her reaction. It’s like her “special little characteristic” that everyone pretends to love. I wish there was a way to address it but everyone seems to just sweep it under the rug. My husband is aware of how I feel about this.

Recently, she’s started dating a new partner, who is absolutely lovely. When she has a big reaction after board games I can also sense him tensing up, so I know this is affecting more than just me. Ultimately, I’m worried for my sister-in-law that if she continues this behaviour, and the family continues to indulge it, she will suffer personal and professional consequences. I also don’t enjoy being around the dynamic, and think it is likely we’ll spend less time with her as a result. What can I do?

Eleanor says: I know someone who ended a relationship because their partner too gleefully teamed up with an ex to lie in a game of wink murder. I know someone who decided not to have kids with their then partner because, when he played with kids, he got a kick out of really scaring them. I know someone whose friendship never recovered after one shouted the c-word in a card game.

Often it’s in the fictional that we most see the real.

It’s not that the way you behave in a game is a straightforward guide to the kind of person you are. The whole reason games are fun is that that isn’t true. Games let you experiment with being a different kind of person; they let you explore different kinds of agency. They are fun and absorbing precisely because you focus on a single goal or way of reasoning. A game is a vacation from the rules and goals of normal life, and an excursion into new ones.

But games aren’t meant to be a moral exemption to your usual self. They’re meant to let you play with and develop your usual self by putting it in unusual circumstances. Treating games as a forum for exorcising the worst parts of yourself with the petulant excuse “it’s just a game” misunderstands the whole enterprise.

So what can you do about your sister in law doing exactly that?

You’re astute to notice that the family going along with it doesn’t help. And you’re astute to notice that their laughter might be a bid to make things less awkward – not a sign that they actually enjoy it. Like how we laugh after an off-colour comment, hoping to social magic it into counting as a joke. They might hope that if they applaud, make this “her thing”, that transforms her behaviour into a fun bit – not just an adult having a tantrum.

Their approach might make things less awkward, but it doesn’t give the disruptive person evidence of how disruptive they are. As always, the more you paper over the cracks someone’s created, the less you can be surprised when they don’t notice them.

Sometimes the best way to puncture “it’s just a game” is to show people that you’re judging them in reality.

You don’t have to say “don’t do that” or “why are you so mad” while they’re heated. (In fact, if it’s a real anger management thing, it’s better not to). You can just let your sincere attitude show in a moment they presumed would be structured by the fiction. A long look without a smile or a laugh. Silence. A hint of the ick it’s giving you in real life. In the same way that laughing along is a bid to turn a tantrum into a joke, reacting as you would in other circumstances can be a bid to separate her behaviour from the game.

Awkward, yes; socially costly, yes. But as with all things, if you want her to know you’d prefer she stopped this, you have to endure the discomfort of her learning how you feel.

The boyfriend who lied in wink murder, the man who scared the kids and the friend who shouted in the card game didn’t realise that the way they acted in games would affect how people saw them in real life until it was too late. A long look across the table now – or even a quiet word from a relative once she’s calmed down – is a much kinder way for her to find out.

My phone thinks my boyfriend is my ‘best friend’. It’s not alone

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:00:46 GMT

Being in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormal

My boyfriend and I invented a game on our recent trip to Italy. We called it “invisible gays”, which might have been an attempt at some kind of word play around “gays” and “gaze” – but I was on holiday and feeling lazy, so I didn’t push it.

The game began when one night he took me out to a little trattoria to celebrate my birthday. It was a warm night, and fairy lights were entangled in the fragrant blooming flowers over our heads, and we drank good wine and ate bowls of perfect pasta, and there was candlelight, and it was so romantic I wouldn’t have blinked if two dogs had started smooching over a strand of spaghetti. Che bello!

We were one of four tables, all couples of various ages looking at each other with disgusting wet amorous eyes. During the evening a man selling roses approached the other tables. One young guy even bought one, presenting the blossom with a flourish to his girlfriend, earning applause from other patrons and a round of toothy photos. Caught up in the moment, my partner pulled out his wallet to buy a rose for me too, despite my wildly insincere protestations – but the rose man didn’t even clock us as a couple and wandered off into the night.

I briefly wondered if it was because my outfit wasn’t chic enough for Rome. Then I realised we were the only couple who weren’t the societal default setting of a man and a woman, having instead made the dire mistake of being two beautiful men dining together. I wonder if he thought we were some kind of complicated interracial brothers?

This continued all around Italy, with more than seven episodes of being passed over at romantic tourist traps marked on our scorecard. When I organised a fancy dinner for my boyfriend’s birthday weeks later, one of the servers said I was a “good friend” for doing so.

I’m used to the way that being in a same-sex couple can make you hyper visible or put a homophobic spotlight on you, so that it feels like every time you kiss in public it’s like Frodo putting on the One Ring, drawing the attention of the Dark Lord and his screeching Nazgûl. I’m used to muttered comments from people you walk by on the streets when you’re holding hands, or of making out with a tall guy outside a bar after our first date only for a car full of men to stop and yell slurs at us. I’m used to holding the hand of a boyfriend as we were chased down the backstreets of Newtown late at night by three silent men.

I’ve also dated enough women to know that there’s a contrast – no woman I’ve ever dated has flinched away from a kiss on the cheek and whispered: “Maybe not in public.” I’ve had men I’ve dated comment on how “openly affectionate” I am, because I haven’t had to learn to self-censor my public love languages. Women I date usually just comment on how clean my legs are and how many Gilmore Girls references I make.

Obviously being hyper visible and therefore at risk of overt and violent homophobia is worse than not being able to buy an overpriced street flower. Over the past year in Australia, hate crimes against gay and bisexual men have been making headlines. As someone who has suffered a hate crime or two, I can confirm that dealing with this should be the authorities’ priority instead of cracking down on the rose men of Rome.

But with the 10-year anniversary of the marriage equality win coming up next year, it’s worth looking at all the ways being in a same-sex relationship can still make you weirdly invisible. It’s another argument for why Mardi Gras, pride flags and Idahobit days in schools are still so necessary – because, when love between queer people goes unseen, it makes it seem as though it isn’t “normal”. And when queer identity is treated as abnormal, it fertilises the ground necessary to justify violence against queer people.

We all know the little “collections” of photos and videos our smartphones occasionally create. This can be anything from “Your trip in Italy 2026” to “Furry pals throughout the years”. It’s been a source of constant amusement to me that it sorts all the photos of my boyfriend and me into a collection called “best friends”. These are photos of two men kissing and, without oversharing, sometimes photos of two men doing things even more intimate than kissing (kayaking).

It shows you that homosexual invisibility is so hardwired into aspects of society that a phone short-circuits and decides that two men in love are just good bros. I’ve never had any of the women I’ve dated put into a folder called “best friends”. In fact, none of the women who are my actual best friends have made it into those folders either. My dog does get filed there, which, when its alongside my boyfriend, feels a little like one of those slippery slope arguments made by the Australian Christian Lobby during the plebiscite.

It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough. Make up your mind!

Not only do I simply want to express my love for my boyfriend publicly and without risk of violence, and for it to be recognised for what it is; I also don’t want my sexuality to be the only thing that people notice me for. I want to be noticed for my abnormally good looks and sex appeal.

Patrick Lenton is a writer. His latest novel is In Spite of You
