How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budget

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:00:45 GMT

John Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customers

The last of five £20 notes disappears into the slot machine as The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony plays over the shop’s sound system.

That’s it, £100 gone in the space of about five minutes, swallowed up by one of the many “slot farms” that dominate the shopping streets of Peterborough.

All that’s left to show for it is a free KitKat, one of the incentives staff use to tempt customers into staying a little longer and losing a little more.

It’s lunchtime on a Thursday and dozens of glassy-eyed hopefuls are having the same experience, feeding in what little cash they have and cursing as it disappears.

The same pattern is repeated across the country. Gamblers in Great Britain lost £2.7bn on slot machines last year, nearly double the annual budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which oversees the sector.

In his inaugural budget this week, the chancellor, John Healey, took direct aim at slot machines by raising “machine games duty”, the tax levied on them, from 20% to 25%. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.

But what is the reality of Britain’s booming slot machine industry and why is it in the government’s crosshairs?

The most popular machines in the UK are so-called category B3 terminals. They allow you to stake £2 every 2.5 seconds for a jackpot of up to £500. A £2 maximum stake may not sound like a lot but losses can stack up quickly. In this test, £100 is gone in just five minutes.

That’s one reason why each machine earns £40,000 a year on average, more than the median pay of a British worker. Slot machines are found in bookmakers, casinos and bingo halls but the venues that really pack them are adult gaming centres (AGCs), sometimes known as slot farms.

They’re on pretty much every British high street, disproportionately in poorer areas. On some, such as this stretch in Peterborough, almost every shop is a bookmaker or an AGC.

By far the two biggest AGC operators are Admiral, which is owned by an Austrian billionaire, and Merkur, owned by a German billionaire. Both have targeted the UK for growth in recent years.

AGCs have their critics, including Andy Burnham, who has accused them of “targeting some of the most vulnerable in our communities”. Notable examples include when Merkur was fined £100,000 in 2025, after the Guardian revealed it had allowed an older woman with terminal cancer to rack up huge losses over two spells lasting 16 hours.

As well as the potential for rapid losses, the machines are associated with higher rates of problem gambling than products such as sports betting. Critics also point to practices apparently designed to keep punters playing and losing. For a start, the majority of venues are open 24 hours a day, while the Guardian has previously revealed that staff are paid bonuses linked to customers’ losses, undermining their incentive to intervene to prevent problem gambling.

Shops are increasingly offering a new breed of super slot machine, featuring a comfy armchair and a highly-immersive, 65-inch screen. Staff will offer drinks and snacks to keep punters playing, there are regular prize draws and “free spin” offers, and you can make cash withdrawals from your bank without leaving the shop.

Punters will sometimes play more than one machine simultaneously. Admiral has introduced a two-machine limit, which it says is designed to reduce harmful gambling.

Many are open under bingo licences, which may sound more benign to local authority planning committees. In practice, most have one bingo machine that is rarely used, if ever.

On a one-off basis, it’s possible to win up to £500. In tests across several AGC venues, the Guardian occasionally won some money, which will be donated to charity. But the machines have a fixed “return to player”, meaning that regular slot machine players will always lose. That’s why slots are a good target for a tax raid, and a valuable cash cow for companies, which like predictable sources of income. It’s also why gambling harm experts think they’re dangerous.

Bookmakers say it will cost them money, leading to shop closures. Entain, which owns Ladbrokes, expects a £25m hit. But shares in the three listed slot machine operators – Entain, the William Hill owner Evoke and the Grosvenor Casinos owner Rank Group – rose sharply after the budget. Relieved investors had feared Healey would opt for a 40% rate.

AGCs were singled out by the chancellor, who said they and vape shops would be excluded from business rates relief, costing them a combined £10m. But AGCs appear well-placed to thrive anyway because of their low overheads and 24-hour opening. For the slot farms, it’s business as usual.

Neither Admiral nor Merkur responded to a request for comment. Bacta, the slot machine trade body, said its members’ venues were “among the safest places to gamble, with experienced staff on hand to identify problems and provide support to customers”.

“Player protection is central to our approach, and machines in AGCs are designed with inbuilt tools to encourage safe play, facilitate self-exclusion and help prevent problem gambling,” it said.

“Games in these venues are low-stake – costing as little as 10p a spin – and these businesses have been a longstanding part of the high street for decades, providing low-stake entertainment, local jobs and a boost to local economies. AGCs tend to open on high streets where there is already footfall, alongside other hospitality and leisure venues, and where planning and licensing permissions allow.

“Our members operate within one of the most tightly regulated licensing regimes in the world. Venues are regularly inspected, must comply with strict conditions, and can have licences refused or revoked where licensing objectives are at risk.”

Russell Brand’s wife tells court he is ‘amazingly attentive husband’

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 13:12:36 GMT

Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand says couple previously split up over his promiscuity

Russell Brand’s wife has told a court that they previously split up over his promiscuity but that he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”.

Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand, 39, said they fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian found monogamy difficult.

“I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people,” she said.

Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Giving evidence at Southwark crown court on Wednesday, Laura told the court she met Brand at the Edinburgh festival in 2006 after his show Shame, which was “very, very, very funny”, “extremely entertaining” and sexually explicit.

She said they met in the foyer of the Assembly Rooms, where Brand complimented her friend, who had a boyfriend. Laura recalled: “And he said to me: ‘But tell me you don’t have a boyfriend,’ and I said: ‘No, I don’t.’”

Laura recalled that Brand contacted her the next day and they had oral sex. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked: “Did he want to have penetrative sex?” to which Laura replied: “I didn’t want to, but I don’t remember it even being a topic. I didn’t intend to and I don’t remember him asking.”

They began dating in September 2006 and Brand “absolutely” respected her wishes sexually, Laura said. Describing his treatment of her, she said: “Very caring, totally at my pace. I was not experienced, I had only had one partner before Russell and I felt entirely cared for, and looked after by Russell.”

But the court heard their relationship broke down over his cheating. Winter asked: “Did you become aware shortly thereafter that he was promiscuous and engaging in sexual activity with others?” Laura replied: “I was aware when I met him that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of that year that he was engaging with other women, yes.”

Laura said the couple split up in February 2007 because of his infidelity. “I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous. We talked about it. I did find that difficult,” she said.

Laura said she was “heartbroken” after the breakup but that the pair resumed contact as friends in summer 2007. She said she became friendly again with Brand when his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry ended, and that they restarted their relationship in 2015, married two years later, and now have three children together.

When asked if she was aware of Brand’s promiscuity during their time apart, Laura said: “I was very aware of it and I would read about it regularly in the papers and he also told me; we talked about it.”

Both the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, and the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, objected when Winter asked Laura what her view was “as to the truth” of the criminal allegations her husband faces.

“She’s not here as an expert witness,” the judge said.

Winter then asked Laura to describe Brand, to which she replied: “Russell, my husband, is caring, he’s kind, he’s a wonderful father to our children, he’s an amazingly attentive husband.

“He’s got an eye for detail I’ve never known before. The way he treats me is to really know me, I feel very seen by him, in a way I’ve never experienced before. I love him very much.”

She continued: “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage. It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest.”

In cross-examination, Karmy-Jones noted that Laura had been present throughout most of the trial and had taken notes. She also challenged Laura about how much contact she had had with Brand after their break up in 2007.

Laura said she had spoken to Brand after his marriage to Perry ended. “He called me after his marriage and gifted me meditation for me and my boyfriend at the time,” she said.

Brand nodded and smiled as Laura insisted that while they had not had a sexual relationship in the years before they got back together in 2015, they had spent time together by going to the theatre and watching TV box sets.

The prosecutor said that in 2017, shortly after the couple had their first child, Brand was a guest on the US talkshow, The Wendy Williams Show. She said the comedian had said of his relationship with Laura: “When we went out with each other we loved each other very much but I was in a phase where I thought the world was an amusement park made out of orgasms.”

Laura replied: “I’m not denying he said that. I probably didn’t watch it.”

Earlier, statements from two of Brand’s ex-girlfriends were read to the court, as they gave good accounts of his character. They also said he had cheated on them and they had supported him financially.

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

The trial continues.

England urged to hold nerve as Rugby League World Cup hopes hang by a thread

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 13:07:17 GMT

England need 68-point swing in final group games

McDermott: ‘It’s a difficult situation to negotiate’

The England head coach, Brian McDermott, has urged his side to keep their nerve as they attempt to hold up their end of the bargain on Friday and secure what would be a remarkable qualification for the semi-finals of the Rugby League World Cup.

Defeat by Tonga in their opening group game a fortnight ago appeared to all but consign England to an early exit, owing in no small part to a complex and shortened format, with the tournament reduced to 10 teams. However, the margin of their 82-0 win against France last Saturday means qualification is still possible, albeit unlikely.

They need to defeat Papua New Guinea in Wollongong and hope Tonga beat Samoa on Sunday, with a 68-point swing required in points difference between England and the Samoans. That essentially means McDermott’s side will once again have to pile on the points against a capable Kumuls side who will pose a sterner challenge than the French.

England Brimson; Young, Savala, Farnworth, Ashton; Williams, Smith; King, Litten, Thompson, Nsemba, Pearce-Paul, Knowles. Interchange Lewis, Walters, Havard, O’Neill, Eckersley, Watkins.

Papua New Guinea Laybutt; Derby, Feledy, Macdonald, Dotoi; Voro, Biondi-Odo; Kapinias, Horne, Moretti, Martin, Putt, Richard. Interchange Glare, Taulani, Mathias, Wabo, John, Tai.

McDermott described the circumstances and permutations as “remarkable” this week, knowing his side must win big to stand a chance of avoiding becoming the first England side in history to fail to reach the semi-finals of the tournament. But he warned his players not to be distracted by the unique task at hand and the need to score points.

“I don’t know how many coaches have been in this position before where they know they need to win by a big score,” he said. “It’s a difficult situation to negotiate because you don’t want to show any disrespect to the opposition. So to suggest we would want to score a lot of points, it sounds disrespectful.

“There’s a discipline in that we don’t start looking for things or searching for things outside of how we want to play. And that was a really impressive trick against France because we knew we had points in us and they weren’t coming for that first 20 minutes. We can’t get to the points first, we’ve got to get through the physicality.”

That patience will be key against a Papua New Guinea side who have a large contingent of England-based players. They were initially resolute against Samoa last week in Port Moresby, trailing 14-6 at half-time before imploding in the second half to lose 64-6. They, like England, need a huge victory to stand any chance of qualification.

But the spotlight is undoubtedly on England, who start as heavy favourites. In the pursuit of points, McDermott’s one significant team change has the Hull KR hooker Jez Litten starting in place of the reigning Man of Steel, Wigan’s Brad O’Neill, who drops down to the bench. Litten has provided a spark in both games so far and his dynamic attacking play will be key again.

“It’s more about the best fit for the gameplan,” McDermott said. “They all understand the concept of it being a squad effort. It’s not just a team effort. We’ve got a specific task against PNG and I think it’ll be a stiffer test than against France. And we find ourselves in a similar situation, because we don’t just need to beat them, we need to beat them convincingly.”

McDermott’s expansive style which produced points aplenty last week will be key again, as will the performances of Mikey Lewis and the captain, George Williams. Lewis will start from the bench and look to stretch a tiring Kumuls side, while Williams has drawn praise from McDermott for his displays so far.

Both possess the running threat that could unlock the requisite scoreline England need to at least ensure Sunday morning’s game between Tonga and Samoa has meaning.

“George was the guy who broke the game open for us last week against France,” McDermott said. “We faced a really determined France in that first 20 and George was the guy who ran.

“That’s why he’s in the team, he’s in the team because he’s the captain and because he’s a good player, but he’s also a runner. And he ran, and broke France’s defensive line down and opened it up for us a bit.”

Meanwhile the permutations for England’s women, who kick off earlier on Friday morning, are more straightforward. Beat Samoa, they and will be in the semi-finals – but defeat means they are going home. England’s wheelchair side begin the defence of their World Cup title against Wales in the early hours of Friday, with Tom Coyd’s side heavy favourites to go all the way once again.

Exploding heads, mutant aliens and bursting chests: horror’s greatest special effects – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 13:00:43 GMT

From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI style

Towards the end of the 20th century, when film-makers’ overreliance on CGI was increasingly making special effects less special, it took the old-school practical approach of Japanese film-maker Hideo Nakata to make one’s hair stand on end. Just when you think the cursed VHS tape has claimed its last victim, Sadako’s vengeful ghost emerges from the well, comes closer … and climbs out of the television screen.

The Swedish director Victor Sjöström makes extensive use of double exposure – all done in-camera because optical printing had yet to be developed – to depict Death’s soul-collecting carriage in this folk-horror classic. Sjöström also plays the dissolute antihero, condemned to be the spectral vehicle’s driver unless he can mend his ways.

Henrik Galeen’s expressionist variation on the Faust legend reunites the stars of The Cabinet of Dr Caligari: Conrad Veidt plays the student who makes a deal with the devil (Werner Krauss), who steals his reflection. This evil doppelganger runs amok until Veidt confronts it in a split-screen climax.

FW Murnau commandeers a variety of in-camera effects for this vampire masterpiece. Flipped negatives, sped-up action and stop-motion add to the unheimlich ambience until, exposed to the sun’s rays, cadaverous Count Orlok (Max Schreck) vanishes in a puff of smoke.

Raise a glass to Jim Krut, who died in August but who will forever be remembered as “Helicopter Zombie” in George A Romero’s undead classic. Thanks to the magic of splatter makeup maestro Tom Savini, he shambles into frame – and gets the top of his head sliced off by a spinning rotor.

Shinya Tsukamoto burst on to the body horror scene with a no-budget semi-experimental cyberpunk nightmare in which a Japanese salaryman’s body parts gradually turn to metal through a combination of juddery time-lapse, stop motion and jump-cutting, all set to a clanging soundtrack. Finally, his penis turns into a giant drill and destroys a coffee table.

James Whale’s adaptation of HG Wells’s novel owes much to the sardonic tones of Claude Rains, whose face is only briefly glimpsed in his Hollywood debut. John P Fulton’s special effects show the actor unwrapping bandages from his head to reveal – nothing!

Fredric March won the best actor Oscar for his performance in this violent, sexy pre-code adaptation of Robert Louis Stevenson’s novella. It would be 38 years before the director, Rouben Mamoulian, revealed how they achieved the groundbreaking onscreen transformation of Jekyll into Hyde: Wally Westmore’s makeup combined with coloured filters over the lens.

A surgeon kidnaps young women and – in explicit black and white – slices their faces off with a scalpel in an attempt to restore the beauty of his disfigured daughter. Georges Franju’s eerie arthouse horror was dismissed on its release, but is now hailed as an influential masterpiece.

The pea-coloured puke popularised the term “projectile vomiting”, and the deleted “spider-walk” became legendary before its restitution. But the signature effect in William Friedkin’s film is Linda Blair’s 360-degree head rotation, an effect at once ludicrous and horrifying, thanks to Dick Smith and Marcel Vercoutere’s lifesize animatronic dummy.

The climbing frame, the schoolchildren, the gas station are impeccable set pieces, but the attack on Tippi Hedren in the attic is particularly terrifying. Much of the impact was achieved by editing, but some birds were attached to her clothes by nylon threads, and one of the beaks nearly took her eye out. The scene took seven days to shoot; Hedren described it as “the worst week of my life”.

David Lynch’s first full-length feature is set in an industrial hellscape, where Jack Nance, he of the tumbleweed hair-do, ends up having to look after a chittering mutant baby. The creature, designed by Lynch himself, was reportedly made from an embalmed calf foetus with added working parts, and was ceremonially buried in a secret location after production wrapped.

Graphic decapitation goes mainstream in a special effect supervised by John Richardson. Photographer Keith Jennings (David Warner) stoops to retrieve the Daggers of Megiddo, the only weapons effective against Damien the Antichrist – and is beheaded by a sheet of glass sliding off a runaway truck. Warner reportedly kept the severed head until his divorce, when his ex-wife claimed custody of it.

Joe Dante’s werewolf satire, co-written by John Sayles, shows Robert Picardo (AKA Star Trek’s holographic doctor) saying “I’m gonna give you a piece of my mind” and offering a bit of his own brain to a horrified Dee Wallace before pulsating air bladders transform him into a beast before our very eyes. Take a bow, Rob Bottin, making his solo special effects debut.

John Cassavetes, darling of American indie cinema, found Brian De Palma’s film “degrading”, but his villain’s comeuppance is so satisfying you wish Rick Baker’s effects could have been retroactively applied to the same actor’s character in Rosemary’s Baby as well. One of the psychic teenagers the scumbag has been trying to control zaps him with her full telekinetic force and kaboom! He explodes!

Brian Yuzna’s body-horror satire unmasks the upper classes as shapeshifting entities who literally feed off the proletariat. The film climaxes with an orgiastic “shunt” in which posh partygoers merge into an orifice-invading mass not unlike Salvador Dalí’s Great Masturbator, surreal effects courtesy of Screaming Mad George.

There is no shortage of mind-boggling effects in the early films of David Cronenberg, but his sci-fi thriller about warring psychics provides one of the most memorable. One telepath’s demonstration of his ability is hijacked by a more powerful scanner (Michael Ironside) who makes his head explode. Dick Smith and Chris Walas packed a plaster skull with “leftover burgers”, then blasted it with an out-of-frame shotgun.

Rick Baker won the inaugural best makeup Oscar for his work on John Landis’s horror-comedy (with a budget three times that of The Howling). As Sam Cooke’s Blue Moon plays on the radio, David Naughton stares aghast at his hand turning into a werewolf’s paw. As his skeleton painfully reconfigures itself, his shrieks of agony turn into a howl.

The rest of the cast knew something was about to happen, but didn’t know precisely what, so when a critter erupts out of John Hurt’s chest, their shock is almost as extreme as the audience’s. For the money shot, Hurt’s torso was replaced by a mechanical one packed with compressed air and animal entrails, with puppeteers hiding beneath the table. Director Ridley Scott designed the creature, Roger Dicken constructed it and sci-fi cinema would never be the same again.

A shapeshifting alien infiltrates a US research station in the Antarctic, sporadically erupting into displays of special effects that have yet to be equalled. Take another bow, Rob Bottin, who riffs on elements of human and animal anatomy in surreal sculptures that are simultaneously repulsive and beautiful. In one of the highlights, a geologist’s head separates from his body, sprouts spider-legs and tries to scuttle away. Palmer the pothead (David Clennon) says what we’ve all been thinking: “You’ve gotta be fucking kidding.”

Is this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election?

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 12:34:24 GMT

There’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandate

Great hopes were invested in Andy Burnham when he became prime minister in July. He went big on the failings of 40 years of neoliberalism, emphasised the need for Britain to start making things again and promised growth in every postcode. Back in the summer, John Healey’s first budget was seen as an opportunity to start delivering on these ambitions, but it has been clear for some time that it wouldn’t do so. The road to the New Jerusalem – judging by the chancellor’s “breathing space” package – will be a slow and arduous one. Healey has taken what he inherited from Rachel Reeves and performed some minor tweaks. Not so much a revolution as continuity Keir Starmer. As has been the hallmark of Burnham’s first 100 days in Downing Street, there was plenty of activity in the budget but the slew of measures – almost 100 in all – was a hotchpotch and had no real semblance of a strategy being fleshed out. Not many budgets linger long in the memory and it is unlikely that Healey’s will break with this tradition.

In essence, it has bought Healey and Burnham some time. For the moment they can argue that the budget was just part one of a three-stage process, to be followed by the government’s 10-year-plan and next year’s spending review. They need to use that time wisely or the glitzy PR will cease to impress. There are, of course, reasons why the chancellor played it safe. Energy prices have rocketed since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February. The consequent higher inflation has resulted in higher interest rates for mortgages, business loans and government borrowing. Optimism about an early resolution to the war is fast fading. Indeed, the prospect of an intensification of the conflict after next week’s US midterm elections has led to a fresh surge in the cost of crude oil and gas in the past couple of weeks. The modest help provided in the budget to reduce energy bills will be dwarfed by the expected price increases in January. A tough winter lies ahead. As the dust settles, a number of conclusions can be drawn. One is that Britain remains – as Burnham once put it – in hock to the bond markets. Healey may well have wanted to come up with a more generous energy support package, but was constrained by the fear that the financial markets would cut up rough. Ever since Liz Truss’s mini budget in 2022, governments have lived in fear of another sell off in government bonds. Healey is like a contestant in Strictly Come Dancing – he knows that the markets always have the casting vote. To be fair to the chancellor, he borrowed £20bn more to invest in infrastructure spending, using the flexibility in meeting the government’s rules for the public finances provided by Reeves. That was welcome and – at first glance – didn’t appear to unsettle the markets. Whether Healey’s array of minor fixes to help with cost of living pressures is enough to keep voters sweet is another matter. The economy has so far showed impressive resilience in the face of the energy shock caused by events in the Middle East, but that strength has been concentrated in the financial and business sectors of the economy, with growth in artificial intelligence particularly striking. Consumer-facing sectors – such as hospitality and housing – have been much weaker, with the most recent report on consumer confidence showing the sharpest monthly fall since the Brexit referendum in 2016. That’s hardly surprising given the fact that taxes as a share of national income are on course next year to be at their highest ever level, and that spending power is being eroded by rising fuel and energy costs. In its latest report on the economy, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that living standards will fall next year and by 2030-31 will be only 2% higher than they were before the Covid pandemic. A lost decade in other words. It is against this unpropitious backdrop that many pundits – particularly in the City – have seen the lack of meat in the budget not as an indication that the government is dithering, but as a sign that Burnham is preparing the ground for an early general election. On this reading, all the big decisions – on social care, relations with the EU, and defence – have been parked until the prime minister has his own mandate. The case for holding a snap poll is not just that voters seem to have taken to Burnham, although he is certainly enjoying a honeymoon period. It is also that Labour is currently benefiting from the lack of a single challenger on the right as the Conservatives and Reform slug it out, and from the problems facing both the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on the left. The polls show Labour in the lead. Even so, an early election would be a colossal risk for a party with a commanding majority and two and a half years of the current parliament still to run. The OBR thinks the economy will grow more slowly in 2027 than in 2026, while living standards will actually fall before picking up in 2028 as the energy shock abates. Next week’s anticipated rise in interest rates from the Bank of England may not be the last. The prime minister is arguably at the peak of his popularity. Burnham has repeatedly said that he has no plans to go to the country early, which if true will be a relief to the many Labour MPs who would almost certainly lose their seats, even now that the polls are looking more favourable. But if that is his intention, he will need to get a move on – because now is as good as it is going to get.

England’s Ivan Toney to stand trial during Euro 2028 after denying assault charge

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 11:55:21 GMT

Striker’s trial due to begin on 12 June 2028

He has denied assaulting man at Soho nightclub

Ivan Toney has in effect been ruled out of Euro 2028 after his trial for assault occasioning actual bodily harm was scheduled for 12 June 2028.

Toney appeared at Southwark crown court and stood in the dock to confirm a not guilty plea. The striker is accused of head-butting and punching Saber Da Silva at a Soho nightclub on 6 December last year.

Setting the trial date for 20 months’ time, Judge Hehir apologised to Toney for the delay. “That’s a long way, I’m sorry about that,” he said. “As you may know, the crown courts are operating under a great deal of pressure.” Toney – wearing a black button-up cardigan, white shirt and tie – was told he was in a queue of defendants awaiting crown court trials.

Toney was part of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad for the 2026 World Cup, coming on against Argentina in the semi-final and starting the third-place playoff victory against France. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged by the Metropolitan police three weeks after the tournament. He was not part of Tuchel’s next squad for the Nations League fixtures at the end of September and early October.

It appears inconceivable the England manager would select a player for Euro 2028, which is due to be held in the UK and Ireland, while the player faces a criminal trial during the group stage.

Toney was released on unconditional bail and told it was “very important” and “a matter of common sense” that he stayed in regular contact with his solicitors while awaiting trial.

Judge Hehir told Toney that the law obliged him to give the footballer a formal warning, as with any defendant on bail awaiting trial, about the consequences of failing to attend court. “It’s a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment,” he said. The case would likely be tried in his absence if he did not appear, the judge added.

When Toney appeared at Westminster magistrates court to enter his plea at the start of October, the court was told by the prosecutor, Tom Heslop, that Toney and Da Silva exchanged words that resulted in them “squaring up” to one another before Toney “lunged forward and head-butted the complainant, followed by a few punches”. Da Silva sustained injuries to his nose and fingers, it was alleged. After pleading not guilty, Toney requested that his trial be heard at a crown court.

After the Metropolitan police announced Toney had been charged, a spokesperson for the player said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney, who has 10 England caps, started his career at Northampton before moving to Newcastle and Peterborough. His career took off at Brentford, where his goals helped them win promotion to the Premier League in 2021 before he established himself as one of the leading top-flight strikers. He moved to Al-Ahli for £40m in 2024.

A simple pub sign led me down a very disturbing rabbit hole

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 11:00:31 GMT

The cleanliness, or otherwise, of a pub’s pipes has never bothered me before. But that was before I read about the potential yeast, bacteria and mould ...

There’s a pub near me with an eye-catching sign outside. I’ve driven past it many times, and it always gives me pause for a little idle thought. On the sign there is a loud and proud notice that in this pub they clean their lines every week.

There’s a lot going on with this simple sign. First and foremost, in a long life of pub observance, I don’t recall ever reading such a boast adorning any other establishment. What’s going on here? Surely it’s not the case that this pub, and only this pub, is so scrupulous about the cleanliness of its lines. (By lines, I assume they refer to the pipes that convey the beer from the kegs or casks to the pump and into the glass.)

Surely all pubs have a weekly flush-through? In which case, this sign is clever, but daft, making a virtue of a norm. Like a restaurant stating its chefs don’t sneeze on the food, or an airline assuring us that the planes’ wings are checked before every flight.

Always on the lookout for a fresh source of worry, I’ve been down a rabbit hole on the subject of beer line issues, and I’ve come up smelling not very nice. There’s a lot going on in those pipes – an awful lot if you’re not careful. Potentially, it’s hell in there. Living wild yeast and bacteria attaching itself to the interior of the tubes; mould around the taps and connectors; sticky protein residue left behind by the grain; and something called beerstone, a stubborn mineral scale that bonds to the plastic lining. Ye gods, it’s enough to put you off your beer.

I’m going to pop into this pub and suggest they clean daily instead of weekly. And as for every other pub I frequent, before I shout up a pint I’ll henceforth be asking for details of their line-cleaning regime. I may carry a hazmat suit to have a poke around in the cellar myself. You can’t be too careful.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfire

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 10:00:31 GMT

With his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to voters

As he criss-crosses the nation, stumping for Republican candidates, Donald Trump keeps asking voters to use their imaginations.

“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just pretend,” he urged at a Kansas rally as he campaigned for the incumbent senator Roger Marshall and gubernatorial challenger Ty Masterson last month.

“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.

But will it work? That seems increasingly unlikely.

Given his own lack of popularity and weird behavior, it’s an egotistical notion – more appealing to himself than to voters.

After all, his approval ratings are in the basement. Gas prices are higher, on average, than at any time during the Biden years. People feel like they need to float a loan before heading to the supermarket.

In that Kansas rally, he referred to the opposition as “Dumocrats”, which is typical of the level of presidential discourse to which the nation has become accustomed.

In his rallies, he appears “increasingly detached from reality”, as one campaign analysis in the Independent put it, as he “vacillates between topics to the point where his remarks border on the nonsensical and he ends every appearance by awkwardly dancing to the Village People’s well-known gay anthem YMCA”.

Stranger still, as the Guardian’s Adam Gabbatt reported recently, Trump has been offering “unsolicited and increasingly unhinged assessments of men’s bodies” over the past few weeks.

“I examined his ass,” the president said in Kentucky, speaking about Republican senator Jon Husted. “And then I looked at his shoulders … I looked at his jawline … I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”

Trump has also been – to put it mildly – stretching the truth on the campaign trail, sometimes merely misleading in his remarks, sometimes straight-up lying.

For example, he promised a North Carolina rally that gas and oil prices would tumble soon and he claimed: “I had it down to the lowest level in years,” apparently speaking about the price of filling up a gas tank at the pump. A PolitiFact examination disputed this, noting that when Trump took office at the beginning of last year, the average gas price was $3.23 a gallon, but by late September of this year, it was $4.61.

But it’s not just what he says at rallies that may backfire on the candidates he hopes to help.

Much of what’s happened in Trump’s second term is working against Republican candidates. That includes the widespread self-dealing that, as the historian Garrett Graff wrote recently, “is so endemic and so obvious that it has broken through to voters”.

It’s also his misguided war, his rants on social media, his disparagement of longtime allies, including Canada. It’s also his obvious plan to declare the election rigged should it not go his way.

“Even Maga die-hards and GOP allies in Congress have grown weary of his erratic behavior,” as the Wall Street Journal’s Jason Riley noted.

And Democrats, including Barack Obama, are only too happy to campaign by associating Republican candidates with Trump.

These midterm elections, Obama told a crowd in Ohio, “is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration. It’s the circuit breaker in the system.”

That blast of sanity and good sense seems far more likely to resonate with potential voters than Trump’s unhinged rants and dangerous threats.

Pretend he’s on the ballot?

Maybe that’s effective with Trump’s remaining cult-like base. And maybe it will bring some of those loyalists out to vote next week if they had been thinking of sitting out this election.

But more likely, the imagined association with Trump will serve to remind most voters that Trump’s malfeasance must be rebuked and rejected. Certainly not encouraged.

Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

If British Library reading rooms become ‘co-working spaces’, what, exactly, is a national library for?

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 08:00:27 GMT

The plan to generate revenue from areas currently used by the public is causing bitter dispute, and raises fundamental questions

In a crowded country that is short of public money, any expansive public building that seems underused in any way is vulnerable. Professional critics of state spending can claim taxpayers’ money is being wasted. Managers of the building who are under financial pressure can argue it needs to be used more intensely, perhaps that some spaces should be commercialised and offered for rent. The original open, uncommodified, egalitarian quality of the building can be steadily sliced away.

The British Library in London is in danger of that fate. A huge brick battleship moored on the Euston Road since 1997, it claims to be the largest public building constructed in the UK in the 20th century. Its both forbidding and exhilarating exterior conceals 11 unusually elegant and comfortable reading rooms and one of the world’s most extensive print and digital collections, free to use for anyone who is over 18. Last week, these readers received an email with the subject line, “Transforming your Library”. Next summer, the library would “begin work on repurposing our [three] Science and Social Sciences Reading Rooms to become a flexible workspace … available for hire by workers and businesses for co-working, collaboration and meetings”. The reason given for removing more than a quarter of the library’s much-loved research space was “ensuring we generate the necessary revenue to keep our core services free”.

The library has a current annual budget of about £170m – a third the size of my local London hospital’s – 84% of which comes from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The rest is from donations, investments and “charitable and other trading activities”, such as the private parties and ticketed exhibitions already frequently held in the sweeping interior connecting its reading rooms. Even with these multiple income streams, the library’s financial reserves are perilously low – according to its latest accounts – thanks to inflation and austerity, which mean its state funding has in real terms declined to two-thirds of what it was in 2010, and also a devastating cyber-attack in 2023, from which the library has still not fully recovered.

Despite this troubled context, and in some ways because of it, the library’s drastic reading room reduction plan has provoked “outrage” from staff, say the Prospect and Public and Commercial Services (PCS) unions that represent them. Reading room staff understandably fear for their jobs, but also for the building’s fundamental purpose, which was set out by law in 1972 – an indication of how hard the complex was to conceive and build – as “the establishment for the United Kingdom of a national library”. Staff are now “the most furious I’ve ever seen them about anything”, says a union source. A strike over the reading room plan, following one last year over low pay, could begin as soon as December.

Behind this potentially explosive dispute – not least because many well-connected authors, academics and journalists use the library – lurks a big question. In a digital age of decentralised study and dispersed online resources, what is a national library for?

During the quarter of a century I’ve been regularly using the library, usually the reading rooms that are now under threat, its hierarchy has been trying to answer that existential question by steadily, not always harmoniously, widening the building’s user base and functions. Reading room passes have been transformed from a rationed credential for a few thousand people with supposedly serious research intentions – though some always ended up snoring at their desks – to something provided in minutes to everyone from elderly amateur family historians to undergraduates, particularly when dissertation deadlines pile up in early summer.

Meanwhile, the library’s lobbies, landings, hallways and outdoor terraces have been lined with hundreds of chairs and tables and turned into study areas, meeting places, cafes and locations for loud laptop video conversations. These are all heavily used: a sign of good, free spaces lacking elsewhere. A “family station” inside the entrance offers play materials, art supplies and reading corners for young children. What Karl Marx, who researched for years in the reading room of the British Museum, precursor to the British Library, would have made of the latter’s invitation this Halloween to “pop in for spooky crafts” and “enjoy a fang-tastic time” is an intriguing question.

I generally like the contrast between the library’s studious and boisterous sides: an antidote to the solitary obsessiveness of research and writing. But there are also tensions between the library’s diverging uses, which its management prefers not to acknowledge – and which the proposed changes would almost certainly worsen. Modern life is noisy, especially in London, and the semi-silence of the long, wood-lined reading rooms, with pages softly turning, keyboards pattering, books being slid on and off shelves, and the odd murmured conversation, is precious and addictive, as the constant influx of new young readers makes obvious. First thing in the morning and last thing in the evening, the rooms are half empty. That will probably be used to argue that fewer are needed. But a half-empty place can be an aid to crucial thinking and concentration. And if the reading rooms become fewer and therefore fuller, then users from outside London, whose taxes also pay for this national library, are less likely to be able to get there in time to grab a desk. In the busiest periods, they already sometimes run out.

The library is straining to cope with its daily crowds. On bad mornings, the entrance queue lasts over half an hour. The toilets are increasingly often out of order. The free lockers are wearing out, partly because of use by travellers from the many stations nearby. And across the reading rooms, a mysterious hissing has been spreading for months, like a kettle that never boils. The library says it is coming from a failing pneumatic ventilation system, and “there is no quick solution”. The library is starting to get old.

In 2032, a towering extension, blander than the original building, is due to open. It is already noisily under construction. Last year, Rebecca Lawrence, then the library’s chief executive, who resigned during the strike, said the extension would “open up the Library even further … [for] future generations of visitors, learners, researchers and budding entrepreneurs”. It will not contain new reading rooms. If you find that ominous, you are not alone.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Fake film deals and emails from top agents: who is behind the explosion in literary scams?

The Guardian Thu, 29 Oct 2026 05:00:22 GMT

Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touch This piece first appeared in the Dial

‘Hello Professor Snigdha Poonam,” the email began. I read that again. Nobody has ever called me “professor” for the obvious reason that I am not a professor. Bracing myself, I read on. The email was from Timothy Firth, organiser of a Seattle-based life-drawing community with 1,943 members that regularly has “thoughtful discussions inspired by creative works”. A recent inspiration was my first book, Dreamers: How Young Indians Are Changing Their World. The group wanted to discuss it, the email said, at one of its upcoming meetups. Attendees would be encouraged to post reviews on Goodreads and Amazon after.

I looked up CAM Life Drawing and found an events page and an Instagram account. The latter had some photos of Timothy Firth – white, male – as well as testimonials from members who said he worked “day and night to create more community space”. Something told me this wasn’t the man who had reached out to me.

Why would a hyperlocal life-drawing community in Seattle be interested in a nonfiction book about the shifting aspirations of young people in India’s small towns? The book was published seven years ago. What did they want from me?

I accepted the invitation. The next email had a slick poster promoting the Zoom event, with the book cover as the backdrop and blurbs from the Economist and other publications. My attention was drawn to something more intriguing: a request for a “contribution fee”, with no amount specified. It would cover promotion, coordination and administration. But, oddly, this email didn’t come from Timothy. Signing off this time was Stephen – “Organiser, Community Improv LA”, which was another group in another city. According to the improv community’s Facebook group, Stephen is indeed the name of the organiser. However, Stephen had written to me using Timothy’s email address. To add to the chaos, Stephen/Timothy had also left what I suspect was an AI prompt in the email, which included the line: “MAKE IT MORE PROFESSIONAL.”

This was undoubtedly a scam. Genuine book clubs don’t ask for money from authors. But who was behind it?

Had these individuals actually read my work, they would have wanted to stay away from me. I have spent the last 10 years reporting on transnational fraud. My first book, Dreamers, closed with a chapter on fake call centres in India; my second, Scamlands, travelled to other low-income countries in Asia to portray an invisible empire that thrives on inequality, technological change and the erosion of trust.

Along the way, I met and interviewed the scammers whose labour keeps this empire running. For some, fraud was a route to upward mobility; for others, an act of revenge against the privileged. Though I have formally emerged from this underworld, I can never delete a scam email without wanting to know more.

I agreed to pay the book club – but after rather than before the event. After clarifying that “Stephen” was a typing error, “Timothy” sent me a Google Meet link for the book discussion. I joined the meeting to find about 20 people already in there: Alexander, Andrew, Mira, Rajnish, another Alexander, and several others. Timothy was also there and so was Stephen. None of them had their cameras on. Going by the profile pictures they used, most of them appeared to be white.

Then the questions began.

“Professor, what was your inspiration for writing Dreamers?”

“Professor, what did you learn while reporting from Indian small towns?”

“Professor, what surprised you?”

While the questions may have been AI-generated, the voices seemed human. They did not always align with their pictures. Timothy seemed to be a woman, not a man, judging by the voice. Who were these people? They left only one clue. All these ostensibly white people, men and women, spoke with a west African accent.

I am not the only author to have found myself stuck in a Zoom book club with fake readers. Countless writers with published books have been receiving invitations from reading communities that start to unravel after a basic Google search.

As often happens with scams, most invitations sound too good to be true – thousands of members, incredible Goodreads clout and, at times, something even more alluring for an author: a deep understanding of their book.

Many authors spot red flags from the first email onward, but not all.

One author who engaged with a book-club impersonator was told a $100 (£75) contribution for the online event would cover snacks for the participants; she withdrew without asking how they would partake of the snacks while on Zoom. Novelist Marsh Rose, playing along, exchanged 29 emails with the Chicago LGBTQ Book Club. “The individuals whose voices I heard on the Zoom didn’t seem to be speaking from Chicago. They all sounded like my friend in Nigeria,” she wrote in a blog post for WritersWeekly. com, an online resource for authors that offers writing opportunities and industry news.

Writers are also being bombarded with offers to publish our next book, market our book, handle social media for us, represent us as agents and get us book-to-movie deals with Netflix and Paramount. Every major publisher, agent, editor, author union and literary award executive is at risk of being impersonated.

The money requested often seems small. “Amounts reported to me range from $55 to $350. In one case, the scammer offered three ‘spotlight packages’ – basic, essential and premium – for between $100 and $200,” Victoria Strauss, co-founder of Writer Beware, an anti-scam watchdog, wrote in a blog post. Often, the paper trail leads to Nigerian third parties holding bank accounts in the US. Author Jon Cocks paid $478.65 to one “Mary Brown,” who claimed a wide network of book clubs across the US, the UK and Australia, only to later notice the name Dayo Oguntuase listed as the recipient on the PayPal statement.

The Writers’ Guild of Great Britain (WGGB) reports “an explosion” in the number of members seeking advice about unusually enticing offers in recent months. “Even the most vigilant of writers are understandably falling prey to these scams,” WGGB’s general secretary, Ellie Piers, said in a statement commenting on new guidance, co-issued with the Society of Authors in May, to help authors protect themselves against scammers. “Our advisory team receives at least a dozen reports of scams each week,” Anna Ganley, chief executive of the Society of Authors, said in her own statement, tracing the spike to the emergence of generative AI. The US Authors Guild says it hears from authors who have been scammed, or nearly scammed, every day. Angela Hoy, the founder of WritersWeekly. com, told me she is in touch with “authors all day long, every day, thinking they got an offer from one of the top five publishers in New York or thinking they’ve been contacted by a famous literary agent”.

A prominent trendsetter was the PageTurner scam, named after a fictitious US-registered publishing company that operated between 2017 and 2024. Call centre staff in Cebu, the Philippines, claimed PageTurner was an intermediary between authors and literary agents, film studios and streaming services and persuaded authors to pay so-called taxes, transaction fees and other costs before their books could be published or adapted.

The scale of the operation became clear after US authorities launched an investigation into the business. According to the Department of Justice, more than 800 authors were defrauded of upwards of $48m (£36m). Writer Beware received hundreds of complaints about PageTurner. One author reportedly lost more than $600,000 (£450,000). The prosecutors found that at least $42m in proceeds were laundered through accounts in the Philippines. One defendant pleaded guilty in May of this year, while three others are awaiting trial.

Judging by the surge in both the number and range of baits used on authors over the past couple of years, the scams seem to be launched from multiple territories. Anyone who has researched publishing would know most authors don’t have bundles of cash lying around. So why are the scammers coming after us?

Hoy, who has dealt with thousands of writers at WritersWeekly. com, puts it down to ego. Brian Whiddon, the site’s managing editor, elaborated: “Not every author is a narcissist, but they all want to be recognised. That’s exactly what these scammers are targeting. They have identified a very, very lucrative niche.”

Writers are waiting “for somebody to read their writing”, Hoy added. She argued that is why many writers believe the praise scammers heap on them. AI makes many of the compliments sound nuanced and personalised. Elderly authors are particularly vulnerable. As Hoy explained, a significant number of people who have a book in them leave off the writing until they have retired. Something else also kicks into the picture at this life stage: a sizable retirement fund. Scammers know American people have worked their whole lives and have retirement accounts, Hoy said.

Some authors are so hell-bent on signing up for the deals the scammers promise that they disregard Hoy’s counsel. Others come to Hoy when it’s too late. She has said one of the writers in her community paid more than $100,000 for a fake book-to-movie deal.

“I’ve actually used some of the verbiage from these emails talking about how fantastic my book is in my advertising,” author Donna Strong commented in the Goodreads discussion forum Readers Group Scams.

Even as a new category of literary scams emerges every few days, authors have very little information about the people behind them.

In August, Danny de Hek, a New Zealand-based scam buster, forwarded me an Excel spreadsheet he received from a scammer in Karachi, Pakistan, with permission from the sender. Titled “LinkedIn Outreach 2026”, it has monthly data on targeted authors from March until August. One sheet has 403 names, each neatly labelled: new author, cookbook author, religious author, investigative author, poetry author, New York Times bestselling author and so on. Most are based in the US; the rest are in Canada, Australia or Europe.

It’s an incredibly detailed document, with columns for the name of the person who found the profile, the person who first reached out, the service the author needs (website development, illustrator, social media visibility), the department handling the author, meeting links shared with the author. In a few cases, the document also lists the outcome of the outreach.

“Paid $1,200 UP FRONT.”

“Not willing to pay, has been scammed before.”

“Meeting booked Wed 12 Aug, 10pm PKT, number confirmed, deep trust-built relationship, ready to invest, needs custom package built around limited budget and multi-project scope.”

Some of the details only make sense if you know the context. 10pm PKT would mean 10am on the US west coast and 1pm in the east. Danny told me that most of the people working on this scam are Pakistani, yet the names of the callers are all American-sounding – Ashley, Jocelyn, Megan – probably to fool the authors into thinking they are Americans working for US-based companies and groups.

Scam recipients often find the emails they receive haphazard and random. But the modern scam industry is a highly organised system modelled on the global corporate setup, with clearly laid out deliverables, salaries, incentives and reporting structures. Even though the schemes are mind-boggling in range, the young people joining these “companies” are given the same targets: Americans on top, followed by gullible foreigners in other western countries. I spent several years reporting from India on its massive scam call-centre network, which employs hundreds of thousands of educated young people trying to beat the dim economic prospects offered by the domestic labour market. Similar Excel spreadsheets are used to organise schemes where Indian scammers in Delhi or Kolkata impersonate Microsoft tech support, the Internal Revenue Service or even the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

De Hek, who exposes transnational scams on his blog and YouTube channel with relentless zeal, told me Pakistan’s fake companies offering literary services operate in a similar fashion to India’s scam call centres. The majority of them maintain physical offices in Karachi and Lahore and employ people aged 20 to 24. Upon joining, the young employees typically get assigned to a unit, each designed around a specific literary swindle. While entry-level employees may only be tasked with outreach, the more experienced ones are entrusted with building long-term relationships aimed at selling multiple “packages” to clients over months and sometimes years.

The most profitable service targets authors lurking outside the notoriously gatekept realm of traditional publishing. Rather than through a cold call or email, the scammers lure them through websites offering self-publishing or vanity publishing.

Scam companies in Pakistan trap writers by impersonating known publishing houses and paying thousands of dollars to influence search results on Google. As a result, someone with a finished manuscript who searches online may find sites such as penguinwriters. com or amazonglobalpublishers. com before any legitimate self-publishing platform. Unlike traditional publishing websites, these feature open calls for new writers. WritersWeekly. com estimates there are at least 3,000 such sites. The biggest tell: a chat box pops up in the bottom right of all fake publishing websites as soon as the page opens, followed by a message from someone with an American-sounding name (such as Mark Anderson or Jessica Parker) and a white person’s face: “How can I help you today?” “Talk to a live agent, not a bot!” claims a ticker. And that much is absolutely true: the person messaging you is a scammer whose shift is dictated by the waking hours in your time zone.

None of the five major trade publishers has sued alleged impersonators. The only recorded instance involves Amazon, which took nearly 20 individuals and associated companies to court in California for falsely claiming affiliation with Amazon Publishing and Kindle Direct Publishing to deceive authors. Amazon won $36.4m (£27m) in February 2025.

M L Stark, a Danish self-published author of several psychological thrillers, is one of the rare victims who has met – and confronted – her scammer in person. Last year, she flew to Thailand to meet with Ethan Williams, a man she believed had become her longtime editor at an LA-based self-publishing house affiliated with Amazon – and a close friend. By this time, she had been talking to him over Zoom and email for more than a year and paid his company about $100,000 for different author services, from editing and cover design to coverage in the New York Times and the Los Angeles Times.

While most of the services she paid for never materialised, the company did follow through on some. They signed her up on IngramSpark, a self-publishing platform, which enabled her to release two books, and Amazon, which made the books available on the platform. Most notably, in 2024, one of her titles was displayed on a digital billboard in Times Square.

“I had paid $10,000 for that,” she told me. Only later, she told me, did she come to see these deliveries as strategic concessions, held back for moments when a long-term client reached the end of her tether. “Each time, it happened when I told them, after months of them stalling, that I wanted my money back.”

The scammers’ last pitch was a Netflix adaptation that they claimed the film-makers wanted to shoot in Thailand – an important setting in her upcoming book, a thriller based on her own life. Stark and Williams were meeting in Thailand to scout locations.

He had told her he was a British citizen, half English and half Arab; as a light-skinned Pakistani, his story was plausible. “He is an artist, he knew how to play the role,” she said. Still, she asked him to show an ID. He produced one that looked clearly faked. “I demanded he show me his passport,” she said. That exposed his real name and citizenship. He came clean. “He said, ‘Yeah, this has been a scam from the beginning. Even Peter is using a fake name; even Ronald is using a fake name. Everybody in the company that you have talked to is a scammer. It’s a huge scam operation, and we are not based in Los Angeles. We are based in Karachi.’” She is still processing her shock.

I clicked on a random website from a list of known scam sites; it happened to be impersonating Red Rock, a real literary agency based in London whose authors have been published by major publishers such as Hurst, which published my first book in the UK. Bold promises greeted me on the homepage.

“Get seen on Times Square.”

“Bring your book and brand on Broadway.”

“Join our authors making their mark in Manhattan.”

A chat window opened, and someone with the username “Rae Donnaelly” asked how she could help. I told her I had an idea for a book. She asked for my contact, then called me on WhatsApp from a US number. She spoke like a South Asian imitating an American accent, something I could easily recognise because I’m South Asian myself, and we’ve all tried it at one point or another.

I told her the truth: I was writing an article about author-baiting scams, and I was hoping she could tell me about her experience working for a fake publishing house.

She told me she wasn’t “authorised” to talk about the company she works for, and she refused to tell me her real name. But she had no qualms spilling the beans on her ex-employer.

Rae has a law degree but found it difficult to find a job in law after university. Her first job after graduating was at a fake publishing company in Karachi. “I started working for a company which was a scam – a guaranteed scam – and I didn’t know it when I started off with them. I was an intern trying to learn how the system really works; what the pros and cons are.”

It took Rae only a few days to figure out the company’s business model: proxy sales. They would tell the author they would get them a guaranteed sale order for 1,000 copies, or something like that, making “fake commitments”. The scam rarely stopped there. After a client signed up for developmental editing, they would be offered a discount on book-cover design, and once they paid for that, the scammer would dangle social media management. “It could start off from as little as $400- $500, and it could go up to the skies, like $10,000, $15,000.”

As with all scams, those executing the con learned how easily people can be manipulated if you know what they desired. “You could see how the human brain works. It’s actually scary when you think about it,” Rae admitted.

She believes Americans make easy scam targets. “People in the US are very nice, they’re very good-hearted people. They trust you. Whatever you’re saying, they trust you. That’s the problem.”

At times, the clients only noticed they had been scammed after they had paid all the way up to a Times Square display and Broadway adaptation. “When the authors did not see results, they would either reverse the charge on their card or accuse us of being scamsters,” Rae recalled.

According to Talal Choudhary, an Islamabad-based tech journalist, there are about 1,000 Pakistani companies running scam sites. “One company runs as many as 25 websites. I personally know a company that had about 200 employees, just offering services to writers.” These companies are “very, very profitable”, he said. “From one client, you can make $60,000.”

In Pakistan, Choudhary told me, the workforce of the author-baiting scams is largely made up of high-school and university graduates. They earn an average salary of about 50,000 Pakistani rupees (£136) a month. For high performers, there is commission. For every sale worth $1,000, they might get a 10-20% commission, he said, upselling until the author backs out.

According to Rae, any guilt the scammers felt was cancelled out by the increasingly skewed conversion rate between the American dollar and Pakistani rupee. “Generally, the mentality was: when you’re making income in dollars, you have a stable life, you have sustainability. So that’s what they did. They just ripped people off.”

I have heard multiple versions of this statement since I first reported on the rise of organised transnational fraud. Earlier this year, Hoy received a message on Facebook from a Nigerian man who offered to market her latest novel. Convinced he was part of the suspected author-scam network, she made him an offer of her own: write an article for Writersweekly. com about how the company he worked for scams Americans while being based overseas.

But he wrote it using AI, which is against the site’s submission rules. He also ignored the brief. Instead, he chose to highlight, as Hoy recalls, “how it’s so hard for people in Africa and therefore it’s OK to scam Americans because all of us are rich over here”.

Salil Mahmood, who asked that I change his name, is another self-described ex-scammer from Karachi. He reached out to me after hearing from Danny de Hek about the article I was writing. Compared with some of the more outrageous deals his seniors offered their clients, his job, as an entry-level recruit, was low-key. He cold-emailed published authors with a proposal to create their official pages on Wikipedia and have those approved. However, many of the pages he created – largely based on information provided by the authors – failed verification because the citations he supplied were fabricated. “The pages would remain active for a while and then disappear.” The authors never got their money back.

While he only worked there for a few months, he said the setup was highly aspirational for those who wanted to make serious money. “The bosses would show us pictures of their lifestyles: mansions, fast cars, parties and lots of alcohol. If you met your targets, they would have a rented car drive you around.” But in keeping with the nature of such enterprises, failure was not an option. “If an employee did not meet the target, they and their families were threatened with violence,” he said.

Rae left the company she had been working for after a disagreement with her manager less than a year into the job. But rather than go back on the job market, she and a few friends started a new company that, as she described, provides American authors with tailored services.

She insisted her company did not defraud its clients. I could have asked her why, if it was a genuine publishing house in Pakistan, it gave clients the impression that it was based in the US; why the website featured books it had not published; or why the individuals who popped up in the chat boxes used fake, American-sounding names, including her. But I left it at that. I could sense she wanted me to believe she had nothing to do with the scammers. She even pointed out that her religion does not allow her to earn money from fraud.

“You can look out for us at the next Frankfurt book fair,” she said. I told her I would.

I still get emails from Timothy Firth – the impersonator – reminding me to send my voluntary contribution in gratitude for the book club discussion. The person writing to me as Timothy probably knows it is not coming. I have a feeling the scammers know I am on to them because of how the meeting ended. After running through all the questions they had prepared, the moderator asked if I had any final comments.

I asked if any of them had thoughts to share about the last chapter in my book. Reported from fake call centres in Delhi, I explained, it is the story of ambitious young people being drawn into an underworld of scams and fraud.

Nobody spoke for a while. Then I saw Timothy unmute herself.

“It is happening all over the world,” she said, “including in Africa.”

That’s all she had to say.

Published in The Dial as The Lucrative World of Literary Scams
