The British actor was 86. He achieved pop-culture stardom as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation.”

Patrick Stewart was Professor X in five “X-Men” movies, Macbeth on Broadway and, recently, the voice of a wise ram in “The Sheep Detectives.”Credit... Ryan Pfluger for The New York Times

Supported by

By Anita Gates and William McDonald

Patrick Stewart, who overcame a bleak childhood in England’s coal-mining country to find acclaim as a Shakespearean actor before making an unlikely career pivot in middle age that would bring him his greatest fame, playing a noble starship captain on the TV series “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.

The death, from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, was announced on social media.

With a commanding baritone voice — he had shed his Yorkshire dialect as an acting student — Mr. Stewart was by his late 40s an eloquent, statesmanlike presence on the British stage. But to many American television viewers, Mr. Stewart was a new face when he made his debut in 1987 as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in “The Next Generation,” the first live-action spinoff of the original “Star Trek” series of the late 1960s.

Old and new fans embraced the balding, graying Picard and the members of his 24th-century crew, among them a pale-skinned android with deadpan comic timing; an intense, half-alien mind-reader; a gruff Klingon; and a blind human engineer wearing a vision visor. Over the show’s seven seasons, as it piled up 18 Emmys and a Peabody Award in first-run syndication, Picard became known for his preternatural calm and his trademark directives “Engage!” and “Make it so.” (Mr. Stewart titled a 2023 memoir “Making It So.”)

Mr. Stewart went on to star in four feature-film spinoffs — “Star Trek Generations” (1994), “Star Trek: First Contact” (1996), “Star Trek: Insurrection” (1998) and “Star Trek: Nemesis” (2002) — before returning to the bridge of the Starship Enterprise in 2020 in a TV sequel that he could call his own, “Star Trek: Picard,” which ran for three seasons.

The Enterprise was neither Mr. Stewart’s first science-fiction home nor his last. He appeared in David Lynch’s original film version of “Dune” (1984) as the weapons teacher Gurney Halleck. Years later, he was Charles Xavier, a. k. a. Professor X, in five “X-Men” movies, playing a wealthy telepath in a wheelchair who leads other mutants with superpowers. Those films, some of which also starred Mr. Stewart’s close friend Ian McKellen, included “X-Men” (2000), “X-Men: United” (2003) and “Logan” (2017).

By the time he became a screen star, Mr. Stewart was a lauded stage veteran in Britain, where he began working with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. After making his first public stage appearance at 19, he performed in both classical and contemporary works alongside fellow up-and-coming actors like Ben Kingsley, Helen Mirren and Glenda Jackson.

In 1986, he won the London Fringe Theater best actor award for his role as the humiliated husband, George, in the Young Vic’s production of Edward Albee’s “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” He also won Olivier Awards (Britain’s equivalent of Broadway’s Tony) for playing Enobarbus, Mark Antony’s best friend, in Shakespeare’s “Antony and Cleopatra” (1979) and Claudius, opposite David Tennant’s Danish prince, in “Hamlet” (2009).

To most American film and television fans, however, he was always Picard, even after the “X-Men” movies. And though in terms of substance the character may have been light years removed from his meatier roles with the R. S. C., Mr. Stewart continued to express pride in his work as that resolute ship captain, dismissing theater-world peers who had looked askance at him when he went to Hollywood.

“They used to ask me ‘Why, why, why?’ as if I was somehow slumming it,” he said in a 2003 interview with the London newspaper The Independent.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

“What snobbery!” he said, adding: “For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that’s fine. I really believe we created an admirable individual.”

Mr. Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, England, a small, industrial river town in West Yorkshire. (He was given no middle name but later invented one, Hewes, when he joined a union that already had a member named Patrick Stewart.) His father, Alfred Stewart, was a regimental sergeant major in the British Army, and his mother, Gladys (Barrowclough) Stewart, was a weaver at a textile factory. Patrick was the youngest of their three sons.

The family scraped by, living in a grim little house with no running hot water. The bathroom was outside, in a brick communal outhouse for the neighborhood, one stall to a family. Patrick used his family’s stall as a reading nook.

Much later in life, he wrote and spoke about the domestic violence that had shattered his childhood. His father was reduced to working as a semiskilled laborer after his military career, and became what Mr. Stewart described as a resentful “weekend alcoholic” who physically attacked his mother for years, sometimes in Patrick’s presence.

As Mr. Stewart recalled in a 2009 article he wrote for The Guardian, “I knew exactly when to insert a small body between the fist and her face, a skill no child should ever have to learn.”

The family dynamic was complicated. Despite the abuse, Patrick’s mother remained with her husband until her death in 1977, and throughout his life Patrick regarded his father with a mixture of anger, fear, sadness and regret. Interviewed by The Sydney Morning Herald in 2023, after his memoir was published, he told a reporter, tapping the cover of a copy, “I wish my father could have seen this.”

Patrick was 12 when an English teacher, Cecil Dormand, with whom he maintained a lifelong friendship, handed out scripts for “The Merchant of Venice” and instructed him to read the part of Shylock. Patrick went on to work with local drama groups.

Graduating from secondary school at 15, he took a job as a junior reporter with the local newspaper but quit after a year; his editor had complained that he was spending too much time on his theater avocation. After that, he worked for a year as a furniture salesman to save money for drama school, though a local arts council ended up giving him a full scholarship so that he could enroll in the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theater School, which accepted him in 1957, when he was 17.

Two years later, he made his professional acting debut, as the marooned pirate Tom Morgan in “Treasure Island,” with the Lincoln Repertory Company in Lincoln, England. In other early appearances, he took the title roles in Shakespeare’s “Henry V” (1963), at the Manchester Library Theater, and Bertolt Brecht’s “The Life of Galileo” (1965), at the Bristol Old Vic.

As part of the R. S. C., Mr. Stewart played more than a dozen roles, mostly supporting, in Stratford-upon-Avon and London between 1966 and 1969. He was the Player King in “Hamlet,” Grumio in “The Taming of the Shrew,” Cornwall in “King Lear” and Hector in “Troilus and Cressida.”

By the age of 19, Mr. Stewart was already balding, a result of hereditary alopecia. (He wore wigs for many screen and stage roles.) And he was already frequently hearing the prediction familiar to many young character actors: The first 20 years of your career will be difficult; true fame, if it ever comes, may take a while. It was a forecast that was largely borne out.

Mr. Stewart continued to find work, including on British television series like “Coronation Street” and “Story Parade.” By the 1970s, he was winning substantial roles in BBC TV movies and mini-series.

He portrayed Lenin in “Fall of Eagles” (1974); the postwar prime minister Clement Attlee in “The Gathering Storm” (1974); John Thornton, a brainy mill owner, in “North and South” (1975); Sejanus, head of the Praetorian Guard, in “I, Claudius” (1976, seen in the United States on “Masterpiece Theater” in 1977); and the Soviet spymaster Karla in brief, nonspeaking appearances in two John le Carré adaptations, “Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy” (1979) and “Smiley’s People” (1982).

Mr. Stewart made his Broadway debut in 1971 in Peter Brook’s acclaimed production of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream.” He was Snout, the tinker who portrays the wall between Pyramus and Thisbe in the comedy’s lowbrow play-within-a-play. It would be 20 years before Mr. Stewart appeared on Broadway again, in a 1991 run of a solo production of “A Christmas Carol” he had developed a few years before. The holiday-season show, which he repeated on Broadway in 1992, 1994 and 2001, received a Drama Desk Award for outstanding solo performance.

He was largely considered an unknown when the “Star Trek” offer came along. At the invitation of a friend, a university professor, Mr. Stewart had been in Los Angeles conducting master classes on Shakespeare when, one evening, he gave a lecture and performed some bits of the plays in a program that was open to the public.

A TV producer who was involved in developing a new “Star Trek” series happened to attend and soon persuaded Mr. Stewart to audition — even though, as Mr. Stewart later wrote, he knew “next to nothing” about the franchise.

Surprised to get the part — the “Star Trek” creator, Gene Roddenberry, who was overseeing the new series, had not been keen to hire him at first — Mr. Stewart expected the project to be a short-term commitment. How, he remembered thinking, could the show possibly succeed with a middle-aged pacifist captain with a French name and a British accent?

After its run ended, Mr. Stewart continued his stage and television career, now with the power of Hollywood fame behind him. Between 1995 and 2013, he starred in a handful of Broadway productions, two of them Shakespearean: He was Prospero in “The Tempest” in 1995 and, in 2008, the title character in “Macbeth,” for which he was nominated for a Tony.

He also played a self-satisfied bigamist in Arthur Miller’s “The Ride Down Mount Morgan” (2000); a desperate, possibly dangerous homeless man in Harold Pinter’s “The Caretaker” (2003); and a veteran actor who has seen it all in David Mamet’s “A Life in the Theater” (2010).

In 2013, Mr. Stewart and Mr. McKellen co-starred in two plays in repertory, an offering that the New York Times critic Ben Brantley called “absurdly enjoyable.” Mr. Stewart was Vladimir, the cerebral one, in Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” and the wealthy man of letters in Pinter’s “No Man’s Land.”

On American television, he portrayed a restless 17th-century spirit in “The Canterville Ghost” (1996); Captain Ahab in “Moby Dick” (1998); Scrooge in “A Christmas Carol” (1999), this time with a cast of 50 or so; a wealthy rancher pointedly named Lear in “King of Texas” (2002); and Henry II, opposite Glenn Close, in “The Lion in Winter” (2003).

Though his rock-steady Picard only rarely seemed to lighten up, Mr. Stewart was, in fact, no stranger to comedy.

He “got rather good at being silly,” The Sydney Morning Herald wrote. He played King Richard in Mel Brooks’s 1993 film spoof “Robin Hood: Men in Tights,” parodying Sean Connery with a thick Scottish accent. He appeared in about 120 episodes of the animated series “American Dad!” as Avery Bullock, a C. I. A. deputy director with too many character flaws to count.

When asked to name the most distinguished moments of his career, Mr. Stewart often mentioned — not altogether facetiously — his appearances on “The Simpsons,” in 1995 and 2013, and “Sesame Street” (1996), on which he performed the soliloquy “B or Not a B.”

When he hosted “Saturday Night Live” in 1994, one of his sketch characters was an erotic-cake baker with a fetish even his customers couldn’t deal with. And the legion of projects for which he served as narrator included “Ted,” Seth MacFarlane’s 2012 movie comedy about a teddy bear with the soul of a frat boy.

After hundreds of screen and stage roles, Mr. Stewart — Sir Patrick since his 2010 knighthood — gave one of his final performances in the “The Sheep Detectives” (2026), in which he was the voice of Sir Richfield, a wise old Boreray Blackface ram in a flock of crime solvers.

Mr. Stewart and Sheila Falconer, a choreographer, married in 1966, had two children, and divorced, almost a quarter-century later, in 1990. His marriage to Wendy Neuss, an American producer, also ended in divorce. The trigger in each divorce, he acknowledged in his memoir, was an affair with a younger woman. “In a life chockablock with joy and success,” he wrote, “my two failed marriages are my greatest regret.”

In 2013, he married Sunny Ozell, an American singer 38 years his junior, in a makeshift ceremony in a Mexican restaurant after a performance of “No Man’s Land” in Berkeley, Calif. His co-star Mr. McKellen, donning a cloak for the occasion, officiated, having been licensed by the Universal Life Church.

Mr. Stewart’s survivors include Ms. Ozell; his son, Daniel, who is also an actor; and his daughter, Sophie.

For Mr. Stewart, acting was a compulsion, he said, something he was driven to do. In 2011, a BBC interviewer asked him to describe the experience of being onstage. Mr. Stewart answered, “It feels like being a giant.”

And he saw no reason to quit, even in his later years.

“Acting was the thing that made me happy when I was 13 years old,” he wrote in his memoir, “and that is still the case 70 years later. I have so much more work to do. I am not done with the stage. I still want to try another TV comedy. I still have so many characters inside me that I need to let out.”

William McDonald was the obituaries editor of The Times from 2006 until 2026.

The New DNA Technology That Linked Ted Bundy to a 52-Year-Old Cold Case

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Software known as STRmix was instrumental in identifying Mr. Bundy’s DNA in a decades-old sample.

By Alexander Nazaryan

Recent advances in forensic science, including a powerful computer program able to reconstruct degraded DNA, allowed law enforcement officials in Utah this week to close a 52-year-old cold case and attribute the 1974 murder of a teenage girl to Ted Bundy, the serial killer.

Scientists at the Utah Bureau of Forensic Services linked Mr. Bundy, one of the nation’s most prolific and notorious spree killers, to the 1974 murder of Melissa Ann Smith. It was the second decades-old murder in the state attributed to Mr. Bundy this year. In April, investigators in Utah County determined that he had also murdered Laura Ann Aime.

Both were 17.

The body of Ms. Smith was found a few weeks before that of Ms. Aime. Now, their cases have been solved months apart, after the DNA found at one crime scene became instrumental in solving the other’s murder.

Before his execution in 1989, Mr. Bundy admitted to killing Ms. Aime. But it was not until this year that sophisticated new technology definitively connected him to her murder.

That technology not only closed the Aime case, but gave investigators new evidence with which to re-examine the Smith case.

“That Laura Aime case was what was key to solving the Melissa Smith case,” said Heather Mills, a forensic scientist manager at the Utah Bureau of Forensic Services.

Forensic scientists were able to connect the cases to each other and Mr. Bundy using a widely-available technology called STR genotyping as well as an innovative software known as STRmix.

STR stands for “short tandem repeat,” repeating DNA blocks found at certain locations throughout our genome. Those locations have names such as CSF1PO, and D8S1179. Each person has STRs of different lengths across the genome, so if two samples have repeating code of identical length at many different places, they are likely to have come from the same source.

“What we’re looking at here are regions that can be distinguished from each other, not on the basis of their sequence, necessarily, but rather on the basis of their length,” said Dan E. Krane, a bioinformatics expert at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio.

In 2011, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement uploaded Mr. Bundy’s DNA to CODIS, the nationwide forensic database, after a vial of his blood was found in a Florida courthouse.

About fifteen years later, investigators in Utah ran a degraded sample of DNA found at Ms. Aime’s crime scene and ran it through STRmix, a software program that performs a type of analysis called probabilistic genotyping.

Developed by scientists in New Zealand and Australia, STRmix, pronounced “star mix,” sorts through multiple sources of DNA found in a single sample. This can be especially useful if the DNA of several people are mixed at a crime scene. The software uses modeling to untangle genetic profiles and gives a statistical readout about the likelihood of a match.

“If two people were wearing the same T-shirt, you might think that that’s unusual or it could still be coincidence,” Shoumita Dasgupta, a biomedical geneticist at Boston University, said of how STRmix works. “However, if two people were wearing the same T-shirt, pants, socks, shoes, watch, necklace and glasses, then coincidence is starting to become less likely of an explanation.”

After identifying a likely DNA profile through STRmix, investigators ran it through the CODIS database. There was a match.

The results, Ms. Mills said, left little doubt that the DNA found on Ms. Aime belonged to Mr. Bundy.

The case of Ms. Smith presented a different challenge. “We had evidence from Melissa Smith, but it was Y-STR evidence,” Ms. Mills explained.

That Y refers to the Y chromosome, which meant that investigators knew it came from a male, but determining its origin would be more difficult.

“Y-STR testing can be really valuable to just target in on male-specific DNA,” Ms. Mills said. “It’s really helpful when you have low-level or degraded samples where you might have a lot of human DNA, but just this very small amount of male DNA,” she added.

That turned out to be the case when it came to analyzing genetic material from the Smith murder.

Y-STR testing looks for exactly the same type of repeating blocks as autosomal STR testing, only it is confined to the Y chromosome, making it a valuable tool in sexual assault cases.

There was, however, a hitch. The Ted Bundy DNA in the federal database was not going to be helpful this time around. “We don’t know what his Y-STR profile is, so we can have evidence, but we don’t have anything to compare it to,” Ms. Mills said of the predicament she and her colleagues in the forensic lab faced.

But investigators already knew that Mr. Bundy was the killer of Ms. Aime from their earlier analysis. “We know he’s the male in that sample,” Ms. Mills said. Y-STR testing, along with non-genetic evidence, confirmed that Ms. Smith was, like Ms. Aime, a victim of Mr. Bundy.

Ms. Mills said it was gratifying to see new technology revive old evidence.

“That’s why we keep working cold cases,” she said.

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The Trump administration is carrying out the most intense pressure campaign on Cuba in decades. The Cuban government says its plan is simply to endure.

Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla of Cuba during an interview with The New York Times this week. Credit... Graham Dickie for The New York Times

Supported by

By Jack Nicas

Reporting from the Cuban mission at the United Nations

Few foreign ministers are in a worse diplomatic position than Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla of Cuba.

His country is nearly out of oil. It can hardly receive other goods. The Trump administration wants to topple the government. And its allies have largely vanished.

But in an exclusive interview this week, Mr. Rodríguez projected confidence that the current Cuban government would survive President Trump. That is because, he said, its strategy is to simply endure, much as it has for six decades, in the hope that Washington moves on or shifts course.

“For as long as it takes,” he said. “U. S. policy toward Cuba will change. It has to. It’s inevitable.”

His reasoning? A majority of Americans and foreign governments oppose the U. S. pressure on Cuba and, for decades, it has failed to cause change.

“For 60 years now, U. S. policy toward Cuba hasn’t worked,” he said, “while Cuba’s policy of resisting and adapting to that aggression has.”

Mr. Rodríguez, 68, has served as foreign minister for 17 years and has been a Cuban diplomat since 1993 — a career primarily focused on countering U. S. policy. But, he said, he has never encountered a U. S. pressure campaign like this one.

Since January, the Trump administration has sought to make the Cuban government submit to its demands by imposing intensifying sanctions and an oil blockade on the island. The measures have triggered Cuba’s worst energy and economic crisis in decades, leading to prolonged blackouts, shuttered schools and a disintegrating health care system. The Cuban government’s frustration broke through on the floor of the United Nations on Tuesday, when Mr. Rodríguez directly confronted Mike Waltz, the U. S. ambassador to the U. N., in a spat that was captured on video.

Less than two minutes into a speech by Mr. Waltz in which he accused Cuban officials of corruption, members of the Cuban delegation began shouting and banging their hands on a table. Mr. Rodríguez formally objected, his third time interrupting a U. S. diplomat’s speech at the U. N. in the past year.

But this time he marched up the aisle with the Cuban delegation in tow, lodging their complaints within a few feet of where Mr. Waltz was standing.

“You’re a liar!” one Cuban diplomat screamed at him.

“Back up!” Mr. Waltz shouted back. “Do you understand who you’re dealing with?”

It was perhaps the most heated altercation between U. S. and Cuban officials in years, and it reflected Havana’s growing desperation and Washington’s increasingly belligerent posture.

On Monday, the U. S. Embassy in Cuba posted a photo of the top American diplomat on the island meeting with the top American military general overseeing the Caribbean. “Much to discuss about Cuba,” read the caption.

Mr. Trump mused about deploying a warship off the island’s coast to intimidate the Cuban government. And Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently made an extraordinary public call to recruit spies in Cuba to aid the U. S. effort against the government. “Seize this opportunity to create the change you desire,” he wrote.

But all the intimidation has failed to make the Cuban government yield.

“Honestly, I have no idea what the secretary of state is trying to do with those posts,” Mr. Rodríguez said of Mr. Rubio’s call for spies. “They come across as a bit childish.”

The Cuban government has lasted longer than many expected under the oil blockade. That is partly because the government has stretched out its fuel supplies by rationing electricity and building solar parks.

In the meantime, the Trump administration has signaled that it is willing to be patient. Mr. Rubio has said change could take years.

In a statement, Tommy Pigott, a State Department spokesman, blamed worsening conditions in Cuba on the Cuban government and said the United States was sending humanitarian aid. “The failing Cuban regime continues to blame the United States and everyone else for their own incompetence and corruption,” he said.

Mr. Pigott added that “President Trump continues to apply pressure to drive much more substantial economic and political reforms” in Cuba.

U. S. officials have acknowledged that they are seeking a sympathetic and malleable figure in the Cuban government, much like Venezuela’s new interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez. But Mr. Rubio’s public plea for informants suggests that they may be struggling to find one.

When asked about his post this week, Mr. Rubio told reporters, “We think Cuba needs very dramatic change,” then added that “it’s a totally different case from Venezuela.”

Mr. Rodríguez said that talks were continuing with U. S. officials — including in-person meetings and phone calls and WhatsApp messages — but that little progress was being made. “It’s very difficult for talks to progress when they’re constantly accompanied by threats,” he said.

Ric Herrero, director of the Cuba Study Group, which pushes for more dialogue between Washington and Havana, said that Mr. Rodríguez’s stance of trying to wait out the Trump administration was shortsighted.

“It’s easy for Bruno to claim that they’re there resisting when the ones that are really bearing the brunt of it are the Cuban people,” he said.

Cuba may also find it much harder to maintain its resilience than in years past. Its government long relied upon Russia or Venezuela to help it stand up to U. S. pressure, but those allies are now largely gone. Russia sent a large tanker of oil in March but has declined to test the U. S. blockade since. Venezuela is effectively controlled by Washington.

“The hard fact is that Cuba is alone,” Mr. Herrero said. “They can resist, but it’s just managed decline. Ultimately you’re heading toward the abyss.”

Mr. Rodríguez disputed any suggestion that Cuba was collapsing or that it had been abandoned on the world stage. He pointed to decades of U. N. resolutions that denounced U. S. trade embargoes on Cuba.

On Wednesday, 130 nations again sided with Cuba on such a resolution, yet it was one of the island’s lowest levels of support ever. Seventeen nations voted against the resolution, or 10 more than last year, with Colombia, Costa Rica and Ecuador switching their votes. Another 25 abstained, or 16 more than last year, including Germany, Italy, South Korea and the Dominican Republic.

Those results largely reflect the Trump administration’s success in persuading and pressuring nations to support its Cuba policy, or to at least look the other away.

Mr. Rodríguez argued that the American lobbying, as well its decision to increase sanctions, showed the Cuban government’s strength.

“If they really think Cuba’s strategy and the Cuban state are so ineffective, why go to all this trouble?” he asked.

Despite Mr. Rodríguez’s contention that Havana can simply ride out the Trump administration, the Cuban government is enacting change. Earlier this year, it announced the most sweeping economic measures since the Cuban revolution in 1959, including allowing private banks, selling shares in state companies and removing many restrictions on foreign investment and private businesses.

Mr. Rodríguez claimed that the slow economic liberalization of Cuba — one of the world’s few communist countries — was being done not to appease the Trump administration but to respond to global economic challenges.

“It opens many new opportunities to private capital, foreign investors and companies from various countries,” Mr. Rodríguez said. “But the Cuban economy will remain socialist.”

At the same time, he said, American companies should invest.

“We wouldn’t allow the United States to control sectors of the Cuban economy,” he said. “But American companies are competitive, and we’d welcome them in Cuba.”

Jack Nicas is The Times’s Mexico City bureau chief, leading coverage of Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

Big Tech’s Data Center Blitz Is Burning Through Cash and Scaring Wall Street

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Amazon on Thursday became the latest tech company to announce swelling investments in A. I. amid stumbling share prices.

By Karen Weise

Reporting from Seattle

Four of the tech industry’s biggest companies set a new spending record in the last quarter as they raced to build artificial intelligence, leading to a worrisome new milestone: most of them are spending more cash on data centers than they get from running their businesses.

Over the past two weeks, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta said they were on track to spend more than $720 billion this year on data centers and other capital expenses — roughly triple what they spent just two years ago. And all are expected to spend even more next year. The investments are so large, the A. I. boom accounts for much of the resilience in the U. S. economy.

The buying binge has sent them scrambling to fund their ambitions by taking out loans and in some cases selling more stock to get the cash they need. While their core businesses generally remain healthy, those moves have unsettled investors who worry whose bets will pay off.

By the time markets closed on Thursday, Google’s stock had fallen more than 12 percent the day after reporting its quarterly earnings. Then, after Amazon reported its results showing heavy spending, its shares traded down too, falling more than 4 percent. Last week, Meta’s shares fell 7 percent after its results showed it was using so much cash that the company was issuing new stock to raise funds.

“Slight differences is causing a lot of volatility,” said David Tsui, a technology credit analyst at S&P Global Ratings. He said there could be several more years of uncertainty because “you’re spending now and a lot of the return is going to be years down the road.”

It’s not just some of the largest tech companies making this giant bet. Oracle and SpaceX have dramatically boosted their spending, and borrowing, and now have capital expenses quickly approaching their much larger rivals.

Investors have increasingly kept an eye on a metric known as free cash flow, which looks at how much cash a company has after paying for both its day-to-day costs and for new capital expenses. For every company but Microsoft, free cash flow has turned negative, a sign of just how much they are banking that their A. I. bets will pan out.

If the companies keep adding to their spending faster than they can increase their sales and cash, “then we get a little bit more nervous,” Mr. Tsui said.

On Thursday, Amazon became the latest big tech company to report its quarterly results. It had $201.9 billion in sales, up 12 percent from a year earlier, and profit fell slightly to $20.7 billion. Both fell slightly short of what investors expected.

Amazon’s cloud computing division saw sales increase 39 percent to $46 billion, and its core retail business in North America grew 6 percent. Investors expected only modest growth because, unlike last year, the company’s popular annual Prime Day deal event was not in the third quarter for most large countries.

Its capital expenditures surpassed $75 billion, far more than doubling what it spent a year earlier.

The business created $168.3 billion in cash over the past year, up 29 percent. But after investments in data centers and other facilities, Amazon’s free cash flow fell to negative $42.4 billion, which it said primarily reflected its investments in A. I.

On Wednesday, Alphabet, Google’s parent company, disclosed that for the second quarter in a row, it had negative free cash flow because of its spending, even though its cloud computing business more than doubled in sales.

But its search business, the source of so much of its free cash, underperformed, underscoring investor worries that A. I. chatbots could erode its core advertising business. Google’s capital expenses more than doubled to $51 billion. It also signaled it could have more than $1 trillion in future commitments on leases and other obligations.

Last week, for the first time since soon after Meta went public in 2012, the company told investors that its free cash flow was negative as well. It also slightly increased what it had told investors it would spend on capital expenses, and disclosed more than $800 billion in additional future leases and other commitments.

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, told investors that making the most of its investments will be essential to expanding the early success of Muse, its personal A. I. agent, into a huge, profitable business.

“We want to make sure that we’ve built enough compute to be able to serve what we think is going to be 1 billion-plus people,” he said.

A number of the companies are issuing new stock, selling bonds and taking out loans to support their spending. On Monday, Meta said it would raise up to $95 billion from selling stock to fund its A. I. ambitions. That same day, SpaceX said it had secured $40 billion in loans to secure specialized A. I. chips.

Microsoft showed growth in its cloud and A. I. business while keeping costs in check. The company said it would have positive free cash flow at least through next summer, and if it needed to tap additional resources to raise cash, it would.

“We have lots of options to be able to tap the finance markets when they make sense and they’re attractive,” Amy Hood, the company’s finance chief said.

Microsoft’s revenue for the quarter was $92.3 billion, up 19 percent, and profit grew 32 percent to $36.6 billion. Sales of Azure, its main cloud computing and A. I. offering, grew 48 percent, and Microsoft told investors it would grow even more in the current quarter.

And its capital spending only grew 30 percent, to $45.2 billion — less than the $50 billion Microsoft previously said to expect. That reduction was at least in part because some of Microsoft’s suppliers were running behind schedule. It said it was still able to sell more computing power because it was using the resources it did have more efficiently.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

On Thursday morning, Microsoft filed the paperwork to issue its first new bonds in almost a decade. While its stock price was up Wednesday in late trading, its shares declined slightly on Thursday.

Tech companies are “in this existential play for market share,” said Will Sommer, a tech market economist at the research firm Gartner. “They’re willing to take losses to be the dominant provider of this market that we think will be worth trillions of dollars.”

Karen Weise writes about technology for The Times and is based in Seattle. Her coverage focuses on Amazon and Microsoft, two of the most powerful companies in America.

U. S. Expels Cuban Diplomat After Fiery Showdown at United Nations

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Tensions have risen between the United States and Cuba as the Trump administration tries to force the island’s Communist government to make drastic changes.

By Michael Crowley

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration expelled a Cuban diplomat from the United States on Wednesday, a day after a fiery shouting match between Cuba’s foreign minister and the U. S. ambassador to the U. N., Michael Waltz, at the United Nations General Assembly.

The State Department said that it told Cuba’s mission to the U. N. that its first secretary, Richard Tur de la Concepción, was “not welcome” in the United States after the Cuban swatted at the phone of a U. S. official who was filming him at close range in the main U. N. hall.

In a social media post on Wednesday, Mr. Waltz accused Mr. Tur de la Concepción of “assaulting” the American. He later told Fox News that the Cuban official would “be on a flight back to Havana and out of this country today.”

The unusual rancor in the typically staid hall came at a moment of renewed tension between Cuba and the United States. The Trump administration is applying intense pressure on Cuba’s Communist government, hoping to force it into dramatic reforms and possibly even collapse.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently called on Cubans to collaborate with the C. I. A. against their government. And President Trump told voters at a recent campaign rally in Florida that U. S. forces may “take care of Cuba” on their way back from Iran.

The drama began on Tuesday, as Mr. Waltz spoke against a resolution calling for an end to the longtime U. S. economic embargo against the island.

Speaking from the podium, Mr. Waltz accused Cuba’s leaders of repression, corruption and self-enrichment. Cuba’s foreign minister, Bruno Rodríguez, and other members of the country’s delegation began pounding on their desks and demanding points of order. Eventually they approached the rostrum to within a few feet of Mr. Waltz, who interrupted his remarks to rebuke them.

“Back up! Back up!” Mr. Waltz barked. “This isn’t Havana. You’re not going to intimidate me. Do you understand who you’re dealing with? This is America!”

The Cubans soon returned to their desks after the presiding officer paused the proceedings. Mr. Rodríguez was then granted time to respond to Mr. Waltz, whom he accused of being a liar. At some point during or after that sequence, Mr. Tur de la Concepción had an altercation with a U. S. official that was captured on video and posted on X by Mr. Waltz.

The video showed Mr. Tur de la Concepción standing near the side of the rostrum, slapping away the phone of the American U. N. official.

When a U. N. staff member approached, Mr. Tur de la Concepción could be heard protesting that the American was “violating my personal space.” The staff member then escorted a compliant Mr. Tur de la Concepción from the area.

Mr. Waltz charged on X that Mr. Tur de la Concepción had been “trying to intimidate UN staff” into cutting off his microphone “to silence me after I exposed the regime for the world to see.”

In a letter to the U. N. secretary general’s office, Cuba’s U. N. ambassador formally protested the episode, insisting that the American who was filming had harassed Mr. Tur de la Concepción.

The resolution calling for an end to the U. S. embargo has become an annual tradition at the United Nations. Even many countries critical of Cuba oppose U. S. sanctions on the island, saying they unduly harm the Cuban people and have accomplished little over many decades.

The Trump administration aggressively lobbied against the nonbinding measure this year, limiting it to 130 votes in favor, down from 165 votes a year ago.

That total marked a 20-year low, according to the U. N.’s news office, which says support peaked at 191 votes in 2015 and 2017. Just 59 countries backed the resolution when it was first proposed in 1992.

Michael Crowley covers the State Department and U. S. foreign policy for The Times. He has reported from nearly three dozen countries and often travels with the secretary of state.

What’s Next for Israel? Four Writers Decode the Election Results.

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Round table

By Diana ButtuYossi Klein HaleviDahlia ScheindlinBret Stephens and Daniel J. Wakin

Ms. Buttu is a former adviser to P. L. O. negotiators. Mr. Halevi is author of “Letters to My Palestinian Neighbor.” Dr. Scheindlin is a enior analyst at Haaretz. Mr. Stephens is an Opinion columnist. Mr. Wakin is an editor in Times Opinion.

Tuesday’s historic elections in Israel ended in deadlock, setting the stage for negotiations and machinations to create a majority in the Knesset that could form a government. Two blocs are now at loggerheads: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right governing coalition and an opposition grouping led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff.

In a written online conversation, Daniel J. Wakin, Times Opinion’s deputy international editor, discussed the election with Diana Buttu, Yossi Klein Halevi, Dahlia Scheindlin and Bret Stephens. The text has been edited for length and clarity.

Daniel J. Wakin: It’s been two days since Israelis went to the polls. It was the highest voter turnout in more than 25 years, but neither of the two main blocs will be able to form a government on its own. What do you think is the most likely solution to this logjam?

Bret Stephens: Likeliest? Mr. Netanyahu fails to form a government but continues to govern and hopes events — like another military confrontation with Iran — turn in his favor when another election is called sometime next year.

Dahlia Scheindlin: It’s hard to keep the permutations straight: political stalemate and new elections? A minority government? A unity government? Bloc defections? The biggest question is whether any bloc will do the obvious and include an Arab party in the coalition — those two parties hold 19 seats combined, a record.

Diana Buttu: Israel uses the claim that Palestinians who hold Israeli citizenship can vote as somehow being a defense against the charge of apartheid. But here we see clearly that despite the fact that Palestinians, who make up about 20 percent of the population, showed they wanted an end to this government, our votes are being discounted. The opposition, despite being given an opportunity to seize power from Mr. Netanyahu by forming a coalition with the Palestinian-led parties, cannot seem to get over their racism to finally oust him.

Yossi Klein Halevi: The opposition has three options, none of them good. The first is to go for new elections, in which Mr. Netanyahu is likely to either maintain his support or even increase it. For example, the many thousands of Israelis living abroad who came in just to vote against Mr. Netanyahu will not come a second time. The second option is to depend on the outside support of the two Arab parties and create a minority government. The third option is to enter a so-called unity government with Mr. Netanyahu, but no one trusts him to uphold a rotation agreement — and in any case the main goal of the opposition has been to unseat him.

Scheindlin: Personally, I think Yossi’s second option is a great one. And why only from the outside? Arab parties should join a coalition directly.

Stephens: I don’t think Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc is going to be eager to team up with an Arab opposition that refuses to describe Hamas as a terrorist organization. The problem is that there are so many poison pills on every side of this vote: The Eisenkot bloc won’t sit with Mr. Netanyahu out of personal suspicion, or with the Haredi — ultra-Orthodox — parties allied with the prime minister because the issue of exempting the Haredi from conscription is at the top of that bloc’s concerns. Mr. Netanyahu isn’t eager to form a power-sharing agreement with Mr. Eisenkot if he sees a path to a full term in office. So deadlock is what I suspect we’re going to get until a new election is called.

Halevi: After Oct. 7, no party can sit in an Israeli government whose members don’t recognize Hamas as an enemy. The Israeli Jewish public will not accept it. This is not about racism, though certainly anti-Arab sentiment has spread since the Hamas massacre.

Scheindlin: All of the Arab party leaders have condemned everything about Oct. 7 — they have condemned terror in all possible ways except signing a metaphorical declaration that Israel’s Zionist political leaders are demanding, mostly to exclude them. Don’t worry — when they want the Arab parties in, they’ll find a way. If they want to keep Arab Palestinian parties in Israel out, nothing will satisfy them.

Buttu: Palestinians do not want to be part of a government that carries out genocide, ethnic cleansing and which supports the occupation, and with it the settler terrorism. The Palestinian-led parties are parties that are calling for equality and justice for all. All Israeli governments have sought to maintain Jewish supremacy.

Stephens: Well, for an “apartheid regime,” as Israel is so inaccurately accused of being, it’s remarkable that Israeli Arabs turned out to vote in record numbers.

Wakin: What do you think the exclusion of Palestinian-led parties from a coalition would say about the nature of Israeli democracy?

Scheindlin: Democracy in Israel has been partial and ambiguous from the start. That’s partly due to a reluctance to clarify religion and state relations or final borders, but very much due to resistance to equality for Palestinians — either as citizens, or later, those under occupation. The effort to delegitimize their vote (via Likud claims of “stop the steal”) or exclude them from coalition-building is the latest manifestation of efforts to claim democracy via elections alone, while eroding the meaning of that process.

Buttu: The exclusion of Palestinian-led parties says that Israel is a racist state founded on apartheid. Can you imagine any other place that claims to be a democracy saying to 20 percent of the population, “Your vote does not count”? But this is Israel.

The Palestinian-led parties are seeking simple things: (1) a halt to the demolition of our homes; (2) finally the addressing of the issue of organized crime rings to which the government has turned a blind eye; (3) an end to the race-baiting that Netanyahu and his government have engaged in as well as the scores of racist pieces of legislation that have been introduced and passed.

Halevi: And yet we have the precedent of Raam, the United Arab List party, participating in the government headed by Naftali Bennett in 2021. Oct. 7 has set the bar higher: Israeli Jews need basic reassurance that their potential Arab partners in governing Israel accept the premise that the country has the right to defend itself against radical Islamism.

Wakin: While this is an election involving many parties, in some ways it came down to a referendum on two men. Yossi, Bret — was Gadi Eisenkot a compelling alternative to Benjamin Netanyahu? Why did he fall short?

Halevi: On paper, he was an ideal alternative to Netanyahu: The first serious Mizrahi — a Jew with family roots in the Arab world — candidate for prime minister, a former chief of staff of the armed forces, a bereaved father who lost a son in Gaza. But he lacks political experience, and Israelis tend to be wary of ex-generals who enter the political system too soon after leaving the army. Mr. Netanyahu succeeded in portraying him — falsely, I believe — as an unsuccessful military commander who would be irresolute against Israel’s enemies.

Stephens: It’s a truism in politics that you can’t run on biography alone. It’s also a truism in Israeli politics never to count Bibi out. He’s an exceptionally skilled politician who, for all of the disasters over which he’s presided — Oct. 7 above all — has also presided over some notable successes. Israel has largely re-established its regional reputation for military fearsomeness. Israel’s economic growth, despite three years of war, is one of the strongest in the world. He has a close personal relationship with Donald Trump, which, distasteful as it may be to many people, is vital to Israel’s security, at least for the next two years.

Wakin: What specifically are you watching in the coming days and weeks as the parties search for a way to form a coalition?

Halevi: I’m hoping that Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, who has already gone so far in reaching out to the Jewish public, will make the essential statement labeling Hamas as a terrorist regime. If he does so, my sense is that the opposition parties will accept him once again as a coalition partner. If that doesn’t happen, Mr. Eisenkot may have no choice but to negotiate a joint government with Mr. Netanyahu, in which the opposition will demand a bill to draft the ultra-Orthodox into the military and end the vast subsidies for the ultra-Orthodox community that are threatening the long-term stability of the Israeli economy.

Scheindlin: Those of us who are committed to liberal democratic principles are longing for the leading politicians of the opposition bloc to invite an Arab party into the coalition or, second best, support it from the outside. There were demonstrations — albeit small — on Wednesday demanding this, and petitions. But we know it’s a long shot. More likely, I’ll look for defections from the known blocs or options for a minority government. But first, President Isaac Herzog has to tap someone to form a government, and it could well be Mr. Netanyahu.

Stephens: The best Israeli governments have been national unity governments: in 1967 during the Six-Day War, in the mid-1980s during the economic crisis, at the beginning of this century during the second intifada. I don’t envision that happening this time, except perhaps for one reason: President Herzog extends a full pardon to Mr. Netanyahu in exchange for a power-sharing deal with Mr. Eisenkot.

Buttu: I will be watching to see just how far this anti-Palestinian campaign of trying to discredit the vote goes and who is supporting it, and who is not. As a Palestinian living in Haifa, I face racism on a daily basis. I have grown used to having my very existence and identity challenged. In a recent poll, roughly a third of Jewish Israelis said that Arabs with Israeli citizenship should not have the right to vote. What’s shocking isn’t just the figure: It’s that the question was asked in the first place.

Wakin: Yossi mentioned earlier that new elections would benefit the Netanyahu camp because the out-of-country voters would not be making another trip back. How else would Mr. Netanyahu — or the opposition — benefit from new elections, if at all?

Halevi: The opposition generated tremendous energy. We haven’t seen this level of optimism for many years. The fact that Netanyahu has proved that he can’t be dislodged will be deeply demoralizing, and will likely affect the ability of the opposition to mobilize its public.

Scheindlin: We don’t know how many returnees actually voted or which side they supported. If we have new elections, Arab turnout will surely be lower.

Stephens: “Events, my dear boy, events.” The line, widely attributed to Harold Macmillan, the midcentury British prime minister, was supposed to describe what politicians most fear. For Mr. Netanyahu it’s what he most wants — crises that give him a chance to change the conversation in his favor. He thinks his life’s mission is to bring about the fall of the regime in Tehran, and he is going to do everything in his power over the next few months to make that happen, probably with the broad backing of the Israeli public. If he succeeds, he could win another mandate by a wide margin.

Wakin: Dahlia, Yossi, Diana — what do you think of the situation with Iran? There are indications that the United States and Israel might already be making preparations for further attacks on Iran after the U. S. midterms. How — if at all — would that action impact negotiations if they are still underway?

Scheindlin: Mr. Netanyahu prefers to cling to every possible day in office, and if there’s a chance that a war would distract or delay coalition negotiations, he would gain. I don’t want to claim that’s the reason he would start a war, though many Israelis would certainly believe this.

Halevi: Mr. Netanyahu has corrupted the political system, divided our society and taken no responsibility for the greatest disaster in the country’s history. But this much needs to be acknowledged: He has consistently led the international campaign to stop Iran from going nuclear. No matter who becomes prime minister, the confrontation with Iran will continue. What began on Oct. 7 was the Iranian-Israeli war. That war is not over.

Stephens: There isn’t much that Tehran, Jerusalem and Washington (under Trump) agree on, except maybe for this: War and diplomacy aren’t opposites. They are complements. What the Trump administration now seems to envisage is a short campaign of intense strikes intended to change Iran’s approach to negotiations. So far that hasn’t succeeded, and I’m not sure how effective it will be going forward. Israel, I think, is prepared for a longer military campaign if there’s a reasonable chance of doing lasting, possibly irreversible damage to the Tehran regime.

Buttu: Mr. Netanyahu’s political career (and in particular this election) is premised on the idea of forever wars. Forever wars keep him in power even though it is abundantly clear that he is the instigator of these wars. In short, he starts the fire and sells Israelis the water needed to put out the fire. So he will try to start another war to make it more difficult to get rid of him. We’ve seen this movie; we know the ending.

Halevi: Diana’s dismissal of Israel’s need to militarily confront Iran, a nuclearizing regime that has declared war against our existence, is itself an indication of why many Israeli Jews are wary of including Arab parties in the coalition. In conversations I’ve had with Arab Israeli political leaders, it was clear that there is no military action on Israel’s part that would be acceptable to them.

Buttu: We have existential concerns, too. Ours are real and being played out in real time before our very eyes as you watch. Our land has been eaten up, we are hearing daily promises about ethnic cleansing, settlers are terrorizing our lives and members of the Knesset are calling for our erasure. This isn’t theoretical; it is real.

Halevi: Absolutely. But alienating even Israeli Jewish liberals by convincing us that the goal of the Palestinian national movement remains the destruction of a Jewish state in any borders is not going to change Jewish attitudes.

Buttu: It isn’t my job to convince Jewish Israelis. The choice is theirs: Mr. Netanyahu or getting over their racism. I suspect they will choose Mr. Netanyahu.

Halevi: Much of the Jewish public voted against Mr. Netanyahu. Portraying us all as racists doesn’t advance the cause of coexistence within Israeli society or peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

Scheindlin: Why are we even distinguishing between Jewish and Arab votes in Israel? That shouldn’t be acceptable in any country striving for democracy.

I think Bret’s comment about Israelis being prepared for a longer-term war with Iran leaves out the precipitous decline in public trust that the war could achieve its goals this spring and the massive disruption to life over just five weeks — not to mention damage and loss of life — that were deeply traumatic for every Israeli citizen, in addition to ongoing war in Gaza and imminent war in the West Bank if conditions don’t change. Jewish Israelis will certainly support it at the start, I guess, but not with a blank check.

Wakin: What will this whole political process mean for Israel’s place in the world?

Scheindlin: Israel enjoyed kind words from international observers in the moment after its high-turnout election. But Israel’s position among Western allies and even the United States will continue to decline — like the sharp decline in U. S. opinion surveys over recent years — without a change of policy.

Buttu: I hope that people truly examine the positions that are being espoused by all of the political parties, including the two Palestinian-led parties. When they do, they will see that with the exception of those two parties (now with 19 seats), Israeli politicians, reflecting Israeli society, believe in the idea of Jewish supremacy; they support genocide, ethnic cleansing, occupation, land theft and a two-tiered system. This is something that needs to be confronted — and it can.

Halevi: A unity government between the opposition and Mr. Netanyahu is a compelling way to help forestall the isolation of Israel. That would mean a government committed to reining in settler violence, forgoing the current government’s goal of annexing the West Bank and ending the assault on Israel’s democratic institutions. My concern is shoring up the resolve of our friends around the world to continue to defend us. They need us to be morally credible.

Stephens: There’s a myth that Israel used to have standing in the world but it somehow dissipated in the last several decades. The truth is that Israel has been fighting for its life, against formidable odds since 1948 by doing what it thought was right irrespective of whether it was popular. The ultimate truth about this election is that Israelis of all backgrounds, including its Arab citizens, voted in record numbers because they care about the future of their state. That’s something to admire, even if the result is nothing anyone on this panel — or, for that matter, most of Israel itself — seems to like.

Diana Buttu is a lawyer and former adviser to P. L. O. negotiators. Yossi Klein Halevi is a senior fellow of the Shalom Hartman Institute and author of “Letters to My Palestinian Neighbor.” Dahlia Scheindlin is a public opinion expert, political strategist and senior analyst at the Haaretz newspaper.

Source photographs by Amir Levy and Chris McGrath and Keystone/Hulton Archive, via Getty Images.

7 Memorable Patrick Stewart Performances

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Patrick Stewart (1940-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

The actor’s long and varied career included Shakespearean roles, “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” comedy and a stint in the Marvel Universe.

By Claire Moses

While Patrick Stewart, who died on Wednesday at 86, might have been best known for his role as the noble starship captain on “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” his long career was filled with memorable roles.

Mr. Stewart was a lauded stage performer, star of the small screen, familiar voice-over actor and an understated comedic presence.

Here are seven performances to remember him by.

Before he became a television star, Mr. Stewart was a celebrated stage actor in his native Britain. He began working with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. Among his best known roles were King Claudius in “Hamlet” and the titular troubled nobleman in “Macbeth.”

“I acted Macbeth for exactly 365 days,” Mr. Stewart told The New York Times in 2023. “The role got into me so deeply it dominated my life at the time and caused me to drink too much alcohol after the performance was over.”

Mr. Stewart’s “Star Trek” captain, Jean-Luc Picard, drank a lot of tea on the deck of the Starship Enterprise. Though Capt. Picard was French, he seemed to like his drinks English: His order from the ship’s food replicator was usually the same: “Tea, Earl Grey, hot.”

“I suggested lapsang souchong,” a Chinese black tea, “but the producers thought that nobody would know what it was,” Mr. Stewart told Britain’s Neon Magazine in 1998.

Mr. Stewart, well known for his many Shakespearean roles, was also versed in comedy. He hosted “Saturday Night Live” in 1994, and in one sketch played an erotic-cake baker with a fetish even his customers couldn’t deal with.

He also lent his voice, with its regal English diction, to a legion of projects for which he served as narrator, including “Ted,” Seth MacFarlane’s comedy about a teddy bear with the soul of a frat boy.

He also sought to take Shakespeare to a younger audience. In 1996, he turned perhaps the most famous passage from “Hamlet” into a rousing performance on “Sesame Street” called “B or Not a B.”

Captain Picard is one of 20th century television’s most famous characters. It was therefore only a matter of time until he became an internet sensation.

Played by Mr. Stewart as stoic and thoughtful, the captain rarely displayed strong emotions but often registered displeasure by putting his palm to his face. The move became an internet meme, the most famous version of which comes from an episode of the third season of the show. “I love that photograph,” Mr. Stewart told the website Nerdist.

He was also not averse to silliness or self-mockery. He appeared on more than 90 episodes of the animated series “American Dad” as Avery Bullock, a C. I. A. deputy director with too many character flaws to count, often poking fun at himself or at “Star Trek.”

Mr. Stewart was Charles Xavier, a. k. a. Professor X, in several “X-Men” movies, playing a wealthy telepath in a wheelchair who leads other mutants with superpowers. Most recently, he reprised the role for “Avengers: Doomsday,” which is scheduled for release in December.

“I still continue to receive interesting offers and I love being challenged by new work,” he told the website TV Insider in July. “I can’t imagine ever officially ‘retiring.’ I’ll always and forever be an actor.”

Claire Moses is a Times reporter in London, focused on coverage of breaking and trending news.

A Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang was found to be passing intelligence to Beijing. President Trump was briefed and took no action.

Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, is influential at the White House on technology policy and has developed a close relationship with President Trump. Credit... Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times

Supported by

By Jonathan SwanMaggie HabermanAna SwansonPaul MozurTripp Mickle and Julian E. Barnes

American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence.

A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A. I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing.

But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive.

For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A. I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump’s, set off alarms at the White House.

Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.

This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts.

American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A. I. chips.

But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Ms. Huang had insights into Mr. Trump’s thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge A. I. models.

Mr. Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services, people briefed on the surveillance said.

The surveillance of Ms. Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia said the company that employed Ms. Huang, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C. E. O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Nvidia is “confident that if the U. S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” Mr. Rizzo said. Customers like Megaspeed, he added, “receive ordinary business information — not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”

The White House, the C. I. A. and the National Security Agency all declined to comment. In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said that its “current leadership” takes the matter “extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations.” It added that “outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U. S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating.”

Megaspeed later added in a statement that it “cannot respond to a media trial and welcomes formal, evidence-based investigation.”

Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment. It is not clear how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed. A person familiar with Megaspeed’s operations said that Ms. Huang had become less active in the company in the wake of the American investigations.

Asked about the American conclusion that Ms. Huang has been collecting intelligence on behalf of Beijing, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said the United States was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China.

When Mr. Trump was initially briefed on the intelligence last year, U. S. officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Ms. Huang was gathering information for the Chinese. It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment, but some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Mr. Huang could have remained unaware of what they had concluded was her intelligence-gathering role for China.

Questions about whether Megaspeed was providing A. I. chips to China became public through articles published last year by The New York Times and Bloomberg News.

Mr. Huang has successfully lobbied the administration during Mr. Trump’s second term to loosen regulations on artificial intelligence companies and roll back tighter restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China. He also negotiated a deal with Mr. Trump that allowed the U. S. government to take a 25 percent stake of certain Nvidia chips that the government allows to be sold to China.

The close relationship between the president and Mr. Huang has impeded efforts to clamp down on Nvidia’s chip sales abroad, current and former U. S. officials said. They described some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia as having ground to a halt within the Commerce Department, the agency in charge of regulating chip exports.

Nvidia has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China. Mr. Rizzo said China’s government has “blocked U. S. AI chips, protecting its own industry.”

Many questions about the situation remain unanswered, at least publicly.

It is unclear whether concerns about protecting the surveillance played a role in the decision not to inform Mr. Huang. Telling him could have alerted Ms. Huang that she was being watched, which is a common reason intelligence officials hesitate to give defensive briefings.

It could not be determined which intelligence agency or agencies have been involved in monitoring Ms. Huang, or what prompted them to start. It is also not clear under what circumstances Ms. Huang began gathering information for Beijing, what information she passed along or its value to China.

The previous reporting about Ms. Huang by The Times described her meteoric and somewhat mysterious rise. A Chinese businesswoman and investor, she eventually became a top official with Megaspeed, which the Commerce Department, toward the end of the Biden administration, began to suspect was helping China evade U. S. prohibitions and gain access to the computing power of Nvidia chips.

The U. S. government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data center in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there.

Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Ms. Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her.

The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed over this year to the Justice Department, administration officials said.

While the U. S. government has restricted companies from exporting the most advanced Nvidia chips into China since 2022, some firms have been found to illegally smuggle them over the Chinese border. Other companies have legally set up businesses that buy large numbers of chips to build data centers in Southeast Asia that serve Chinese firms.

Some U. S. officials and lawmakers consider this to be a problematic loophole, and the Biden administration restricted this practice. Mr. Trump rolled back those rules. The administration is weighing whether to tighten them again.

Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centers and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. It has bought Nvidia chips from the American arm of Inspur, a Chinese server maker. The U. S. has blacklisted Inspur’s parent company for funneling technology to the Chinese military, though the U. S. firm remains free of sanctions.

Megaspeed has then provided that computing power to Alibaba and other Chinese companies. U. S. officials believe the firm is one piece of a sprawling international effort by Chinese companies to access the chips needed to build and run A. I. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China.

Megaspeed’s sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced A. I. equipment containing Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records obtained from ImportGenius, a trade platform. It was an exceptional amount of money for a small, obscure company.

Nvidia and Megaspeed have continued to do business this year. The limited data available for most of this year shows that Megaspeed and its affiliates kept buying Nvidia products, often through intermediaries.

To prevent chips from being smuggled to China, Nvidia evaluates buyers before approving a chip purchase and sometimes checks later whether the buyer still has the chips. The company continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. Megaspeed advertised the relationship as recently as this month. In a job ad, Megaspeed’s Indonesian branch called itself “a premier business partner of Nvidia.”

Megaspeed has continued serving its primary client, Alibaba, according to that person and other tech industry analysts.

In June 2024, just weeks before Megaspeed began its purchases, photos posted to LinkedIn showed Mr. Huang alongside Ms. Huang at a bar in Taipei following a local technology trade show. They drank whiskey with other A. I. executives.

One year later, in May 2025, they were seen together again, leaving a restaurant in Taipei after a business dinner with other A. I. suppliers. She waited behind Mr. Huang as he spoke to Taiwanese journalists outside the restaurant.

Those details were described in a Times article last October. But the deeper intelligence involving Ms. Huang remained closely held inside the administration.

People with knowledge of the matter said U. S. agencies had been conducting electronic surveillance of Ms. Huang. That surveillance showed that she was in contact with an American citizen.

U. S. intelligence agencies generally cannot legally surveil American citizens without a court order. But when communications involving Americans turn up in surveillance, citizens can be identified to government agencies who can show a need for the information through a process known as unmasking. In this case, the unmasking process identified Mr. Huang as the U. S. citizen.

Before 2025, Mr. Huang seldom visited Washington and stayed out of politics.

But as the Trump administration was considering a ban on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Mr. Huang and his wife traveled to Mar-a-Lago, the president’s private club and residence in Florida, to meet with Mr. Trump at a high-end donors’ dinner and sell him on the idea of allowing chip companies to do business with Beijing.

At the event, according to people briefed on the discussion there, the Nvidia executive appeared to wow the president with his descriptions of his own rise.

Nvidia later donated at least $20 million to Mr. Trump’s ballroom fund, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The company also pledged to invest $500 billion on manufacturing in the United States.

And when the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, visited the White House for a state dinner last month, Mr. Huang was at the head table.

Last year, Mr. Trump approved the sale of an older generation of Nvidia chips to China in return for a cut of the revenue. As the president sought warmer ties with China ahead of his meeting with Mr. Xi, he entertained a push by Mr. Huang to sell the Chinese even more powerful technology, rankling some administration officials and Republicans in Congress, before ultimately deciding against it.

People who have watched the two men interact say Mr. Trump has been won over by the lavish praise Mr. Huang has given the president in public, and his immense wealth and success.

It is not clear when Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang of Megaspeed first met. Before The Times reported last year on her role in purchasing Nvidia chips, Ms. Huang posted photos of herself with Mr. Huang on her social media feed, according to a person who viewed it.

Ms. Huang has a slim profile on the Chinese internet. She has described herself as Megaspeed’s chief executive, and the company listed her as its managing director for its first eight months before removing her from that role in its corporate paperwork. Megaspeed’s current director is from Singapore but has recently lived in Shanghai, according to business records and his social media accounts.

According to information posted online by a Chinese investment fund where Ms. Huang worked, she was formerly employed in China as a TV reporter, but The Times could not find any information to verify that. She later worked at several major Chinese banks, then joined a Shanghai-based fund, Hexi Capital, which has invested in a variety of semiconductor- and A. I.-related firms, according to WireScreen, a data platform.

According to tech investors familiar with the company, Ms. Huang and her associates bragged about her connections to Mr. Huang and used it to raise funds and promote their fast-expanding network of businesses, which has invested alongside the Chinese government in data centers around China. In Southeast Asia, Megaspeed has continued to pitch new data centers, hire employees and trumpet its close connections to Nvidia, according to industry analysts, online job posts and other records.

Megaspeed is pushing ahead with construction of a large data center in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new A. I. facilities have risen between palm oil plantations. In a stock filing last month, a Malaysian property developer said it had received the final payment for the 53-acre plot where a Megaspeed subsidiary has promised to build the data center.

When a Times journalist visited recently, rows of construction materials sat between the skeletal frames of partially built data centers. Outside the park, backhoe loaders dug into the reddish brown earth as workers installed concrete pipes.

The company had already secured the chips necessary for the build out, according to a person with knowledge of the plans.

Pei-Lin Wu and Zunaira Saieed contributed reporting.
