Why Miami Is a Destination for Latin America’s Political Exiles

The New York Times October 29, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The city’s Hispanic majority, news media reach and air links to Latin America have made it an ideal base for politicians escaping their home countries.

By Francesca Regalado and Victor Mather

When Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday from Brazil, he joined a long list of Latin American politicians who have fled to the city to escape arrest or prosecution at home.

Mr. Bolsonaro lost Sunday’s election to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and Brazilian authorities asked him to surrender his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation. He crossed to Argentina by land on Tuesday night with his wife and two daughters, then took a private plane to Ecuador and onward to Miami.

From there, he issued a statement claiming that the election was fraudulent and declared himself the “legitimate president-elect” of Brazil.

Exiled political leaders from Venezuela, Cuba, Nicaragua and other countries have found supporters in the Miami area, which is home to large Latino immigrant communities and is connected to major cities in the Caribbean and Central and South America by dozens of daily nonstop flights.

“Miami is the hub,” said Guilherme Casarões, an associate professor of political science at Florida International University in Miami.

He noted that the influx of anti-Castro Cubans starting in the 1960s, and especially since the 1980s, fomented a strong anti-communism sentiment in the city and a rightward drift in general. Many who have been exiled to or sought refuge in Miami, including Mr. Bolsonaro, come from the right side of the political spectrum.

Mr. Bolsonaro also has the support of President Trump, who is ever-present in South Florida. Mar-a-Lago, the president’s private club and residence in Palm Beach, “is the informal capital of the country,” Dr. Casarões said.

Many Latin American exiles may also find it comfortable.

“Miami is a crossroads, with direct flights to nearly every Latin American capital, a language and daily life that feel familiar, and lawyers, banks and media already experienced in receiving people from the region,” said Luisa Turbino Torres, an assistant professor of political science at Florida Atlantic University in Boca Raton who studies Brazilian politics and social movements. “This makes it feel less like exile and more like an extension of home.”

Here are some of the prominent political exiles who have made the Miami area home:

South Florida has the largest population of Venezuelans in the United States. Thousands of them gathered in Miami in early 2020 for a rally headlined by Juan Guaidó, the former opposition leader who declared himself interim president in 2019 after leading protests against the authoritarian government of Nicolás Maduro.

Mr. Guaidó ended up in Miami in 2023, after he said he was put on a plane by U. S. and Colombian officials following his arrival in Bogotá to attend talks about Venezuela’s future. Later that year, the authorities in Venezuela said they would issue a warrant for his arrest on accusations of misusing state money.

In Miami, he has continued to speak about the political situation in Venezuela. He told CBS News in January that Mr. Maduro’s capture by the United States was “justice” for Venezuelans. “This is a criminal regime,” he said, and called for it to be dismantled. He also expressed a desire to return to Venezuela, if possible.

José Daniel Ferrer, the leader of a prominent dissident group in Cuba, arrived in Miami last year after being released from prison at the request of the U. S. government. He joined hundreds of thousands of Cubans who have fled to Miami in the decades since Fidel Castro took power in 1959 in the Communist revolution.

Mr. Ferrer’s departure dealt a blow to the opposition in Cuba, as he was one of the few remaining leaders not in exile. He had asked to leave Cuba because of harsh prison conditions and threats against his family, the U. S. government said at the time. (Cuba has denied that it holds political prisoners.)

He was welcomed to Miami by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a native of the city who is the son of Cuban immigrants.

Ricardo A. Martinelli, who was president of Panama from 2009 to 2014, left his country in 2015, days before the nation’s Supreme Court could issue a warrant for his arrest on charges of corruption and illegally spying on political rivals. He denied the allegations and requested political asylum in the United States.

In 2017, he was living in Coral Gables, a Miami suburb, when the U. S. Marshals took him into custody at the request of the Panamanian government. He was extradited to Panama the next year. A court in Panama City found him not guilty of political espionage in 2019 and ordered his release.

He was sentenced to 10 years in prison for embezzlement in 2024 but was given passage to Colombia after a year.

Félix Maradiaga was running for president of Nicaragua in 2021 when he was arrested by the government of President Daniel Ortega, who has controlled the country for nearly 20 years. Mr. Maradiaga was released abruptly in 2023 and headed for the Miami area. He and roughly 200 other political prisoners were stripped of their Nicaraguan citizenship after their release.

From Miami, Mr. Maradiaga has led an opposition party, Path to Change, which includes exiles but also operates in secret in Nicaragua.

Mr. Maradiaga is part of a large population of Nicaraguans who live in Sweetwater, a city near Miami. Many of the political prisoners who were released to the United States chose to settle in South Florida.

Francesca Regalado is a Times reporter covering breaking news.

Victor Mather, who has been a reporter and editor at The Times for 25 years, covers sports and breaking news.

Trump and His Aides Helped Bolsonaro Flee Brazil for the U. S.

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Brazil’s Presidential Election

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump ensured Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost a presidential election in Brazil and faces multiple criminal investigations there, could enter the United States, U. S. officials said.

By Edward WongAna IonovaHamed Aleaziz and Tyler Pager

The four correspondents have reported for years on U. S. policy in Latin America from Washington and Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

Flávio Bolsonaro, the Brazilian presidential candidate who faces multiple criminal investigations, is staying in Florida on a temporary status that was given following orders by President Trump, and will likely be granted permanent residency later, U. S. officials said.

Mr. Bolsonaro fled Brazil after losing an election this week. U. S. border agents allowed him and his family to enter the United States on what is called parole, usually given for humanitarian reasons, after they landed in Miami on a private jet on Wednesday morning, a U. S. official said that day.

The jet had been arranged by a White House official. President Trump said later that afternoon that Mr. Bolsonaro had been given “a pass” to enter the country.

The White House and the State Department referred questions about Mr. Bolsonaro’s parole status and Mr. Trump’s involvement to the Department of Homeland Security. That agency said Mr. Bolsonaro and his family “were met and inspected by U. S. Customs and Border Protection in accordance with applicable immigration laws and procedures. At the conclusion of the inspection, Mr. Bolsonaro and his accompanying family members were released.”

A public U. S. government record suggests that Mr. Bolsonaro presented a canceled Brazilian diplomatic passport on arrival, according to a review by The New York Times. The record lists a document with a number issued in Brazil that public disclosures show is linked to Mr. Bolsonaro’s diplomatic passport.

The State Department said through an official on Tuesday that it planned to issue visas to Mr. Bolsonaro and his family allowing them to enter the country. The White House said the same thing that day, citing an administration official.

The U. S. government grants parole status to people “for urgent humanitarian reasons or significant public benefit,” according to a federal website. The status allows a person to remain in the United States while “treated as an applicant for admission,” the site says.

Mr. Bolsonaro is expected to apply at some point for permanent resident status in the United States, known as a green card, a U. S. official said. That normally would happen after he is given an immigrant visa. Mr. Bolsonaro’s application for a green card would be processed quickly, similar to that of his younger brother before him, the official said.

The officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s younger brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, lives in Texas and maintains close ties to the Trump administration, and was granted permanent resident status in July. The process takes years for most immigrants, but the younger Bolsonaro got expedited approval, a U. S. official said.

Flávio Bolsonaro set off for the United States after Brazilian police asked him to turn over his passports on Monday because he is being investigated in relation to a money laundering scheme.

While Mr. Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator who has held elected office for more than two decades, has not been formally charged with a crime, he will be stripped of his parliamentary immunity in early 2027 because he lost the presidential election on Sunday. He could then potentially face prosecution in relation to multiple criminal investigations.

He flew late Tuesday from Argentina to Ecuador for refueling and finally to Miami, all on a private jet arranged by Jason Miller, a White House communications official, according to a person familiar with the logistics. Mr. Bolsonaro’s younger brother Eduardo has been in touch with Mr. Miller. The plan was put into motion on Monday, after Mr. Bolsonaro was told to turn in his passports, the person said.

On Sunday, Mr. Bolsonaro was decisively defeated in the election by the incumbent, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Mr. Miller, who is listed as a special U. S. government employee, declined to comment, and the White House referred only to public remarks by Mr. Trump, which did not address the private jet. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Mr. Miller’s involvement. He is an ally of the Bolsonaro family, and has said he was briefly detained on a visit to Brazil in 2021.

After landing in Miami, Mr. Bolsonaro declared himself the legitimate leader of Brazil.

Just after 9:30 a. m. Monday, Mr. Bolsonaro could be seen leaving a small jet at an airport outside Miami along with his family. The group was ushered into a dark S. U. V. shortly after exiting the airport, hidden under umbrellas.

His journey took place during a whirlwind 24 hours in which officials and journalists from multiple countries tried to determine where he was and how he was getting to the United States. Mr. Bolsonaro crossed into Argentina late Tuesday before traversing South America on the private plane.

Mr. Bolsonaro, in a lengthy statement on social media on Wednesday afternoon, said he had left Brazil because he faced political persecution and thanked Mr. Trump and President Javier Milei of Argentina. After initially declaring himself the “legitimate president-elect” of Brazil, Mr. Bolsonaro deleted his statement and reposted it using the word “leader” instead.

“I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the leader of Brazil,” Mr. Bolsonaro said. Without offering credible evidence, he claimed the election that he lost was fraudulent and that he was the subject of a “witch hunt” by Brazil’s judiciary.

The White House’s assistance to Mr. Bolsonaro could escalate tensions between the Trump administration and Mr. Lula, who has accused Mr. Trump of interfering in Brazil’s internal affairs.

When asked about Mr. Bolsonaro on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said, “We gave him a pass to come into the country, so we’ll see. But I won’t get involved. It was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”

On Thursday, Mr. Trump declined to say who was the election’s legitimate winner. He said he had not taken sides in the vote because Mr. Lula had asked him to refrain from doing so. “I thought the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil,” he said.

This year, the State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio took actions on Brazil after lobbying by the two Bolsonaro sons, The New York Times reported.

The two are sons of a former right-wing president, Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a lengthy sentence under house detention for attempting a coup. Flávio Bolsonaro conceded this week’s election, but seized on a change in the voting hours on Sunday to demand the outcome be annulled.

The change in hours, though, affected only 0.03 percent of the vote and Brazil’s electoral authorities said it did not make any difference to the result, given Mr. Lula’s winning margin of 4.4 million votes. International independent observers have certified the integrity of the election and dozens of countries have recognized the result. The United States and Argentina are not among them.

Mr. Bolsonaro, in his statement on Wednesday, doubled down on his complaints. He also insisted that Mr. Lula had unfairly used government funds to win, citing the president’s move to raise a welfare stipend in the last stretch of the campaign. (Mr. Lula’s government has said the increase was an overdue inflation adjustment.)

Mr. Bolsonaro crossed from Brazil to Argentina by land on Tuesday night with his wife and two daughters, Argentina’s National Directorate of Migration said Wednesday. It said that he then boarded a private fight to Guayaquil, Ecuador, and from there went on to the United States.

On Monday, Brazilian authorities asked Mr. Bolsonaro to hand over his passports within 24 hours because of investigations into his links to a Brazilian lawyer accused of laundering more than $1 billion through a scheme involving online gambling.

Separately, Mr. Bolsonaro is the subject of a police inquiry over millions of dollars he raised to finance a biopic about his father from a disgraced banker at the center of a huge corruption scheme.

When Mr. Bolsonaro did not turn in his passports by Tuesday morning, Brazilian authorities canceled the documents and issued an alert to immigration authorities barring Mr. Bolsonaro’s exit from the country. It is not clear how he was able to cross into Argentina.

Brazil’s federal police said it had no official record of Mr. Bolsonaro exiting the country. The police also said in a statement that the restrictions on Mr. Bolsonaro’s travel did not necessarily make him a fugitive or allow for his arrest. The police said they are now “investigating the circumstances surrounding the senator’s failure to comply with court orders.”

Argentina’s federal police also said they had not registered his entry. Still, Argentina’s immigration authorities said that Mr. Bolsonaro and his family had entered the country at 10:50 p. m. Tuesday. They traveled in a van across what is known as the “Fraternity Bridge,” connecting Foz do Iguaçu in southern Brazil to Puerto Iguazú in Argentina.

The area is popular with tourists because of the majestic waterfalls along the border.

Some 40 minutes later, Mr. Bolsonaro and his entourage embarked on a plane owned by Baires Fly, a private company that has transported Mr. Milei in the past.

Alice Maciel and Thayz Guimarães contributed reporting from Brasília, and Emma Bubola and Lucía Cholakian Herrera from Buenos Aires and Adam B. Ellick from São Paulo.

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

Ana Ionova is a correspondent for The Times, covering Brazil and neighboring countries.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Critic’s Notebook

The photographer Taryn Simon spent a decade channeling an F. B. I. agent’s life into pictures. Is it good art? Does it matter?

Credit...

Supported by

By Jason Farago

Visuals by Daniel Terna

Quality takes time to surface; quantity is easier to see. For the New York-based artist Taryn Simon, the challenge of making a photography exhibition has regularly been expressed in metrics: this many years of research, this many miles traveled, this many images, this many texts. The numbers always spiral upward, as does her current show at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum — which, true to form, arrived in September with quantitative honors. The first photographer given a solo show in the museum’s spiraling galleries. The largest debut of new artwork ever staged at the Guggenheim.

Count how many photos: over 1,700, plus the videos and sculptures too. Clock how many years: almost 10. When this show opened, Vogue praised Simon’s bespoke outfits in equally numerical terms: She has “dozens, maybe hundreds” of the same practical skirt with suspenders. The Wall Street Journal, a statistics-loving newspaper, counted how much she walks: “Sometimes I’ll hit 30,000 steps before 11 or 12.”

What is the function of this quantitative shock and awe? Do numbers have powers that a picture does not? (And most pictures, these days, are made of numbers: ones and zeros, computed billions of times into cyan, magenta, yellow and black.) Since her earliest days, when she photographed exonerated convicts for her series “The Innocents” (2000-03), Simon has tried to visualize murky currents of power with an unrelenting work ethic, not to mention hefty budgets. The force of her pictures lay not just in what they depicted, but in the diligence and effort required to capture them. She is the hardest-working woman in the darkroom, and she wants you to know it.

I’m not convinced all this hard work pays off, certainly not in the case of “Father Country I Do Love You,” now filling the Guggenheim. It is the second most solipsistic exhibition I have ever seen at this museum (last year’s Rashid Johnson exhibition is still the vainest), and tragic besides, because Simon really can be an impressive photographer when she uses her powers of persuasion and technical skill more precisely. This show has pictures of real strength and surprise, but they’re submerged in a mock-paranoid mapping of recent American history riddled with banalities, affectations, off-key jokes and literal toys. She cannot get out of her own way, and no one at the Guggenheim — which commissioned the work, and has now acquired it for its permanent collection — seems to have helped her.

Here’s the conceit of “Father Country I Do Love You”: In 2017, Simon had lunch with an agent at the Federal Bureau of Investigation. She does not tell us his name, offering instead the James Ellroy-esque detail that they met “at Los Portales, a Mexican restaurant off an airport service road in Maryland.” Artist and agent hit it off, and over the coming decade he tells her about his career. At least as he narrates it, it intersected with almost every major episode of political upheaval from the end of the Cold War to the first election of President Trump, when the agent retired. (A frame narrative at the show’s start and end invokes Simon’s father, who also worked for the U. S. government in a shadowy role; more on that in a spoiler-laden postscript.)

From these conversations, Simon produced 42 sequences of artworks, mostly color-coded photographs: count them, forty-two. The agent describes wiretapping a small-time cocaine dealer in Washington in the early 1990s; here now is the drug dealer, photographed from the back. The agent let Jodie Foster shadow him at Quantico in preparation for “The Silence of the Lambs,” and here now is Jodie Foster, 35 years older, her fingers inked with proper F. B. I. technique.

Simon travels to Kenya to photograph 36 blinded survivors of the 1998 bombings at the American embassy in Nairobi, where the agent was stationed; each picture has excessive headroom and plain lighting, and hangs in a uniform tiled display. She heaps McDonald’s French fries against a backdrop of Communist Party red: not just any McDonald’s fries, but fries purchased at the specific Pennsylvania McDonald’s where Mr. Trump staged an election photo op at the drive-through.

We know the artist schlepped to that particular McDonald’s because the French-fry photos come, as do most images here, with extended captions. These not only specify that the F. B. I. agent enjoyed eating McDonald’s at the Beijing Olympics, but offer extraneous details about earlier McDonald’s sponsorships, about limited-edition hamburgers only available in Beijing, and about Mr. Trump’s stated desires to serve McDonald’s to Xi Jinping, the Chinese president.

You will have noticed the tone: connecting the dots, unmasking the truth. These photographs, the show wants us to believe, are not just images, but evidence — shot in the cool style of courtroom exhibits, or stock photography. These extended wall labels are not just texts, but disclosures — and at the Guggenheim I saw visitors training their camera phones on the labels, rather than the photographs, as if that were where the real work lay. (It takes hours on your feet here to read them all.)

Hanging over this exhibition-as-evidence-locker is Simon’s deep-state Zelig, popping up at terrorist attacks, political conventions, at a Capitol shooting. Yet behind the patina of disclosure, Simon behaves like someone who wants her own cover blown. Numerous biographical details in the interviews Simon conducted appear to match the life of Jeffrey Bedford, who served in the F. B. I. from 1989 to 2016, rising to the rank of unit chief. My repeated efforts to contact him at work and through relatives were unsuccessful, but Bedford was born in Exeter, N. H., as was Simon’s agent. He attended Phillips Exeter, Amherst College and Golden Gate University School of Law before joining the police force in Manchester, N. H.; Simon’s agent, she lets him tell us, did all that too.

She does not redact the names of her agent’s parents — also the names of Bedford’s parents — when she interviews them in a nursing home. Nor does she redact the name of her agent’s partner, killed in the line of duty, when she photographs the chaplain who led her funeral; Bedford has publicly discussed his partner’s killing on a podcast.

By the show’s end she even lets Simon’s retired agent disclose that he left the bureau to work in campus security at a “pretty hoity-toity, all girls” school, whose alumnae include Jackie Kennedy. No secret, then, what school that was: the Holton-Arms School, in Bethesda, Md. In 2020, one Jeffrey Bedford published an article on his campus safety work at Holton-Arms, complete with smiling headshot.

These are not secret details; I found them with two minutes’ searching on my phone at the Guggenheim’s coffee bar. They are so unclassified that Bedford’s own LinkedIn profile mentions “overseas assignments” in Kenya and Saudi Arabia, which Simon’s agent also undertook, “as well as 9/11 at the Pentagon.”

In other words, Simon’s cloak of privacy over her agent is a MacGuffin of the most classic Hitchcockian vintage — a performance of protective anonymity, to invest each photograph with the frisson of a political thriller. She even winks at this in the show’s one truly great gag: five portraits of Valerie Plame, outed as a covert C. I. A. agent in 2003, posing for Simon in the disguises of a cowgirl, a Hollywood star, a Starbucks-sipping corporate lackey.

So the question becomes: Why has Simon propped up this giant show with a secret that is not a secret? Asked for comment, the Guggenheim would not confirm his identity either: “It was an artistic decision not to reveal the identity of the agent. Simon kept him unnamed because she wanted him to represent the ‘everyman.’”

Yet this is exactly the trouble: the distraction of an undisclosed narrator suggests she doesn’t trust her photographs alone. The agent’s pseudo-anonymity is functioning just like the large grids, the long captions and the neutral backgrounds: it sheathes her pictures with a veneer of objectivity. The supposed disclosures assign to the pictures an assumption of credibility that has been draining away from photography for well over a century, and that is now, with the arrival of computational imagery from artificial intelligence, very close to death. But if all the pictures here are true — corroborated through the extended texts — then we don’t have to ask if any one picture is good.

That isn’t how truth in photography works, and someone as smart as Simon already knows this. Whether the agent really did meet Jodie Foster is totally irrelevant for whether Simon has made a good photograph of Jodie Foster (and she really has). Whether he ate McDonald’s in Beijing cannot make a still life of Pennsylvania-terroir French fries any less heavy-handed (which it really is).

Any truth in photography inheres in the image, not in the caption. The sensation I felt at the Guggenheim was uncannily similar to what I feel reading the A. I. summaries that now appear above web search results, which declare (with total confidence and putative neutrality) that such-and-such really happened, but are as likely to be wrong as right.

“Truths are illusions which we have forgotten are illusions,” Nietzsche insisted, and his skepticism of a rigid truth/fiction binary would animate so much art and philosophy of the 20th century: Truth is only a social convention, the malleable product of institutions and discourses, and no “outside” reality exists to evaluate a claim. The truth has had a rough ride in America lately. Nietzsche had an answer, though: In art, at least, we still have one last place where the true dimensions of the world can be grasped. Art happens through allusions, metaphors, stylizations. Art admits its constructedness openly, and it is honest about what it cannot know. And through that craft, it keeps our larger will to know alive.

But Simon plays hide-and-seek in one other way at the end of this show: a video of her father, whose memories of his own government activities have been lost to Alzheimer’s. This should be the moment of metaphor: the agent merges with the parent, America into Lethe. And yet she can’t help herself — dad, yet another text recounts, manufactured arcade games after his government service, and so Simon has embedded the video of her father into a giant marble run, with a chute spanning half the museum. As Guggenheim attendants encouraged families to send the balls sliding down the ramp, like the seabirds in “Mr. Popper’s Penguins,” I watched in disbelief. After all this work, the truth was only a game.

Taryn Simon: Father Country I Do Love YouThrough March 14, 2027, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1071 Fifth Avenue, Manhattan, 212-423-3500; guggenheim. org.

Jason Farago, a critic at large for The Times, writes about art and culture in the U. S. and abroad.

Expectations are cresting for Democrats, and some kind of wave seems likely, but so much will depend on a few close Senate races.

By Nate Cohn

There’s no formal definition of a “wave” election, but by some measures a blue wave appears all but inevitable.

Whether a big wave translates into a large Democratic House majority and Democratic control of the Senate is a very different question. Republicans have major structural advantages that give them a chance to avoid major losses, even if a big blue wave comes ashore. Under some scenarios, Republicans might even feel like the winners.

If the Democratic Party’s strength can be thought of as a growing blue wave, the Republican Party’s advantage is that its House members and especially its senators are already far uphill. The big question isn’t whether a big wave is forming, but whether it will be large enough to overwhelm those Republicans standing on high ground.

Most G. O. P. seats in Congress are in heavily Republican areas, shown at the top of the hill. But some are in less safe states or districts, seen toward the bottom of the hill. A higher “blue wave” would threaten more of these seats.

Democraticlead innational polls

Republican seats

Note: Seats shown are held by Republicans or were targeted by them during redistricting. The vote margins of each House and Senate seat reflect 2024 presidential election results adjusted so that the national margin is even. Source: 2024 presidential election results from The New York Times. By June Kim and Rachel Buigas-Lopez/The New York Times

The Republicans are well prepared. They have seen this possibility coming for a long time. Historically, midterm elections tend to go poorly for the president’s party and, this cycle, President Trump’s approval ratings are among the lowest on record.

To try to preserve their majority, Republicans redrew the House map so that more of them would be in safer districts — to continue with this metaphor, they tried to evacuate away from the shoreline. They have also spent billions trying to shore up red states and districts — the equivalent of Elon Musk and other donors spending billions on sandbags and life jackets.

Notice on the wave graphic how many more Republicans represent districts that lean eight to 15 points toward the G. O. P. than eight points or below. This is not an accident; it is deliberate. When Republicans redrew maps, they created districts that were intended to survive previous wave elections, which in recent decades have usually been in the range of +6 to +8.5 for the party out of power.

Nonetheless, these extraordinary preparations probably won’t be enough to keep the House under Republican control. The wave appears big enough that Democrats seem likely to take the chamber under almost any scenario short of a polling error larger than in 2016 or 2020. The big question is whether they can win a large majority.

The Senate is a very different story. There the Democratic challenge is much greater: They will need to flip at least two seats in states that Mr. Trump won by double digits in 2024. Not even the largest waves in memory would make the Democrats plainly favored to win such reliably Republican states. That might take a tsunami.

Here are four scenarios for how the election might unfold.

Wave size: D+5 to D+7 popular vote (similar to 2010 or 2014).

Polling error: Democratic strength substantially overestimated (similar to 2016 or 2020).

Outcome: Republicans hold the Senate fairly easily. Democrats win only a narrow-to-modest House majority. That House victory may not be called for days or even a week, as Democrats wait for states like California to count their mail-in ballots.

How it happens: Imagine you’re standing alongside Republicans in districts that voted for Mr. Trump by eight to 12 percentage points, when an enormous blue wave crashes ashore.

Fortunately, you are on high ground — and well prepared.

In this first scenario, the wave sweeps away the Republicans along the beach, like the Republican Senate seat in North Carolina, but by the time the water reaches you uphill, it gently sloshes over your feet like a peaceful day on the beach. The blue wave is big, but it doesn’t reach beyond what Republicans are prepared to withstand.

It’s not implausible to imagine how Republicans hold the Senate and keep the House close. To do it, Republicans merely need Republican-leaning voters to show up for them on Election Day, despite these voters’ reservations about Mr. Trump’s job performance. In today’s polarized era, Republicans voting Republican is never a far-fetched possibility.

It’s even easier to imagine when you consider just how far Republicans are positioned uphill. If Democrats win only the seats where Mr. Trump won by 8.5 points or less, they would win a modest 223 seats (just five more than needed for a majority), and they would fall two seats short of taking the Senate.

And the polls have underestimated Republicans before. If the polls are off by as much as they were in 2016 or 2020, the current Democratic polling lead — around nine points nationwide — might only yield a Democratic victory of five to seven points. That would be comparable to the size of some prior wave elections (like Republican victories in 1994, 2010 and 2014), but it would not necessarily yield a large Democratic House majority or Democratic control of the Senate.

It may count as a blue wave in terms of the national vote, but it would feel like a ripple in Congress.

Wave size: D+7 to D+9 (similar to 2006 or 2018).

Polling error: The polls are generally accurate, but Republicans are modestly underestimated — either nationally or in crucial red states. (Similar to 2018 or 2024.)

Outcome: A big blue wave that nonetheless leaves Republicans breathing a sigh of relief — and Democrats disappointed. The Senate only narrowly remains Republican, even though Democrats fare better in safely Republican states than either party has fared on opposing turf in decades. Democrats make significant gains in the House.

How it happens: This is a big wave. It’s as large or larger than any midterm in decades. In this scenario, the wave doesn’t slosh up against the feet of the Republicans on high ground; it surges over the sandbags and washes them away. Republicans are fighting for political survival.

On a national scale, it would mean a seat-by-seat battle for control of the Senate, while Democrats cruise to a large majority in the House. The polls aren’t far off in this scenario: Democrats are winning big nationwide and are highly competitive in Republican states and districts. In Scenario 1, states like Kansas and Iowa might not even be close. This time, the core Senate battlegrounds in red states remain too close to call late into the night.

But in this scenario, Republicans hold on in just enough of the key Senate battlegrounds. The life vests do their job. Democrats have their best night in decades in red states like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, but they fall short. Or maybe Susan Collins, the renowned political surfer who has thrived in wave elections before, manages to stay on her surfboard in Maine yet again.

How could this happen? To hold the Senate, Republicans merely need enough support and turnout from Republican-leaning voters to prevent Democrats from taking states that Mr. Trump won by 13 points. No party has flipped a Senate seat that leans so heavily toward the other party in a regularly scheduled election since Republicans won in Illinois in 2010.

Over the last three blue waves — 2006, 2008 and 2018 — Democrats flipped Republican-leaning Senate seats facing that kind of double-digit deficit only three times: Montana in 2006, North Carolina in 2008 and Alaska in 2008 (which required the Republican senator Ted Stevens to be convicted of a felony just one week before the election).

This scenario does not require a major polling error. Today, the polls show Democrats up by a couple of points in states like Ohio, Texas, Maine and Alaska. It would be pretty typical for the polls to be off by a few points in a few states, and it’s particularly common in states that typically lean heavily toward one side or the other. Historically, polls tend to underestimate Republicans in red states (and underestimate Democrats in blue states).

Wave size: D+8 to D+10 (similar to 2006 or 2018).

Polling error: Reasonably accurate, including in the key Senate battlegrounds. (Similar to 2006 or 2022.)

The outcome: Democrats win control of the Senate. They win an even larger House majority than they did in 2018.

How it happens: This is mostly like Scenario 2. The wave is just as high. The Republicans are swept off their feet. Except this time, the Republicans can’t hold on. Democrats win the double-digit Trump states they need to flip the Senate. Maybe even Ms. Collins is flipped off her surfboard.

The difference between Scenarios 2 and 3 might be only tens of thousand votes in a few key states. From the standpoint of polling, public opinion or wave height, it’s barely a difference. Politically, it’s everything: the difference between Democratic or Republican control of the Senate.

Whether Scenario 2 or Scenario 3 unfolds on election night comes down to a crucial sliver of Republican-leaning voters who disapprove of the president. These are not the voters who usually decide the outcome of American elections. They’re usually safely in the Republican camp, including in prior blue waves. But the polls suggest that these voters are so dissatisfied with Mr. Trump that enough of them will either stay home or vote Democratic.

The 2006 midterm election makes for a nice comparison. Democrats needed to win at least three Senate seats that President George W. Bush had won by eight points or more. In the end, they won the seats they needed, but by a razor-thin margin: Two of the three were decided by less than one point.

Wave size: D+10 and higher (similar to 2008 or larger than any modern electoral victory).

Polling error: Democrats outperform the polls in the most closely watched states or nationwide. (Similar to 2012, 2022 or 2025.)

Outcome: A large Democratic majority in the House (maybe 250 seats), a comfortable one in the Senate (53 or more), and the beginning of a new chapter of American politics.

How it happens: In this scenario, the G. O. P.’s structural advantages are swept away. Maybe Democrats win the key Senate races with room to spare, with the party’s candidates winning reliably red states like Ohio, Alaska, Texas or even Kansas by a modest but comfortable margins. The wave is just that high.

The consequences of this kind of Democratic victory would reverberate for years. The closest Senate races — which in this scenario might be Iowa, Kansas or even Mississippi and South Carolina — might not decide control of the Senate in 2026, but could determine which side has the advantage heading into 2028. Farther down the ballot, Democrats would have a once-in-a-generation chance to break the Republican grip on solidly red-state legislatures. Texas wouldn’t just go blue in the Senate race but in the governor’s one as well.

In today’s polarized era, it can be hard to believe that any party could win in this kind of tsunami. The last time a party won by more than 10 points in the national vote was 2008, when House Democrats outran Barack Obama while benefiting from the giant turnout on his behalf.

But this scenario is consistent with the latest polls and the president’s approval rating, which is lower than any president’s heading into a midterm since Harry Truman. It’s nearly 10 points lower than it was in 2018, when Republicans lost the popular vote by almost nine points but held the red-state Senate races.

Back then, Republicans held those states by rallying Mr. Trump’s supporters. A majority of voters approved of his performance in the key red states, like Texas, Tennessee, Indiana, North Dakota and Missouri. This time, winning just the voters who approve of Mr. Trump won’t be anywhere near enough. It wouldn’t even be enough in a state like South Carolina, let alone the top-tier Senate battlegrounds.

With Republican-leaning voters outright disapproving of Mr. Trump, this time they really do stay home or even cast a ballot for the other party. If that happens, Democrats could win by a larger margin than we’ve seen in recent memory.

As I’ve said on The Daily, this election will mark the moment when we begin to turn the page and look toward a new chapter of American politics. No matter what, the next chapter is going to be different. There will be new issues like artificial intelligence, new candidates trying to capitalize on deep dissatisfaction with the parties, and a presidential primary — without Mr. Trump. If the midterm is a tsunami, the end of the Trump era might start to feel as if it’s in sight.

Of course, it’s just as easy to imagine — maybe even easier to imagine — that Republican-leaning voters will ultimately decide to show up and vote for Republicans, as they usually do. We will find out on election night.

Nate Cohn is The Times’s chief political analyst. He covers elections, public opinion, demographics and polling.

The world can be tough to navigate with one working ear. Even now with two, I still face challenges.

Credit... Vincent Alban/The New York Times

Supported by

By Scott Dodd

Scott Dodd edits Times fellows who report on disability issues. This is his personal disability story.

My right ear hasn’t worked since I suffered a brain injury in middle school. Hearing on only one side makes life more complicated. For the nearly 25 years my wife and I have known each other, whenever we want to have a conversation, we need to make sure she’s on my good side.

“Left is best” is how she remembers it.

So it definitely broke the rules for us to sit on a blue plastic couch in a busy waiting room, with a loud TV to my left and my wife, Jaime, on my right. But we were at my audiologist’s office, following the doctor’s orders: Make small talk.

Jaime caught me up on the kids’ schedules and our weekend plans, then weighed our dinner options. It was the kind of conversation we’d had thousands of times.

But I had never been able to hear it from this direction. Now I could.

It seemed like such a small thing, but it felt profound. A lifetime of single-sided deafness had trained me to avoid this exact situation — a loud noise on my left, someone talking on my right.

And yet here we were, conversing casually like a normal couple that didn’t have to constantly triangulate seating arrangements.

I told Jaime to scoot over, and she slid down to the other end of the blue couch and kept talking. I could still hear her. Then she moved to a row of chairs about 20 feet away. The TV was still loud, and I could still hear her.

Just like that, a couple of small electronic devices tucked behind my ears changed how I experienced the world.

There are many forms of hearing loss, some more difficult to correct than others. Mine is particularly tricky.

The concussion I suffered in middle school destroyed my right auditory nerve, making most forms of hearing assistance ineffective for me.

It was a stupid accident. Some classmates and I were goofing around in the auditorium, and someone knocked me off the stage. As I fell, my head hit one of the built-in desks in the front row, knocking me unconscious. I’m not sure for how long.

Today, we understand the danger of head injuries like that. But back in the 1980s, I wasn’t even sent to the nurse’s office.

I first noticed something was wrong that afternoon as I walked home from school. A plane flew overhead, and the engine sounded weird, in a way that I couldn’t describe. But it wasn’t until the next morning, when my mother had to yell from my bedroom door to wake me up for school, that I knew I had serious trouble.

I had been sleeping on my left side, and I hadn’t heard my clock radio alarm going off.

We went to the hospital, and doctors determined that I had a type of traumatic brain injury known as a contrecoup, which is French for “counterblow.”

The impact of the fall had rocked my brain back and forth, crushing my auditory nerve against the side of my skull. Signals from my right ear can’t reach my brain through the ruined nerve, which won’t heal.

The official name of my condition is single-sided deafness, which is a serious form of bilateral hearing loss, though I’ve always just referred to it as being half deaf. People with single-sided deafness struggle to decipher speech, screen out background noise and localize sounds, all of which I’ve experienced on a daily basis.

I’m sure the doctors explained all this to me back then, but I still remember being surprised the first time a teacher clapped me on the right shoulder in the school hallway. He was saying my name and thought I was ignoring him. Amid the chatter of classmates and slamming lockers, I didn’t realize he was there.

I’m still pretty easy to sneak up on. My skull blocks sound waves coming from the right, preventing them from reaching my left ear. It’s called the head shadow effect.

Every noise I do pick up seems as if it’s coming from my left side, giving me no real spatial awareness. My world is a sonic blur. When someone shouts to me from across the street or tries to get my attention in the newsroom, I have to twist my head around to try to figure out where the sound is coming from.

The usual follow-up of “Over here!” doesn’t help.

Every dinner out, every birthday party, every sporting event or bar mitzvah is a chessboard where I calculate moves: Sit at the right side of the table. Keep my back to a quiet corner. Pay more for a seat on the right aisle so no one can sit on my bad side.

The mental stress can be overwhelming. My nerves fray in a noisy environment. I’ll get home from work and a long bus commute feeling exhausted. My family has learned to let me hide away sometimes for an hour or so to recover.

It’s called listening fatigue, and medical studies have linked it to anxiety, depression, social isolation and increased risk of suicide.

For most of my life, I coped pretty well. But over the last few years, things felt as if they were getting worse. I became anxious, tired and irritable more easily. I started skipping more events, or ducking out early. I left my wife behind at a good friend’s birthday party when their house got too loud.

In the newsroom, I had to stop joining video calls during breaking news stories, because I couldn’t process the input from so many sources. At home, any background noise at all — running water in the sink, the vent on the kitchen stove — would block out the voices of my wife and kids while I was cooking dinner.

For the first time in decades, at age 54, I decided to see an audiologist again.

Sitting in an audio testing booth, I raised my hand when I could hear the doctor play a tone or a beep through special earphones. I vividly remembered doing the same thing for specialists after my head injury more than 40 years ago.

When the volume was turned up on the right, I could feel my skull vibrating from the loudest tones. But I couldn’t hear them.

The tests confirmed what I had feared. Now, along with the flat line indicating severe hearing loss in the right ear, another dip on the chart showed deterioration in my “good” ear, too.

This happens to a lot of people in their 50s and 60s, the audiologist, Dr. Phyllis Schaffer-Cohen, said. And after decades of single-sided deafness, I was more vulnerable than most, to both additional hearing loss and other associated issues.

“You’re at a real disadvantage,” she said. “No hearing in one ear, reduced hearing in the other.”

After the accident, the doctors told me and my parents that there was nothing anyone could do. The nerve damage was permanent, and the hearing aids available at the time wouldn’t help.

Even years later, when cochlear implants became common, I wasn’t a candidate. For decades, the only options for my condition were awkward, expensive and invasive. That had changed, Dr. Schaffer-Cohen told me in January.

She recommended that I try a system called contralateral routing of signal, or CROS. I’d wear a receiver on my right side, and it would pick up sounds, transmitting them to an amplifier on my left ear. I still wouldn’t know which direction to turn, but I would hear more.

CROS was around when I had my accident, but systems back then were primitive, requiring transmission wires across the back of a user’s head, or sometimes hidden in thick glasses. Even later, when they got smaller, the sounds often didn’t sync. Many users gave up in frustration.

But in the last decade, Dr. Schaffer-Cohen said, CROS hearing aids had improved, even incorporating artificial intelligence to help measure head movements and make adjustments. She now recommends them to patients like me. I did some research, and the medical literature bore her out.

Two weeks later, I went with Jaime to Dr. Schaffer-Cohen’s office at Summit Health in Montclair, N. J. She said the best test drive was to have a normal, everyday conversation with my wife.

I tucked sleek black devices roughly the size and shape of garlic cloves behind my ears. The doctor usually sent couples outside, but it was frigid that day. Her waiting room would have to do.

With the television blaring a TLC program on my left and Jaime chatting normally on my right, I stared straight ahead, keeping my good ear from turning toward her.

The device behind my right ear was picking up her voice and broadcasting to its twin on the left, which routed it through a tiny speaker on the end of a wire snaking into my ear canal.

“Do you know how weird this is?” I asked her.

It was weird for her, too. We decided to take them.

I wanted to bring the hearing aids home right away, but Dr. Schaffer-Cohen needed insurance approval first.

Good CROS systems aren’t cheap; mine ran about $5,000 from a supplier called Oticon. UnitedHealthcare covered roughly three-quarters of that amount. Apple, Bose and other big names in audio make hearing aids now, too. Some are available over the counter.

Steve Martin and other celebrities helped test a new system from a start-up called Fortell that uses A. I. to screen out background noise. At $6,800 a set, it’s even pricier than mine.

Back in Dr. Schaffer-Cohen’s office a few weeks after my tryout, I sat across from her, learning how to operate and clean the new devices. They looked a lot different from the chestnut-size beige hearing aids my grandfather used to wear.

“That’s what most people remember,” Dr. Schaffer-Cohen said. “They were bulky. They whistled.” My grandfather was always taking his out, adjusting them to try to cut down the static.

The stigma has lessened as the devices have gotten smaller, and other kinds of wearables have grown more common. But it’s still there. “We sell a product that people don’t want,” the doctor said.

I jumped as a noise like a buzz saw whirred from under her desk. It was the printer, she told me, and pulled out papers for me to sign.

I had heard printers before. They didn’t sound like that.

I had the same thought driving home. My turn signals sounded like beating electronic drums. Over the next few weeks, I realized how much of the noisy world around me I had been missing.

I started a list on my phone of things that stood out:

The sidewalk salt and gravel that crackled under my feet like firecrackers as I walked to the bus on a cold morning

The incessant squish-squish of rubber-soled shoes in my building’s lobby on a rainy day

The distracting noise of a colleague folding a piece of paper while sitting next to me during a meeting

A conversation between two reporters sitting about 30 feet away, coming in loud and clear

Months later, I’m still hearing new things. Recently it was the sound of ice cubes clinking in a metal carafe as I poured cream into my coffee. Some of it is amazing. Some I could do without.

The listening fatigue hasn’t gone away. It might even have gotten worse. There’s more sound for my single ear to process now, and I still find myself in need of recovery time.

I often leave the hearing aids in their recharging cases on the weekends, or take them out on the bus home, to give myself a break. My wife can tell right away if I’m wearing them when I walk through the door at night, based on the volume of my voice.

I knew I was a loud talker. People have told me that for years. When I struggle to hear, my voice gets louder to compensate.

Once, my boss asked me to move into a conference room when I was on a video call, managing a busy news story. My voice kept getting louder, disturbing co-workers around me.

But it’s one thing to hear it from other people. It’s another to hear your noisy voice for yourself. And a little embarrassing.

“Do you realize how much less loud your voice is now?” a colleague asked me a few days after I started wearing the hearing aids. I do. And now I’m the one who sometimes finds others too noisy.

Fortunately, I can do something about that. My hearing aids came with an equalizer and volume control, in the form of an app on my phone.

The day I got them, my older son received his driver’s license. I rode with him to pick up his brother from swim practice and sat in the back seat on the short drive home.

In the front, with satellite radio playing a U2 song, they talked about school and sports. I adjusted the volume and mixed the audio settings so I could hear them better over the music.

When we got home, I showed my younger son how it worked. “Bro,” he said, impressed. “You got superpowers now!”

This essay focuses mainly on my personal experience with single-sided deafness, but I dug into a lot of scientific literature while working on it. I was particularly interested in studies that confirmed my experience with impacts on mental health and cognitive function. If anyone else here has dealt with hearing loss, I’d love to know if you’ve experienced issues like “listening fatigue,” and how they affect your life.

Scott Dodd is an editor overseeing national news coverage for The Times.

Third-Party Spoilers, Long Fueled by Both Parties, Could Matter This Year

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

The other Dan Sullivan in Alaska has drawn the most attention, but both parties are quietly trying to use little-known candidates in other battlegrounds to siphon votes, too.

By Reid J. Epstein

Reporting from Washington

Sly maneuvering around third-party candidates is a time-honored, bipartisan tradition in politics.

Democrats and Republicans alike have long stealthily tried to help little-known names on the ballot who might siphon votes away from the opposing party’s nominees. The issue has suddenly become a top midterm story line because of remarkable drama in Alaska, where Democrats carried out a gambit to place a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot, alongside a Republican senator with the same name.

But several other midterm battlegrounds also have outsider candidates who could swing a close race.

In Ohio, Republicans have spent more than $2.2 million to promote a socialist candidate in the state’s vital Senate race, aiming to pull votes from the Democratic nominee, former Senator Sherrod Brown.

In Virginia, a Republican group has sent mailers highlighting the Democratic-leaning positions of a self-described “radical centrist” running as an independent in a competitive House race.

And in Nebraska, both major parties are jockeying to help minor candidates peel votes away from Senator Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent, and his Democratic-backed independent challenger, Dan Osborn.

With modern elections often decided by extremely thin margins and billions of dollars sloshing through campaigns, both parties have ample incentives and opportunities to gain an edge through mischief involving third parties.

The jockeying around spoiler candidates is widely considered a legal yet shadowy part of political campaigning that has gone on for decades. The Sullivan episode in Alaska is far from the first time that multiple candidates with the same name have run for the same office, with the lesser-known one often deliberately trying to confuse voters. There was even an Eddie Murphy movie in 1992 based on the concept of his character’s winning a seat in Congress previously held by a deceased politician with the same name.

Usually the actors propping up spoiler candidates are careful enough about wiping away their fingerprints that they do not get caught in the kind of uproar that Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign now faces in Alaska. After a New York Times report detailing how allies of Ms. Peltola, a Democrat, had recruited little-known candidates to try to stack the ballot, Gov. Mike Dunleavy of Alaska ordered an investigation into whether the Peltola campaign should face criminal charges or civil penalties, and President Trump demanded that she be removed from the ballot. Neither suggested a specific law that had been violated.

“Ghost voters are a bad phenomenon, but it’s a phenomenon that’s been in American politics for decades,” said Benjamin Ginsberg, a prominent Republican election lawyer. “At this point there’s no legal violation. Coming when it does, it’s purely up to Alaska voters, who, after all, put both Dan Sullivans on the ballot with their votes.”

He added, “The whole thing is clearly political.”

History offers plenty of precedent of third-party candidates playing spoiler.

Former Senator Jon Tester of Montana, a Democrat, won his first two elections with a margin of victory that was less than the vote total for the Libertarian candidates in those contests. In 2000 and 2016, the number of votes that left-wing presidential candidates received could have been enough to flip the results had they gone to the Democrats running in those years.

It does not always work. Mr. Trump’s allies tried to engage in this when they encouraged Kanye West to run for president in 2024, in an effort to shave off some Black voters from Mr. Trump’s Democratic rivals. The musician failed to get on the ballot in most battleground states.

Usually, the third-party candidates are relatively innocent bystanders to the political drama swirling around them.

This year in Ohio, Greg Levy, a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation, is making a long-shot run for the Senate, his first bid for public office. He has raised about $132,000 mostly from small donors, is still working full time as a mover and is squeezing in his campaign stops in the evenings.

So it came to his great surprise when a shadowy Republican group began what has become a nearly $2.3 million campaign to promote him to Democratic voters, mostly through mail and text messages, funded by a weeks-old super PAC with ties to Mr. Trump and Ohio Republicans. The group is itself entirely funded by a Republican group that regularly meddles in Democratic politics.

“Say yes to the revolution,” one piece of mail pushing for Mr. Levy reads. “Vote Greg Levy for U. S. Senate.”

Mr. Levy, 49, said in an interview that he opposed on principle the idea “that billionaires subvert the democratic process.”

“I’m the only candidate that’s running that openly opposes political donations, period,” Mr. Levy said. “We want money out of politics, and we need to have an honest political system.”

Republicans are trying to help Mr. Levy because polls show that the top of the ticket is a tight race between Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, and Mr. Brown, a Democrat trying to return to the chamber. In a contest that has drawn nearly $500 million in advertising spending so far, the money for the texts and mail on Mr. Levy’s behalf is a relative pittance.

Ohio Democrats are aiming to help their own spoiler candidate in the Senate race.

The state Democratic Party and Mr. Brown’s campaign have sent mail promoting the Libertarian candidate, Bill Redpath, as “a proud supporter of gun rights” — an apparent attempt to appeal to Republican voters.

Tony Wen, a spokesman for the Ohio Democratic Party, declined to comment on the Redpath mailers. Mr. Redpath did not respond to messages.

It is often hard to tell before an election how many voters are attracted to third-party candidates. The polling is complicated because research has shown that simply including a third-party candidate in a poll can lead to a drastic overstatement of their support, while not including them forecloses on voters’ opportunity to demonstrate any support for them.

Pollsters typically err on the side of not including these minor-party candidates, largely because the candidates have not historically received much support. In 2024, third-party presidential candidates drew less than 2 percent of the vote nationally.

This year, most of the late spending to help third-party candidates has come from groups that will not have to disclose their donors before Election Day. One such group, Our Heritage Matters, revealed last week that it had spent $340,000 to help Libertarian candidates in Senate races in Iowa and Kansas as well as in six House contests.

In New Jersey, Republicans have tried to elevate a mysterious candidate named Seamus O’Toole. He is on the ballot in the House district where the Republican incumbent, Representative Tom Kean Jr., is running for re-election against Rebecca Bennett, a top Democratic recruit.

Mr. O’Toole’s party is listed as “Stop Israel’s Genocide” — a position that could catch the eye of left-wing voters.

Mr. O’Toole did not respond to messages from The New York Times and has not responded to New Jersey news outlets that have tried to reach him.

In Virginia, Matt Baker, a retired Marine from Norfolk, decided to run for Congress as an independent because he was dissatisfied with both parties. In an interview, he described himself as a “radical centrist” and said that he borrowed policy ideas from both parties.

Yet only his ideas that align with Democratic views — that he believes in abortion rights and that the 2020 election was not stolen, among others — showed up in mail sent by a Republican group called Progressive Champions PAC that called him “the independent choice for Congress.”

The other side of the mailer called the Democrat in the race, former Representative Elaine Luria, “a corporate candidate.”

The House Democratic campaign arm, however, signaled to outside groups that they should spend money to call Mr. Baker “a staunch supporter of the 2nd Amendment,” a detail reported earlier by Axios.

Mr. Baker was not pleased to be used this way.

“It makes me mad as hell,” he said. “They didn’t coordinate with me. They’re only telling half my story. I am a retired Marine, 28 years of service, and I think integrity is incredibly important. These shadowy people are going around trying to use me to trick people.”

Other potential spoiler candidates are more sanguine about their situation.

Two years ago, Lynn Chapman, a conservative political activist from Sparks, Nev., earned 5 percent of the vote as the Independent American Party candidate in Nevada’s Second Congressional District. It did not matter much, since Representative Mark Amodei, a Republican, won re-election by 19 percentage points.

But this year Mr. Amodei is retiring. The race to succeed him is competitive. And Ms. Chapman is back, this time with some Democratic support. She is well aware that her vote total could be enough to swing the result to the Democratic nominee, Teresa Benitez-Thompson.

Ms. Chapman, 77, said that, given the choice, she would rather see the Republican, David Flippo, an Air Force veteran, win the general election over Ms. Benitez-Thompson, a former state legislator. How would she feel if Ms. Benitez-Thompson won?

“Oh, well,” she said. “Gee whiz, too bad.”

Alaska’s Senate race is just the latest episode of Democratic and Republican candidates and their allies trying to elevate spoiler candidates to siphon off votes from their main rivals. This has been going on for decades in politics and Alaska is hardly the only example of it this year. If you are in a battleground state or district, have you gotten mail or texts or seen ads trying to boost candidates you didn’t know about? How do you feel about this legal but shadowy phenomenon?

Ruth Igielnik contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Consumers and A. I. Spending Push U. S. Economic Growth Higher

The New York Times October 29, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

The economy grew 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year. Strong spending and growth contrast with the poor marks many voters are giving the economy.

Note: Data is annual rate of change, adjusted for seasonality and inflation.

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis.

By The New York Times

By Ben Casselman

U. S. economic growth was robust over the summer, as businesses poured money into artificial intelligence and consumers kept spending despite high prices that have soured their mood ahead of midterm elections next week.

Gross domestic product, the broadest measure of goods and services produced in the country, increased at a 3.4 percent annual rate in the third quarter, adjusted for inflation, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said Thursday.

That was an acceleration from the 2.2 percent rate in the spring, and was the fastest growth in a year. Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of economic output, grew at a 3.8 percent rate.

The strong spending and growth figures contrast with the poor marks that many voters are giving the economy as they head to the ballot box for next week’s midterm elections. Polls consistently show that Americans are frustrated with the high cost of living and hold President Trump and congressional Republicans responsible for failing to deliver on their promises to improve affordability.

Those frustrations are grounded in reality. Consumer prices were up 3.5 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier, driven in part by high gas prices that are the direct result of Mr. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. Americans are increasingly dipping into their savings to keep up with rising costs. Households, in the aggregate, saved just 4.1 percent of their after-tax income in the third quarter, the lowest rate in nearly four years. After-tax income, adjusted for inflation, rose in the third quarter as a whole but fell in September.

“The data on the economy are something to celebrate, but they look better on paper than they feel to most Americans,” said Diane Swonk, chief economist for KPMG, the accounting firm. And while the strength in the economy is real, she said, it is unequally distributed: Wealthy households are benefiting from growing stock portfolios, while wages, adjusted for inflation, have fallen over the past year.

“When you have a very large middle class and all boats are lifting with the tide, more people feel good about the economy,” Ms. Swonk said. “This has more of the feeling of some people in yachts and some people with no boats at all.”

Still, the data released Thursday, which is preliminary, is the latest evidence that while Americans may be unhappy about inflation, they haven’t pulled back their spending. That has helped keep the economy on track through a tumultuous period, but it could also be contributing to inflation by making it easier for businesses to pass on price increases to customers.

“This is a hot economy,” said Aditya Bhave, head of U. S. economics for Bank of America. “That’s the good news. The bad news is that inflation is the price we pay for that hot economy, and inflation is going to remain elevated.”

That could be a problem for officials at the Federal Reserve, who are trying to bring down inflation after five years above their goal of 2 percent annual price increases. On Wednesday, policymakers decided against raising interest rates for a second straight meeting, a gradual approach that some economists warn runs the risk of allowing inflation to become more entrenched.

Appearing on Fox Business, Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, said the “really huge” growth figures last quarter reflected a strong economy under President Trump.

“You can pick and choose specific prices and say, ‘Oh, I’m very frustrated about that,’ and it’s a legitimate concern, a legitimate feeling, but as an economist, you’ve got to look at things in the aggregate,” he said.

The A. I. investment boom is responsible, directly and indirectly, for much of the economy’s resilience. Companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars into building data centers and related infrastructure this year, with trillions more planned by 2030. That has rippled through the economy, lifting the fortunes not just of chipmakers and computer equipment manufacturers but also of companies seemingly far removed from the tech sector, like the producer of the gray paint used inside many data centers.

Investment in equipment grew at an astonishing 20.9 percent annual rate in the third quarter, and overall business investment grew at a 12.7 percent annual rate, accounting for more than half of G. D. P. growth. Those numbers are somewhat misleading, because many of the computer chips and other parts used in data centers are produced overseas, and therefore aren’t considered part of domestic output. Imports grew at a nearly 20 percent rate in the third quarter, in large part because of shipments of computer equipment.

Companies’ A. I. investments require domestic parts and labor too, however. That is helping to offset weakness elsewhere in the economy, particularly the housing market, which has been hit hard by high interest rates. Residential investment, which includes housing construction, contracted for the sixth time in the past seven quarters.

“Interest rates have been high, input prices have been ramping higher, the midterms have been approaching, other sources of uncertainty are intensifying, and yet we are in the midst of this data center construction boom,” said Anirban Basu, chief economist at Associated Builders and Contractors, a trade group. If not for A. I., he said, “we’d be talking about a very different economy, a very different stock market and a very different construction industry.”

Not all companies are benefiting. Smaller construction companies have struggled to win giant data center contracts, and are being squeezed as A. I. projects drive up the cost of materials and labor.

Power & Construction Group, an industrial construction company in upstate New York, has been shut out of the A. I. boom by the state’s moratorium on large data center projects. Projects unrelated to A. I. have dried up because of high interest rates and weak demand, said Thomas “Murph” Murphy, a vice president at the company.

The company is still growing because of strong demand for utility and infrastructure projects, he said. But it is competing with A. I. projects in other states for skilled workers.

“There are very attractive opportunities to go to some of these data centers,” Mr. Murphy said. “Especially our electrical guys and our welding guys, because they get paid huge money.”

Investor enthusiasm for all things A. I. has also helped push up share prices, which, in turn, has supported consumer spending, especially among wealthy households. Economists disagree about exactly how big a role this “wealth effect” is playing in the strong spending figures, but few doubt that it is important.

“The resiliency story has been about the connection between A. I.-related spending, asset markets and the upper-end consumer,” said Michael Gapen, chief U. S. economist for Morgan Stanley.

The economy’s reliance on A. I. as a source of growth could turn into a vulnerability if the boom falters. Concerns have mounted in recent weeks as investors have begun to scrutinize some of the companies behind the A. I. build-out, and to raise questions about whether the massive spending will pay off. Community opposition has also led to the delay or cancellation of data center projects around the country.

“The way I look at the economy now is, in one word, fragile,” said Ryan Cummings, the chief of staff for the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research. “You have this fragile consumption happening from the stock-market gains. And the stock market gains themselves in my view are incredibly fragile.”

Other economists are more optimistic, arguing that demand for A. I.-related infrastructure is likely to keep growing even if investors sour on individual companies. And they point to sources of strength outside A. I., especially the low unemployment rate, which has allowed Americans to keep spending.

“Never, ever underestimate the capacity of the American consumer to find things to spend money on as long as they have jobs,” Mr. Bhave said.

Tony Romm contributed reporting.

Ben Casselman is the chief economics correspondent for The Times. He has reported on the economy for nearly 20 years.
