Why Are We Having Less Sex? Ask a Pornographer.

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

interesting times

Erika Lust wants to excite you.

By Julia Yost

Produced by Raina Raskin and Charlotte Gartenberg

This episode includes a detailed discussion of pornography and descriptions of sex.

Pornography gets the blame for a lot of societal problems, including the so-called “sex recession.” Can porn ever really be ethical? Erika Lust thinks so. The adult filmmaker sees porn as an art form. She’s a self-described feminist who centers women’s desires and fantasies in her work. But how different is the product she’s making?

Lust sits down with Julia Yost, senior editor at “First Things,” to make the case for porn. Together, they discuss the adult film industry, stigmas around sex and translating fantasy into reality.

Below is an edited transcript of an episode of “Interesting Times.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.

Julia Yost: Erika Lust, welcome to “Interesting Times.”

You’re the first pornographer I’ve ever met.

Erika Lust: Oh!

Yost: As far as I know. And you’re a great advocate for porn and the cultural work that it can do.

I am not, to be clear. Nonetheless, I think we can find some common ground.

Tell me, how did Erika Hallqvist, a good girl from Sweden, become Erika Lust, world renowned adult filmmaker?

Lust: Well, it is a longer story. I try to tell it in the book, obviously, that has just come out here in the U. S. It’s an unexpected story, I think, for many people. Most think that people who are working in porn are doing it because they come from poor circumstances, that they had no other choice, and then somehow, they ended up in this industry.

Well, I studied political science in Sweden. I grew up in Sweden, one of the countries in this world with a feminist background, with sex education. We have a tradition of being a country that is a little bit more sexually liberated.

When I was growing up and I started to get in contact with my sexuality and wanted to figure out more about myself, I watched porn. Back then it was a whole different situation, because we didn’t have access to the internet that young people have access to today.

What I felt was that there was this discrepancy in my body. My body got turned on by looking at these images, but at the same time I felt conflict. I felt that something was not working for me.

It felt like the women were there mostly to please the men. But it wasn’t really their story.

And I asked myself: Why is it this way? Can it be different? Does another kind of porn exist?

When I started to talk to people and search for some things on that early internet, I found a book by a wonderful film professor from Berkeley, Linda Williams, called “Hard Core.” That book really changed my mind about pornography.

Through that book, I realized that pornography is not just porn. It’s more than that. It’s a discourse about sexuality and about gender and about how we relate to each other sexually.

Yost: Walk me through a day on set — without getting too explicit. How do you direct people to have sex?

Lust: What I’m doing is independent filmmaking, so I shoot with mostly female and queer crews. We are sometimes 50 people behind the camera. They are films that have been developed, that have characters. They have a narrative, they have a visual style to it.

What most people are curious about is: How do you work with performers? How does this really work? Do you put them at risk? Do they have a say?

We talk all the time to performers — the production team, the talent managers — to get to know them, to see who they are, what they like, and what they don’t like. Then, when they get cast for a film, we talk through everything in detail, about the film and about how they feel. What do they want to do with these characters? How do we develop the sexual tension and situation together?

And we don’t only talk about their boundaries and things that they don’t want to do, which is obviously something we do talk about, but we also talk a lot about the pleasure side of sex. What do they like? How do they like to get touched? We get into detail here. What is the easiest way to make them come? Can we make it happen on camera?

Then when we actually shoot this, we do the sex talk again in the morning when we arrive on set. We look at different angles. We also get the technical crew involved — our D. O. P. [director of photography, or cinematographer] and the camera operators — and then we will look at it from a more cinematic angle. Where do we have the good light? What kind of positions work in this scenario so that everything around feels great for everyone?

Yost: You have a lot of protocols to ensure safety and consent for everyone involved in your shoots. Can you describe those?

Lust: We have something that we call the “Bill of Rights” that every performer gets to see and read and sign before a shoot. We agree on how the process is going to work out. It’s also so that we both understand our responsibilities, because when you come in as a performer, it’s very important that you are aware that if anything doesn’t feel right, you need to voice that. But to be able to voice that, it’s important that they really feel that they are in an environment where they can speak up and they’re not going to get punished for it.

Yost: I wanted to ask about that. It strikes me that these are not normal labor practices. When you talk about your performers, your emphasis is always on the way in which they’re expressing themselves, they’re finding themselves, they’re connecting with each other, and then sharing that with viewers. But then you also need to follow up with them after the shoot and make sure they’re OK.

I wanted to ask, what do you feel that you’re protecting them from?

I was excited to talk to Erika Lust, and she did not disappoint. Erika makes “ethical pornography.” She seeks to liberate people by actualizing their fantasies, depicting the pleasure of women and minorities, and fostering erotic connections between porn users in real life. She is critical of ethical problems, including misogyny, in the porn industry at large. Her position is, “I love porn enough to criticize it.”I am skeptical that porn can be saved, or should be. I suspect that watching other people have sex teaches us to objectify one another, increases sexual dissatisfaction, and exacerbates the epidemic of loneliness. As the trend line for porn use rises, the trend lines for dating and sex are falling. Can porn be used to combat our social problems? Or is it a cause of many of them?

Lust: It’s being a support to make sure that afterward they don’t have second thoughts or other feelings. Because when you are on set, it is also somehow a euphoric experience. You come in, you are being taken care of, you feel like a star for that day. So many things are happening or going on, so many decisions are being made, and what I really want to do is to check in afterward whether they have any second thoughts about anything that could have happened.

Yost: So if someone does have second thoughts, what does that tend to look like? What kind of ambivalence or distress are they expressing to you, and how do you handle that?

Lust: I haven’t had that kind of situation where someone has said: Oh, I didn’t feel good at all — but I have had small comments on certain situations. There might have been someone spanking someone on the ass and then a performer saying: Hey Erika, I’ve been thinking, and I don’t want that part to be part of the film — for example. This is the kind of conversation that we are having .

Yost: What distinguishes pornography from a project like, say, “Euphoria,” which is an HBO drama that incorporates a lot of explicit elements but is certainly not classified as porn in genre terms?

You’re always emphasizing the cinematic and narrative elements of your work. You describe it as boutique, but you’re not trying to shed the porn label. In fact, you embrace it. So to you, what is it that makes your work porn?

Lust: Because I’m interested in exciting you. That’s part of the work. I’m interested in finding these erotic narratives, the stories, taking you as the audience on an erotic journey.

And when you talk about a series like “Euphoria” — I couldn’t watch the last season myself because I’m very sensitive to violence, and from what I’ve seen from the trailers it felt too violent to me — but the idea behind it is not to excite you.

Yost: Your project is not just aesthetic, it’s also moral or ethical. You’ve been called the “queen of ethical porn.” So explain ethical porn.

Lust: Well, always when we talk about “ethical,” it becomes very complicated, because what I’m really talking about when we say “ethical porn” is about the working conditions, the working standards, the whole process. How do we put it in practice? That’s the main goal of talking about ethical porn.

I also think it extends — we also have to think about how we market it, how we distribute it, and how we consume it. The whole ethical aspect also enters for consumers. For me, it’s essential that people understand that to make great pornography, it has a cost. You have to pay people a fair salary — crew and performers and staff, obviously. To do that, we need a budget. And to be able to have the support of that budget, you need to find a system that works.

I’m an independent production company owned by me and my husband. There are no big investors. There is nobody else in this. But the way we make this work is through our audience. It’s through our community of subscribers to our online cinema or streaming platform. They are the ones that are supporting the way we can actually make these films.

I would ask people that when they consume porn, don’t do it from the free online platforms. Don’t do it!

Yost: Yeah, support your local pornographer. Absolutely.

Lust: Exactly. Think the same way as you’re thinking about food or restaurants…

Yost: Fair trade, this and that.

Lust: … Or fair trade or clothes. We should all be more responsible consumers here, and we need to understand that as consumers, we have a great deal of power. We do. People and big industries and businesses, they see where you click and how much time you spend on something. You actually vote by spending your time online on certain sites.

I really would like to ask people to think twice and look for independent — independent — pornography.

Yost: Could you talk about realism as an aspect of your pornographic ethics?

Lust: Realism?

Yost: Yeah. It seems to me that you’re very interested in being realistic about the mechanics of female pleasure.

Lust: I am, definitely. I want it to feel real to my audience. I want my audience to feel that we are representing sex the way that they can find pleasure in real life.

This is also something that has upset me when I have watched what we call mainstream porn. Normally women are not portrayed in a realistic sexual context. It looks and feels very fake. I’m especially thinking about clitoral stimulation, that most women need during intercourse to be able to come.

[Laughs.] Can we say this? Can we say clitoral stimulation?

Yost: I believe we can. We may get an explicit label, but we can say it.

So you would consider your style of porn feminist? That’s part of your ethics?

Lust: I consider myself a feminist.

Yost: OK.

Lust: And I make porn. That’s how I would put it.

Yost: What does feminism mean for you in the context of porn?

Lust: In the context of porn, I would go to two things: Participation behind the camera. Who’s making this film? Who’s in the process? Who has the right to make decisions? And then I will talk about representation. What do we see onscreen? Not only women, obviously, but how is gender portrayed? Do we see different kinds of power relations where the films are helping us to understand who is who and how they are negotiating?

I feel that many times in regular mainstream kinds of pornography, that conversation is happening outside the camera. It’s not happening in the film. But I know from experience and from working with many performers that this is standard in the adult industry today. It’s standard to have all these negotiations. So even if you don’t see it in the scene, it’s probably happened before.

But I think it really can help the audience if they get to see it onscreen.

Yost: Yeah. So you really emphasize character and narrative and context and all these forms of complexity. I’m listening to you talk and thinking: Wow, she makes porn sound like a George Eliot novel.

[Lust laughs.]

But your account of porn’s positive work is not universally accepted by feminists. In the ’70s and ’80s, Andrea Dworkin argued that pornography inherently subjugated women, like other forms of sex work.

Archival recording of Andrea Dworkin: “Pornography… is a system of sexual exploitation, in which women are devalued. Women are turned into commodities. Women are sold as meat. Women are in fact tortured… Pornography creates both physical aggression toward women and attitudes and behaviors of discrimination, and it makes every struggle that we have toward civil equality essentially ridiculous.”

Yost: So why should women embrace porn and sex work broadly?

Lust: Well, there’s many types of feminism, just as there’s many kinds of porn, obviously. Part of the feminist movement believes that there could never exist a fair feminist kind of pornography.

Obviously I don’t agree with them. I think that we as women have the right to our pleasure, to our sexuality, and we need space to try things out and to get into our own fantasies and desire and to revise them.

I am also a product of this world we live in. I’m a product of this patriarchy, and my fantasies are not only my fantasies, but they are a construct of what I have learned in this society since I was a little girl. And pornography is helping us to get rid of that sexual shame that so many of us somehow feel.

Yost: So far we’ve been focusing on your work and talking around the other world of porn out there, the type that floods the internet. What is the nonfeminist pornography that you are working against?

Lust: It’s almost everything that’s out there. It’s lots of people and creators who really have no interest in how to show female pleasure onscreen, but are more interested in the business of pornography. They’re interested, not so much in the actual sex, but in the clicks and in the algorithms.

What I’ve seen is a business that has been taken over by many of these tech guys. If we look back at the ’60s and the ’70s, when we had this golden era of porn and the porn was even in the theaters, many of the creators back then, they were filmmakers, they were artists. They were people who had a vision and who had this reaction to a conservative world that they lived in back then and wanted to show a more liberated sexuality.

But then, as society advanced, we got into the videocassette era, and then to the beginning of the internet, with this pay site and the photo archives with images that you could slowly download. And then we get to the era we now live in, with the “tube” sites taking over.

This is where these tech guys really come in. They’re not that interested in the sex anymore, but rather in the technology of it.

Yost: So what kind of porn do those sites tend to host? What are the mechanics of it? What’s the style of it? Is it substantively misogynistic?

Lust: It’s phallocentric. I would use that as the first way of describing it. It’s about men and their sexuality. And women are many, many times reduced to some kind of object in that sexuality, but it’s not really their stories.

Yost: There’s a big audience surely for this misogynistic porn which you critique. Is there something wrong with the millions of men who are using it to fantasize? You say that women have a right to their desires, including desires that have been shaped by the patriarchy. Do men not?

Lust: No, of course, they also have a right to fantasizing and desire. But I think we have to think … How should I put it? It’s a job each of us have to understand what we are desiring and what we are fantasizing about and how it affects us in our life.

I also think it’s very important that we understand that we are cultural products. We are socialized with the general ideas that we have as human beings, and if we understand those and we criticize them and we think about them, we are also able to change.

So I think sometimes men haven’t even realized that what they are attracted to in some sexual circumstances is this misogynistic concept.

Yost: What if a woman were attracted to a misogynistic concept?

Lust: Well, they are. Many, many women are. We all are. But we have to be able to explore it and to think about it.

When it comes to porn, it’s also interesting how we all have this personal relationship to it, to what we enjoy when nobody watches us, and then how we talk about it when we’re in front of other people, when we are in contact with other people. Sometimes what we see is how that conversation changes.

Yost: How does it change as a whole?

Lust: It changes in the sense that we feel that what we like is shameful and is something that we shouldn’t like. And then when we talk about it to other people, we don’t recognize what actually turns us on.

Yost: Where does it come from, that idea that what we like is shameful, that our desires are shameful? What’s your sense of that?

Lust: It has a long tradition. We can go back many, many years in history and what we see is a change from Roman culture to Christian culture, where we start seeing how the church somehow is dividing all these goddesses — women — that we had in the past, who were representing so many things, representing power, representing fertility, representing sexuality.

And then when we get into this moment of history, they are being divided into different roles. Suddenly we have the whore on the one side, and we have the respectable mother figure Maria, the saint, on the other side.

Yost: My understanding of the scholarship around the transition from pre-Christian to Christian Rome is that Christianity was the force that accorded rights to women in the domain of sex and marriage, and also basically said: Hands off the little boys.

I was struck by that moment in your book where you describe going to, I think it was Pompeii?

Lust: Yes.

Yost: Yes. And you saw the frescoes, and there was ——

Lust: The erect penises.

Yost: Yes, exactly. And, I don’t know, orgies or whatever, depicted on walls. You felt that was a very liberating moment, and you thought, yes, there was a time when sex was just so elaborately incorporated into art, and it was out in the open, and it was not consigned to the red-light district. It’s just in people’s dining rooms or whatever.

And I thought, yeah, but that was part of a sexual dispensation that was actually quite cruel to both women and children. I’m not sure you really want to live in Pompeii before the volcano.

Lust: [Chuckles.] I would rather live there today than in any period of the past.

Yost: Yeah, I’m sure you would.

We’re recording this conversation in the midst of a pretty big story here in the U. S. I’m not sure if you’ve been following the story of the Cornell Seven. Seven young men are accused of sexually assaulting a young woman in the context of group sex under the influence of drugs and alcohol on a college campus.

I was thinking about this story as I read your book and wondering whether the students had drawn on some scenario they had picked up from porn — a gangbang scenario.

I wanted to ask you, when pornographic fantasy meets reality, as it will sometimes do, is there potential for risk or danger?

Lust: What we see in cinema, we see it in film, we see it in video games, we read it in books and obviously some of these stories are also portrayed in porn. But I don’t think that porn has this kind of magical power that it’s so much bigger than other media in influencing people in doing exact acts.

What I see is a huge lack of sex education. I see a huge lack of conversation around sex and around consent and respecting women. And I think that those conversations and that sex education is what we really, really need to focus on now.

We cannot continue censoring voices who are speaking about eroticism and who are speaking about sexuality. We cannot censor books in school. We cannot cut sex education programs when it’s so clearly seen that it’s needed.

Yost: This is interesting. What do you think sex education should encompass? Because in the United States it tends to be how not to get pregnant, how not to get an S. T. D. — I guess we’re calling them S. T. I. s [sexually transmitted infections] now.

Lust: That’s the basics.

Yost: That’s the basics?

Lust: That’s the absolute basics.

Yost: But you had the Nordic model growing up, and that’s much more extensive. What would you have children learning, and from what age?

Lust: Right from the beginning. For me, it’s not one sex conversation that you have to have and when suddenly your kid is ——

Yost: So we’re talking first grade?

Lust: —— Yes. We’re talking parents who need to be part of this from the beginning. I think we need to be more natural with conversations around sex. People are discovering their bodies from a very young age, and what we are doing is giving them messages. Sometimes if we don’t give them vocabulary, they don’t even know how to name their sexual organs.

If we don’t have these conversations with them, we are sending them directly into trouble.

Yost: Yeah, they’ll learn it from Pornhub or whatever.

Lust: Well, they’ll learn it from all over our society. Some might learn it from Pornhub, others might learn it from “Euphoria.” We have to be aware of the importance in today’s society of being media literate, of being porn literate, of being able to think critically of anything you read or see.

We all know that on socials there are messages being passed on to our kids and teens and young adults and adults all the time.

Yost: So a sex ed curriculum for you would certainly include porn literacy and also …

Lust: Gender identity questions.

Yost: OK, gender identity. So kids being asked about their pronouns every week? Because you get that in some of the toniest schools.

Lust: It’s not that they have to be asked every week about their pronouns. What we need to be able to do is to stop this heteronormative culture that we have. We need to enter a queer perspective into all sex education. We need to make people feel that they have a right over their bodies and their identities, and that they can safely express that and be respected and that they can get an inclusive, diverse sex education without having this very heteronormative perspective that is still the most powerful that we see in sex education in most countries.

Yost: To return us to the Cornell case, the question about fantasy versus reality, you’re proposing a pretty sturdy border between those two. For you, it’s just kind of: OK, porn is porn, and remember these are trained professionals on a closed course, and do not attempt unless you really, really want to, and you’re going to be really careful — or something like that.

Lust: Correct.

Yost: One of the reasons I wanted to bring up the Cornell case is because gangbangs feature prominently in your new book. The first chapter is titled “Does Every Woman Deserve a Gang-Bang?” In it, you write about overcoming your discomfort with gangbangs in order to film one.

Why was it important for you to push past that discomfort and make that film?

Lust: Because I had, like so many people, this idea that we are talking about, that a gangbang is a situation where a group of men are preying on a woman.

Then I met a performer, an actor, Kazumi. We were in a meeting, talking about potentially making a film together. I had maybe more romantic ideas for this film, but then when we started to talk about what she really liked and what she wanted to do, this idea of her wanting to do a gangbang with five men came up time after time after time. So I had to challenge my own prejudices.

Then when she started to explain how she felt about it and she told me real life stories of her life outside the adult industry and situations she had had, and she told me about all the fun and how it made her feel to be the center of so much attention and so much care, it really opened up my mind.

Yost: You write: “A woman enjoying sex with multiple men on her own terms for her own gratification is the ultimate anti-patriarchal sex fantasy. No wonder it’s taboo.” That’s kind of the understanding of the gangbang that you finally reached.

But I do wonder whether that taboo, and perhaps also your discomfort, arose in part from an intuition that was arguably vindicated by the Cornell case, namely that one woman having sex with multiple men is objectively a risky situation.

I wonder whether some stigmas on sex may exist for good reason because the activities that are stigmatized are intrinsically risky.

Lust: I think many of the stigmas we have come from these kinds of situations from the past where a woman feels that she’s in a risky situation. Walking through a park at night, I would feel that that’s a risky situation. It’s a situation where many women would hold their keys in their hands. But also, if we don’t face some of these risky situations, then we don’t have the same opportunities, the same possibilities ——

Yost: So every woman deserves a gangbang, is what I’m getting from you.

Lust: —— To go out, to live, to feel. I think that this was also something that was in Virginie Despentes’s book, “King Kong Theory,” where she talks a lot about this idea that even if there’s risk, go out into the world and experience and take up space and learn on the way.

Yost: Your advocacy of porn seems to presume that we live in a patriarchy in which girls and women are taught to feel shame about their bodies and desires, and that demonizing pornography is an extension of that.

But is this true? It seems to me that most of the messaging to girls and women is sex-positive, and pornography certainly has been normalized to the extent that it’s been widely adopted. So who needs to hear the good news of sexual liberation?

Lust: I don’t agree. Sex-positive messages — yes, some of them we have. Empowerment messages — yes, some of them are out there. But at the same time, I still see so many women worrying about their own sexuality, about what they project to the world, how they are dressing, what kind of sex they want to have, what kind of sex they accept having.

I still hear so many stories of women being in sexual relationships, especially with heterosexual men, where not only is the orgasm gap really, really happening, but also the whole sex act is focused on pleasing their men instead of really having a life-fulfilling moment for themselves.

And when I talk to them and they describe how they’re having sex by themselves, it’s a whole different story.

Yost: Do you think there’s too much reticence around the question of the mechanics of female pleasure? That people don’t talk enough about that?

Lust: People talk about it, but I think they could still talk lots more about it. It’s also different in different generations.

I’m hearing a lot lately about people stuck on social media, stuck on their cellphones, connecting much less with people. We hear reports about young people not having as much sex anymore.

Yost: Yeah, I wanted to ask you about that.

Lust: We hear reports about the A. I. girlfriends. That seems easier for some young men to connect to than real people.

Sex involves intimacy, it involves negotiation, it involves friction, it involves difficult conversations sometimes.

Yost: Yeah. So we’re talking about, what I’ll call, in-person sex.

Lust: Mm-hmm. In-person sex.

Yost: Whereas porn is other people’s sex that you’re watching. So I think that for you, porn can facilitate in-person sex or can foster connections between flesh and blood human beings who watch it. But I wonder whether that’s universally the case. Do you see the abundance of porn on the internet as contributing to the problem of the decline of sex?

Lust: I think it starts with the people who have anxieties about sex, fear, shame, difficulties connecting to other people. I think that technology really has worsened this situation, because we have less interaction with real people, and people are afraid of getting humiliated somehow through connecting, through not being accepted by a potential partner or not knowing how to reach out. They are scared that it’s going to go wrong somehow.

I think that all this kind of anxiety has led to many people having an easier time fulfilling their sexual needs watching porn online than connecting with other people.

Yost: So it’s kind of old-fashioned shame at bottom? That’s the issue?

Lust: I think so.

Yost: So you don’t see the availability of porn as a replacement for actual partners?

Lust: I don’t think it is. I honestly don’t think it is. You want to connect with someone.

Yost: No, I agree!

Lust: You want to touch someone. You want to be in the same room.

Yost: I’m with you.

Lust: You want the bodies to be active in this.

Yost: I’m completely with you, but not everybody’s with us on that.

Lust: But I think they are fearing it. I don’t know if it’s that they don’t want it or that the fear is so big and they have so little knowledge in how to connect to others.

Yost: Oh, I think the revealed preferences are that a lot of people do actually prefer to have perfect control over their sexual experiences, which they can get with a vibrator and Pornhub — whatever. I don’t know.

Lust: It’s hard! It’s hard to ask another person.

Yost: It is.

Lust: It’s hard to ask for what you want. And here we get to the point again, where so many people don’t even know what they want. They don’t know what they want.

Sex education — here we go. We need sex education.

Yost: But I guess I wonder whether too much exploration can make sex actually less enjoyable. There’s a recent report that was written up in “The Atlantic” that found that married churchgoing Americans have the most sex of any demographic group in the country.

It would seem that the most vanilla people have the hottest sex lives. Explain that to me.

Lust: Maybe it’s the connection after church on Sunday.

Yost: Maybe.

Lust: Maybe.

Yost: But I just wonder about the relation of porn to satisfaction. Is it possible that people who spend a lot of time watching other people have sex and thinking about the kinds of sex they could be having but probably aren’t — could they be more prone to sexual dissatisfaction?

Lust: Here it’s also a question of how much porn are we really watching? This is also an interesting subject because many people who consider themselves porn addicts, when they actually look at the numbers of how much porn they’re watching, they watch much less porn than people who don’t consider themselves porn addicts.

And there’s this idea, the moral incongruence idea ——

Yost: Yeah, the funny thing about that though is that, to me, that doesn’t undermine their position. It’s just a description of their struggle. Because if you’re a person who doesn’t want to be using porn, you have some kind of objection to it — maybe it’s religious, maybe it’s not religious, maybe you just want to practice more temperance in your life or discipline or whatever, or you find it’s getting in the way of your finding other people to connect with — you’re going to try not to use it. You will probably use less of it.

But to the extent that you do use it, it’s because you feel compelled, you feel like you have a compulsion. I think that’s where the language of compulsion and addiction comes from, the sense that people feel sort of captured by porn. They feel that they cannot quit it, even though they want to.

I did want to ask you about people like that. What would you say to them? Is their job simply to put away their shame? Or could there be a way in which their desire to be rid of porn is valid?

Lust: I think you have to find a balance that works for you in your own life. I feel that, first of all, it’s also a question of what kind of porn are you watching? I would like to watch porn that I feel represents my value, and I would not connect to a kind of pornography that I feel is not representing me.

For me, it’s important to use these moments as a connection with my own erotic self. It’s almost a moment of erotic mindfulness somehow.

Yost: You’re a virtuoso of porn. I think that for most people it’s not a mindfulness moment probably.

Lust: [Chuckles.] But maybe it’s also because the porn that I watch, the porn I make, the porn that I’m in contact with, it’s so great. It’s so beautiful.

Yost: Yeah, you have a good porn diet, no doubt.

Lust: So it’s true that I live in a bubble of sex positivity and people who are wanting to explore their identity through this kind of pornography.

Yost: But I just repeatedly hear you describing the psychology of that refusal as arising from shame, that everybody has shame over their bodies, shame over their desires. They think sex is dirty, and we have to use sex education and whatnot to train people out of that.

I have to say that that does not ring true to me. My social and professional networks are very conservative on sex, and the idea of shame about desire and sex being dirty, those are not sentiments that I would attribute to anyone I know.

Lust: Seriously?

Yost: Oh, no. No.

Lust: You don’t feel that people are thinking …

Yost: I think that they agree with you that sex is extremely important and meaningful.

Lust: Yes.

Yost: And they take that insight in a different direction. They say because of that, we honor it by putting certain parameters on it, which not everybody needs to accept, obviously. It’s a free society.

But that is the logic. I would say that is my logic. That’s the logic of pretty much everyone I know. If they do think that sex is shameful, they’re not saying it out loud, so they’re ashamed of the idea that they think sex is shameful.

Lust: But I think that that is happening. I think that that is also happening.

Yost: What is?

Lust: That some people think that they don’t want to say that they think that sex is shameful. In a conversation, they want to be open and liberal and make other people feel that they are not judging anyone.

Yost: Yeah, sure. I mean, I’m talking about people who tend to have five or more kids, so they’re definitely having sex.

Lust: Right.

Yost: So they’re definitely not inhibited from it in their own lives. I think one thing I would suggest is that America’s favorite ice cream flavor is vanilla.

Lust: Uh-huh.

Yost: And so you could say—

Lust: But it’s a good flavor

Yost: It’s a great flavor.

Lust: Why not?

Yost: Why not? One could say that in a patriarchy death by chocolate is taboo because people think that cocoa powder is dirty. But then you would just get a lot of American women saying: “No, thank you. I’m just a vanilla gal.”

It’s not that there’s a fear of porn. There’s often just the kind of thing that it’s private like my finances are private. Sex is private for reasons that don’t have to do with its intrinsically shameful nature, which I just don’t think that all that many people believe in anymore.

It just comes down to how you want to play it, and that often implicates values, but I don’t think that the values are this kind of patriarchal misogynistic thing that I feel like is your mission to oppose.

Lust: I don’t want to push porn on anyone.

Yost: Oh, no. Agreed, agreed.

Lust: If you don’t want to watch it, I think that’s the one thing.

Yost: No, certainly. I don’t take you to be saying that.

Lust: What I do want is to offer an alternative for people who felt that we couldn’t find the kind of pornography that we wanted to watch. And I think that we are, quite a lot of people, feeling that way.

Yost: Well, this has been fascinating. Erika Lust, it’s been a pleasure.

Lust: Thank you very much.

Ilhan Omar Investigation Involves New Scrutiny of Long-Disputed Marriage

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

Several current and former law enforcement officials said an Obama-era investigation found some evidence that Ms. Omar had entered into a sham marriage with a man suspected of being her brother.

By Ernesto Londoño

Reporting from Minneapolis

The federal investigation of Representative Ilhan Omar is focused in part on whether she entered into a sham marriage in 2009 to help a man suspected of being her brother obtain a green card, according to current and former officials familiar with the matter.

The F. B. I. and Department of Homeland Security investigated the marriage in summer 2016, during the Obama administration, and found some evidence that it was fraudulent, current and former officials said.

Speculation that Ms. Omar committed marriage fraud with a brother has shadowed the Minnesota Democrat’s political career for more than a decade and President Trump repeated the accusation last week. She has long called it a right-wing conspiracy theory that federal officials debunked during her first race for elected office in 2016.

But that case stalled chiefly because prosecutors concluded that the potential crime, a felony, fell outside a five-year statute of limitations, according to the current and former officials, most of whose law enforcement careers spanned several presidential administrations.

Now the Trump administration, whose top leaders have long reviled Ms. Omar, has revived the scrutiny as one element of a sprawling investigation into the Omar family’s journey to the United States as refugees from war-torn Somalia. At issue is her marriage in 2009, when she was already a U. S. citizen, to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, a British citizen whom she divorced in 2017.

The reporting for this article is based on interviews with three current and former officials familiar with the present-day investigation and six current and former officials with knowledge of the 2016 investigation.

It is unclear what evidence prosecutors, then or now, have showing that the person Ms. Omar married was her brother. Marrying anyone for the sole purpose of securing a green card is illegal under federal law. Marrying a sibling is illegal under state law, but it is not clear whether state authorities ever investigated the matter.

It is also unclear whether federal prosecutors could find a path to charging Ms. Omar that skirts the statute of limitations that applies to marriage-based immigration fraud, a crime that would not threaten her citizenship.

Regardless, they could cite the marriage in an indictment or civil action that describes a family immigration fraud conspiracy — a broader case that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said could lead to Ms. Omar’s deportation.

The extraordinary investigation burst into public view when agents searched Ms. Omar’s Washington home on Oct. 12. Democrats have loudly condemned it as a political persecution and said it violates a Justice Department policy to avoid overt measures that could be seen as affecting the vote in the weeks before Election Day. Ms. Omar is seeking her fifth term in next week’s midterms.

Up to now, officials have said investigators are examining whether Ms. Omar’s late father lied or omitted information in immigration forms before becoming an American citizen. Another subject of inquiry is whether Ms. Omar, who was a child when she immigrated to the United States, was too old to have qualified for citizenship through her father in 2000, The New York Times reported last week.

Last week, the Justice Department referred to the congresswoman as Ilhan Nur Said Elmi in a court filing and suggested that the name she has long used is an alias. In a statement Thursday, Mr. Trump drew attention to the similarity of the name to that of the man she had married in 2009. He suggested that the two might be siblings.

Ms. Omar, an ardent critic of the president, strongly rejected the claim through a spokeswoman.

“Rep. Omar has repeatedly and unequivocally denied this baseless, disgusting conspiracy theory,” Jackie Rogers, the spokeswoman, said in a statement. “This is a desperate political smear designed to distract from Trump’s failed presidency and two years of Republican failure in Congress.”

Mr. Elmi, who is listed on the University of Bristol’s website as a doctoral student writing a thesis about Kenya’s L. G. B. T. community, did not respond to several requests for comment by email, LinkedIn and through a friend.

Murmurs that Ms. Omar married a brother first surfaced publicly in 2016, when she was on the brink of making history as the first Somali American elected to a state legislature. A first-time candidate, she had just defeated a 44-year incumbent in the Democratic primary to represent a Minneapolis district when Somali community message boards and conservative outlets claimed that she had once married a sibling.

Federal agents in Minnesota opened an investigation, according to several people familiar with the matter. They found evidence suggesting that Mr. Elmi and Ms. Omar were siblings, according to the six former and current officials familiar with the case. But, because prosecutors did not pursue the matter, the agents had limited investigative tools, the officials said.

Mr. Elmi had obtained a provisional two-year green card based on the marriage, two former officials said. But when he sought to make that status permanent, immigration officials requested additional evidence about the validity of the marriage. Instead of responding, Mr. Elmi left the United States and abandoned his green card petition, the officials said.

The officials who investigated the matter in its early phase included an F. B. I. agent who specializes in public corruption and civil rights cases, and two agents at Homeland Security Investigations, a division of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Two of the investigators remain employed at their agencies in Minnesota.

The F. B. I. and the U. S. attorney’s office in Minnesota declined to comment. The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to an inquiry.

In August 2016, a local news station reported that the U. S. attorney’s office in Minnesota had opened an investigation into Ms. Omar.

That prompted the campaign to form a “crisis management committee,” Carla Kjellberg, a lawyer who represented Ms. Omar, said in a 2018 deposition related to a state campaign finance inquiry. Ms. Kjellberg added that the campaign worried that the story, which was being covered by right-wing publications, could gain traction in mainstream outlets.

A means to quash it came on Aug. 22, 2016, when the campaign released a letter it had requested from Andrew M. Luger, then the U. S. attorney in Minnesota. In the three-sentence letter, Mr. Luger wrote that “my office is not investigating, nor have we requested an investigation into Ms. Omar.”

Ms. Omar at the time characterized the letter as an exoneration that put to rest “flat-out falsehoods.” Ms. Kjellberg said in the deposition that the credibility of the claim “fell drastically once Andy Luger said that’s false.”

But in an interview last week, Mr. Luger said that the letter “was never meant to say anything about the substance of the claims.” Instead, he said, it was narrowly written to rebut the news station’s report that Mr. Luger had asked ICE to investigate Ms. Omar, which he called erroneous.

Federal agents may have been pursuing the matter without his knowledge, Mr. Luger said. He added that he had never shielded Ms. Omar from scrutiny, and that he later backed primary candidates who ran against her.

After Mr. Luger’s letter became public, local news coverage of the marriage controversy waned. Ms. Omar won her first race in a blowout, and she quickly became a rising star on the left.

In 2018, two years into the first Trump administration, Ms. Omar made history again, becoming the first African refugee and the first hijab-wearing woman elected to Congress.

She and Mr. Trump began trading insults soon after she arrived in Washington.

As Mr. Trump sought to limit immigration, including from several Muslim countries, Ms. Omar became a visible foil, calling her own presence in the U. S. Capitol a “nightmare” for the president.

In summer 2019, Mr. Trump told reporters that there was “a lot of talk about the fact that she was married to her brother.”

Those remarks turbocharged interest in Ms. Omar’s marital history, which conservative journalists and operatives have spent years scrutinizing.

According to her own accounts, Ms. Omar has been married three times. In her 2020 memoir, “This is What America Looks Like,” Ms. Omar wrote that she first wed a fellow Somali immigrant, Ahmed Hirsi, in an Islamic ceremony in 2001, when she was 18. The two did not file paperwork to make the union legal at that time, she wrote.

In the book, she described a second marriage in 2009 to a British man as an impulsive elopement during a low point in her life. That was a reference to Mr. Elmi, though Ms. Omar did not use his name.

Several aspects of the marriage to Mr. Elmi have long been murky. For instance, although Ms. Omar is an observant Muslim, the couple’s marriage certificate was signed by a Christian pastor rather than an imam.

In 2014 and 2015, when she was still legally married to Mr. Elmi, Ms. Omar filed joint federal tax returns with Mr. Hirsi, the campaign finance inquiry found.

Ms. Omar later said that she amended the tax filings but declined to explain what led to the error. Her marriage to Mr. Elmi was dissolved in court in 2017, and Ms. Omar said in a divorce filing at that time that they had been separated and had no contact for years.

Ms. Omar had said she and Mr. Hirsi — the father of her children — reconciled after her relationship with Mr. Elmi ended. She and Mr. Hirsi got legally married in early 2018 and divorced in late 2019, marriage and court records show. Mr. Hirsi did not respond to several messages requesting comment by phone, text and Facebook.

In March 2020, Ms. Omar announced her marriage to a third spouse, Tim Mynett, a political consultant her campaign had employed.

Mr. Trump returned to the White House last year after promising the biggest deportation push in history. Last fall, he and top aides became engrossed by a social services fraud scandal in Minnesota in which scores of Somali Americans were charged with stealing hundreds of millions of dollars.

Around then, the Justice Department began prioritizing a new inquiry into Ms. Omar’s immigration issues, several officials familiar with the inquiry said.

In March, as Mr. Trump announced an anti-fraud task force led by Vice President JD Vance, the president called Ms. Omar “one of the ringleaders.” Days later, Mr. Vance told a conservative commentator that the administration had conclusively established that Ms. Omar committed immigration fraud and was exploring ways to hold her accountable.

In September, Mr. Mullin, the homeland security secretary, disclosed that the inquiry had broadened from questions about the 2009 marriage to determine whether the lawmaker and her relatives committed fraud after they were admitted to the country as refugees.

“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place,” he said, “we’ll deport you.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research and Alan Feuer and Megan Specia contributed reporting.

Ernesto Londoño is a Times reporter based in Minnesota, covering news in the Midwest and drug use and counternarcotics policy. He welcomes tips and can be reached at elondono.81 on Signal.

on Comedy

Swiping jokes word for word, these bodacious bots mainly lift from young female comedians. What’s so insidious is how they’re subtly changing us, the audience.

Credit...

Supported by

By Jason Zinoman

Where were you when the A. I. revolution came for stand-up comedy?

I was looking at my phone this month when all of a sudden my social media scrolls filled with teasingly seductive female comedians in front of brick walls, drawing hundreds of thousands of followers through flirty onstage punchlines.

If the jokes of these Stepford stand-ups, packed into crop tops and body suits, seemed familiar, that’s because they were stolen.

This taut, deftly crafted joke by Olivia Carter …

… was copied word for word, with a less expressive delivery:

In another, Olga Namer, a real stand-up, exuberantly acted out a date she had with a nice guy …

… with timing and language that was aped by this realistic-looking bot whose more deadpan version ends on a slightly darker note:

I had been a skeptic about the threat that artificial intelligence poses to stand-up comedy. Sure, ChatGPT may spell doom for the screenwriter of “Toy Story 12.” But I’ve spent enough time experimenting with large language models to conclude that they would figure out how to destroy a city before an audience.

That’s because laughter is inherently social. So much of the appeal of stand-up is in its connection with another human face, sensibility, consciousness. Or at least, that’s what I believed until the invasion of virtual comedians shook my confidence. Now I am here with a warning: Saucy synthetics are coming for our jokes and they might end up taking much more.

Strikingly, this industrial-scale heist swiped from one demographic almost exclusively: young, non-famous female comics making jokes about dating or sex. No bots were aping Jim Gaffigan or Dave Chappelle. But the New York club comic Natalie Cuomo, whose crowd-work videos often go viral, told Deadline. com that seven to 10 of her jokes were taken.

It now seems obvious that A. I. comedy would find success with a bot less like the Terminator than the one in “Ex Machina,” the film in which a tech billionaire designs a sexy android to appeal to the male gaze.

After all, Mark Zuckerberg’s empire began with male students rating their female classmates. Instagram sex-robot comedy builds on a similar impulse.

What might have been more disturbing than the theft was the response to it. For one thing, I thought the uncanny valley would protect human comedy, because the closer A. I. came to imitating real people, the creepier it would seem. But the comments on the accounts of these fake comics suggested viewers either couldn’t tell the difference between real stand-ups and bots or didn’t mind. Being creepy might not matter on a site that can appeal to the creep in everyone.

In early October, many comics whose jokes were stolen posted videos sounding the alarm.

Would it shock you that the response from the platforms was tepid? Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram, commented on the account of one comic, saying he wanted to drive more traffic to original artists, but that it wasn’t practical to ban A. I.

Joke stealing has long been considered a reputation-ruining offense. But unlike humans, A. I. comics can’t be shamed.

You might say that A. I. is just using the same old Hollywood playbook: selling a version of reality with more sex appeal. The difference is that the tech companies have already manipulated the market to give themselves a better chance of success. As traditional networks decline, young comics rely on social media to make a living. It’s where they market their work and make money by going viral — and everyone knows the way to gain followers is through outrage or sex appeal.

Comedians feel pressure to post bikini pics to promote shows. And comment sections filled with men assessing female comics’ looks has become normalized. It wasn’t that long ago that being attractive was slightly taboo in comedy. Now there’s a premium on it.

The message received by female comedians is grim. Olga Namer saw a joke of hers get more engagement for an A. I. version of a comic. She posted a video concluding: “I know my writing is good. It’s my boobs that are the problem.”

We don’t know who is behind the fake comedian accounts, but the strategy of stealing from young female comics has a dystopian business logic. Because social media incentives led the real stand-ups to post sexual material, A. I. conveniently has a large supply of jokes to steal. If comedy is a bellwether, this represents a dark future in which tech players exploit human labor until the quality of the imitation is good enough that it can cut us out of the equation.

They started with comics without much fame and clout. But stars shouldn’t get too comfortable. Recently, the virtual comedians have moved from standing in clubs to sitting near the desk of fake versions of late night talk-show hosts:

One video combines O’Brien’s hair with Fallon’s face, creating a bizarre creature out of a talk-show version of David Cronenberg’s “The Fly.”

The other advantage that the A. I. creations have is that they can more easily adjust to the increasingly globalized comedy market, telling the same joke in English …

… and in French:

The most damaging part of this trend might be how A. I. is training audiences what to expect. The first time a young viewer sees stand-up these days, it’s more likely to be in front of a digital brick wall than an actual one.

Audiences want well-crafted jokes, clever premises, punchlines that pop out of nowhere. But some viewers will settle, then develop a taste for that reduced quality. Then a nostalgia for it. Audiences will not only grow less discerning. They will become increasingly docile, easily manipulated and even replaced.

The popularity of videos of comics doing crowd work, long considered a less ambitious way to get a laugh than crafted material, is already an example of how social media has lowered standards. Outsourcing this cheap trick to a collection of raunchy pixels is just the next step.

Take a closer look at those videos of fake comedians: The crowds are computer-generated as well. Whether we realize it or not, those canned laughs have a job to do: They encourage us to laugh. It works.

It’s a pleasing fiction that laughter is always a purely honest response to what we think is funny. The truth is that humans are easier to manipulate than we think. We laugh more if we see others doing it. A. I. surely knows this and is using the social aspect of comedy against us. If we’re not careful, the most human of activities — cracking up — could be slowly drained of humanity.

Produced by Tala Safie

I recently received an email from Felicia Madison, a standup comic who runs the Westside Comedy Club, with the attention-grabbing title: “So this is a new phenomenon.” She pointed me a video of an A. I. comic who stole one of her jokes. Asked how she felt about it, she joked that she was flattered because the targets of such theft were “usually hot girls.”

Jason Zinoman is a critic at large for the Culture section of The Times and writes a column about comedy.

A Monkey King and a Maiden Fell in Love. For China’s Regulator, It Crossed a Line.

The New York Times October 29, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mash-up videos of beloved characters from Chinese classics — some made with A. I. — have caught the attention of the authorities.

By Tiffany May

Reporting in Hong Kong

In wholesome videos that have delighted the Chinese internet in recent weeks, the Monkey King in a yellow martial arts outfit and a maiden swathed in embroidered silks walk hand in hand. They frolic on sandy beaches and lush forest trails. They ride roller coasters and sample ice cream in a lantern-lit night market.

The unlikely couple are Sun Wukong and Lin Daiyu, who hail from “Journey to the West” and “Dream of the Red Chamber,” classic Chinese novels that were turned into television shows in the 1980s.

The pair had never met in literature — or onscreen — until now. Their love story has been concocted by fans, some using artificial intelligence and some splicing old TV footage together.

While they are popular with audiences in China, the videos have attracted the attention of the authorities, who believe they take too much creative license by bringing characters from disparate worlds together.

An editorial this month in People’s Daily, a Communist Party mouthpiece, acknowledged the appeal of rewriting the destiny of the characters, but said it risked eroding the meaning of the original stories, which are considered among the four most important Chinese classical novels. The editorial called for red lines to be drawn over videos depicting “malicious alterations that ridicule heroes.”

Citing a government directive to remove A. I. animations that “seriously violate” the spirit of original works of classical literature and their characters, platforms said in October that they had taken down thousands of videos featuring the Monkey King and Lin Daiyu as a couple, one citing “improper romantic associations” between them.

The two 1980s televised adaptations were the childhood staples of a generation of Chinese millennials, and the characters are beloved for being misfits unbound by convention. The novels have also been reinterpreted into films and operas.

Sun Wukong, the Monkey King from “Journey of the West,” was the irrepressible companion of a guileless monk seeking nirvana. He often found himself in trouble with the gods.

Lin Daiyu was an orphaned girl who had been taken in by wealthy relations in “Dream of the Red Chamber.” Sentimental and sickly, she was prone to sulky ripostes. Ultimately, she died of a broken heart after her lover was married off to another woman.

Liang Ge, a lecturer in sociology at the University of Manchester in Britain, said that the Chinese government demanded a reverential interpretation of the classics and, while the novels had always been rewritten, these retellings seemed to have crossed that line.

The use of the phrase “improper romantic association” by the video platform Kuaishou was telling, the academic added, saying that the authorities seemed concerned by “unauthorized authorship of intimacy at scale.”

Some adaptations of the classics have been encouraged by the Communist Party. China’s leader, Xi Jinping, has urged a revival of traditional culture, saying that classic literature is part of the foundation of modern Chinese identity, along with revolutionary heroes. The blockbuster video game, “Black Myth: Wukong,” with hyper-realistic depictions also drawn from “Journey of the West,” was hailed as such a soft power triumph that the tourism authorities in Shanxi Province released a promotional video featuring landmarks that appeared in the game.

Yucong Hao, an assistant professor of Asian studies at Vanderbilt University, said in an email that the freedom to reinterpret Chinese history, mythology and classics remained bounded by “ideological correctness.”

“The boundary between telling China’s stories well and telling them in ways that may be deemed subversive is often ambiguous,” she added.

In January, the National Radio and Television Administration launched a campaign to remove A. I. animations that it said maligned revolutionary heroes, presented counterfactual history and misrepresented the spirit of characters from classic literature.

Social media and video streaming apps, including WeChat and Douyin, said in October that they had deleted A. I.-generated videos referencing classical literature that violate the rules.

Afra Wang, a technology writer and cultural critic from China, said that the Lin Daiyu and Monkey King pairing was so popular “because of how different those two characters are, and at the same time, how deeply those two character are baked in the psyche of the generation.”

Viewers seemed to enjoy the characters finding happiness together and seeing Lin Daiyu finally content, Ms. Wang said. The most liked comment under the People’s Daily editorial was: “May all great people have great lives. But reality is often so cruel.” Even the Guangzhou Railway posted a commercial comparing its relationship with customers to the chemistry between the pair.

Internet users have largely mocked the removal of the videos. One joked that all relationships that make women happy are labeled “inappropriate romantic associations.”

Eileen Chengyin Chow, a Sinologist at Duke University, said that with Mao Zedong identifying himself as a havoc-wreaking Monkey King in 1961, reinterpreting the canon was a political exercise dating back to the early days of the People’s Republic of China.

“Fans feel — rightly so — that it is very much in their rights to reinvent the classics,” she wrote in an email. “After all, ‘who doesn’t want Daiyu to be happy?’ seems to be the most popular sentiment!”

Siyi Zhao contributed research in Beijing.

Tiffany May is a reporter based in Hong Kong, covering the politics, business and culture of the city and the broader region.

The 2,000-Nit OLED in Apple’s New MacBook Is a Big Deal

Wired October 28, 2026

Laptops with OLED screens aren’t particularly special. They’ve been around for a decade. You can currently buy a touchscreen OLED machine for as little as $700, and even the iPad Pro has had an OLED screen since 2024.

So, why did Apple wait over a decade to release its own touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro? The simple answer for the long wait is that the company wanted to do it “the Apple way.” But in this case, “the Apple way” involves somehow cranking up the display to 2,000 nits, solving both the brightness and glare problems that OLED laptops have always suffered from.

Having seen the thing with my own eyes at a media event today in Los Angeles, I can tell you that this screen is the real deal.

Apple is using a tandem OLED panel, the same layer-stacking technology used in the OLED iPad Pro. The real innovation here, however, is that the panel has been optimized to hit a new peak brightness of 2,000 nits, and that’s a result that matters.

That big number is meaningless on its own, but here’s the context. Nits are the standard measure of screen brightness used across the consumer tech industry. A cheap OLED laptop maxes out around 300 nits. A higher-end OLED laptop might get you up to 1,000 nits of brightness—but only in brighter and more colorful High Dynamic Range content like specific streaming apps, YouTube videos, and games. In other words, the vast majority of the time you’re using an OLED, it’ll feel like a dimmer screen than normal. The iPad Pro can get up to 1,600 nits for HDR content, and 1,000 nits for the less bright, less colorful Standard Dynamic Range content. That’s closer.

But this MacBook Pro’s screen is on an entirely different level. It’s a ground-up redesign of the tandem OLED layer arrangement in the iPad Pro, even down to the manufacturing process. And the result is that it can blast your eyes with 2,000 nits of brightness in both SDR and HDR. That means whether you’re looking at some generic wallpaper, a website, or an HDR-compatible movie, you’ll feel that extra brightness. That’s why, I assume, Apple gave it the name PROLED XDR. In a world where the words “OLED” and “HDR” don’t necessarily indicate how good the experience is, more weighty jargon is needed.

As with all tech, bigger numbers don’t always add up to a noticeable difference for the user. But when it comes to HDR performance, we’ve been waiting a long time for OLED to catch up.

HDR, or High Dynamic Range, serves as a measure of color depth, brightness, and contrast—and in the past, this has always involved a trade-off. An OLED screen can turn each individual pixel any color, and it can turn off individual pixels in the display. This allows OLED to have great color control and unbeatable contrast, since when you turn a pixel off, it renders absolutely black.

But OLEDs couldn’t get super bright, and other screen tech like mini-LED could get much brighter, which is why Apple stuck with mini-LED for years, using it on the MacBook Pro and Studio Display XDR. This technology allowed Apple to have the laptops with the best HDR performance out there.

With the 2026 MacBook Pro, that compromise no longer exists. This OLED screen has both the brightness and contrast in its pocket, and you can see it.

An OLED panel has lots of more benefits over conventional backlighting beyond just contrast. Mini-LED struggles with an effect called blooming, where bright parts of images bleed light to the surrounding area, which is where lots of detail is lost in the image. OLED completely fixes that, giving each pixel a much wider range of control (up to completely turning off). As part of the Apple event I attended, we were shown a selection of HDR images with lots of contrast, a number of which had fields of darkness at the edges that made it look like the image simply disappeared into the bezel. Very pretty. We also watched a darker scene in the show Widow’s Bay in HDR, which was an excellent showcase of the range of detail this screen can show.

The new screen helps this MacBook stay exceedingly light, as well. Much of the savings in weight comes from the OLED design, since the screen uses thinner and lighter materials than screens past. Despite the computer using the same aluminum chassis as the previous MacBook Pro, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs just 3 pounds, which is 12 percent lighter than before.

To put the new screen into context, we were also shown a comparison between Apple’s OLED and the OLED of a high-end competitive Windows laptop. The difference was striking, especially in off-axis viewing. At its worst, there were visible rainbow effects on the Windows machine’s screen.

There’s a catch, though. While Apple’s screen can get up to 2,000 nits, it’s normally capped at 1,000 nits. When the laptop’s built-in adaptive brightness sensor thinks you need a boost, the screen’s brightens increases up to 2,000 nits. So the brightness only hits the high end when you’re outside or working under really harsh lighting conditions. The previous-gen MacBook Pros also did this, but to a lesser degree. With this machine, you’re getting 400 more nits of SDR brightness right out of the box, with the ability to crank it up to twice as much.

Glare is another issue with conventional, low-brightness OLED laptops that the MacBook Pro improves. When deeper blacks are rendered on the screen, it often results in harsher reflections. Sometimes it can get so bad, it feels like you’re looking into a mirror. The brightness alone on the MacBook Pro goes a long way toward overpowering glare and reflections, but Apple is also using what it claims is a “state-of-the-art” anti-reflective coating. Almost every laptop screen uses some kind anti-reflective coating, so one can hope that Apple’s “state-of-the-art” coating is at least on par with those, but I can attest that this is the very best I’ve seen.

The ultimate solution to cutting glare and reflections is still the option for a nano-texture display, where the anti-reflective pattern is actually etched into the screen itself rather than layered on top. That’s available as an upgrade on both the 14-inch and 16-inch models.

The other major innovation happening with the MacBook Pro’s screen is the introduction of touch. Like OLED itself, this is a feature we’ve seen on many other laptops for well over a decade. I came in hoping Apple would swing for the fences here, but its use of touch interaction feels much more modest. (Let us quickly forget the failure of the Touch Bar from 2016.)

The implementation itself is impressive. Interacting with elements on the screen feels every bit as fluid as it does on an iPad. The screen also supports many of the familiar trackpad gestures, such as pinch to zoom or a three-fingered swipe to switch Spaces.

The most natural feeling touch optimizations have been lifted directly from iPadOS. If you tap in the top left window controls, they zoom in to let you select more precisely. You can even grab a window and flick it to the side to quickly get into Split View. My favorite optimization is the ability to tap, hold, and slide down to select an item within the Menu Bar. Very clever. And yet, I was still hoping for a stronger commitment on the software side. You can’t use an Apple Pencil on this screen, and nothing in the hardware of the MacBook Pro has been adjusted to make touching the screen feel any more ergonomic.

The bigger issue is with third-party apps, though. While touch-to-click will work on all apps automatically, it’s up to developers to do any more than that. Even the third-party apps we were shown during demos had varying degrees of touch optimization.

The 3D modeling application ZBrush was a good example. While certain aspects were touch-enabled, none of the controls or menus had the useful optimizations that Apple’s first-party apps had. Hopefully this touch option will become more widely adopted, but I can foresee a future in which these fingers-first interactions are mostly forgotten outside of occasionally scrolling down a webpage with your thumb. And let me be clear: All of this is more than what Microsoft has ever done to optimize Windows 11 for touch. (And Microsoft even has Windows 2-in-1 tablets to support!)

With the 2026 MacBook Pro, Apple is doubling down on what’s working well for it: leading the way in high-end hardware. There’s plenty more testing to do on the MacBook Pro in the coming weeks, but this OLED screen already looks like the one the entire industry will be chasing for years to come.

This Is What the GOP’s Final Midterms Push Looks Like

Wired October 28, 2026

Republicans are spending the final week ahead of the midterm elections defending historically red Senate seats that have suddenly become competitive, according to federal filings and sources familiar with the matter.

A significant focus is now on four Senate races in ​K​ansas, ​South Carolina, ​Nebraska, and even ​Mississippi, all traditionally red seats, in what’s ​an ominous development for Republicans in their effort to at least keep control of the upper chamber.

Trump operatives tell Inner Loop that they do not expect ​Democrats to win those Senate seats and that they have ​mainly directed GOP outside groups to spend there to ​​help boost incumbents that only have a narrow lead.

But ​t​he operatives also concede that they are having to divert an increasing amount of resources ​to those states—states that president Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and where Republicans never dreamed of having to spend tens of millions of dollars.

In total, in the penultimate week of the campaign, the Senate Republican–aligned Senate Leadership Fund spent $14 million across those four states, according to a WIRED review of federal filings. The biggest spend has been in Kansas, where SLF has abruptly dumped more than $5 million.

Trump operatives say Kansas has been a major headache since the start of October, when Trafalgar Group​, a GOP pollster, found Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton one point ahead of ​incumbent GOP senator Roger Marshall.

Marshall, a doctor, has had an unusually tough race following a slew of negative stories about how he pursued legal action against his patients with unpaid bills and how much time he spends in Florida. Some political operatives have also complained that he has not taken his race seriously, sources say.

​But the last-minute spending is also coming in places like South Carolina, where SLF spent another roughly $5 million to help incumbent Darline Graham, who has struggled to galvanize Trump's base despite having the president’s endorsement that propelled her to victory in the primary.

SLF also spent nearly $3 million in Nebraska to help Republican incumbent senator Pete Ricketts, who has been behind in some polls, and in Mississippi, the fund put just under $1 million toward Republican incumbent senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The final sprint has highlighted the fraught predicament for Republicans, who are having to patch a seemingly ever-growing number of vulnerabilities.

Trump's campaign schedule has also added several deep-red states that are flashing warning signs, in addition to the expected campaign stops in battleground states. Last week, Trump went to Kansas and South Carolina. This week, he has been in Mississippi and will return to Kansas and South Carolina, as well.

Still, several Trump operatives tell Inner Loop they have been encouraged by the fact that Democratic candidates lately have not expanded their leads in several key Senate races—a concern that has cropped up among some Senate Democratic leadership aides.

Chief among their concerns is Michigan, the best GOP pickup opportunity. Many of the most viable paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority pass through the state, but Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has suffered lingering issues with key voting blocs.

Black voters turned out in droves to help Barack Obama carry the state in 2008 and 2012, and the conventional wisdom in Washington is that El-Sayed will need similar support in order to keep the seat blue, one of the Democratic aides tells Inner Loop.

But the trouble for El-Sayed, they add, has been the decades-long animosity between Arab and Black communities in Michigan, a divide that was further strained during the primary when supporters of his challenger, Haley Stevens, ran ads featuring Barack Obama praising her earlier work during the financial crisis.

In an effort to rebuild at least part of that coalition, Obama held a joint rally with El-Sayed in Detroit over the weekend, which aides are hoping could persuade some voters. Operatives aren’t sure if it’ll be enough.

We will have to see how it pans out. See you next week, on the other side!

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
